0.title: If the LORD Is God, Follow Him

1.text: <sup>1</sup>Now King David was old and advanced in years. And although they covered him with clothes, he could not get warm.<sup>2</sup>Therefore his servants said to him, "Let a young woman be sought for my lord the king, and let her wait on the king and be in his service. Let her lie in your arms, that my lord the king may be warm."<sup>3</sup>So they sought for a beautiful young woman throughout all the territory of Israel, and found Abishag the Shunammite, and brought her to the king.<sup>4</sup>The young woman was very beautiful, and she was of service to the king and attended to him, but the king knew her not.<sup>5</sup>Now Adonijah the son of Haggith exalted himself, saying, "I will be king." And he prepared for himself chariots and horsemen, and fifty men to run before him.<sup>6</sup>His father had never at any time displeased him by asking, "Why have you done thus and so?" He was also a very handsome man, and he was born next after Absalom.<sup>7</sup>He conferred with Joab the son of Zeruiah and with Abiathar the priest. And they followed Adonijah and helped him.<sup>8</sup>But Zadok the priest and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada and Nathan the prophet and Shimei and Rei and David's mighty men were not with Adonijah.<sup>9</sup>Adonijah sacrificed sheep, oxen, and fattened cattle by the Serpent's Stone, which is beside En-rogel, and he invited all his brothers, the king's sons, and all the royal officials of Judah,<sup>10</sup>but he did not invite Nathan the prophet or Benaiah or the mighty men or Solomon his brother.<sup>11</sup>Then Nathan said to Bathsheba the mother of Solomon, "Have you not heard that Adonijah the son of Haggith has become king and David our lord does not know it?<sup>12</sup>Now therefore come, let me give you advice, that you may save your own life and the life of your son Solomon.<sup>13</sup>Go in at once to King David, and say to him, 'Did you not, my lord the king, swear to your servant, saying, "Solomon your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne"? Why then is Adonijah king?'<sup>14</sup>Then while you are still speaking with the king, I also will come in after you and confirm your words."<sup>15</sup>So Bathsheba went to the king in his chamber (now the king was very old, and Abishag the Shunammite was attending to the king).<sup>16</sup>Bathsheba bowed and paid homage to the king, and the king said, "What do you desire?"<sup>17</sup>She said to him, "My lord, you swore to your servant by the LORD your God, saying, 'Solomon your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne.'<sup>18</sup>And now, behold, Adonijah is king, although you, my lord the king, do not know it.<sup>19</sup>He has sacrificed oxen, fattened cattle, and sheep in abundance, and has invited all the sons of the king, Abiathar the priest, and Joab the commander of the army, but Solomon your servant he has not invited.<sup>20</sup>And now, my lord the king, the eyes of all Israel are on you, to tell them who shall sit on the throne of my lord the king after him.<sup>21</sup>Otherwise it will come to pass, when my lord the king sleeps with his fathers, that I and my son Solomon will be counted offenders."<sup>22</sup>While she was still speaking with the king, Nathan the prophet came in.<sup>23</sup>And they told the king, "Here is Nathan the prophet." And when he came in before the king, he bowed before the king, with his face to the ground.<sup>24</sup>And Nathan said, "My lord the king, have you said, 'Adonijah shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne'?<sup>25</sup>For he has gone down this day and has sacrificed oxen, fattened cattle, and sheep in abundance, and has invited all the king's sons, the commanders of the army, and Abiathar the priest. And behold, they are eating and drinking before him, and saying, 'Long live King Adonijah!'<sup>26</sup>But me, your servant, and Zadok the priest, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and your servant Solomon he has not invited.<sup>27</sup>Has this thing been brought about by my lord the king and you have not told your servants who should sit on the throne of my lord the king after him?"<sup>28</sup>Then King David answered, "Call Bathsheba to me." So she came into the king's presence and stood before the king.<sup>29</sup>And the king swore, saying, "As the LORD lives, who has redeemed my soul out of every adversity,<sup>30</sup>as I swore to you by the LORD, the God of Israel, saying, 'Solomon your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne in my place,' even so will I do this day."<sup>31</sup>Then Bathsheba bowed with her face to the ground and paid homage to the king and said, "May my lord King David live forever!"<sup>32</sup>King David said, "Call to me Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada." So they came before the king.<sup>33</sup>And the king said to them, "Take with you the servants of your lord and have Solomon my son ride on my own mule, and bring him down to Gihon.<sup>34</sup>And let Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet there anoint him king over Israel. Then blow the trumpet and say, 'Long live King Solomon!'<sup>35</sup>You shall then come up after him, and he shall come and sit on my throne, for he shall be king in my place. And I have appointed him to be ruler over Israel and over Judah."<sup>36</sup>And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada answered the king, "Amen! May the LORD, the God of my lord the king, say so.<sup>37</sup>As the LORD has been with my lord the king, even so may he be with Solomon, and make his throne greater than the throne of my lord King David."<sup>38</sup>So Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and the Cherethites and the Pelethites went down and had Solomon ride on King David's mule and brought him to Gihon.<sup>39</sup>There Zadok the priest took the horn of oil from the tent and anointed Solomon. Then they blew the trumpet, and all the people said, "Long live King Solomon!"<sup>40</sup>And all the people went up after him, playing on pipes, and rejoicing with great joy, so that the earth was split by their noise.<sup>41</sup>Adonijah and all the guests who were with him heard it as they finished feasting. And when Joab heard the sound of the trumpet, he said, "What does this uproar in the city mean?"<sup>42</sup>While he was still speaking, behold, Jonathan the son of Abiathar the priest came. And Adonijah said, "Come in, for you are a worthy man and bring good news."<sup>43</sup>Jonathan answered Adonijah, "No, for our lord King David has made Solomon king,<sup>44</sup>and the king has sent with him Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and the Cherethites and the Pelethites. And they had him ride on the king's mule.<sup>45</sup>And Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet have anointed him king at Gihon, and they have gone up from there rejoicing, so that the city is in an uproar. This is the noise that you have heard.<sup>46</sup>Solomon sits on the royal throne.<sup>47</sup>Moreover, the king's servants came to congratulate our lord King David, saying, 'May your God make the name of Solomon more famous than yours, and make his throne greater than your throne.' And the king bowed himself on the bed.<sup>48</sup>And the king also said, 'Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who has granted someone to sit on my throne this day, my own eyes seeing it.'"<sup>49</sup>Then all the guests of Adonijah trembled and rose, and each went his own way.<sup>50</sup>And Adonijah feared Solomon. So he arose and went and took hold of the horns of the altar.<sup>51</sup>Then it was told Solomon, "Behold, Adonijah fears King Solomon, for behold, he has laid hold of the horns of the altar, saying, 'Let King Solomon swear to me first that he will not put his servant to death with the sword.'"<sup>52</sup>And Solomon said, "If he will show himself a worthy man, not one of his hairs shall fall to the earth, but if wickedness is found in him, he shall die."<sup>53</sup>So King Solomon sent, and they brought him down from the altar. And he came and paid homage to King Solomon, and Solomon said to him, "Go to your house."
1.overview:
The book of Kings opens with an old man who cannot get warm. It is a deliberate first sentence: the last two books gave us a boy with a sling, a soldier who killed his ten thousands, a king who danced in front of his whole capital — and here he is under a pile of blankets while other people arrange things around him.

Then Adonijah exalted himself and got chariots and horsemen and fifty men to run before him, which is word for word what Absalom did (2 Sam. 15:1). He was alive when his brother did it. He watched the gate, the rebellion, the flight, and the oak — and he is doing it again, prop for prop, and he is handsome too, as Absalom was and as Saul was, in a history that said the LORD looks on the heart.

And then the parenthesis that explains him, which is not about him at all: his father had never at any time displeased him by asking, "Why have you done thus and so?" Not once, in the man's whole life, and the example the writer picks is the mildest question available. The historian of Kings has read Samuel, and he has condensed the entire domestic catastrophe of 2 Samuel 13 to 19 into one clause about a question that was never asked.

Nathan moves first — and does not once say thus says the LORD in this chapter. Bathsheba's argument is not ambition but arithmetic: a new king with a live rival does not leave the rival's mother alive either. The old man then gives eight exact orders in a row, and the first is about an animal that everyone in Jerusalem can identify at a distance. Twenty minutes after a trumpet, Adonijah is sitting alone at En-rogel with the dishes, and his guests have not said goodbye.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David is old and cannot get warm, so they find Abishag the Shunammite to lie in his arms — and the king knew her not (vv. 1-4). Now Adonijah the son of Haggith exalted himself, saying, "I will be king." And he prepared for himself chariots and horsemen, and fifty men to run before him (v. 5). And the narrator explains him in a parenthesis: his father had never at any time displeased him by asking, "Why have you done thus and so?" He was also a very handsome man, and he was born next after Absalom (v. 6). Joab and Abiathar the priest support him; Zadok, Benaiah, Nathan, Shimei, Rei and the mighty men do not (vv. 7-8). He holds a sacrificial feast at En-rogel and invites all his brothers except Solomon (vv. 9-10).
verseByVerse.theology: The props are Absalom's, exactly: chariots and horsemen, and fifty men to run before him is what Absalom got himself at 2 Samuel 15:1, the day after his father kissed him. And he is handsome, as Absalom was, and as Saul was — in a history that said the LORD looks on the heart.
verseByVerse.examples: But verse 6 is not about Adonijah. It is about his father, and it is one of the saddest parentheses in Scripture: David had never once, in the man's whole life, asked him why he had done something.

So they sought for a beautiful young woman throughout all the territory of Israel, and found Abishag the Shunammite, and brought her to the king. The young woman was very beautiful, and she was of service to the king and attended to him, but the king knew her not. Now Adonijah the son of Haggith exalted himself, saying, "I will be king." Adonijah sacrificed sheep, oxen, and fattened cattle by the Serpent's Stone, which is beside En-rogel, and he invited all his brothers, the king's sons, and all the royal officials of Judah, but he did not invite Nathan the prophet or Benaiah or the mighty men or Solomon his brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now King David was old and advanced in years. And although they covered him with clothes, he could not get warm.'

The book of Kings opens with an old man who is cold.

That is a deliberate first sentence. The last two books have given us a boy with a sling, a soldier who killed his ten thousands, a king who danced in front of his whole capital, and a fugitive who walked up a hill barefoot. Here he is under a pile of blankets and the heat will not come.

'Therefore his servants said to him, "Let a young woman be sought for my lord the king, and let her wait on the king and be in his service. Let her lie in your arms, that my lord the king may be warm."'

'So they sought for a beautiful young woman throughout all the territory of Israel, and found Abishag the Shunammite, and brought her to the king.'

'The young woman was very beautiful, and she was of service to the king and attended to him, but the king knew her not.'

The last clause is put there for a reason, and it will matter enormously in the next chapter.

The king knew her not. She is in the household and she is not his wife, and the writer establishes it so that we understand exactly what Adonijah is asking for at 2:17 and why Solomon reacts as he does.

It should also be said what this arrangement is. A young woman is fetched from her village and put in a dying man's bed as a source of warmth, and nobody asks her anything. She has a name and a home town and no recorded word in the whole of Scripture. The narrator does not condemn the plan and does not commend it; he tells us her name, which is more than the ten concubines of 2 Samuel 20 ever got.

'Now Adonijah the son of Haggith exalted himself, saying, "I will be king." And he prepared for himself chariots and horsemen, and fifty men to run before him.'

Now read that verse and then read 2 Samuel 15:1.

After this Absalom got himself a chariot and horses, and fifty men to run before him.

It is the same sentence. The same equipment, the same number of runners, the same act of a king's son announcing himself in the street before anybody has given him anything.

Adonijah was alive when Absalom did it. He was a boy or a young man in that palace when his brother stood at the gate for four years, stole the hearts of Israel, drove their father barefoot out of Jerusalem, and died hanging in an oak with three javelins in him. He watched the whole thing happen and he is doing it again, prop for prop.

And exalted himself is the writer's own verdict, placed before the quotation. Nobody exalted him. He did it, and then said I will be king, which nobody had told him.

'His father had never at any time displeased him by asking, "Why have you done thus and so?" He was also a very handsome man, and he was born next after Absalom.'

Here is the explanation, and it is not about Adonijah at all.

Take the sentence slowly, because it is one of the saddest parentheses in Scripture and it is easy to read as a throwaway.

His father had never at any time displeased him by asking, "Why have you done thus and so?"

Not once. In the whole of the man's life. Not a rebuke, not a correction, not even a question — and the question the writer chooses to give as the example is the mildest one available. Not you are forbidden. Not you will be punished. Just: why have you done that?

David never asked it.

Now put that beside what the previous book recorded. When Amnon raped Tamar, David was very angry and did nothing (2 Sam. 13:21). When Absalom murdered Amnon, he mourned and then longed for the murderer and brought him home without a trial and without a pardon. When Absalom sat at the city gate for four years collecting a rebellion, nobody asked him what he was doing.

The historian of Kings has been reading Samuel, and he has condensed the entire domestic catastrophe of chapters 13 to 19 into one clause about a question that was never asked.

And it is not a small point about temperament. A father who will not ask why have you done that? is not being gentle. He is withholding the one thing that tells a child there is a standard and that somebody is watching. Adonijah reached his thirties having never been asked to account for anything, and the first large thing he does is help himself to a kingdom.

There is a warning in it that lands on any parent, and the shape of it matters: it is not the harsh father who produces Adonijah. It is the one who cannot bear the discomfort of the question.

Then two more facts in the same verse.

He was also a very handsome man. This history keeps saying that about the wrong men. Saul was the handsomest man in Israel and a head taller than anybody (1 Sam. 9:2). Absalom had no blemish in him from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head (2 Sam. 14:25). And the sentence that stands over all of them was said to Samuel in a courtyard at Bethlehem: the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart (1 Sam. 16:7).

And he was born next after Absalom, which is the writer telling us the succession as the country would have counted it. Amnon is dead. The second son, Chileab, is never mentioned again and had presumably died. Absalom is dead. Adonijah is next, and by every ordinary rule of inheritance the throne is his.

That is what makes this chapter a real contest rather than a squalid grab. He has a case.

'He conferred with Joab the son of Zeruiah and with Abiathar the priest. And they followed Adonijah and helped him.'

These two names are a shock, because both of them have been with David since the wilderness.

Joab has run his army for forty years. Abiathar is the boy who escaped the massacre at Nob with the ephod in his hand and ran to David in a cave, and to whom David said stay with me... with me you shall be in safekeeping (1 Sam. 22:23).

Why they go is not stated. Joab has reason to fear a new reign: David has been promising for years to deal with him and never has, and Adonijah is the candidate least likely to. Abiathar has watched Zadok rise beside him for a generation.

Both of them are ruined by this decision within two chapters, and it is the last decision either of them makes.

'But Zadok the priest and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada and Nathan the prophet and Shimei and Rei and David's mighty men were not with Adonijah.'

Here is the other list, and the chapter is decided by it.

Zadok, the other priest. Benaiah, who commands the royal bodyguard and killed a lion in a pit on a snowy day. Nathan, who once walked into this palace and said you are the man. And David's mighty men — the thirty-seven whose names close the book of Samuel.

Adonijah has the general and one priest. Solomon's side has the bodyguard, the other priest, the prophet, and the men from the cave.

'Adonijah sacrificed sheep, oxen, and fattened cattle by the Serpent's Stone, which is beside En-rogel, and he invited all his brothers, the king's sons, and all the royal officials of Judah,'

'but he did not invite Nathan the prophet or Benaiah or the mighty men or Solomon his brother.'

The invitation list is the coronation, and the omissions are the plot.

He has held a sacrificial feast — a religious event, at a spring outside the city — with all the king's sons and the officials of Judah present. That is not a party; it is an acclamation being arranged.

And he has left out precisely the four the previous verse named. Which means he knows exactly where he stands with them, and has decided to present the country with a finished fact before they can react.

He is a day too slow.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nathan goes to Bathsheba: Adonijah is king and David does not know it, now therefore come, let me give you advice, that you may save your own life and the life of your son Solomon (vv. 11-12). She is to go in and remind the king of his oath, and Nathan will come in behind her and confirm her words (vv. 13-14). She does it, and adds what the king has not thought about: the eyes of all Israel are on you, to tell them who shall sit on the throne... otherwise it will come to pass, when my lord the king sleeps with his fathers, that I and my son Solomon will be counted offenders (vv. 15-21). Nathan follows, and asks his question carefully: have you said, "Adonijah shall reign after me"? (vv. 22-27).
verseByVerse.theology: Bathsheba's argument is not sentiment and it is not a mother's ambition. When a new king takes a throne with rivals alive, the rivals and their households die. She is telling an old man that his failure to say anything will kill two people, and she is right.
verseByVerse.examples: And Nathan does not say thus says the LORD anywhere in this chapter. At 2 Samuel 12 he came with a word from God and told the king he was a murderer. Here he plans a sequence, briefs a queen, and times his own entrance. The writer records the difference and does not comment on it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Nathan said to Bathsheba the mother of Solomon, "Have you not heard that Adonijah the son of Haggith has become king and David our lord does not know it? Now therefore come, let me give you advice, that you may save your own life and the life of your son Solomon. Go in at once to King David, and say to him, 'Did you not, my lord the king, swear to your servant, saying, "Solomon your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne"? Why then is Adonijah king?' Then while you are still speaking with the king, I also will come in after you and confirm your words." So Bathsheba went to the king in his chamber (now the king was very old, and Abishag the Shunammite was attending to the king). Bathsheba bowed and paid homage to the king, and the king said, "What do you desire?" She said to him, "My lord, you swore to your servant by the LORD your God, saying, 'Solomon your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne.' And now, behold, Adonijah is king, although you, my lord the king, do not know it. He has sacrificed oxen, fattened cattle, and sheep in abundance, and has invited all the sons of the king, Abiathar the priest, and Joab the commander of the army, but Solomon your servant he has not invited. And now, my lord the king, the eyes of all Israel are on you, to tell them who shall sit on the throne of my lord the king after him. Otherwise it will come to pass, when my lord the king sleeps with his fathers, that I and my son Solomon will be counted offenders." While she was still speaking with the king, Nathan the prophet came in. And they told the king, "Here is Nathan the prophet." And when he came in before the king, he bowed before the king, with his face to the ground. And Nathan said, "My lord the king, have you said, 'Adonijah shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne'? For he has gone down this day and has sacrificed oxen, fattened cattle, and sheep in abundance, and has invited all the king's sons, the commanders of the army, and Abiathar the priest. And behold, they are eating and drinking before him, and saying, 'Long live King Adonijah!' But me, your servant, and Zadok the priest, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and your servant Solomon he has not invited. Has this thing been brought about by my lord the king and you have not told your servants who should sit on the throne of my lord the king after him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Nathan said to Bathsheba the mother of Solomon, "Have you not heard that Adonijah the son of Haggith has become king and David our lord does not know it?"'

Nathan moves first, and he goes to the mother.

The last time these two were mentioned in the same paragraph, Nathan was standing in front of David saying you are the man about her husband's murder. That was thirty years ago and the child of that week is dead, and the second child is the one this chapter is about.

'"Now therefore come, let me give you advice, that you may save your own life and the life of your son Solomon."'

Note what he says is at stake, because it is not a career.

That you may save your own life and the life of your son.

That is not alarmism. It is how the ancient world worked and everybody in that palace knew it. A new king with a live rival does not leave the rival alive, and does not leave the rival's mother alive either. Bathsheba is being told, correctly, that she and Solomon have hours.

'"Go in at once to King David, and say to him, 'Did you not, my lord the king, swear to your servant, saying, "Solomon your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne"? Why then is Adonijah king?'"'

'"Then while you are still speaking with the king, I also will come in after you and confirm your words."'

He plans the sequence, and what kind of thing this is deserves to be said plainly.

Nathan is a prophet. He is the man who was sent by God to David in 2 Samuel 12, who told a story about a lamb and then named the king a murderer to his face, and who did not soften a syllable of it.

In this chapter he does not say thus says the LORD once. He does not claim a word from God, does not report a vision, and does not tell David what God requires. He assesses a political situation, works out a two-stage approach, briefs the person who will go first, and times his own entrance for maximum effect.

That is a court manoeuvre. It may well be a righteous one — there was an oath, Solomon was God's choice, and the alternative was two murders — and it is still not the same kind of act as chapter 12, and the writer lets both stand without explaining the difference.

It is a useful thing to notice, because people who serve God are frequently doing ordinary work with ordinary judgment, and pretending every such decision is a revelation does not help anybody.

'So Bathsheba went to the king in his chamber (now the king was very old, and Abishag the Shunammite was attending to the king).'

The parenthesis is a picture. She comes into the room where her husband is dying and there is another woman there looking after him.

'Bathsheba bowed and paid homage to the king, and the king said, "What do you desire?"'

'She said to him, "My lord, you swore to your servant by the LORD your God, saying, 'Solomon your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne.'"'

She begins with the oath, and there is no record of it anywhere before this chapter.

The writer of Kings has not told us about it and neither did Samuel. Both Nathan and Bathsheba refer to it as a known thing, David does not dispute it, and he confirms it under oath in verse 30. Chronicles reports God's word to David that Solomon would build the house and that his kingdom would be established (1 Chron. 22:9-10), so the promise is not being invented here.

'"And now, behold, Adonijah is king, although you, my lord the king, do not know it."'

'"He has sacrificed oxen, fattened cattle, and sheep in abundance, and has invited all the sons of the king, Abiathar the priest, and Joab the commander of the army, but Solomon your servant he has not invited."'

She reports the facts, including the guest list, and lets the omission speak.

'"And now, my lord the king, the eyes of all Israel are on you, to tell them who shall sit on the throne of my lord the king after him."'

And this is the sentence that gets through, and it is well judged.

The eyes of all Israel are on you. Not: you owe me. Not: Adonijah is unworthy. She tells a king who has been lying under blankets that the country is waiting for him to speak, and that his silence is itself an answer being read.

'"Otherwise it will come to pass, when my lord the king sleeps with his fathers, that I and my son Solomon will be counted offenders."'

Then the consequence, and she puts it plainly.

Counted offenders. The word means guilty, liable, condemned — and what she is describing is what actually happens. If Adonijah takes the throne, she and Solomon are not rivals to be watched; they are criminals to be dealt with.

She is not asking for a crown for her son. She is asking not to be executed, and she is asking a man who has never once protected any of his children from the consequences of his own inaction.

'While she was still speaking with the king, Nathan the prophet came in.'

The timing works exactly as arranged.

'And they told the king, "Here is Nathan the prophet." And when he came in before the king, he bowed before the king, with his face to the ground.'

'And Nathan said, "My lord the king, have you said, 'Adonijah shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne'?"'

Look at the form of it. He asks a question.

He does not accuse Adonijah of treason or tell David what to do. He asks whether the king has authorised this — which forces David to answer, and there are only two possible answers, and one of them requires him to act within the hour.

'"For he has gone down this day and has sacrificed oxen, fattened cattle, and sheep in abundance, and has invited all the king's sons, the commanders of the army, and Abiathar the priest. And behold, they are eating and drinking before him, and saying, 'Long live King Adonijah!'"'

'"But me, your servant, and Zadok the priest, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and your servant Solomon he has not invited."'

'"Has this thing been brought about by my lord the king and you have not told your servants who should sit on the throne of my lord the king after him?"'

He ends where he began, on the question, and the second time it has an edge: if you did authorise it, why were your closest servants not told?

Which is either a courtier's tact or a prophet's way of letting a man see what he has allowed. It works either way.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–40 — On the King's Own Mule
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David swears: as the LORD lives, who has redeemed my soul out of every adversity... Solomon your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne in my place (vv. 29-30). He gives the orders himself — put Solomon on my own mule, take him down to Gihon, let Zadok and Nathan anoint him, blow the trumpet and say Long live King Solomon! (vv. 32-35). Benaiah answers amen! May the LORD, the God of my lord the king, say so (v. 36). It is done, and the people come up playing pipes and rejoicing, so that the earth was split by their noise (vv. 38-40).
verseByVerse.theology: The oath he swears is the sentence he has been saying his whole life — the LORD, who has redeemed my soul out of every adversity is 2 Samuel 4:9, spoken to two assassins thirty years earlier. It is the last recorded oath of his reign and it names God as the one who got him out of everything.
verseByVerse.examples: And the mule is his own, which is the whole point of naming it: everybody watching knows whose animal that is. The last royal son to ride a mule in this history was Absalom, and it went out from under him and left him hanging in an oak.

verseByVerse.quote: Then King David answered, "Call Bathsheba to me." So she came into the king's presence and stood before the king. And the king swore, saying, "As the LORD lives, who has redeemed my soul out of every adversity, as I swore to you by the LORD, the God of Israel, saying, 'Solomon your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne in my place,' even so will I do this day." Then Bathsheba bowed with her face to the ground and paid homage to the king and said, "May my lord King David live forever!" King David said, "Call to me Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada." So they came before the king. And the king said to them, "Take with you the servants of your lord and have Solomon my son ride on my own mule, and bring him down to Gihon. And let Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet there anoint him king over Israel. Then blow the trumpet and say, 'Long live King Solomon!' You shall then come up after him, and he shall come and sit on my throne, for he shall be king in my place. And I have appointed him to be ruler over Israel and over Judah." And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada answered the king, "Amen! May the LORD, the God of my lord the king, say so. As the LORD has been with my lord the king, even so may he be with Solomon, and make his throne greater than the throne of my lord King David." So Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and the Cherethites and the Pelethites went down and had Solomon ride on King David's mule and brought him to Gihon. There Zadok the priest took the horn of oil from the tent and anointed Solomon. Then they blew the trumpet, and all the people said, "Long live King Solomon!" And all the people went up after him, playing on pipes, and rejoicing with great joy, so that the earth was split by their noise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then King David answered, "Call Bathsheba to me." So she came into the king's presence and stood before the king.'

The old man moves, and for the length of this section he is the David of the middle of his reign again.

Watch what happens to the prose. For twenty-seven verses he has been lying in a bed while other people arranged things around him. From here he gives eight consecutive orders and every one of them is exact.

'And the king swore, saying, "As the LORD lives, who has redeemed my soul out of every adversity,"'

Stop on that oath, because it is the last one he swears in Scripture and it is a quotation of himself.

As the LORD lives, who has redeemed my soul out of every adversity.

He said that thirty years earlier, standing in front of two men who had brought him the head of Ish-bosheth expecting to be thanked: as the LORD lives, who has redeemed my life out of every adversity (2 Sam. 4:9). It was his answer then to men who thought he needed help getting a throne.

And it is what he swears by now, at the end, arranging a succession from a bed. A lion and a bear. A giant. Four spears. A window and a rope. Two caves. A burnt town. A forest. Every one of them, and he names God as the one who got him out.

'"as I swore to you by the LORD, the God of Israel, saying, 'Solomon your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit on my throne in my place,' even so will I do this day."'

'Then Bathsheba bowed with her face to the ground and paid homage to the king and said, "May my lord King David live forever!"'

'King David said, "Call to me Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada." So they came before the king.'

The three names from verse 8, summoned together.

'And the king said to them, "Take with you the servants of your lord and have Solomon my son ride on my own mule, and bring him down to Gihon."'

The first order is about an animal, and everybody in Jerusalem will understand it before the day is out.

My own mule. Not a mule. The king's personal mount, which nobody else rides, and which every person in that city can identify at a distance. Putting Solomon on it is a public statement that requires no herald: whatever is happening at En-rogel, this is the king's own son on the king's own animal with the king's own guard around him.

And there is one other royal son in this history who rode a mule. He was riding it through a wood when it went under an oak, and his head caught in the branches, and the mule that was under him went on (2 Sam. 18:9).

The writer does not mention Absalom. He does not have to; he has already put the chariot and the fifty runners in verse 5.

Gihon is the other half of the instruction and it is equally deliberate. Adonijah's feast is at En-rogel, outside the city to the south. Gihon is the spring on the east side, close in, within earshot of the walls — and it is the spring that fed the city through the shaft David's men climbed to take Jerusalem in the first place.

'"And let Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet there anoint him king over Israel. Then blow the trumpet and say, 'Long live King Solomon!'"'

Priest and prophet together, and then a trumpet.

The anointing is the thing that matters and the trumpet is the thing that carries. Adonijah has been holding a feast; Solomon is being anointed by the priest and the prophet and proclaimed with a horn that can be heard a mile away.

'"You shall then come up after him, and he shall come and sit on my throne, for he shall be king in my place. And I have appointed him to be ruler over Israel and over Judah."'

'And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada answered the king, "Amen! May the LORD, the God of my lord the king, say so."'

Benaiah's answer is better than an acclamation.

Amen! May the LORD, the God of my lord the king, say so.

The king has spoken and the soldier says: let God say the same. He is not doubting the order and he is not flattering it. He is asking that the thing David has just arranged should turn out to be what God has arranged, which is the only thing that will make it stand.

'"As the LORD has been with my lord the king, even so may he be with Solomon, and make his throne greater than the throne of my lord King David."'

And then a wish that no courtier would risk unless he meant it: may this son's throne be greater than yours. Said to David's face, in David's bedroom.

It comes true, and the next nine chapters are about how, and chapter 11 is about what it cost.

'So Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and the Cherethites and the Pelethites, went down and had Solomon ride on King David's mule and brought him to Gihon.'

The Cherethites and the Pelethites go with them — the foreign professionals who have guarded David since the wilderness. The bodyguard has chosen.

'There Zadok the priest took the horn of oil from the tent and anointed Solomon, and they blew the trumpet, and all the people said, "Long live King Solomon!"'

The horn of oil from the tent. The tent is the one David pitched for the ark in 2 Samuel 6, after the second attempt, after Uzzah.

'And all the people went up after him, playing on pipes, and rejoicing with great joy, so that the earth was split by their noise.'

The last clause is the writer enjoying himself: the earth was split by their noise.

Which is a figure, and it is also the tactical fact of the chapter. Adonijah is half a mile away at a spring, and what ends his coronation is a sound.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–53 — The Horns of the Altar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Adonijah's feast hears the noise, and Jonathan the son of Abiathar arrives with the news: the king has made Solomon king, sent him to Gihon on the royal mule, and the king has bowed himself on his bed saying blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who has granted someone to sit on my throne this day, my own eyes seeing it (vv. 41-48). The guests get up and scatter (v. 49). And Adonijah feared Solomon. So he arose and went and took hold of the horns of the altar (v. 50). Solomon's answer: if he will show himself a worthy man, not one of his hairs shall fall to the earth, but if wickedness is found in him, he shall die (vv. 51-53).
verseByVerse.theology: Every guest at that feast worked out the same thing at the same moment and left without speaking to their host. That is what a claim on a throne is worth the instant it fails.
verseByVerse.examples: The altar was sanctuary for a man who had killed without intending it, and the law is explicit that a wilful murderer is taken even from there (Ex. 21:14). Adonijah has killed nobody, so he gets terms rather than a sentence — and the terms are conditional, and the condition is his own future conduct.

verseByVerse.quote: Adonijah and all the guests who were with him heard it as they finished feasting. And when Joab heard the sound of the trumpet, he said, "What does this uproar in the city mean?" While he was still speaking, behold, Jonathan the son of Abiathar the priest came. And Adonijah said, "Come in, for you are a worthy man and bring good news." Jonathan answered Adonijah, "No, for our lord King David has made Solomon king, and the king has sent with him Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and the Cherethites and the Pelethites. And they had him ride on the king's mule. And Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet have anointed him king at Gihon, and they have gone up from there rejoicing, so that the city is in an uproar. This is the noise that you have heard. Solomon sits on the royal throne. Moreover, the king's servants came to congratulate our lord King David, saying, 'May your God make the name of Solomon more famous than yours, and make his throne greater than your throne.' And the king bowed himself on the bed. And the king also said, 'Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who has granted someone to sit on my throne this day, my own eyes seeing it.'" Then all the guests of Adonijah trembled and rose, and each went his own way. And Adonijah feared Solomon. So he arose and went and took hold of the horns of the altar. Then it was told Solomon, "Behold, Adonijah fears King Solomon, for behold, he has laid hold of the horns of the altar, saying, 'Let King Solomon swear to me first that he will not put his servant to death with the sword.'" And Solomon said, "If he will show himself a worthy man, not one of his hairs shall fall to the earth, but if wickedness is found in him, he shall die." So King Solomon sent, and they brought him down from the altar. And he came and paid homage to King Solomon, and Solomon said to him, "Go to your house."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Adonijah and all his guests heard it as they finished feasting. And when Joab heard the sound of the trumpet, he said, "What does this uproar in the city mean?"'

The old soldier hears a trumpet in the city and knows immediately that something is wrong.

'While he was still speaking, behold, Jonathan the son of Abiathar the priest came. And Adonijah said, "Come in, for you are a worthy man and bring good news."'

That is a bleak line, because a reader of Samuel has heard it before.

David sat between two gates waiting for word from a forest and saw a runner and said he is a good man and comes with good news (2 Sam. 18:27). He was wrong, and the news was that his son was dead.

Jonathan the son of Abiathar is one of the two young men who spent a day hiding in a well at Bahurim with a covering of grain over the mouth of it, carrying messages for David during Absalom's rebellion. He has been a runner before.

'Jonathan answered Adonijah, "No, for our lord King David has made Solomon king,"'

No. He does not soften it and he does not build up to it. One word, and then the facts.

'"and the king has sent with him Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and the Cherethites and the Pelethites. And they had him ride on the king's mule."'

He lists the four names and then the mule, which is exactly the order in which the news would land on a man who understands the court. Not the crowd, not the noise — who went, and what he was riding.

'"And Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet have anointed him king at Gihon, and they have gone up from there rejoicing, so that the city is in an uproar. This is the noise that you have heard."'

'"Solomon sits on the royal throne."'

Four words, and the matter is finished.

'"Moreover, the king's servants came to congratulate our lord King David, saying, 'May your God make the name of Solomon more famous than yours, and make his throne greater than your throne.' And the king bowed himself on the bed."'

'"And the king also said, 'Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who has granted someone to sit on my throne this day, my own eyes seeing it.'"'

This is the last recorded blessing of David's life, and it should stop a reader.

Blessed be the LORD... who has granted someone to sit on my throne this day, my own eyes seeing it.

He is dying, and what he is glad about is that he lived long enough to watch it. Not that the son is his, or that the dynasty is secure, or that his enemies were outmanoeuvred. That God let him see it happen.

And the writer has him bow himself on the bed — too weak to get up, and worshipping where he lies.

Remember what was said to him about this throne: your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me. Your throne shall be established forever (2 Sam. 7:16). He is watching the first instalment of that arrive while he is still alive to see it, and the man who told him is standing at Gihon anointing the boy.

'Then all the guests of Adonijah trembled and rose, and each went his own way.'

One verse, and it is devastating.

They had been eating and drinking and shouting long live King Adonijah an hour earlier. Now every one of them stands up, and they do not confer, and they do not offer their host anything. Each went his own way. Nobody says goodbye.

That is what a following is worth when the thing it was following stops looking likely, and it is worth a moment before it is passed over. Adonijah had the general, a priest, all his brothers and the royal officials of Judah at his table. Twenty minutes after a trumpet, he is sitting alone at En-rogel with the dishes.

'And Adonijah feared Solomon. So he arose and went and took hold of the horns of the altar.'

He runs to the altar.

The horns were the projections at the four corners of the altar, and taking hold of them was a recognised appeal for sanctuary. The law behind it is specific: a man who killed without intending it could flee, but if a man wilfully attacks another to kill him by cunning, you shall take him from my altar, that he may die (Ex. 21:14).

So the altar is not a place where anybody can hide from anything. It shelters the man who did not mean it, and hands over the man who did.

Adonijah has killed nobody. He exalted himself and threw a feast and was abandoned by his own guests, and he is now holding on to a piece of stonework because he expects to be executed by his brother.

Hold the altar in mind. Joab runs to it in the next chapter, and Joab is a wilful murderer twice over, and the law is applied to him exactly as it is written.

'Then it was told Solomon, "Behold, Adonijah fears King Solomon, for behold, he has laid hold of the horns of the altar, saying, 'Let King Solomon swear to me first that he will not put his servant to death with the sword.'"'

'And Solomon said, "If he will show himself a worthy man, not one of his hairs shall fall to the earth, but if wickedness is found in him, he shall die."'

The new king's first recorded ruling is a conditional, and it is a good one.

Adonijah asked for an oath. He does not get one. What he gets is terms.

If he will show himself a worthy man — the word means whole, sound, a man of substance — not one of his hairs shall fall to the earth. Total protection, and the phrase is the strongest guarantee of safety in the language.

But if wickedness is found in him, he shall die.

Nothing in that is arbitrary. Solomon has not pardoned him and has not condemned him; he has told him precisely what the rest of his life depends on, in advance, in public, in terms he cannot misunderstand.

Set that beside what his father did with a son in exactly this position. Absalom came home from Geshur, and David neither tried him nor forgave him, and left him in a house for two years with the door shut and nothing said — and the country burned for it.

Solomon says the thing out loud on the first afternoon.

'So King Solomon sent, and they brought him down from the altar. And he came and paid homage to King Solomon, and Solomon said to him, "Go to your house."'

He is brought down, he bows, and he is sent home.

Go to your house. No punishment, no exile, no guard. The condition has been stated and the man is free.

Everything now depends on whether Adonijah can leave it alone, and the first thing he does in chapter 2 is ask for the dead king's nurse.

1.theology:
Absalom, prop for prop (v. 5). Chariots and horsemen, and fifty men to run before him is 2 Samuel 15:1 repeated exactly. Adonijah was in that palace when his brother stood at the gate for four years, stole the hearts of Israel, drove their father barefoot out of Jerusalem and died in an oak with three javelins in him. He saw the whole thing and is doing it again. And exalted himself is the writer's verdict, set before the quotation: nobody exalted him.

The saddest parenthesis in Scripture (v. 6). Not a rebuke, not a punishment — the example chosen is the mildest question there is: why have you done thus and so? David never asked it, not once, in Adonijah's whole life. Set that beside the record: Amnon raped Tamar and David was very angry and did nothing; Absalom murdered Amnon and was brought home without trial or pardon; Absalom sat at the gate for four years and nobody asked him what he was doing. A father who will not ask that question is not being gentle. He is withholding the one thing that tells a child there is a standard and somebody is watching — and it is not the harsh father who produces an Adonijah, it is the one who cannot bear the discomfort of asking.

Handsome, again (v. 6). Saul was the handsomest man in Israel and a head taller than anyone (1 Sam. 9:2); Absalom had no blemish in him (2 Sam. 14:25). And the sentence standing over all of them was spoken in a Bethlehem courtyard: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart (1 Sam. 16:7). Note too that Adonijah has a real case — Amnon dead, Chileab never mentioned again, Absalom dead, and he is next. By every ordinary rule of inheritance the throne is his, which makes this a contest rather than a squalid grab.

The two lists (vv. 7-8). Joab has run David's army for forty years and has reason to fear any reign but this one. Abiathar is the boy who ran from the massacre at Nob with the ephod in his hand, to whom David said with me you shall be in safekeeping (1 Sam. 22:23). Both are ruined within two chapters, and this is the last decision either of them makes. Against them: Zadok, Benaiah, Nathan, and the mighty men whose names close the book of Samuel.

What Bathsheba is actually asking for (vv. 12, 21). Not a crown for her son — her life. Counted offenders means guilty, liable, condemned, and it is an accurate forecast: a new king with a live rival does not leave the rival or his mother alive. And the sentence that gets through to David is neither a claim nor a complaint: the eyes of all Israel are on you, and your silence is itself an answer the country is reading.

A court manoeuvre, not a prophetic word (vv. 12-14). Nathan does not say thus says the LORD once in this chapter, claim a vision, or tell David what God requires. He assesses a situation, plans a two-stage approach, briefs the person who goes first, and times his own entrance. It may well be righteous — there was an oath, and the alternative was two murders — and it is not the same kind of act as 2 Samuel 12, and the writer lets both stand. People who serve God are frequently doing ordinary work with ordinary judgment, and pretending every such decision is a revelation helps nobody.

The last oath of his life (v. 29). As the LORD lives, who has redeemed my soul out of every adversity is a quotation of himself: he said it thirty years earlier to two men who brought him a rival's head expecting thanks (2 Sam. 4:9). A lion and a bear, a giant, four spears, a window and a rope, two caves, a burnt town, a forest — and he names God as the one who got him out of all of it.

The mule (v. 33). Not a mule — my own mule, the royal mount nobody else rides and every person in the city can identify at a distance. It is a public statement requiring no herald. And there is one other royal son in this history who rode a mule: it went under an oak, his head caught, and the mule that was under him went on (2 Sam. 18:9). The writer never mentions Absalom here. He put the chariot and the fifty runners in verse 5 and trusts the reader.

Benaiah's amen (vv. 36-37). The king has spoken and the soldier says: let God say the same. Not doubt, and not flattery — a request that what David has arranged should turn out to be what God arranged, which is the only thing that will make it stand. And then a wish no courtier would risk unless he meant it, said in David's own bedroom: may this son's throne be greater than yours.

Each went his own way (v. 49). An hour earlier they were shouting long live King Adonijah. Now every guest stands up, and they do not confer, and nobody says goodbye to their host. That is what a following is worth the instant the thing it was following stops looking likely.

What the altar does and does not do (v. 50). The law is specific: a man who killed without intending it could flee there, but if a man wilfully attacks another to kill him by cunning, you shall take him from my altar, that he may die (Ex. 21:14). It shelters the man who did not mean it and hands over the man who did. Adonijah has killed nobody. Joab runs to the same altar in the next chapter, and he is a wilful murderer twice over.

Terms, stated out loud on the first afternoon (v. 52). Adonijah asked for an oath and gets a condition instead, and nothing in it is arbitrary: he is neither pardoned nor condemned, and he is told precisely what the rest of his life depends on, in advance and in public. Set that beside what his father did with a son in exactly this position — Absalom home from Geshur, neither tried nor forgiven, left in a house for two years with the door shut and nothing said, and the country burned for it.
1.examples:
Then: A king's son who had never once in his life been asked why he had done something helped himself to a throne, hired fifty men to run in front of him exactly as his dead brother had, threw a coronation feast for the whole court — and within twenty minutes of hearing a trumpet half a mile away, every guest at his table stood up and left without speaking to him.

Now: Two things. Verse 6 is the one that lands hardest, and it lands on parents: the failure recorded there is not harshness but the refusal to ask an uncomfortable question, and the child it produced reached his thirties having never accounted to anybody for anything. And Solomon's first ruling is the contrast worth keeping. His father managed a dangerous son by leaving everything unsaid, which felt like restraint and was in fact the only course that could not work. Solomon says the terms out loud, on the first day, in public, so that the man knows exactly where he stands. Clarity is kinder than silence, even when what it has to say is hard.

2.text: <sup>1</sup>When David's time to die drew near, he commanded Solomon his son, saying,<sup>2</sup>"I am about to go the way of all the earth. Be strong, and show yourself a man,<sup>3</sup>and keep the charge of the LORD your God, walking in his ways and keeping his statutes, his commandments, his rules, and his testimonies, as it is written in the Law of Moses, that you may prosper in all that you do and wherever you turn,<sup>4</sup>that the LORD may establish his word that he spoke concerning me, saying, 'If your sons pay close attention to their way, to walk before me in faithfulness with all their heart and with all their soul, you shall not lack a man on the throne of Israel.'<sup>5</sup>"Moreover, you also know what Joab the son of Zeruiah did to me, how he dealt with the two commanders of the armies of Israel, Abner the son of Ner, and Amasa the son of Jether, whom he killed, avenging in time of peace for blood that had been shed in war, and putting the blood of war on the belt around his waist and on the sandals on his feet.<sup>6</sup>Act therefore according to your wisdom, but do not let his gray head go down to Sheol in peace.<sup>7</sup>But deal loyally with the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite, and let them be among those who eat at your table, for with such loyalty they met me when I fled from Absalom your brother.<sup>8</sup>And there is also with you Shimei the son of Gera, the Benjaminite from Bahurim, who cursed me with a grievous curse on the day when I went to Mahanaim. But when he came down to meet me at the Jordan, I swore to him by the LORD, saying, 'I will not put you to death with the sword.'<sup>9</sup>Now therefore do not hold him guiltless, for you are a wise man. You will know what you ought to do to him, and you shall bring his gray head down with blood to Sheol."<sup>10</sup>Then David slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David.<sup>11</sup>And the time that David reigned over Israel was forty years. He reigned seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem.<sup>12</sup>So Solomon sat on the throne of David his father, and his kingdom was firmly established.<sup>13</sup>Then Adonijah the son of Haggith came to Bathsheba the mother of Solomon. And she said, "Do you come peacefully?" He said, "Peacefully."<sup>14</sup>Then he said, "I have something to say to you." She said, "Speak."<sup>15</sup>He said, "You know that the kingdom was mine, and that all Israel fully expected me to reign. However, the kingdom has turned about and become my brother's, for it was his from the LORD.<sup>16</sup>And now I have one request to make of you; do not refuse me." She said to him, "Speak."<sup>17</sup>And he said, "Please ask King Solomon—he will not refuse you—to give me Abishag the Shunammite as my wife."<sup>18</sup>Bathsheba said, "Very well; I will speak for you to the king."<sup>19</sup>So Bathsheba went to King Solomon to speak to him on behalf of Adonijah. And the king rose to meet her and bowed down to her. Then he sat on his throne and had a seat brought for the king's mother, and she sat on his right.<sup>20</sup>Then she said, "I have one small request to make of you; do not refuse me." And the king said to her, "Make your request, my mother, for I will not refuse you."<sup>21</sup>She said, "Let Abishag the Shunammite be given to Adonijah your brother as his wife."<sup>22</sup>King Solomon answered his mother, "And why do you ask Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? Ask for him the kingdom also, for he is my older brother, and on his side are Abiathar the priest and Joab the son of Zeruiah."<sup>23</sup>Then King Solomon swore by the LORD, saying, "God do so to me and more also if this word does not cost Adonijah his life!<sup>24</sup>Now therefore as the LORD lives, who has established me and placed me on the throne of David my father, and who has made me a house, as he promised, Adonijah shall be put to death today."<sup>25</sup>So King Solomon sent Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and he struck him down, and he died.<sup>26</sup>And to Abiathar the priest the king said, "Go to Anathoth, to your estate, for you deserve death. But I will not at this time put you to death, because you carried the ark of the Lord GOD before David my father, and because you shared in all my father's affliction."<sup>27</sup>So Solomon expelled Abiathar from being priest to the LORD, thus fulfilling the word of the LORD that he had spoken concerning the house of Eli in Shiloh.<sup>28</sup>When the news came to Joab—for Joab had supported Adonijah although he had not supported Absalom—Joab fled to the tent of the LORD and caught hold of the horns of the altar.<sup>29</sup>And when it was told King Solomon, "Joab has fled to the tent of the LORD, and behold, he is beside the altar," Solomon sent Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, saying, "Go, strike him down."<sup>30</sup>So Benaiah came to the tent of the LORD and said to him, "The king commands, 'Come out.'" But he said, "No, I will die here." Then Benaiah brought the king word again, saying, "Thus said Joab, and thus he answered me."<sup>31</sup>The king replied to him, "Do as he has said, strike him down and bury him, and thus take away from me and from my father's house the guilt for the blood that Joab shed without cause.<sup>32</sup>The LORD will bring back his bloody deeds on his own head, because, without the knowledge of my father David, he attacked and killed with the sword two men more righteous and better than himself, Abner the son of Ner, commander of the army of Israel, and Amasa the son of Jether, commander of the army of Judah.<sup>33</sup>So shall their blood come back on the head of Joab and on the head of his descendants forever. But for David and for his descendants and for his house and for his throne there shall be peace from the LORD forevermore."<sup>34</sup>Then Benaiah the son of Jehoiada went up and struck him down and put him to death. And he was buried in his own house in the wilderness.<sup>35</sup>The king put Benaiah the son of Jehoiada over the army in place of Joab, and the king put Zadok the priest in the place of Abiathar.<sup>36</sup>Then the king sent and summoned Shimei and said to him, "Build yourself a house in Jerusalem and dwell there, and do not go out from there to any place whatever.<sup>37</sup>For on the day you go out and cross the brook Kidron, know for certain that you shall die. Your blood shall be on your own head."<sup>38</sup>And Shimei said to the king, "What you say is good; as my lord the king has said, so will your servant do." So Shimei lived in Jerusalem many days.<sup>39</sup>But it happened at the end of three years that two of Shimei's servants ran away to Achish, son of Maacah, king of Gath. And when it was told Shimei, "Behold, your servants are in Gath,"<sup>40</sup>Shimei arose and saddled a donkey and went to Gath to Achish to seek his servants. Shimei went and brought his servants from Gath.<sup>41</sup>And when Solomon was told that Shimei had gone from Jerusalem to Gath and returned,<sup>42</sup>the king sent and summoned Shimei and said to him, "Did I not make you swear by the LORD and solemnly warn you, saying, 'Know for certain that on the day you go out and go to any place whatever, you shall die'? And you said to me, 'What you say is good; I will obey.'<sup>43</sup>Why then have you not kept your oath to the LORD and the commandment with which I commanded you?"<sup>44</sup>The king also said to Shimei, "You know in your own heart all the harm that you did to David my father. So the LORD will bring back your harm on your own head.<sup>45</sup>But King Solomon shall be blessed, and the throne of David shall be established before the LORD forever."<sup>46</sup>Then the king commanded Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and he went out and struck him down, and he died. So the kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon.
2.overview:
The last charge of David's life begins as well as it possibly could. I am about to go the way of all the earth — no self-pity, no evasion. Be strong, and show yourself a man, and then the substance: keep the law of Moses. He does not tell his son how to hold a throne, which alliances to make, or what the treasury needs. He tells him to keep what is written, which was already available and was the same for a king as for anybody.

And then, with no transition whatever, the speech turns into a list of people to kill. The writer runs the two halves together without a seam and the effect is deliberate. The Joab charge is true and specific — two commanders killed by cunning in peacetime, the blood of war on the belt around his waist — and what is uncomfortable is the timing, since David had forty years to do it himself and confessed at 2 Samuel 3:39 that he could not. The Shimei instruction is worse: he names the oath he swore, quotes it accurately, and hands the killing to somebody who did not swear it. No reading of that makes it admirable.

And in the middle of the two death sentences sits Barzillai — the eighty-year-old who fed David's army at Mahanaim at his own expense and asked for nothing but a grave. Forty years later, dying, David has not forgotten the bedding. The writer arranged the speech that way and made no comment.

Then four men are dealt with. Adonijah asks for a dead king's woman, which is a claim on his throne, and Solomon hears it before his mother finishes the sentence. Abiathar is sent to a field at Anathoth — and the writer stops the narrative to say that a word spoken over Eli at Shiloh a century earlier has just been completed. Joab holds the horns of the altar that sheltered Adonijah a chapter ago, and Exodus 21:14 distinguishes the two cases exactly. And Shimei keeps a sworn boundary for three years and crosses it for two runaway slaves.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Be Strong, and Show Yourself a Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David charges Solomon: I am about to go the way of all the earth. Be strong, and show yourself a man, and keep the charge of the LORD your God, walking in his ways and keeping his statutes... that you may prosper in all that you do (vv. 2-3), and that God may keep his word about the throne (v. 4). Then Joab — you also know what Joab the son of Zeruiah did to me... avenging in time of peace for blood that had been shed in war — do not let his gray head go down to Sheol in peace (vv. 5-6). Then Barzillai: deal loyally with the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite, and let them be among those who eat at your table (v. 7). Then Shimei, who cursed him at Mahanaim: I swore to him by the LORD, "I will not put you to death with the sword." Now therefore do not hold him guiltless (vv. 8-9). He dies after forty years, and the kingdom was firmly established in the hand of Solomon (vv. 10-12).
verseByVerse.theology: The first half of this speech is as good as anything in the book. The second half is a list of two men to kill, and the writer runs them together in one breath without a seam.
verseByVerse.examples: And the Shimei instruction is the hard one, because David names the oath while telling his son to get round it. He swore at the Jordan that the man would not die (2 Sam. 19:23), and here he remembers the oath, quotes it, and hands the killing to somebody who did not swear it. Between the two death sentences sits Barzillai, and that instruction is pure gratitude.

verseByVerse.quote: When David's time to die drew near, he commanded Solomon his son, saying, "I am about to go the way of all the earth. Be strong, and show yourself a man, and keep the charge of the LORD your God, walking in his ways and keeping his statutes, his commandments, his rules, and his testimonies, as it is written in the Law of Moses, that you may prosper in all that you do and wherever you turn, that the LORD may establish his word that he spoke concerning me, saying, 'If your sons pay close attention to their way, to walk before me in faithfulness with all their heart and with all their soul, you shall not lack a man on the throne of Israel.' "Moreover, you also know what Joab the son of Zeruiah did to me, how he dealt with the two commanders of the armies of Israel, Abner the son of Ner, and Amasa the son of Jether, whom he killed, avenging in time of peace for blood that had been shed in war, and putting the blood of war on the belt around his waist and on the sandals on his feet. Act therefore according to your wisdom, but do not let his gray head go down to Sheol in peace. But deal loyally with the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite, and let them be among those who eat at your table, for with such loyalty they met me when I fled from Absalom your brother. And there is also with you Shimei the son of Gera, the Benjaminite from Bahurim, who cursed me with a grievous curse on the day when I went to Mahanaim. But when he came down to meet me at the Jordan, I swore to him by the LORD, saying, 'I will not put you to death with the sword.' Now therefore do not hold him guiltless, for you are a wise man. You will know what you ought to do to him, and you shall bring his gray head down with blood to Sheol." Then David slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David. And the time that David reigned over Israel was forty years. He reigned seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem. So Solomon sat on the throne of David his father, and his kingdom was firmly established.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When David's time to die drew near, he commanded Solomon his son, saying,'

'"I am about to go the way of all the earth. Be strong, and show yourself a man,"'

The last charge of David's life begins as well as it possibly could.

I am about to go the way of all the earth. No self-pity and no evasion. He is dying and he names it, and the phrase is the oldest way of saying it in the language — Joshua used it at the end of his own life (Josh. 23:14).

Be strong, and show yourself a man. Two imperatives, and the first is the one Moses gave Joshua and God repeated to him at the Jordan.

'"and keep the charge of the LORD your God, walking in his ways and keeping his statutes, his commandments, his rules, and his testimonies, as it is written in the Law of Moses, that you may prosper in all that you do and wherever you turn,"'

And here is the substance of it, and it is entirely right.

Read what he does not say. He does not tell his son how to hold a throne, or which alliances to make, or how to handle the army, or what the treasury needs. He tells him to keep the law of Moses.

Note also the specific form: as it is written in the Law of Moses. Not according to your own judgment, not according to what I did, not according to what the prophets tell you. Written, and already available, and the same for a king as for anybody else. Israel's law required a king to copy the thing out for himself and read it every day of his life (Deut. 17:18-19).

'"that the LORD may establish his word that he spoke concerning me, saying, 'If your sons pay close attention to their way, to walk before me in faithfulness with all their heart and with all their soul, you shall not lack a man on the throne of Israel.'"'

And then he quotes the covenant of 2 Samuel 7 back to his son, and notice which half he quotes.

The promise had two sides. God said the throne would be established forever and that his steadfast love would not depart as I took it from Saul — which is the unconditional half. And he said when he commits iniquity, I will discipline him with the rod of men — which is the half about conduct.

David gives Solomon the conduct half: if your sons pay close attention to their way... you shall not lack a man on the throne.

That is not a distortion; it is what a father says to a son who is about to inherit. The covenant holds whatever the house does, and what happens to the house depends a great deal on what it does, and both are true. Solomon is being told the part that is his responsibility.

Chapter 11 records how he handled it.

'"Moreover, you also know what Joab the son of Zeruiah did to me, how he dealt with the two commanders of the armies of Israel, Abner the son of Ner, and Amasa the son of Jether, whom he killed, avenging in time of peace for blood that had been shed in war, and putting the blood of war on the belt around his waist and on the sandals on his feet."'

Now, with no transition of any kind, the speech turns into a list of people to kill.

The writer sets the two halves side by side and does not put a seam between them, and the effect is deliberate and uncomfortable. One breath: walk in the ways of the LORD as it is written in the Law of Moses. Next breath: you know what Joab did.

Take the Joab charge on its own first, because it is the strongest of the three.

Everything David says is true and specific. Joab killed Abner at the gate of Hebron under a pretence of private conversation, in a city of refuge, in peacetime, when Abner had come under safe conduct (2 Sam. 3:27). He killed Amasa in the road at Gibeon with the same greeting and the same wound, when Amasa was the king's own appointed commander (2 Sam. 20:10). Both were time of peace, and both were unlawful killings by a serving officer.

And the image is exact: putting the blood of war on the belt around his waist and on the sandals on his feet. He wore a soldier's kit and did murder in it.

What is uncomfortable is not the verdict but the timing. David has had forty years to do this himself. He said after Abner's murder, publicly, these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are more severe than I (2 Sam. 3:39) — which is a confession that he could not touch the man. He could not touch him after Absalom either, when Joab disobeyed a public order and killed the king's son. And he needed him, every time.

So the account is genuine and the man rendering it is handing it to somebody else.

'"Act therefore according to your wisdom, but do not let his gray head go down to Sheol in peace."'

'"But deal loyally with the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite, and let them be among those who eat at your table, for with such loyalty they met me when I fled from Absalom your brother."'

In the middle of the list there is this, and it changes the shape of the whole speech.

Barzillai was eighty years old and very rich, and he fed David's army at Mahanaim when the king arrived across the Jordan with nothing — beds, basins, wheat, honey, curds and cheese, at his own expense, at an age when nobody would have blamed him for staying out of it (2 Sam. 17:27-29). He declined a place at court because he could no longer taste food or enjoy music, asked only to be buried near his parents, and sent his son instead.

Forty years later, dying, David has not forgotten the bedding.

Let them be among those who eat at your table. It is the same phrase he used of Mephibosheth, and it is the highest thing an Israelite king had to give.

So the last instructions of David contain two death sentences and one act of remembered kindness, and the kindness sits between them. The writer arranged it that way and did not comment.

'"And there is also with you Shimei the son of Gera, the Benjaminite from Bahurim, who cursed me with a grievous curse on the day when I went to Mahanaim. But when he came down to meet me at the Jordan, I swore to him by the LORD, saying, 'I will not put you to death with the sword.'"'

Here is the hard one, and it should not be smoothed over.

David remembers the oath. He states it accurately, quotes his own words, and names the God he swore by.

Go back and read what that day looked like. Shimei walked along a hillside throwing stones and dirt at a barefoot king and shouting get out, get out, you man of blood, and Abishai offered to take his head off, and David refused with one of the finest answers in Scripture: let him alone, and let him curse, for the LORD has told him to... it may be that the LORD will look on the wrong done to me (2 Sam. 16:11-12).

And when the man came grovelling at the Jordan with a thousand Benjaminites, Abishai asked again, and David said: shall anyone be put to death in Israel this day? For do I not know that I am this day king over Israel? And he swore it (2 Sam. 19:22-23).

'"Now therefore do not hold him guiltless, for you are a wise man. You will know what you ought to do to him, and you shall bring his gray head down with blood to Sheol."'

There is no reading of that which makes it admirable, and this commentary is not going to attempt one.

The defences that exist should be stated, because they are not worthless. The oath was David's own and personal — I will not put you to death — and did not bind the crown after him. A king has a duty to justice as well as to his word, and cursing the LORD's anointed was a capital matter that had gone unpunished. Shimei may well have remained dangerous: he was a Benjaminite of Saul's house who had commanded a thousand men, and the north had already broken away twice.

All of that is arguable. And what it amounts to is keeping the letter of an oath while arranging for its substance to be broken by somebody who did not swear it.

The book records the mercy at the Jordan and it records this, and it reconciles neither. Both are David. The man who would not touch Saul in a cave, who wrote a lament for the king who hunted him, who fed Mephibosheth for twenty years and remembered Barzillai's bedding for forty, also said this on his deathbed.

One thing should be added in fairness, since Solomon acts in verse 46. When Shimei dies it is not for the cursing. It is for breaking a fresh oath he swore himself, under terms he accepted, three years later, of his own free will. Solomon does not simply execute the sentence he was given.

'Then David slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David.'

Eleven words for the death of David.

There is no lament, no funeral described, no crowd, no oration. The man who wrote the elegy for Saul and Jonathan and the one for Abner gets a formula — and it becomes the formula, used of king after king for the rest of the two books.

'And the time that David reigned over Israel was forty years. He reigned seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem.'

'So Solomon sat on the throne of David his father, and his kingdom was firmly established.'

Hold that last clause, because the chapter ends with it again in verse 46, and everything between the two is what it took.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–25 — Ask for Him the Kingdom Also
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Adonijah comes to Bathsheba peaceably, says the kingdom was his and all Israel expected him to reign, however, the kingdom has turned about and become my brother's, for it was his from the LORD (vv. 13-15), and asks her to request Abishag the Shunammite as his wife (vv. 16-18). She takes it to Solomon, who has a throne brought for his mother and sits her at his right hand (vv. 19-21). His reaction is instant: and why do you ask Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? Ask for him the kingdom also, for he is my older brother (v. 22). He swears by the LORD and sends Benaiah, and Adonijah dies that day (vv. 23-25).
verseByVerse.theology: Asking for a dead king's woman is a claim on his throne, and everybody in that world knew it. Abner took Saul's concubine and Ish-bosheth read it as a bid; Ahithophel told Absalom to take his father's concubines publicly for exactly this reason (2 Sam. 3:7; 16:21-22).
verseByVerse.examples: Whether Bathsheba understood what she was carrying, the text does not say, and it is not honest to decide. What is certain is that Solomon understood it before she finished, and that Adonijah had been given terms in public on the first afternoon and had been told precisely what would end them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Adonijah the son of Haggith came to Bathsheba the mother of Solomon. And she said, "Do you come peacefully?" He said, "Peacefully." Then he said, "I have something to say to you." She said, "Speak." He said, "You know that the kingdom was mine, and that all Israel fully expected me to reign. However, the kingdom has turned about and become my brother's, for it was his from the LORD. And now I have one request to make of you; do not refuse me." She said to him, "Speak." And he said, "Please ask King Solomon—he will not refuse you—to give me Abishag the Shunammite as my wife." Bathsheba said, "Very well; I will speak for you to the king." So Bathsheba went to King Solomon to speak to him on behalf of Adonijah. And the king rose to meet her and bowed down to her. Then he sat on his throne and had a seat brought for the king's mother, and she sat on his right. Then she said, "I have one small request to make of you; do not refuse me." And the king said to her, "Make your request, my mother, for I will not refuse you." She said, "Let Abishag the Shunammite be given to Adonijah your brother as his wife." King Solomon answered his mother, "And why do you ask Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? Ask for him the kingdom also, for he is my older brother, and on his side are Abiathar the priest and Joab the son of Zeruiah." Then King Solomon swore by the LORD, saying, "God do so to me and more also if this word does not cost Adonijah his life! Now therefore as the LORD lives, who has established me and placed me on the throne of David my father, and who has made me a house, as he promised, Adonijah shall be put to death today." So King Solomon sent Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and he struck him down, and he died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Adonijah the son of Haggith came to Bathsheba the mother of Solomon. And she said, "Do you come peaceably?" He said, "Peaceably."'

Her first question is whether he means harm, which tells you what the atmosphere in that palace is like.
