'He said, "You know that the kingdom was mine, and that all Israel fully expected me to reign. However, the kingdom has turned about and become my brother's, for it was his from the LORD."'

This is a strange speech, and both halves of it need weighing.

The first half is a grievance, and it is not baseless. He was the eldest surviving son, and by every ordinary rule of inheritance the throne was his, and the country did expect it. He is telling the truth.

The second half is orthodox and it is what a submitted man would say: it was his from the LORD. He concedes not merely that he lost but that God gave it to Solomon.

And then he asks for something, which is why he said the second half.

'"And now I have one request to make of you; do not refuse me." She said to him, "Speak."'

'And he said, "Please ask King Solomon — he will not refuse you — to give me Abishag the Shunammite as my wife."'

Now here is what he is actually asking for, and the first chapter told us the fact that makes it possible.

Abishag was brought to the palace to keep an old man warm, and the writer said plainly the king knew her not (1:4). So she is not David's widow in the ordinary sense. She is a young woman of the royal household, unmarried, with no claim on anybody.

And in that world she is also part of the estate of a dead king, and taking a dead king's woman is how a man announces that he has taken his place.

This history has shown it twice. When Abner slept with Rizpah, Saul's concubine, Ish-bosheth accused him of it — and the accusation was a political one, because it meant Abner was reaching for the throne, and it cost Ish-bosheth his kingdom (2 Sam. 3:7). And when Ahithophel wanted Absalom to make his rebellion irreversible, the advice was to take his father's concubines publicly, on a roof, in the sight of all Israel (2 Sam. 16:21-22).

So the request is not romantic. It is a move.

Whether Adonijah understood that is a fair question. He is not a clever man — he announced himself king with fifty runners and lost a kingdom to a trumpet — and it is possible he simply wanted the girl. It is also possible that a man who had been told in public that his life depended on his conduct was testing exactly how far the terms extended.

The text does not say, and the outcome does not depend on it.

'Bathsheba said, "Very well; I will speak for you to the king."'

And she agrees, and here is the question everybody asks about this chapter.

Did she know?

Two readings are available and the text supports neither decisively. On one, she is an older woman who does not follow the politics, hears a modest-sounding request from a defeated man, and carries it in good faith. On the other, she has lived in that palace since before Absalom, watched Ahithophel advise a rebellion, and knows precisely what taking a king's woman means — and she carries the request because she can see what her son will do with it.

Nothing in the chapter settles it. What can be observed is that she says very well without a word of warning to Adonijah, and that she must have known what happened on that roof.

It is better to leave the question open than to decide it on the strength of a preference.

'So Bathsheba went to King Solomon to speak to him on behalf of Adonijah. And the king rose to meet her and bowed down to her. Then he sat on his throne and had a seat brought for the king's mother, and she sat on his right.'

The king gets up, bows to his mother, and has a throne brought for her, and seats her at his right hand.

That is the honour position, and it is a picture worth keeping: the woman the previous book met on a roof, whose first child died, who lay in a bed while a prophet told her husband he was a murderer, is now seated beside the king of Israel while the court watches.

'Then she said, "I have one small request to make of you; do not refuse me." And the king said to her, "Make your request, my mother, for I will not refuse you."'

One small request. She uses Adonijah's own framing, and Solomon commits before he hears it, which is the one careless thing he does in this chapter.

'She said, "Let Abishag the Shunammite be given to Adonijah your brother as his wife."'

'King Solomon answered his mother, "And why do you ask Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? Ask for him the kingdom also, for he is my older brother, and on his side are Abiathar the priest and Joab the son of Zeruiah."'

The reaction is instant, and it is not paranoia.

Ask for him the kingdom also. He has heard the request and understood it as a constitutional claim before his mother has finished the sentence, and then he says the two things that make it dangerous.

He is my older brother. The hereditary case, which Adonijah stated himself twelve verses ago.

On his side are Abiathar the priest and Joab the son of Zeruiah. A priest and the commander of the army. That is not a disappointed man asking for a wife; that is a faction with a candidate and a claim, testing the ground.

Solomon is right about the facts. What is not settled is whether the sentence he passes is proportionate to them, and the writer does not tell us.

'Then King Solomon swore by the LORD, saying, "God do so to me and more also if this word does not cost Adonijah his life!"'

'"Now therefore as the LORD lives, who has established me and placed me on the throne of David my father, and who has made me a house, as he promised, today Adonijah shall be put to death."'

Note what he swears by: the God who has established me and placed me on the throne... and who has made me a house, as he promised.

He is quoting the covenant. Made me a house is 2 Samuel 7:11 word for word, the promise God made his father in a night vision. Solomon knows exactly whose throne he is sitting on and why, and he invokes it while ordering an execution.

Whether the covenant authorised that particular order is a different question, and one the writer leaves alone.

'So King Solomon sent Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and he struck him down, and he died.'

One sentence, and Adonijah is gone.

He was given terms in public on the first afternoon of the reign, in language he could not misunderstand: if he will show himself a worthy man, not one of his hairs shall fall to the earth, but if wickedness is found in him, he shall die (1:52). He had one thing to do, which was to stay away from anything that looked like a claim, and within a chapter he had asked for the dead king's woman through the king's own mother.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–35 — Take Him from My Altar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Abiathar is banished to his fields at Anathoth — you deserve death. But I will not at this time put you to death, because you carried the ark of the Lord GOD before David my father, and because you shared in all my father's affliction (v. 26). So Solomon expelled Abiathar from being priest to the LORD, thus fulfilling the word of the LORD that he had spoken concerning the house of Eli in Shiloh (v. 27). Joab hears and flees to the tent of the LORD and takes hold of the horns of the altar (v. 28). Sent to bring him out, he answers no, I will die here (v. 30). Solomon's order stands on the law and on two names: strike him down... and take away from me and from my father's house the guilt for the blood that Joab shed without cause (v. 31), naming Abner and Amasa, better men and more righteous than himself (v. 32). Benaiah kills him there and he is buried at his own house in the wilderness (v. 34).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 27 closes a thread opened in the first chapters of 1 Samuel. A man of God told Eli that his house would be cut off and that God would raise up for myself a faithful priest (1 Sam. 2:31-35). Eli's great-grandson Ahimelech died at Nob; Abiathar escaped with the ephod and served David forty years; and here the line ends in a field at Anathoth, and the writer stops to tell us why.
verseByVerse.examples: And the altar does exactly what the law says it does. Adonijah held these horns in chapter 1 and was given terms, because he had killed nobody. Joab holds them here, and Exodus 21:14 says a wilful murderer is taken from my altar, that he may die. Solomon names the two men.

verseByVerse.quote: And to Abiathar the priest the king said, "Go to Anathoth, to your estate, for you deserve death. But I will not at this time put you to death, because you carried the ark of the Lord GOD before David my father, and because you shared in all my father's affliction." So Solomon expelled Abiathar from being priest to the LORD, thus fulfilling the word of the LORD that he had spoken concerning the house of Eli in Shiloh. When the news came to Joab—for Joab had supported Adonijah although he had not supported Absalom—Joab fled to the tent of the LORD and caught hold of the horns of the altar. And when it was told King Solomon, "Joab has fled to the tent of the LORD, and behold, he is beside the altar," Solomon sent Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, saying, "Go, strike him down." So Benaiah came to the tent of the LORD and said to him, "The king commands, 'Come out.'" But he said, "No, I will die here." Then Benaiah brought the king word again, saying, "Thus said Joab, and thus he answered me." The king replied to him, "Do as he has said, strike him down and bury him, and thus take away from me and from my father's house the guilt for the blood that Joab shed without cause. The LORD will bring back his bloody deeds on his own head, because, without the knowledge of my father David, he attacked and killed with the sword two men more righteous and better than himself, Abner the son of Ner, commander of the army of Israel, and Amasa the son of Jether, commander of the army of Judah. So shall their blood come back on the head of Joab and on the head of his descendants forever. But for David and for his descendants and for his house and for his throne there shall be peace from the LORD forevermore." Then Benaiah the son of Jehoiada went up and struck him down and put him to death. And he was buried in his own house in the wilderness. The king put Benaiah the son of Jehoiada over the army in place of Joab, and the king put Zadok the priest in the place of Abiathar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And to Abiathar the priest the king said, "Go to Anathoth, to your estate, for you deserve death. But I will not at this time put you to death, because you carried the ark of the Lord GOD before David my father, and because you shared in all my father's affliction."'

Abiathar is spared, and the two reasons Solomon gives are both about the past.

Because you carried the ark of the Lord GOD before David my father. He was there when the ark came up to Jerusalem, and before that he was the one who brought the ephod out of the ruins of Nob.

And because you shared in all my father's affliction. He was in the caves. He ran to David at Keilah with the ephod in his hand after Doeg killed eighty-five priests, and David said to him then, stay with me; do not be afraid, for he who seeks my life seeks your life. With me you shall be in safekeeping (1 Sam. 22:23).

Fifty years of that, and it ends with a man being sent to a village to farm.

'So Solomon expelled Abiathar from being priest to the LORD, thus fulfilling the word of the LORD that he had spoken concerning the house of Eli in Shiloh.'

Here the writer stops the narrative and tells us what has just happened, and the thread runs back a hundred years.

An unnamed man of God came to Eli at Shiloh, when Israel had judges and no king, and told him what would come of his sons: behold, the days are coming when I will cut off your strength and the strength of your father's house, so that there will not be an old man in your house... and all the descendants of your house shall die by the sword of men. And then the sign, and the promise underneath it: and I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who shall do according to what is in my heart and in my mind. And I will build him a sure house, and he shall go in and out before my anointed forever (1 Sam. 2:31-35).

Now follow it out.

Hophni and Phinehas died in one afternoon at Aphek, and Eli fell backward off his seat when he heard it, and his daughter-in-law named her son Ichabod. Eli's great-grandson Ahimelech was slaughtered at Nob on Saul's order with eighty-four other priests, and one son escaped with the ephod, which was the survivor the oracle had promised: the only one of you whom I shall not cut off from my altar shall be spared to weep his eyes out (1 Sam. 2:33).

That son was Abiathar. He served David for forty years, backed the wrong brother in one afternoon, and here the line ends, in a field at Anathoth, and Zadok stands in his place.

The writer will not let it pass as court politics. He interrupts to say that a word spoken in a tent at Shiloh, before there was a king in Israel, has just been completed.

And note what completed it. Not a plague and not an execution. A man made a bad political judgment at a feast, and God's word about his great-great-grandfather's household came true through it.

There is one more thing about Anathoth worth having. Three centuries later a boy is born in that village to a priestly family, and his book opens: the words of Jeremiah, the son of Hilkiah, one of the priests who were in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin (Jer. 1:1). The line that was put out of the priesthood here produced the prophet of the exile.

'When the news came to Joab — for Joab had supported Adonijah although he had not supported Absalom — Joab fled to the tent of the LORD and caught hold of the horns of the altar.'

The parenthesis is the writer being dry.

Joab had supported Adonijah although he had not supported Absalom. Forty years of absolute loyalty to David through a civil war, a rebellion, and every crisis of the reign — and at the very end, with nothing left to gain, he picked the losing son.

'And it was told King Solomon, "Joab has fled to the tent of the LORD, and behold, he is beside the altar." Then Solomon sent Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, saying, "Go, strike him down."'

'So Benaiah came to the tent of the LORD and said to him, "The king commands, 'Come out.'" But he said, "No, I will die here." Then Benaiah brought the king word again, saying, "Thus said Joab, and thus he answered me."'

No, I will die here.

Four words, and they are entirely in character. He is not pleading and he is not repenting. He has worked out that he is a dead man either way, and he has decided where.

Whether he thought the altar would protect him is doubtful; he knew the law as well as anybody. More likely he is doing the last calculation of a long career: make them kill me at the sanctuary, in front of the priests, so that the blood is on the new king's reign.

Benaiah, to his credit, will not simply do it. He goes back and asks.

'The king replied to him, "Do as he has said, strike him down and bury him, and thus take away from me and from my father's house the guilt for the blood that Joab shed without cause."'

Solomon's answer stands on the law, and the law is explicit about this exact case.

The altar was sanctuary for a man who killed without intending it. And Exodus says: but if a man wilfully attacks another to kill him by cunning, you shall take him from my altar, that he may die (Ex. 21:14).

By cunning. Joab took Abner aside at the gate as though to speak privately with him. Joab took Amasa by the beard with his right hand to kiss him. Both times the weapon was in the other hand.

The altar does not cover that, and the law says so in as many words, and the writer expects his reader to know it — because Adonijah held these same horns one chapter ago and was sent home alive.

'"The LORD will bring back his bloody deeds on his own head, because, without the knowledge of my father David, he attacked and killed with the sword two men more righteous and better than himself, Abner the son of Ner, commander of the army of Israel, and Amasa the son of Jether, commander of the army of Judah."'

He names them, and he says two things about them that repay attention.

Without the knowledge of my father David. Solomon is careful about this, because a king is responsible for what his officers do in his name. He is establishing that these were not royal acts.

And more righteous and better than himself. Abner ran a rebellion against David for seven years and killed Asahel; Amasa commanded the army that killed twenty thousand men in the forest of Ephraim. Neither was a saint, and both are called better than Joab, and the comparison is not about their careers. It is that they were killed by cunning, in peacetime, by a man they trusted enough to stand still for.

'So Benaiah the son of Jehoiada went up and struck him down and put him to death. And he was buried in his own house in the wilderness.'

He is buried at his own house, in the wilderness, which is where he came from.

'The king put Benaiah the son of Jehoiada over the army in place of Joab, and the king put Zadok the priest in the place of Abiathar.'

Both posts change hands in one verse, and both were held by men who went to Adonijah's feast.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 36–46 — You Shall Know for Certain
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Solomon confines Shimei to Jerusalem: build a house and live there, and do not go out from there to any place whatever. For on the day you go out and cross the brook Kidron, know for certain that you shall die (vv. 36-37). Shimei agrees and swears to it (vv. 38, 42-43). Three years later two of his slaves run to Gath and he saddles a donkey and goes after them and brings them back (vv. 39-40). Solomon summons him: did I not make you swear by the LORD and solemnly warn you...? Why then have you not kept your oath to the LORD and the commandment with which I commanded you? (vv. 42-43). Benaiah strikes him down. So the kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon (v. 46).
verseByVerse.theology: The terms are exact and public and generous: a house in the capital and a boundary he chose to swear to. He kept it for three years and then crossed it for two runaway slaves.
verseByVerse.examples: And the chapter ends on the sentence it began with. Verse 12 said the kingdom was firmly established in his hand; verse 46 says it again, after four deaths and a banishment. The writer puts the same clause at both ends and lets the reader see what filled the space between them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king sent and summoned Shimei and said to him, "Build yourself a house in Jerusalem and dwell there, and do not go out from there to any place whatever. For on the day you go out and cross the brook Kidron, know for certain that you shall die. Your blood shall be on your own head." And Shimei said to the king, "What you say is good; as my lord the king has said, so will your servant do." So Shimei lived in Jerusalem many days. But it happened at the end of three years that two of Shimei's servants ran away to Achish, son of Maacah, king of Gath. And when it was told Shimei, "Behold, your servants are in Gath," Shimei arose and saddled a donkey and went to Gath to Achish to seek his servants. Shimei went and brought his servants from Gath. And when Solomon was told that Shimei had gone from Jerusalem to Gath and returned, the king sent and summoned Shimei and said to him, "Did I not make you swear by the LORD and solemnly warn you, saying, 'Know for certain that on the day you go out and go to any place whatever, you shall die'? And you said to me, 'What you say is good; I will obey.' Why then have you not kept your oath to the LORD and the commandment with which I commanded you?" The king also said to Shimei, "You know in your own heart all the harm that you did to David my father. So the LORD will bring back your harm on your own head. But King Solomon shall be blessed, and the throne of David shall be established before the LORD forever." Then the king commanded Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and he went out and struck him down, and he died. So the kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then the king sent and summoned Shimei and said to him, "Build yourself a house in Jerusalem and dwell there, and do not go out from there to any place whatever."'

The terms are generous, and it should be said so.

David's instruction was to bring the man's grey head down with blood. Solomon does not do that. He gives him a house in the capital, at his own expense but on his own land, and one restriction: do not leave the city.

That is house arrest in a comfortable form, and for a man who publicly cursed the LORD's anointed and threw stones at him it is a good deal less than he could have expected.

'"For on the day you go out and cross the brook Kidron, know for certain that you shall die. Your blood shall be on your own head."'

The condition is stated in advance, in the plainest possible language.

Know for certain. Your blood shall be on your own head. There is no ambiguity anywhere in it, and no discretion left to anybody. The line is a named brook on the east side of the city, and it is the one David crossed barefoot and weeping on the day Shimei came out to curse him.

Note also that this is the second time in two chapters that Solomon has done this. Adonijah was given terms on the first afternoon. Shimei is given terms here. Both are told exactly what will end their lives, in public, before anything happens.

His father, faced with a dangerous man, said nothing at all for two years and let a rebellion grow.

'And Shimei said to the king, "What you say is good; as my lord the king has said, so will your servant do." So Shimei lived in Jerusalem many days.'

He accepts. And verse 42 will tell us he did more than accept: Solomon made him swear by the LORD, so there is now an oath of Shimei's own on the arrangement.

'But it happened at the end of three years that two of Shimei's servants ran away to Achish, son of Maacah, king of Gath. And when it was told Shimei, "Behold, your servants are in Gath,"'

Three years, and then two slaves run.

'Shimei arose and saddled a donkey and went to Gath to Achish to seek his servants. Shimei went and brought his servants from Gath.'

He goes and gets them.

Look at how small the thing is. Not a conspiracy, not a message to Benjamin, not a plot with the house of Saul — two runaway slaves, and a piece of property he wanted back. He saddles a donkey and rides out of the city and fetches them and rides home, and it probably took a week.

He kept a sworn boundary for three years and crossed it for a debt he could have written off.

Sit with that, because it is the ordinary shape of ruin. Nobody talks themselves into the large disobedience. They keep the line for years and then step over it for something that seemed too minor to count — and the boundary was never about the size of what was on the other side.

Gath is also worth a note. It is Philistine territory, the town Goliath came from and David hid in twice, and Achish is the name of the king David dealt with there. Shimei has gone out of Israel altogether.

'And when Solomon was told that Shimei had gone from Jerusalem to Gath and returned,'

'the king sent and summoned Shimei and said to him, "Did I not make you swear by the LORD and solemnly warn you, saying, 'Know for certain that on the day you go out and go to any place whatever, you shall die'? And you said to me, 'What you say is good; I will obey.'"'

The charge is not the cursing. It is the oath.

Solomon quotes the terms, quotes the warning, and quotes Shimei's own answer back at him. Every element of the case is something Shimei said or agreed to himself three years ago.

'"Why then have you not kept your oath to the LORD and the commandment with which I commanded you?"'

Your oath to the LORD. That is the head of the charge, and it puts this chapter in line with everything the two books of Samuel have been arguing about promises with God's name on them. Saul broke one to the Gibeonites and there was a famine. David kept one to a dead friend and fed a crippled man for twenty years. Shimei swore one and rode to Gath for two slaves.

'The king also said to Shimei, "You know in your own heart all the harm that you did to David my father. So the LORD will bring back your harm on your own head."'

Then the old matter is added, and it is not the ground of the sentence but it is not pretended away either.

'"But King Solomon shall be blessed, and the throne of David shall be established before the LORD forever."'

'Then the king commanded Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and he went out and struck him down, and he died.'

Now the honest reckoning on this chapter, because a reader is owed it.

Four men are dealt with in forty-six verses. Two of them — Joab and Shimei — were on a list David gave from his deathbed, and one of those was under an oath David himself had sworn. That much is genuinely troubling and the previous chapter said so.

And what Solomon actually does is not simply to execute the list.

Abiathar is on nobody's list and is spared, with reasons given. Adonijah dies for breaking terms he was given in public. Joab dies under a written law that covers his case exactly, and Solomon names the two men and the manner. Shimei dies for breaking an oath he swore himself, three years later, over two slaves — not for the cursing, which is mentioned second and is not the charge.

None of that makes the chapter comfortable. Four men are dead at the start of a reign and the writer does not soften it. What it does mean is that the new king is not merely settling his father's scores; he is doing something his father could not do, which is to state a rule, apply it, and be seen to apply it the same way twice.

'So the kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon.'

The chapter ends where verse 12 began.

Verse 12: so Solomon sat on the throne of David his father, and his kingdom was firmly established. Verse 46: so the kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon.

The same clause at both ends, and everything in between is what the space was filled with. A throne, a charge, a deathbed list, a request for a young woman, an old priest sent to a village, a soldier holding the horns of an altar and refusing to come out, and a man who rode to Gath for two slaves.

That is what establishing a kingdom looked like, and the writer states it twice without a word of approval or regret, and turns the page to Gibeon.

2.theology:
What he tells him to do (v. 3). Not statecraft, not alliances, not the army — as it is written in the Law of Moses. Not according to your own judgment, not according to what I did, not according to what prophets tell you: written, available, and the same for a king as for anybody, which is what Deuteronomy 17:18-19 had required of Israel's kings in the first place.

Which half of the covenant he quotes (v. 4). The promise had two sides: the throne established forever and steadfast love that would not depart as I took it from Saul, and discipline with the rod of men for iniquity. David gives Solomon the conduct half, which is not a distortion but what a father says to a son about to inherit. The covenant holds whatever the house does, and a great deal depends on what the house does. Chapter 11 records how Solomon handled it.

The seam that is not there (v. 5). One breath: walk in the ways of the LORD as it is written. Next breath: you know what Joab did. Everything David says about Joab is true and specific — Abner at the gate of Hebron under a pretence of private conversation, in a city of refuge, in peacetime, under safe conduct (2 Sam. 3:27); Amasa in the road at Gibeon with the same greeting and the same wound, when Amasa was the king's own appointed commander (2 Sam. 20:10) — and the image is exact: he wore a soldier's kit and did murder in it. What is uncomfortable is that the man rendering this account had forty years to render it himself and said instead these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are more severe than I.

Barzillai, between the two death sentences (v. 7). He fed the king's army at Mahanaim at his own expense at eighty, when nobody would have blamed him for staying out of it; declined a place at court because he could no longer taste food or enjoy music; asked only to be buried near his parents and sent his son instead (2 Sam. 17:27-29; 19:34-38). Let them be among those who eat at your table is the phrase used of Mephibosheth, and it is the highest thing an Israelite king had to give.

The oath, named while being got round (vv. 8-9). He remembers it, states it accurately, and names the God he swore by. That day he had refused Abishai twice and said one of the finest things in Scripture — let him alone, and let him curse... it may be that the LORD will look on the wrong done to me (2 Sam. 16:11-12) — and at the Jordan, shall anyone be put to death in Israel this day?, and swore it (2 Sam. 19:22-23). The defences are not worthless: the oath was personal and did not bind the crown; a king owes justice as well as his word; and a Benjaminite of Saul's house who could raise a thousand men was a live danger in a country that had already broken away twice. And they amount to keeping the letter of an oath while arranging for somebody who did not swear it to break its substance. The book records the mercy at the Jordan and this, and reconciles neither. Both are David.

Eleven words for the death of David (v. 10). No lament, no funeral, no oration. The man who wrote the elegy for Saul and Jonathan and the one for Abner gets a formula — and it becomes the formula, used of king after king through both books.

Why the request is a move (vv. 17, 22). Chapter 1 established the fact that makes it possible: the king knew her not (1:4). Abishag is not a widow in the ordinary sense — and in that world she is part of a dead king's estate, and taking a dead king's woman is how a man announces he has taken his place. This history showed it twice: Ish-bosheth's accusation over Rizpah cost him his kingdom (2 Sam. 3:7), and Ahithophel's advice to make a rebellion irreversible was to take the father's concubines publicly (2 Sam. 16:21-22). Whether Adonijah grasped it is a fair question — he is not a clever man — and the outcome does not depend on it. Solomon's reading is not paranoia: an older brother with a hereditary case, a priest, and the commander of the army is a faction with a candidate.

Did Bathsheba know? The text does not say. On one reading she is an older woman who does not follow the politics and carries a modest-sounding request in good faith. On the other she has lived in that palace since before Absalom, watched Ahithophel advise a rebellion, and knows exactly what taking a king's woman means. Nothing settles it; what can be observed is that she says very well with no warning to Adonijah, and that she must have known what happened on that roof. Better to leave the question open than decide it on a preference.

A word from Shiloh, completed (v. 27). The writer interrupts the narrative to say so. A man of God told Eli his house would be cut off, with a survivor spared to weep his eyes out, and a faithful priest raised up in his place (1 Sam. 2:31-35). Hophni and Phinehas died in one afternoon; Ahimelech and eighty-four others were slaughtered at Nob; one son escaped with the ephod and served David forty years — and here that line ends in a field, and Zadok stands in his place. Note what completed it: not a plague and not an execution, but a bad political judgment at a feast. And Anathoth should be kept in mind: three centuries later a boy is born there to a priestly family, and his book opens the words of Jeremiah... one of the priests who were in Anathoth (Jer. 1:1).

The altar, and what the law actually says (vv. 28-31). Adonijah held these same horns one chapter ago and was sent home alive, because he had killed nobody. Exodus is explicit: if a man wilfully attacks another to kill him by cunning, you shall take him from my altar, that he may die (Ex. 21:14). By cunning — Joab took Abner aside as though to speak privately, and took Amasa by the beard to kiss him, and both times the weapon was in the other hand. No, I will die here is entirely in character: not pleading and not repenting, but a last calculation, probably to put the blood on the new reign. And Benaiah will not simply do it; he goes back and asks.

Better men than himself (v. 32). Abner ran a rebellion for seven years and killed Asahel; Amasa commanded the army that left twenty thousand dead in a forest. Neither was a saint, and the comparison is not about their careers — it is that they were killed by cunning, in peacetime, by a man they trusted enough to stand still for. Note too Solomon's care over without the knowledge of my father David: a king answers for what his officers do in his name.

The ordinary shape of ruin (vv. 39-40). Not a conspiracy, not a message to Benjamin, not a plot with the house of Saul — two runaway slaves and a piece of property he wanted back. He kept a sworn boundary for three years and crossed it for a debt he could have written off. Nobody talks themselves into the large disobedience; they keep the line for years and then step over it for something too minor to count, and the boundary was never about the size of what lay on the other side. And the charge Solomon brings is not the cursing: it is your oath to the LORD, which puts the chapter in line with everything Samuel argued about promises with God's name on them.

The honest reckoning. Four men in forty-six verses, two of them from a deathbed list and one of those under an oath David swore. That is troubling and the chapter does not soften it. And what Solomon does is not simply to execute the list: Abiathar is on nobody's list and is spared with reasons given; Adonijah dies for breaking terms he was given in public; Joab dies under a written law that covers his case exactly, with the two men named; Shimei dies for breaking his own oath three years later, and the cursing is mentioned second and is not the charge. Four men are dead at the start of a reign. What has also happened is that the new king has stated a rule, applied it, and been seen to apply it the same way twice — which his father, faced with a dangerous son, could not do.

The same clause at both ends (vv. 12, 46). His kingdom was firmly established, and then so the kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon. Everything between is what filled the space: a charge, a deathbed list, a request for a young woman, an old priest sent to a village, a soldier holding an altar and refusing to come out, and a man who rode to Gath for two slaves. The writer states it twice without a word of approval or regret, and turns the page to Gibeon.
2.examples:
Then: A man was given a house in the capital and one condition — do not cross the brook — and he swore to it in the name of the LORD and kept it for three years. Then two of his slaves ran off to a Philistine town, and he saddled a donkey and went and fetched them back, and it cost him his life.

Now: Three things. Shimei is the study in how boundaries actually get broken: not by defiance, and not over anything large. He held the line for three years and stepped over it for a piece of property, because the thing on the other side looked too small to count — and the line had never been about the size of it. Second, David's speech, which should be read whole rather than in the half that flatters him: the finest charge in the book about walking in God's written word, an accurate account of a murderer he had never been willing to touch, an oath he named while arranging for someone else to break it, and in the middle of all of it a decades-old debt of kindness he had not forgotten. And third, Solomon's method, which is the contrast the chapter is built on: terms stated out loud, in advance, in public, and then applied. His father managed dangerous men by leaving everything unsaid, and it cost him a kingdom and a son.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>Solomon made a marriage alliance with Pharaoh king of Egypt. He took Pharaoh's daughter and brought her into the city of David until he had finished building his own house and the house of the LORD and the wall around Jerusalem.<sup>2</sup>The people were sacrificing at the high places, however, because no house had yet been built for the name of the LORD.<sup>3</sup>Solomon loved the LORD, walking in the statutes of David his father, only he sacrificed and made offerings at the high places.<sup>4</sup>And the king went to Gibeon to sacrifice there, for that was the great high place. Solomon used to offer a thousand burnt offerings on that altar.<sup>5</sup>At Gibeon the LORD appeared to Solomon in a dream by night, and God said, "Ask what I shall give you."<sup>6</sup>And Solomon said, "You have shown great and steadfast love to your servant David my father, because he walked before you in faithfulness, in righteousness, and in uprightness of heart toward you. And you have kept for him this great and steadfast love and have given him a son to sit on his throne this day.<sup>7</sup>And now, O LORD my God, you have made your servant king in place of David my father, although I am but a little child. I do not know how to go out or come in.<sup>8</sup>And your servant is in the midst of your people whom you have chosen, a great people, too many to be numbered or counted for multitude.<sup>9</sup>Give your servant therefore an understanding mind to govern your people, that I may discern between good and evil, for who is able to govern this your great people?"<sup>10</sup>It pleased the Lord that Solomon had asked this.<sup>11</sup>And God said to him, "Because you have asked this, and have not asked for yourself long life or riches or the life of your enemies, but have asked for yourself understanding to discern what is right,<sup>12</sup>behold, I now do according to your word. Behold, I give you a wise and discerning mind, so that none like you has been before you and none like you shall arise after you.<sup>13</sup>I give you also what you have not asked, both riches and honor, so that no other king shall compare with you, all your days.<sup>14</sup>And if you will walk in my ways, keeping my statutes and my commandments, as your father David walked, then I will lengthen your days."<sup>15</sup>And Solomon awoke, and behold, it was a dream. Then he came to Jerusalem and stood before the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and offered up burnt offerings and peace offerings, and made a feast for all his servants.<sup>16</sup>Then two prostitutes came to the king and stood before him.<sup>17</sup>The one woman said, "Oh, my lord, this woman and I live in the same house, and I gave birth to a child while she was in the house.<sup>18</sup>Then on the third day after I gave birth, this woman also gave birth. And we were alone. There was no one else with us in the house; only we two were in the house.<sup>19</sup>And this woman's son died in the night, because she lay on him.<sup>20</sup>And she arose at midnight and took my son from beside me, while your servant slept, and laid him at her breast, and laid her dead son at my breast.<sup>21</sup>When I rose in the morning to nurse my child, behold, he was dead. But when I looked at him closely in the morning, behold, he was not the child that I had borne."<sup>22</sup>But the other woman said, "No, the living child is mine, and the dead child is yours." The first said, "No, the dead child is yours, and the living child is mine." Thus they spoke before the king.<sup>23</sup>Then the king said, "The one says, 'This is my son that is alive, and your son is dead'; and the other says, 'No; but your son is dead, and my son is the living one.'"<sup>24</sup>And the king said, "Bring me a sword." So a sword was brought before the king.<sup>25</sup>And the king said, "Divide the living child in two, and give half to the one and half to the other."<sup>26</sup>Then the woman whose son was alive said to the king, because her heart yearned for her son, "Oh, my lord, give her the living child, and by no means put him to death." But the other said, "He shall be neither mine nor yours; divide him."<sup>27</sup>Then the king answered and said, "Give the living child to the first woman, and by no means put him to death; she is his mother."<sup>28</sup>And all Israel heard of the judgment that the king had rendered, and they stood in awe of the king, because they perceived that the wisdom of God was in him to do justice.
3.overview:
Three verses open the chapter that anybody reading quickly would take as favourable, and each has something in it the rest of the history comes back for. A marriage alliance with Egypt — a political triumph, since Egypt did not give daughters to foreign kings — and the law had told Israel's king not to send people back there and not to take many wives lest his heart turn away, in consecutive clauses. Chapter 11 names the daughter of Pharaoh first in the list of the women who turned him.

Then the finest compliment in the book: Solomon loved the LORD, which this writer says of nobody else. And then his needle: only he sacrificed at the high places — the word he will attach to almost every good reign for the rest of both books.

At Gibeon God asks him what he wants, with no terms and no hint of a right answer, which is why the request is a photograph of the heart taken from the inside. He asks for lev shomea, a hearing heart — not a clever mind, not a quick answer, but a deciding faculty that takes things in before it rules, which is exactly what his father had stopped having. And God names the three things he did not ask for: long life, riches, the life of his enemies — the three things every king in that world wanted, and Solomon had reason to want the third. Two of them are given anyway, outright. Long life is the one with an if attached.

And then, straight after a thousand burnt offerings and an appearance of God, two prostitutes are standing in a room. No husbands, no witnesses, no standing, nothing to offer — the least important case in the kingdom and the hardest to decide, and it goes to the king in person. He cannot detect the liar, so he makes a situation in which love has to reveal itself, because love acts against its own interest and a false claim never does.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Only at the High Places
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Solomon made a marriage alliance with Pharaoh king of Egypt. He took Pharaoh's daughter and brought her into the city of David until he had finished building his own house and the house of the LORD and the wall around Jerusalem (v. 1). The people were sacrificing at the high places, because no house had yet been built for the name of the LORD (v. 2). Solomon loved the LORD, walking in the statutes of David his father, only he sacrificed and made offerings at the high places (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The first fact recorded about the reign after the executions is a foreign marriage, and to Egypt of all places. The law had told Israel's king not to send people back there and not to take many wives lest his heart turn away (Deut. 17:16-17). The writer states it and adds nothing.
verseByVerse.examples: And verse 3 has the needle in it: Solomon loved the LORD — which is said of nobody else in Kings — only he sacrificed at the high places. The word only is the verdict this writer keeps attaching to good kings, and the high places are the thing that will still be standing at the end of both books.

verseByVerse.quote: Solomon made a marriage alliance with Pharaoh king of Egypt. He took Pharaoh's daughter and brought her into the city of David until he had finished building his own house and the house of the LORD and the wall around Jerusalem. The people were sacrificing at the high places, however, because no house had yet been built for the name of the LORD. Solomon loved the LORD, walking in the statutes of David his father, only he sacrificed and made offerings at the high places.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Solomon made a marriage alliance with Pharaoh king of Egypt. He took Pharaoh's daughter and brought her into the city of David until he had finished building his own house and the house of the LORD and the wall around Jerusalem.'

The first thing recorded about the reign, once the executions are over, is a wedding to Egypt.

Politically it is a triumph and everybody at the time would have read it that way. Egypt did not give daughters to foreign kings; the Amarna correspondence has a pharaoh saying flatly that a daughter of Egypt is given to nobody. That Solomon got one is a measure of how large Israel had suddenly become.

And the writer records it in the flattest possible sentence and moves on.

Hold two things against it.

The first is the law about Israel's kings, which this history keeps quietly measuring people by. Only he must not acquire many horses for himself or cause the people to return to Egypt in order to acquire many horses... And he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away (Deut. 17:16-17). Egypt and wives, in consecutive clauses, and this verse has both.

And there is the older command about marrying into the nations of the land: you shall not intermarry with them... for they would turn away your sons from following me, to serve other gods (Deut. 7:3-4). The reason given in the law is never about race. It is about what happens to worship in a household.

The second is what chapter 11 says happened. Now King Solomon loved many foreign women, along with the daughter of Pharaoh... For when Solomon was old his wives turned away his heart after other gods (11:1-4).

The daughter of Pharaoh is named first in that list, and she arrives here, in verse 1, before the temple is built and before Gibeon.

This writer does not editorialise. He plants and waits, and this is a plant.

'The people were sacrificing at the high places, however, because no house had yet been built for the name of the LORD.'

The high places are open-air sanctuaries on hilltops, and they are going to be the running problem of both books.

And the writer gives the excuse himself, which is unusually generous of him: because no house had yet been built. There is no temple yet. The tabernacle is at Gibeon and the ark is in a tent in Jerusalem, and worship is scattered.

'Solomon loved the LORD, walking in the statutes of David his father, only he sacrificed and made offerings at the high places.'

Now read that verse twice, because it holds the whole reign in one line.

Solomon loved the LORD. That is a remarkable thing to say and the writer of Kings says it of nobody else. Not of Asa, not of Jehoshaphat, not of Hezekiah or Josiah, who get his highest marks. Solomon alone is said to have loved God.

Then: only.

That little word is this writer's needle and he uses it for the rest of both books. King after king will be told he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, only the high places were not taken away, only the people still sacrificed there. It is the standing qualification on almost every good reign in the history.

Here it appears for the first time, and it is attached to Solomon on the page before he asks for wisdom.

So the chapter opens with three verses that anybody reading quickly would take as a favourable introduction: a magnificent alliance, a plausible explanation for irregular worship, and the finest compliment in the book. And each of the three has something in it that the rest of the history will come back for.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Gibeon Solomon offers a thousand burnt offerings, and God appears to him in a dream by night: ask what I shall give you (vv. 4-5). He answers with what God did for David, and then: I am but a little child. I do not know how to go out or come in... Give your servant therefore an understanding mind to govern your people, that I may discern between good and evil, for who is able to govern this your great people? (vv. 7-9). It pleased the Lord that Solomon had asked this (v. 10), and God names what he did not ask for — long life, riches, the life of his enemies — and gives him a wise and discerning mind, so that none like you has been before you and none like you shall arise after you, and riches and honour as well (vv. 11-13). And one condition: and if you will walk in my ways... then I will lengthen your days (v. 14). He wakes, and it was a dream (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: The Hebrew of verse 9 is a hearing heart. Not a clever mind and not a large one — a heart that listens, which is what a judge needs before anything else, and what his father stopped having.
verseByVerse.examples: And the gifts are not given on the same terms. Wisdom and riches are given outright; length of days has an if attached to it. Chapter 11 is where that matters.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king went to Gibeon to sacrifice there, for that was the great high place. Solomon used to offer a thousand burnt offerings on that altar. At Gibeon the LORD appeared to Solomon in a dream by night, and God said, "Ask what I shall give you." And Solomon said, "You have shown great and steadfast love to your servant David my father, because he walked before you in faithfulness, in righteousness, and in uprightness of heart toward you. And you have kept for him this great and steadfast love and have given him a son to sit on his throne this day. And now, O LORD my God, you have made your servant king in place of David my father, although I am but a little child. I do not know how to go out or come in. And your servant is in the midst of your people whom you have chosen, a great people, too many to be numbered or counted for multitude. Give your servant therefore an understanding mind to govern your people, that I may discern between good and evil, for who is able to govern this your great people?" It pleased the Lord that Solomon had asked this. And God said to him, "Because you have asked this, and have not asked for yourself long life or riches or the life of your enemies, but have asked for yourself understanding to discern what is right, behold, I now do according to your word. Behold, I give you a wise and discerning mind, so that none like you has been before you and none like you shall arise after you. I give you also what you have not asked, both riches and honor, so that no other king shall compare with you, all your days. And if you will walk in my ways, keeping my statutes and my commandments, as your father David walked, then I will lengthen your days." And Solomon awoke, and behold, it was a dream. Then he came to Jerusalem and stood before the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and offered up burnt offerings and peace offerings, and made a feast for all his servants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the king went to Gibeon to sacrifice there, for that was the great high place. Solomon used to offer a thousand burnt offerings upon that altar.'

Gibeon is where the tabernacle was — the tent Moses made, with the bronze altar, still standing there (2 Chron. 1:3-5). So this is not one of the irregular hilltop shrines; it is the national sanctuary, at the town whose people tricked Joshua into a treaty and were spared for the sake of an oath.

A thousand burnt offerings is an enormous act. A burnt offering is the sacrifice that is entirely consumed, with nothing kept back for the worshipper to eat.

'At Gibeon the LORD appeared to Solomon in a dream by night, and God said, "Ask what I shall give you."'

God asks him what he wants.

It is the only time in Scripture the question is put quite like this, to one person, open. There are no terms attached and no hint of what would be a good answer. Ask what I shall give you.

Any reader knows immediately that this is a test, and the reason should be clear. Nothing reveals a person like what they ask for when they can have anything. The request is a photograph of the heart taken from the inside.

'And Solomon said, "You have shown great and steadfast love to your servant David my father, because he walked before you in faithfulness, in righteousness, and in uprightness of heart toward you. And you have kept for him this great and steadfast love and have given him a son to sit on his throne this day."'

He does not begin with a request. He begins with what God has already done, and the word he uses twice is hesed — the covenant love that keeps its promises after the reasons for keeping them are gone.

And note his description of his father: he walked before you in faithfulness, in righteousness, and in uprightness of heart.

A reader who has just finished 2 Samuel may find that hard to take, and it needs saying plainly that it is a son's account and not a full one. It is also not false. David never served another god, and repented when he was confronted, and the covenant of 2 Samuel 7 was grounded in God's character rather than his. Solomon is describing the shape of a life, not auditing it.

'"And now, O LORD my God, you have made your servant king in place of David my father, although I am but a little child. I do not know how to go out or come in."'

Here is the beginning of the answer, and it is an admission.

I am but a little child. He is not literally a child; he is a grown man who has just executed four people and married a princess of Egypt. Josephus says he was fourteen, and most estimates put him around twenty. Whatever the figure, the phrase is a confession of competence, not of age.

I do not know how to go out or come in. That is a soldier's idiom for leading an army out and bringing it home, and it is what the elders said about David when they made him king — it was you who led out and brought in Israel (2 Sam. 5:2).

Solomon is saying: I cannot do what my father did.

'"And your servant is in the midst of your people whom you have chosen, a great people, too many to be numbered or counted for multitude."'

Note whose people they are. Your people whom you have chosen. He has been on the throne for a matter of months and he already knows that the nation is not his.

And there is a small barb in too many to be numbered, since the last thing his father did before the plague was count them.

'"Give your servant therefore an understanding mind to govern your people, that I may discern between good and evil, for who is able to govern this your great people?"'

Here is the request, and it is the sentence the first half of this book turns on.

Take the Hebrew exactly. What he asks for is lev shomea — a hearing heart.

Not a clever mind. Not a large memory or a quick answer or the ability to out-argue people. A heart that listens.

In Hebrew the heart is not the seat of the feelings as it is in English; it is where a person thinks and decides. So a hearing heart is a deciding faculty that takes things in before it rules — and it is precisely what a judge needs and precisely what his father had stopped having. Two men came to David with stories in 2 Samuel: he heard one side from Ziba and handed over an estate in a sentence, and then heard the other side and split the land rather than admit he had judged carelessly.

And note the purpose he attaches to it: to govern your people, that I may discern between good and evil. The request is not for his own benefit. It is a tool for a job, and the job is other people.

The last clause is the honest one. Who is able to govern this your great people? That is not modesty; it is a real question with an implied answer, which is nobody. He has looked at what is in front of him and concluded that it cannot be done, and asked for the one thing that would let him try.

'It pleased the Lord that Solomon had asked this.'

'And God said to him, "Because you have asked this, and have not asked for yourself long life or riches or the life of your enemies, but have asked for yourself understanding to discern what is right,"'

God names what he did not ask for, which is the most revealing verse in the chapter.

Three things, and they are the three things every king in the ancient world wanted, in order.

Long life. To stay on the throne and not be killed on it.

Riches. The measure of a reign, then as now.

The life of your enemies. To have the men who threaten you dead.

Solomon had reason to want the third. He had spent his first year dealing with a brother, a general, a priest and a Benjaminite, and there were more where they came from.

He asked for none of the three.

Here is what makes this passage useful rather than merely admirable. God did not tell him the right answer beforehand. There was no hint, no list of approved requests, no indication that asking for wealth would disappoint. The question was genuinely open, and what came out of him was a hearing heart to do a job for somebody else's people.

That is why it pleased God. Not the eloquence of it — the fact that when a man could have had anything at all, this is what was in him.

'"behold, I now do according to your word. Behold, I give you a wise and discerning mind, so that none like you has been before you and none like you shall arise after you."'

He gets exactly what he asked for, and more of it than anyone before or since.

'"I give you also what you have not asked, both riches and honor, so that no other king shall compare with you, all your days."'

Then two of the three things he did not ask for, given anyway.

There is a principle here that the Lord Jesus states directly, and he may well have this chapter in view: seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you (Matt. 6:33). The order is the whole of it. Solomon did not get riches because he declined to want them as a technique; he got them because the man who asks for a hearing heart is the man it is safe to give them to.

Whether it stayed safe is chapter 10's question.

'"And if you will walk in my ways, keeping my statutes and my commandments, as your father David walked, then I will lengthen your days."'

Now read the difference between this verse and the two before it, because it is deliberate and it is the hinge of Solomon's whole life.

Wisdom: behold, I give you. Riches and honour: I give you also. Given. No condition, no requirement, no test.

Long life: if you will walk in my ways... then I will lengthen your days.

The one thing he did not receive outright is the one thing hedged with an if, and the condition is conduct, and the standard named is his father.

Keep it, because the writer will come back for it. In chapter 11 God says to Solomon: since this has been your practice and you have not kept my covenant and my statutes that I have commanded you, I will surely tear the kingdom from you (11:11). The gifts were never withdrawn — he died the wisest and richest man in the world — and the conditional promise was.

'And Solomon awoke, and behold, it was a dream. Then he came to Jerusalem and stood before the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and offered up burnt offerings and peace offerings, and made a feast for all his servants.'

He wakes up, and the writer says plainly what it was.

Behold, it was a dream. That is not scepticism; the writer has just told us God appeared to him. It is precision. Solomon did not have a vision he could point to or a stone he could show anybody. He woke up in the dark at Gibeon with a conversation in his head.

Look at what he does with it.

He goes to Jerusalem, and he stands in front of the ark, and he offers burnt offerings and peace offerings, and he throws a feast for his whole household.

Burnt offerings are wholly consumed; peace offerings are eaten. So there is a sacrifice that keeps nothing back, and then a meal, and everybody who works for him is at it.

A man is given the greatest promise of his life in his sleep, and the first thing he does when he wakes is go and worship where the ark is, and then feed his servants.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–28 — Give Her the Living Child
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two prostitutes come to the king. They live in one house; both bore sons three days apart; one child died in the night, and each says the living one is hers (vv. 16-22). The king states the deadlock — the one says, "This is my son that is alive"... and the other says, "No; but your son is dead" — and calls for a sword: divide the living child in two, and give half to the one and half to the other (vv. 23-25). Then the woman whose son was alive said to the king, because her heart yearned for her son, "Oh, my lord, give her the living child, and by no means put him to death." But the other said, "He shall be neither mine nor yours; divide him." (v. 26). The king gives the child to the first — she is his mother (v. 27). And all Israel hears, and they stood in awe of the king, because they perceived that the wisdom of God was in him to do justice (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology: Note who gets a hearing. Two prostitutes with no husbands, no witnesses, no standing and nothing to offer, in a case turning entirely on one woman's word against another's — and it goes to the king in person. That is justice and equity to all his people (2 Sam. 8:15) actually operating.
verseByVerse.examples: And he does not detect a liar. He makes a situation in which love has to show itself, because love will act against its own interest and a false claim will not. The real mother gives up the child to keep him alive; the other says let him be neither mine nor yours.

verseByVerse.quote: Then two prostitutes came to the king and stood before him. The one woman said, "Oh, my lord, this woman and I live in the same house, and I gave birth to a child while she was in the house. Then on the third day after I gave birth, this woman also gave birth. And we were alone. There was no one else with us in the house; only we two were in the house. And this woman's son died in the night, because she lay on him. And she arose at midnight and took my son from beside me, while your servant slept, and laid him at her breast, and laid her dead son at my breast. When I rose in the morning to nurse my child, behold, he was dead. But when I looked at him closely in the morning, behold, he was not the child that I had borne." But the other woman said, "No, the living child is mine, and the dead child is yours." The first said, "No, the dead child is yours, and the living child is mine." Thus they spoke before the king. Then the king said, "The one says, 'This is my son that is alive, and your son is dead'; and the other says, 'No; but your son is dead, and my son is the living one.'" And the king said, "Bring me a sword." So a sword was brought before the king. And the king said, "Divide the living child in two, and give half to the one and half to the other." Then the woman whose son was alive said to the king, because her heart yearned for her son, "Oh, my lord, give her the living child, and by no means put him to death." But the other said, "He shall be neither mine nor yours; divide him." Then the king answered and said, "Give the living child to the first woman, and by no means put him to death; she is his mother." And all Israel heard of the judgment that the king had rendered, and they stood in awe of the king, because they perceived that the wisdom of God was in him to do justice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then two prostitutes came to the king and stood before him.'

Now watch what the writer does, because the placement of this story is the argument.

The previous paragraph had a thousand burnt offerings, an appearance of God, and a promise that no king would compare with him. The very next sentence is two prostitutes standing in a room.

Consider what these women are and are not. They have no husbands and no male relative to speak for them. They have no standing in any court. They have nothing to give and nobody to bribe, and their profession puts them at the bottom of the society. The whole case rests on one woman's word against another's, in a house with no other adults in it, and there are no witnesses of any kind.

It is the least important case in the kingdom and the hardest to decide, and it goes to the king in person.

That is the point. The wisdom that was promised in a dream at Gibeon shows up first in a hearing that nobody powerful cared about, and the writer put the two paragraphs next to each other so that the reader would see it.

And it is the sentence that summarised David's reign at its best, operating: David administered justice and equity to all his people (2 Sam. 8:15). All was always the test, because the courts of that world were judged by how they treated the people nobody had to be fair to.

'The one woman said, "Oh, my lord, this woman and I live in the same house, and I gave birth to a child while she was in the house."'

'"Then on the third day after I gave birth, this woman also gave birth. And we were alone. There was no one else with us in the house; only we two were in the house."'

She states the evidential problem herself: there was no one else with us in the house. No witnesses. She knows it, and says it, and comes anyway.

'"And this woman's son died in the night, because she lay on him."'

'"And she arose at midnight and took my son from beside me, while your servant slept, and laid him at her breast, and laid her dead son at my breast."'

'"When I rose in the morning to nurse my child, behold, he was dead. But when I looked at him closely in the morning, behold, he was not the child that I had borne."'

There is the detail that makes the story real: when I looked at him closely in the morning.

She woke to feed a baby and the baby was dead, and in the half-light she did not know at first. It took looking properly.

'But the other woman said, "No, the living child is mine, and the dead child is yours." The first said, "No, the dead child is yours, and the living child is mine." Thus they spoke before the king.'

Two women shouting the same two sentences at each other in front of a throne.

'Then the king said, "The one says, 'This is my son that is alive, and your son is dead'; and the other says, 'No; but your son is dead, and my son is the living one.'"'

He states the deadlock back to them, exactly, and that is the first thing a hearing heart does.

He has listened closely enough to reproduce both positions without favouring either, and he has established out loud that there is nothing to choose between them on the evidence. No amount of further questioning will settle it.

'And the king said, "Bring me a sword." So a sword was brought before the king.'

'And the king said, "Divide the living child in two, and give half to the one and half to the other."'

The room stops.

It has to be said that this is a terrible thing to say in front of a woman holding a baby, and the writer does not soften it. A sword is fetched. The order is given in plain words. Neither woman knows it is a test, and one of them is about to watch her child be cut in half.

Whether Solomon would have gone through with it is not a question the text raises, and the answer is obviously not. But she does not know that.

Now see what he has actually done, because it is not a trick and it is not cleverness for its own sake.

He could not tell which woman was lying. Nobody could; there was no evidence and no witness. So he stopped trying to detect a liar and made a situation in which love would have to show itself.

The insight underneath it is this: love acts against its own interest, and a false claim never does. A woman who wants a baby will not give it up. A woman who loves a baby will give up anything, including the baby, to keep him alive.

So the sword does not test their honesty. It tests what each of them wants more — the child, or winning.

'Then the woman whose son was alive said to the king, because her heart yearned for her son, "Oh, my lord, give her the living child, and by no means put him to death."'

There it is.

Take the narrator's clause first, because he tells us the reason before he gives us her words: because her heart yearned for her son.

The Hebrew verb is physical. It is about the inward parts turning over — the churn a person feels in the body when someone they love is in danger. It is the word used of Joseph, when he saw his brother Benjamin and had to leave the room because his compassion grew warm for his brother, and he sought a place to weep (Gen. 43:30).

That is what is happening in her while she speaks.

Now what she says. Give her the living child.

She loses. That is the whole point and it should not be hurried past. In order to keep her son alive she has to hand him to the woman who stole him, and go home without him, and live the rest of her life knowing where he is and unable to say a word about it.

She does it in one sentence, and the second half of the sentence is the only thing she cares about: and by no means put him to death.

'But the other said, "He shall be neither mine nor yours; divide him."'

The other one says the coldest sentence in the chapter.

He shall be neither mine nor yours.

Notice what she is actually choosing. She is not choosing the child; she has already lost that option, because the king has ruled that neither gets him whole. She is choosing that the other woman shall not have him either.

That is what a grief with nothing underneath it turns into when it is refused. She lost her own son in the night and lay there and swapped the bodies, and what she wants now is not a baby. It is that the woman across the room should not be happy.

Anybody who has watched a bitter dispute go past the point where either party can gain anything has seen this exact sentence. Neither mine nor yours. If I cannot have it, destroy it.

'Then the king answered and said, "Give the living child to the first woman, and by no means put him to death; she is his mother."'

He gives the verdict in her own words. By no means put him to death is what she said, and he says it back, and then three words: she is his mother.

'And all Israel heard of the judgment that the king had rendered, and they stood in awe of the king, because they perceived that the wisdom of God was in him to do justice.'

The last verse is careful about what it is praising.

Not that the king was clever. They perceived that the wisdom of God was in him to do justice.

The wisdom is God's, given at Gibeon a page ago, and it is identified by what it produced: a right verdict in a case nobody could have decided, for a woman with no standing whatever.

That is what Solomon asked for. He wanted a hearing heart to discern between good and evil so that he could govern God's people, and the first thing it did was find a baby's mother.

And there is something in the shape of it that runs further than this courtroom. A real mother gave up her claim so that her son could live. A while later, in the same city, God gave up a Son so that people with no standing and no case and nothing to offer could live — and both of them did it by surrendering the thing they had every right to keep.

3.theology:
The plant in verse 1. The first fact recorded about the reign after the executions is a wedding to Egypt, stated flatly and left there. The law is specific in consecutive clauses — do not cause the people to return to Egypt, and he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away (Deut. 17:16-17) — and the older command against intermarriage gives its reason, which is never race but worship: they would turn away your sons from following me (Deut. 7:3-4). Chapter 11 opens: King Solomon loved many foreign women, along with the daughter of Pharaoh. She arrives here, before the temple and before Gibeon. This writer does not editorialise; he plants and waits.

The word only (v. 3). Solomon loved the LORD is said of no other king in Kings — not Asa, not Jehoshaphat, not Hezekiah or Josiah, who get the highest marks. And the qualification attached to him on the page before he asks for wisdom is the one this writer will attach to almost every good reign that follows: the high places were not taken away. He is generous enough to give the excuse himself in verse 2 — there was no temple yet.

An open question is a photograph of the heart (v. 5). No terms, no hint of an approved answer, no indication that asking for wealth would disappoint. Nothing reveals a person like what they ask for when they can have anything.

He begins with what God has already done (v. 6). The word twice is hesed. And his description of his father — faithfulness, righteousness, uprightness of heart — is a son's account and not a full one, and it is also not false: David never served another god, and repented when confronted, and the covenant of 2 Samuel 7 was grounded in God's character rather than his.

I am but a little child (v. 7). Not literally — he is a grown man who has just executed four people and married a princess of Egypt. It is a confession of competence, not of age. And I do not know how to go out or come in is the soldier's idiom the elders used of David when they crowned him (2 Sam. 5:2). He is saying: I cannot do what my father did. Note also whose people they are — your people whom you have chosen — and the small barb in too many to be numbered, since the last thing his father did before the plague was count them.

A hearing heart (v. 9). The Hebrew is lev shomea. In Hebrew the heart is where a person thinks and decides, not where they feel — so this is a deciding faculty that listens before it rules, which is what a judge needs before anything else. It is precisely what David had lost: he heard one side from Ziba and handed over an estate in a sentence, then heard the other and split the land rather than admit he had judged carelessly. And the purpose Solomon attaches is not his own benefit — it is a tool for a job, and the job is other people. Who is able to govern this your great people? is not modesty; it is a real question whose answer is nobody.

What he did not ask for, named by God (v. 11). Long life, riches, the life of his enemies — the three things every king in that world wanted, in order. He had reason to want the third, having spent his first year on a brother, a general, a priest and a Benjaminite. He asked for none of them. And this is what makes the passage useful rather than merely admirable: there was no hint beforehand. When a man could have had anything at all, this is what came out of him.

Two of the three, given anyway (v. 13). The Lord Jesus states the principle directly and may well have this chapter in view: seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you (Matt. 6:33). The order is the whole of it. Solomon did not decline riches as a technique for getting them; he got them because the man who asks for a hearing heart is the man it is safe to give them to. Whether it stayed safe is chapter 10's question.

The one gift with an if (v. 14). Read the difference deliberately: wisdom, behold, I give you; riches and honour, I give you also. Given outright, no condition. Long life: if you will walk in my ways... then I will lengthen your days, and the standard named is his father. Chapter 11 is the payoff: since this has been your practice and you have not kept my covenant... I will surely tear the kingdom from you (11:11). The gifts were never withdrawn — he died the wisest and richest man alive — and the conditional promise was.

It was a dream (v. 15). Not scepticism — the writer has just said God appeared to him. Precision. Solomon had no vision to point to and no stone to show anybody; he woke in the dark at Gibeon with a conversation in his head. And what he does with it: goes to Jerusalem, stands before the ark, offers burnt offerings (wholly consumed) and peace offerings (eaten), and feeds his whole household.

Who gets a hearing (v. 16). The placement is the argument. A thousand burnt offerings, an appearance of God, and a promise that no king would compare with him — and the next sentence is two prostitutes standing in a room. No husbands, no male relative to speak for them, no standing in any court, nothing to give and nobody to bribe, and a case turning entirely on one woman's word against another's with no witnesses, which she states herself. The wisdom promised at Gibeon shows up first in a hearing nobody powerful cared about. That is 2 Samuel 8:15 operating, and all his people was always the test, because the courts of that world were judged by how they treated those nobody had to be fair to.

He stops trying to detect a liar (v. 25). It is a terrible thing to say in front of a woman holding a baby, and the writer does not soften it: a sword is fetched and the order is given plainly, and neither woman knows it is a test. He could not tell which was lying — nobody could — so he made a situation in which love would have to show itself. The insight underneath is that love acts against its own interest and a false claim never does. A woman who wants a baby will not give him up; a woman who loves him will give up anything, including him, to keep him alive. The sword does not test honesty. It tests what each of them wants more: the child, or winning.

Her heart yearned (v. 26). The narrator gives the reason before the words, and the verb is physical — the inward parts turning over, the churn in the body when someone you love is in danger. It is the word used of Joseph, who saw Benjamin and had to leave the room to weep (Gen. 43:30). And she loses, which is the point: to keep him alive she must hand him to the woman who stole him and go home without him and live the rest of her life knowing where he is. She does it in one sentence, and the half she cares about is the second: by no means put him to death.

Neither mine nor yours (v. 26). The coldest sentence in the chapter, and notice what she is choosing. Not the child — that option is gone, since the ruling gives him whole to nobody. She is choosing that the other woman shall not have him either. That is what a grief with nothing underneath it becomes when it is refused: she lost her own son in the night and swapped the bodies, and what she wants now is not a baby but that the woman across the room should not be happy. Anyone who has watched a bitter dispute pass the point where either side can gain has heard that sentence.

What the last verse praises (v. 28). Not that the king was clever: they perceived that the wisdom of God was in him to do justice. The wisdom is God's, given a page earlier, and it is identified by what it produced — a right verdict in a case nobody could have decided, for a woman with no standing whatever. He asked for a hearing heart to govern God's people, and the first thing it did was find a baby's mother. And there is a shape here that runs further than the courtroom: a real mother gave up her claim so that her son could live, and later, in the same city, God gave up a Son so that people with no standing and no case could live — both by surrendering what they had every right to keep.
3.examples:
Then: God appeared to a young king in his sleep and told him to ask for anything at all, with no hint of what a good answer would be — and he asked for a heart that could listen, so that he could do the job properly for people who were not his. The first case it was used on was two prostitutes and a baby, with no witnesses and nothing to decide it by.

Now: Three things. Verse 5 is the test that never stops being a test: what you would ask for if you could have anything is a photograph of you, and nobody is going to tell you the right answer beforehand. Second, what he asked for was a tool for a job, and the job was other people — which is the difference between wanting wisdom and wanting to be thought wise. And third, the sword.
