He could not tell who was lying, so he stopped trying and made a situation in which love had to declare itself, because love will act against its own interest and nothing else will. Know that about other people, and know it about yourself: the question is never what you claim to care about but what you will give up to keep it.

4.overview:
A cabinet list, and the reader has seen two of these before at the end of 2 Samuel 8 and 20, both times to say the kingdom was in working order. This one is longer, and the difference is the point: two secretaries where David had one, an officer over the officers, a household manager, and a minister of forced labour. This is a state rather than a court.

The name to keep is last on the list where nobody looks. Adoniram... was in charge of the forced labor — the same office, and almost certainly the same man, as the Adoram of 2 Samuel 20:24. Eight chapters from now the ten tribes stone him to death and walk out of the kingdom, and the one thing they ask Rehoboam for is that his father's yoke be lightened. The writer puts him eleventh on a list and says nothing.

And the twelve districts are not the twelve tribes. Several are named by town or region rather than tribe, cutting straight across the old inheritances — which were not administrative conveniences but allotments given by lot under Joshua, each family's portion of the land promised to Abraham. A revenue map is drawn over the top of them. It is more efficient, and when the north finally walks out the slogan is about inheritance.

Then the high-water mark of the Old Testament, in Abraham's own vocabulary: as many as the sand by the sea, and borders from the Euphrates to Egypt, and every man under his vine and under his fig tree. And in the middle of it, forty thousand stalls of horses, stated as one more item of glory, against a command his father had obeyed at cost by hamstringing a captured cavalry on the field. The father cut the tendons; the son built the stables.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–19 — The Officials and the Twelve
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: King Solomon was king over all Israel, and the cabinet is listed: Azariah son of Zadok the priest; two secretaries; Jehoshaphat the recorder; Benaiah over the army; Zadok and Abiathar as priests; Azariah over the officers; Zabud son of Nathan, priest and king's friend; Ahishar over the household; and Adoniram the son of Abda was in charge of the forced labor (vv. 1-6). Then twelve officers over all Israel, who provided food for the king and his household. Each man had to make provision for one month in the year (v. 7), and the districts are set out one by one (vv. 8-19).
verseByVerse.theology: The list looks like David's at 2 Samuel 8 and 20, and it is not the same kind of thing. There are two secretaries where there was one, an officer over the officers, a household manager, and a minister of forced labour. This is a state rather than a court.
verseByVerse.examples: And the twelve districts are not the twelve tribes. Several are named by town or region rather than by tribe, and the old boundaries are cut across — which turns a confederation of families into a revenue map. It is efficient, and chapter 12 is what it cost.

verseByVerse.quote: King Solomon was king over all Israel, and these were his high officials: Azariah the son of Zadok was the priest; Elihoreph and Ahijah the sons of Shisha were secretaries; Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder; Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was in command of the army; Zadok and Abiathar were priests; Azariah the son of Nathan was over the officers; Zabud the son of Nathan was priest and king's friend; Ahishar was in charge of the palace; and Adoniram the son of Abda was in charge of the forced labor. Solomon had twelve officers over all Israel, who provided food for the king and his household. Each man had to make provision for one month in the year. These were their names: Ben-hur, in the hill country of Ephraim; Ben-deker, in Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth-shemesh, and Elonbeth-hanan; Ben-hesed, in Arubboth (to him belonged Socoh and all the land of Hepher); Ben-abinadab, in all Naphath-dor (he had Taphath the daughter of Solomon as his wife); Baana the son of Ahilud, in Taanach, Megiddo, and all Beth-shean that is beside Zarethan below Jezreel, and from Beth-shean to Abel-meholah, as far as the other side of Jokmeam; Ben-geber, in Ramoth-gilead (he had the villages of Jair the son of Manasseh, which are in Gilead, and he had the region of Argob, which is in Bashan, sixty great cities with walls and bronze bars); Ahinadab the son of Iddo, in Mahanaim; Ahimaaz, in Naphtali (he had taken Basemath the daughter of Solomon as his wife); Baana the son of Hushai, in Asher and Bealoth; Jehoshaphat the son of Paruah, in Issachar; Shimei the son of Ela, in Benjamin; Geber the son of Uri, in the land of Gilead, the country of Sihon king of the Amorites and of Og king of Bashan. And there was one governor who was over the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'King Solomon was king over all Israel, and these were his high officials: Azariah the son of Zadok was the priest;'

A cabinet list, and the reader has seen two of these before — at the end of 2 Samuel 8 and again at the end of 2 Samuel 20, both times to say that the kingdom was in working order.

This one is longer, and the difference is the point of the chapter.

'Elihoreph and Ahijah the sons of Shisha were secretaries; Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder;'

'Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was in command of the army; Zadok and Abiathar were priests;'

Two secretaries where David had one. Jehoshaphat the recorder is the same man who held the post under David, which means somebody in that administration has now served two kings.

Note that Abiathar is still listed, although he was expelled to Anathoth in chapter 2. The writer is giving the offices, not a snapshot of one afternoon.

'Azariah the son of Nathan was over the officers; Zabud the son of Nathan was priest and king's friend;'

An officer over the officers — a layer of administration that did not exist under David.

And two sons of Nathan in one verse. If this is the prophet who confronted David and then arranged the succession at Gihon, his family is now inside the government, and one of them holds the title Hushai held: king's friend.

'Ahishar was in charge of the palace; and Adoniram the son of Abda was in charge of the forced labor.'

There is the name to keep, at the bottom of the list where nobody looks.

Adoniram the son of Abda was in charge of the forced labor.

That office appeared once before, in the last cabinet list in 2 Samuel, and it was new even then: Adoram was in charge of the forced labor (2 Sam. 20:24). Same post, and almost certainly the same man under a fuller form of his name.

Now follow him forward. Under Solomon the forced labour becomes enormous — chapter 5 has thirty thousand men conscripted in shifts, and seventy thousand burden-bearers, and eighty thousand quarrymen. And when Solomon dies, the northern tribes come to his son with exactly one request: your father made our yoke heavy. Now therefore lighten the hard service of your father and his heavy yoke on us, and we will serve you (12:4).

Rehoboam refuses, with the line about scorpions. And then: then King Rehoboam sent Adoram, who was taskmaster over the forced labor, and all Israel stoned him to death with stones (12:18).

The man in this verse is stoned to death by the ten tribes eight chapters from now, and the kingdom splits over his department.

The writer puts him last on a list of eleven officials and says nothing whatever.

'Solomon had twelve officers over all Israel, who provided food for the king and his household. Each man had to make provision for one month in the year.'

Twelve districts, each responsible for feeding the court for one month.

It is an elegant arrangement, and look exactly at what it does. The burden is spread, so no region is ruined; the supply is continuous, so the court never runs short; and the whole country is now organised around the maintenance of the capital.

'These were their names: Ben-hur, in the hill country of Ephraim; Ben-deker, in Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth-shemesh, and Elonbeth-hanan;'

'Ben-hesed, in Arubboth (to him belonged Socoh and all the land of Hepher); Ben-abinadab, in all Naphath-dor (he had Taphath the daughter of Solomon as his wife);'

'Baana the son of Ahilud, in Taanach, Megiddo, and all Beth-shean which is beside Zarethan below Jezreel, and from Beth-shean to Abel-meholah, as far as the other side of Jokmeam;'

Now read the district list as a whole rather than name by name, because the shape of it is the information.

These are not the twelve tribes.

Some districts carry a tribal name — Naphtali, Asher, Issachar, Benjamin, Gilead. Others are defined by towns and regions that cut straight across the old inheritances: the hill country of Ephraim, Makaz and Shaalbim and Beth-shemesh, Arubboth, Naphath-dor, Taanach and Megiddo and Beth-shean.

The tribal boundaries were not administrative conveniences. They were allotments, given by lot under Joshua, each family's portion of the land God promised Abraham, and the law made them almost impossible to alienate permanently. A man's field was his tribe's and his tribe's was God's gift.

The new map is drawn over the top of them, for the purpose of collecting food.

It is more efficient. It is also the beginning of the dissolution of the thing that made Israel a covenant people rather than a country, and when the north finally walks out in chapter 12 the slogan they use is about inheritance: what portion do we have in David? We have no inheritance in the son of Jesse (12:16).

'Ben-geber, in Ramoth-gilead (he had the villages of Jair the son of Manasseh, which are in Gilead, and he had the region of Argob, which is in Bashan, sixty great cities with walls and bronze bars);'

'Ahinadab the son of Iddo, in Mahanaim;'

Mahanaim is where David crossed the Jordan when Absalom drove him out, and where three men brought him beds and cheese.

'Ahimaaz, in Naphtali (he had taken Basemath the daughter of Solomon as his wife);'

'Baana the son of Hushai, in Asher and Bealoth;'

Two of Solomon's daughters are married to district officers, and a son of Hushai holds a district. Hushai is the old man in the torn coat who walked into a captured Jerusalem and lied to Absalom's face to save David's life.

The families that stood by the father are being provided for by the son.

'Jehoshaphat the son of Paruah, in Issachar;'

'Shimei the son of Ela, in Benjamin;'

'Geber the son of Uri, in the land of Gilead, the country of Sihon king of the Amorites and of Og king of Bashan. And there was one governor who was over the land.'

Twelve names, twelve districts, and one man over the whole system.

A reader who counts will notice something the writer does not mention: Judah is not on the list.

The Hebrew of the last verse is difficult and translations differ over whether a twelfth district in Judah is being referred to. What is not in doubt is that eleven of the districts named are in the north and centre, and that the tribe the king belongs to does not appear among them.

Whether Judah was exempt from the monthly provision, the text does not say outright. But the ten tribes will say something in chapter 12 that sounds very much as though they thought so.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–28 — Every Man Under His Vine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judah and Israel were as many as the sand by the sea. They ate and drank and were happy (v. 20). Solomon rules from the Euphrates to the border of Egypt, and they bring tribute all his life (v. 21). The daily provision of his table is thirty cors of fine flour and sixty of meal, ten fat oxen, twenty pasture-fed cattle, a hundred sheep, besides deer, gazelles, roebucks, and fattened fowl (vv. 22-23). He has peace on every side (v. 24), and Judah and Israel lived in safety, from Dan even to Beersheba, every man under his vine and under his fig tree, all the days of Solomon (v. 25). Solomon also had 40,000 stalls of horses for his chariots, and 12,000 horsemen (v. 26), and the officers keep the supply coming without fail (vv. 27-28).
verseByVerse.theology: As the sand by the sea is Abraham's promise arriving (Gen. 22:17), and the borders in verse 21 are the land as it was described to him (Gen. 15:18). This is the high-water mark of the whole Old Testament story, and the writer says so in that vocabulary on purpose.
verseByVerse.examples: And in the middle of it, forty thousand stalls of horses. The law said Israel's king must not acquire many horses (Deut. 17:16), and the reader has just watched his father hamstring seventeen hundred captured chariot horses on the day he won them, in obedience to that command (2 Sam. 8:4). The father cut the tendons. The son built the stables.

verseByVerse.quote: Judah and Israel were as many as the sand by the sea. They ate and drank and were happy. Solomon ruled over all the kingdoms from the Euphrates to the land of the Philistines and to the border of Egypt. They brought tribute and served Solomon all the days of his life. Solomon's provision for one day was thirty cors of fine flour and sixty cors of meal, ten fat oxen, and twenty pasture-fed cattle, a hundred sheep, besides deer, gazelles, roebucks, and fattened fowl. For he had dominion over all the region west of the Euphrates from Tiphsah to Gaza, over all the kings west of the Euphrates. And he had peace on all sides around him. And Judah and Israel lived in safety, from Dan even to Beersheba, every man under his vine and under his fig tree, all the days of Solomon. Solomon also had 40,000 stalls of horses for his chariots, and 12,000 horsemen. And those officers supplied provisions for King Solomon, and for all who came to King Solomon's table, each one in his month. They let nothing be lacking. Barley also and straw for the horses and swift steeds they brought to the place where it was required, each according to his duty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Judah and Israel were as many as the sand by the sea. They ate and drank and were happy.'

This is the high-water mark of the Old Testament, and the writer signals it with a phrase.

As many as the sand by the sea is not a general expression for a lot of people. It is the promise God swore to Abraham on the mountain in the land of Moriah, after the ram was found in the thicket: I will surely multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven and as the sand that is on the seashore (Gen. 22:17).

Here it is, in a sentence about ordinary people eating dinner.

They ate and drank and were happy. That is the whole of it. Not conquering, not building, not fighting. Eating, drinking, and content.

'Solomon ruled over all the kingdoms from the Euphrates to the land of the Philistines and to the border of Egypt. They brought tribute and served Solomon all the days of his life.'

The borders are Abraham's too. To your offspring I give this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates (Gen. 15:18).

Nothing before this and nothing after it comes as close. Joshua took the land; David subdued the neighbours; and here, for one generation, the map matches the promise.

'Solomon's provision for one day was thirty cors of fine flour and sixty cors of meal,'

'ten fat oxen, and twenty pasture-fed cattle, a hundred sheep, besides deer, gazelles, roebucks, and fattened fowl.'

Per day.

A cor is something like six bushels, so this is several tons of flour and meal daily, thirty head of cattle, a hundred sheep, and game and poultry on top. Estimates of how many people that fed run into the thousands.

The passage is set down as splendour, and it is splendour, and it is also an invoice.

Somebody grew that grain and raised those animals, and the twelve districts of the previous paragraph exist precisely to deliver it, one month each. What reads as a description of the king's glory is, from the other end, a description of the country's tax burden — and the writer has put the two paragraphs in that order.

Hold both. The prosperity is real and the people are happy, and the machinery underneath it is what the north will complain about the day Solomon dies.

'For he had dominion over all the region west of the Euphrates from Tiphsah to Gaza, over all the kings west of the Euphrates. And he had peace on all sides around him.'

He had peace on all sides around him.

His name means peace, and there is a reason he has it. God told David he would not build the temple because you have shed much blood and have waged great wars (1 Chron. 22:8), and promised instead a son who would be a man of rest.

This verse is that promise in operation. The wars were fought by the father so that the son could build.

'And Judah and Israel lived in safety, from Dan even to Beersheba, every man under his vine and under his fig tree, all the days of Solomon.'

Here is the picture the prophets will use for the age to come.

Every man under his vine and under his fig tree.

It is a domestic image and that is its power. Not an empire, not a temple, not an army — a man sitting outside his own house in the shade of things he planted himself. A vine takes years to bear and a fig tree longer, so nobody sits under either unless he has been in one place long enough to plant them and safe enough to wait.

Micah takes it up for the day when the nations beat their swords into ploughshares: they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree, and no one shall make them afraid (Mic. 4:4). Zechariah uses it of the day God removes the iniquity of the land in a single day (Zech. 3:10).

So the settled prosperity of Solomon's reign becomes the standing Old Testament shorthand for what God intends to give the world, and notice what shape it takes. Peace, in Scripture, does not look like a throne. It looks like an ordinary person, unafraid, sitting in the shade of his own fig tree.

'Solomon also had 40,000 stalls of horses for his chariots, and 12,000 horsemen.'

Then this, in the middle of it, stated as one more item of glory.

The law about Israel's kings has three prohibitions, and the first is: only he must not acquire many horses for himself or cause the people to return to Egypt in order to acquire many horses, since the LORD has said to you, "You shall never return that way again" (Deut. 17:16).

Forty thousand stalls.

And the reader has watched somebody obey this command, recently and at cost. When David captured Hadadezer's cavalry he had almost all of the chariot horses hamstrung on the field, keeping enough for a hundred chariots and destroying the rest — the finest military asset in the region, deliberately ruined, because of one clause in a book (2 Sam. 8:4).

The father cut the tendons. The son built the stables.

And chapter 10 will complete it: Solomon's import of horses was from Egypt (10:28), which is the other half of the same prohibition, the half about sending people back where they came from.

The reason the law gives is never economic. It is that a chariot corps is the thing a nation leans on instead of God, and a psalm of David says so directly: some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God (Ps. 20:7).

The writer records the forty thousand stalls between a verse about men sitting under their fig trees and a verse about the officers never letting the supply fail, and he does not say one word about it.

'And those officers supplied provisions for King Solomon, and for all who came to King Solomon's table, each one in his month. They let nothing be lacking.'

'Barley also and straw for the horses and swift steeds they brought to the place where it was required, each according to his duty.'

They let nothing be lacking. The system works perfectly, and the last verse of the section is about feeding the horses.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–34 — Wisdom Like the Sand on the Seashore
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God gave Solomon wisdom and understanding beyond measure, and breadth of mind like the sand on the seashore (v. 29), surpassing all the east and all Egypt (v. 30). He is wiser than Ethan, Heman, Calcol and Darda, and his fame was in all the surrounding nations (v. 31). He also spoke 3,000 proverbs, and his songs were 1,005 (v. 32). He spoke of trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall. He spoke also of beasts, and of birds, and of reptiles, and of fish (v. 33). And people of all nations came to hear the wisdom of Solomon (v. 34).
verseByVerse.theology: The catalogue in verse 33 runs the categories of Genesis 1. This wisdom is not mysticism and not a technique; it is sustained attention to what God has made, from the largest tree in the region to the weed in a wall.
verseByVerse.examples: Two of the men he is measured against — Ethan and Heman — have psalms in the psalter with their names in the headings (Pss. 88, 89). And the last verse points forward: people came from everywhere to hear him, and one of them arrives in chapter 10, and the Lord Jesus says of himself something greater than Solomon is here (Matt. 12:42).

verseByVerse.quote: And God gave Solomon wisdom and understanding beyond measure, and breadth of mind like the sand on the seashore, so that Solomon's wisdom surpassed the wisdom of all the people of the east and all the wisdom of Egypt. For he was wiser than all other men, wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite, and Heman, Calcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol, and his fame was in all the surrounding nations. He also spoke 3,000 proverbs, and his songs were 1,005. He spoke of trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall. He spoke also of beasts, and of birds, and of reptiles, and of fish. And people of all nations came to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and from all the kings of the earth, who had heard of his wisdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And God gave Solomon wisdom and understanding beyond measure, and breadth of mind like the sand on the seashore,'

The promise at Gibeon is being reported as fact, and the writer uses the same figure he used of the population two paragraphs ago: like the sand on the seashore.

Breadth of mind is literally largeness of heart. It is not a moral phrase here; it means range — the capacity to hold a great many things and see how they fit.

'so that Solomon's wisdom surpassed the wisdom of all the people of the east and all the wisdom of Egypt.'

Those were the two great wisdom traditions of the ancient world, and the writer names them because his readers would have known the comparison was a real one. Egypt had centuries of instruction literature; the east had its own. Solomon is being placed above both.

'For he was wiser than all other men, wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite, and Heman, Calcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol, and his fame was in all the surrounding nations.'

Four named men, evidently famous enough that no explanation was needed.

Two of them turn up in the psalter. Psalm 88 is a maskil of Heman the Ezrahite, and it is the darkest psalm in the book — the one that ends darkness is my closest friend. Psalm 89 is a maskil of Ethan the Ezrahite, and it is the long meditation on the covenant with David that asks, when the crown has been thrown to the ground, Lord, where is your steadfast love of old, which by your faithfulness you swore to David?

The men Solomon is measured against wrote about unanswered grief and a broken covenant. That is what wisdom was understood to be in Israel: not a stock of good advice, but the ability to look steadily at things that do not resolve.

'He also spoke 3,000 proverbs, and his songs were 1,005.'

Three thousand proverbs, and the book of Proverbs contains a few hundred of his. A thousand and five songs, and the Song of Songs is one, and two psalms carry his name (Pss. 72, 127).

Almost all of it is lost. The writer records the numbers so that we understand what a small fraction survived.

'He spoke of trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall. He spoke also of beasts, and of birds, and of reptiles, and of fish.'

This is the verse that tells us what kind of thing his wisdom actually was.

Read the categories: trees, beasts, birds, reptiles, fish.

That is Genesis 1. It is the order of the created world as the first chapter of the Bible sets it out, and Solomon went through it and paid attention.

The range within the first category is the whole point: from the cedar that is in Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall. The cedar is the largest and most valuable tree in the region, the timber kings imported for palaces and temples. Hyssop is a small bushy plant that grows in cracks in masonry, and it is what the Israelites used to daub blood on the doorposts in Egypt, and what was lifted to the cross with a sponge of sour wine.

The biggest tree and the weed in the wall. He looked at both.

So the wisdom God gave was not a mystical faculty or a stock of clever rulings. It was attention — sustained, curious, unembarrassed attention to what God had made, from the cedars down to whatever is growing out of the brickwork.

That is what the book of Proverbs does on every page. Go to the ant. Look at the badger and the locust and the lizard. Watch how a lazy man's field looks in the spring. Israel's wisdom tradition believed the world was made by a God who is consistent, and that a person who watches it carefully will learn how to live.

'And people of all nations came to hear the wisdom of Solomon, from all the kings of the earth, who had heard of his wisdom.'

People came from everywhere, and one of them gets a chapter to herself.

The Queen of Sheba arrives in chapter 10, tests him with hard questions, and says the half was not told her.

And there is one more thing to say about this verse, because the Lord Jesus said it. Speaking to a generation that wanted a sign from him, he said: the queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here (Matt. 12:42).

A foreign queen crossed a desert on a rumour. And the people standing in front of the wisdom of God in person asked him to do a trick.

4.theology:
A state, not a court (vv. 2-6). Two secretaries, an officer set over the officers, a palace manager, and a department of forced labour — layers David never had. Note also two sons of Nathan inside the government, one of them holding the title Hushai held, king's friend; and Jehoshaphat the recorder, who has now served two kings.

The seed of the split, eleventh on the list (v. 6). The office was new when it first appeared at 2 Samuel 20:24. Under Solomon it becomes enormous — chapter 5 has thirty thousand conscripted in shifts, seventy thousand burden-bearers, eighty thousand quarrymen. And when he dies, the north asks Rehoboam for exactly one thing: lighten the hard service of your father and his heavy yoke (12:4). He refuses, sends this man, and all Israel stoned him to death with stones (12:18).

A revenue map over an inheritance (vv. 7-19). Some districts carry tribal names; others are defined by towns that cut across the old boundaries. Those boundaries were allotments given by lot under Joshua, each family's portion of what was promised to Abraham, and the law made them nearly impossible to alienate permanently. Drawing a new map over them for the purpose of collecting food is efficient, and it begins dissolving the thing that made Israel a covenant people rather than a country — and the slogan the north eventually uses is about inheritance (12:16). A reader who counts will also notice that Judah does not appear among the districts named; the Hebrew of the last verse is difficult, and what is not in doubt is that the tribe the king belongs to is not on the list.

Abraham's promise arriving (vv. 20-21). As many as the sand by the sea is what God swore on the mountain in Moriah after the ram was found in the thicket (Gen. 22:17), and the borders in verse 21 are the land as described to him (Gen. 15:18). Nothing before this and nothing after comes as close. And the sentence it is put in is about ordinary people eating dinner: they ate and drank and were happy.

Splendour, and an invoice (vv. 22-23). Several tons of flour and meal a day, thirty head of cattle, a hundred sheep, and game and poultry besides. Somebody grew that and raised it, and the twelve districts exist to deliver it a month each. What reads from one end as the king's glory is from the other end the country's tax burden, and the writer put the paragraphs in that order. Hold both: the prosperity is real and the people are happy, and the machinery underneath is what the north complains about the day he dies.

Peace on all sides (v. 24). His name means peace, and there is a reason he has it. God told David he would not build the temple because you have shed much blood and have waged great wars, and promised instead a son who would be a man of rest (1 Chron. 22:8-9). The wars were fought by the father so the son could build.

What peace looks like in Scripture (v. 25). Not a throne, not an empire, not an army — a man sitting outside his own house in the shade of things he planted himself. A vine takes years to bear and a fig tree longer, so nobody sits under either unless he has been somewhere long enough to plant them and safe enough to wait. Micah takes it up for the day the nations beat their swords into ploughshares (Mic. 4:4), and Zechariah for the day God removes the iniquity of the land (Zech. 3:10). The settled prosperity of this reign becomes the standing shorthand for what God intends to give the world.

Forty thousand stalls (v. 26). The first of the three prohibitions on Israel's kings is he must not acquire many horses for himself or cause the people to return to Egypt in order to acquire many horses (Deut. 17:16) — and the reader has just watched somebody obey it at real cost, hamstringing the finest cavalry in the region on the day he captured it (2 Sam. 8:4). Chapter 10 completes the breach: Solomon's import of horses was from Egypt (10:28). The reason the law gives is never economic; a chariot corps is the thing a nation leans on instead of God, and a psalm of David says so: some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God (Ps. 20:7). The writer sets the forty thousand stalls between men under their fig trees and officers who let nothing be lacking, and says nothing.

Who he is measured against (v. 31). Two of the four turn up in the psalter. Psalm 88 is Heman's, the darkest psalm in the book, ending darkness is my closest friend. Psalm 89 is Ethan's, the long meditation on the covenant with David that asks, with the crown thrown to the ground, Lord, where is your steadfast love of old? The men Solomon surpasses wrote about unanswered grief and a broken covenant. That is what wisdom meant in Israel: not a stock of good advice but the capacity to look steadily at what does not resolve.

What his wisdom actually was (v. 33). Trees, beasts, birds, reptiles, fish — the categories of Genesis 1, gone through with attention. And the range inside the first one is the point: from the cedar that is in Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall. The cedar is the timber kings imported for palaces; hyssop is a weed in masonry, and it is what daubed blood on the doorposts in Egypt and what lifted a sponge to the cross. The biggest tree and the plant in the brickwork, and he looked at both. That is what Proverbs does on every page — go to the ant, watch the badger and the locust and the lizard, look at a lazy man's field in spring. Israel's wisdom believed the world was made by a consistent God and that watching it carefully teaches you how to live. Note also how little survived: three thousand proverbs and a thousand and five songs, of which we have a few hundred proverbs, one song, and two psalms.

Something greater (v. 34). People came from everywhere, and one of them gets a chapter to herself in chapter 10. And the Lord Jesus used this verse against a generation that wanted a sign from him: the queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here (Matt. 12:42). A foreign queen crossed a desert on a rumour; the people standing in front of the wisdom of God in person asked him to do a trick.
4.examples:
Then: A king whose court ate thirty head of cattle and a hundred sheep a day reorganised the whole country into twelve supply districts drawn straight across the tribal inheritances — and the minister he put in charge of the conscripted labour that built it all was stoned to death by ten of the tribes on the day the kingdom broke in half.

Now: Two things. Verse 33 is what wisdom looks like when the Bible describes it, and it is more ordinary and more demanding than most people expect: not a mystical faculty and not a stock of clever answers, but sustained attention to what God has actually made, from the cedars of Lebanon down to whatever is growing out of a wall. Solomon was the wisest man alive and he spent it looking at fish and lizards. And the second is the shape of the chapter. Everything in it is a genuine good — peace, plenty, safety, a man under his own fig tree, a promise to Abraham arriving — and the writer lays the machinery that pays for it right alongside, and drops forty thousand stalls of horses into the middle without a word. Prosperity is not neutral. It has a bill attached and somebody is carrying it, and it quietly acquires the things it was told not to.

5.overview:
The first foreign act of the reign is an embassy arriving unasked, and the reason given is personal: Hiram always loved David. He had sent cedar and craftsmen to build David a house years earlier, unasked — and that cedar is what made David uncomfortable enough to say I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of God dwells in a tent, which produced the greatest promise in the Old Testament. The man who supplied the timber that started the conversation now supplies the timber for the building.

Solomon's account of why his father could not build is the warfare, and it is true and it is not the reason God gave. Chronicles has David reporting it himself, twice: you have shed much blood... you shall not build a house to my name. It was not that David was too busy; his hands were too bloody. The two accounts touch, since the same wars are the cause of the disqualification — and they are not the same, and the one Solomon gives is the one that reflects better on his father, in a letter to a foreign king he wants a timber contract from.

And the warrant for the whole project is a quotation. He is not building because it seems fitting or because kings have temples: as the LORD said to David my father — a sentence spoken in a night vision before he was born. Every stone in the next three chapters goes up on the strength of it. Then a Phoenician king blesses the LORD by name and credits him rather than Solomon with the wisdom, and the writer lets it stand.

And then the levy: thirty thousand Israelites conscripted in monthly shifts, a hundred and fifty thousand labourers in all, under a minister named Adoniram. The terms are humane for the age and the work is glorious — these men are building the place where Israel will meet God for four hundred years. And this is the department the kingdom eventually dies of.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Now the LORD My God Has Given Me Rest
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hiram king of Tyre sends servants to Solomon, for Hiram always loved David (v. 1). Solomon writes back: you know that David my father could not build a house for the name of the LORD his God because of the warfare with which his enemies surrounded him, until the LORD put them under the soles of his feet. But now the LORD my God has given me rest on every side. There is neither adversary nor misfortune (vv. 3-4). And so I intend to build a house for the name of the LORD my God, as the LORD said to David my father (v. 5). He asks for cedars of Lebanon and offers wages for the Sidonian woodcutters, for you know that there is no one among us who knows how to cut timber like the Sidonians (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: The reason Solomon gives for his father's exclusion is the warfare, and it is not the reason God gave. Chronicles has David reporting it himself: you have shed much blood and have waged great wars. You shall not build a house to my name (1 Chron. 22:8). Both are true and they are not the same thing, and a diplomatic letter to a Phoenician king is not where a son would put the second.
verseByVerse.examples: Rest on every side is the condition that makes building possible, and it is the word that opened the covenant chapter: when the king lived in his house and the LORD had given him rest from all his surrounding enemies (2 Sam. 7:1). The wars were fought by the father so that the son could build.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Hiram king of Tyre sent his servants to Solomon when he heard that they had anointed him king in place of his father, for Hiram always loved David. And Solomon sent word to Hiram, "You know that David my father could not build a house for the name of the LORD his God because of the warfare with which his enemies surrounded him, until the LORD put them under the soles of his feet. But now the LORD my God has given me rest on every side. There is neither adversary nor misfortune. And so I intend to build a house for the name of the LORD my God, as the LORD said to David my father, 'Your son, whom I will set on your throne in your place, shall build the house for my name.' Now therefore command that cedars of Lebanon be cut for me. And my servants will join your servants, and I will pay you for your servants such wages as you set, for you know that there is no one among us who knows how to cut timber like the Sidonians."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now Hiram king of Tyre sent his servants to Solomon when he heard that they had anointed him king in place of his father, for Hiram always loved David.'

The first foreign policy act of the reign is a condolence and congratulation embassy arriving unasked, and the reason given is personal.

Hiram always loved David. The word is the ordinary one for love, and in treaty language of that period it also carried the sense of loyal alliance — but the writer chooses it, and he has used it of Jonathan and of Michal and of Solomon toward the LORD.

Hiram had sent cedar and craftsmen to build David a house at Jerusalem, unasked, years earlier (2 Sam. 5:11). That cedar is what made David uncomfortable enough to say I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of God dwells in a tent — which produced the greatest promise in the Old Testament.

So the man who supplied the timber that started the whole conversation is now going to supply the timber for the building.

'And Solomon sent word to Hiram,'

'"You know that David my father could not build a house for the name of the LORD his God because of the warfare with which his enemies surrounded him, until the LORD put them under the soles of his feet."'

Now note carefully what Solomon says, because it is true and it is not the whole truth, and the difference matters.

His account is that his father was prevented by the wars. There was never a season clear enough; the enemies were on every side until God put them under his feet.

That is accurate as far as it goes. And it is not the reason God gave.

The reason is recorded twice, in David's own mouth, in Chronicles. Speaking to Solomon: the word of the LORD came to me, saying, "You have shed much blood and have waged great wars. You shall not build a house to my name, because you have shed so much blood before me on the earth" (1 Chron. 22:8). And again to the assembled leaders: God said to me, "You may not build a house for my name, for you are a man of war and have shed blood" (1 Chron. 28:3).

It was not that David was too busy. It was that his hands were too bloody.

Both things are true at once, and Solomon is not lying. The wars did fill the reign, and the same wars are the reason for the disqualification — so the two accounts touch. But they are not the same, and the one he gives is the one that reflects better on his father.

It is also, in fairness, a letter to a foreign king with whom he wants a timber contract. A man does not open a trade negotiation by telling a Phoenician that his father was refused a building permit by God on account of bloodshed.

The writer records what was said and lets a reader who knows Chronicles hold the other half.

'"But now the LORD my God has given me rest on every side. There is neither adversary nor misfortune."'

Rest on every side.

That is the condition, and it is the word the whole thing turns on. When God made the covenant with David, the chapter opened: when the king lived in his house and the LORD had given him rest from all his surrounding enemies (2 Sam. 7:1). Rest was what prompted David to think about the tent in the first place.

Rest is what Solomon has been given rather than won. He has fought nobody. His father broke the Philistines from Geba to Gezer, destroyed a Syrian army twice, subdued Moab and Edom and Ammon, and hamstrung the horses; and the son inherits a country with neither adversary nor misfortune and builds in the quiet.

Note the name he uses, twice in two verses: the LORD my God. Not the LORD his God, which is what he called him when speaking of David in verse 3. He has taken possession of the relationship.

'"And so I intend to build a house for the name of the LORD my God, as the LORD said to David my father, 'Your son, whom I will set on your throne in your place, shall build the house for my name.'"'

Here is the whole warrant for the project, and it is a quotation.

He is not building because he wants to, or because it seems fitting, or because a king ought to have a temple. He is doing it because God said this would happen, to his father, in a night vision before he was born.

Go back to it: he shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever (2 Sam. 7:13).

David wanted to build and was told no, and told instead that God would build him a house, and that a son would build the other kind. Every stone that goes up in the next three chapters goes up on the strength of that sentence.

'"Now therefore command that cedars of Lebanon be cut for me. And my servants will join your servants, and I will pay you for your servants such wages as you set, for you know that there is no one among us who knows how to cut timber like the Sidonians."'

He asks for the timber and he asks for the men, and he concedes the point that makes the request necessary.

There is no one among us who knows how to cut timber like the Sidonians.

Israel had no forests of that kind and no tradition of felling and hauling and rafting great timber. The Phoenicians did it for the whole eastern Mediterranean, and Egypt bought from them, and so did Assyria later.

So the temple of the LORD is going to be built out of foreign wood, cut by foreign hands, by an arrangement in which Israel admits it cannot do this part.

Solomon offers to pay the going rate: such wages as you set. He does not ask for a gift and he does not name his own price.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Blessed Be the LORD This Day
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As soon as Hiram heard the words of Solomon, he rejoiced greatly and said, "Blessed be the LORD this day, who has given to David a wise son to be over this great people" (v. 7). He agrees to the cedar and the cypress, floating it down the coast in rafts to a place Solomon names, and asks for food for his household in return (vv. 8-9). So Hiram supplies timber and Solomon supplies twenty thousand cors of wheat and twenty of beaten oil, year by year (vv. 10-11). And the LORD gave Solomon wisdom, as he promised him. And there was peace between Hiram and Solomon, and the two of them made a treaty (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: A Phoenician king blesses the LORD by name and credits him with Solomon's wisdom. It should not be overclaimed — Hiram's own gods were Baal and Astarte, and Tyre is where Jezebel comes from two hundred years later — and it should not be skipped either. The writer records a foreigner getting the credit right.
verseByVerse.examples: And read the terms as terms. Tyre had the finest timber and craftsmen in the region and almost no farmland; Israel had grain and oil and no cedar. This is not charity in either direction. It is two kings each supplying what the other could not grow.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as Hiram heard the words of Solomon, he rejoiced greatly and said, "Blessed be the LORD this day, who has given to David a wise son to be over this great people." And Hiram sent to Solomon, saying, "I have heard the message that you have sent to me. I am ready to do all you desire in the matter of cedar and cypress timber. My servants shall bring it down to the sea from Lebanon, and I will make it into rafts to go by sea to the place you direct. And I will have them broken up there, and you shall receive it. And you shall meet my wishes by providing food for my household." So Hiram supplied Solomon with all the timber of cedar and cypress that he desired, while Solomon gave Hiram 20,000 cors of wheat as food for his household, and 20,000 cors of beaten oil. Solomon gave this to Hiram year by year. And the LORD gave Solomon wisdom, as he promised him. And there was peace between Hiram and Solomon, and the two of them made a treaty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'As soon as Hiram heard the words of Solomon, he rejoiced greatly and said, "Blessed be the LORD this day, who has given to David a wise son to be over this great people."'

A Phoenician king blesses the LORD by name.

Take it carefully, in both directions.

What he says is right in every particular. He blesses the LORD — using the covenant name, not a generic word for god. He credits God rather than Solomon with the wisdom. He calls Israel this great people. And he identifies the thing that has actually happened: a wise son given to David.

That is better theology than a great many Israelites managed, and the writer records it without comment.

It should not be turned into a conversion. Hiram is the king of Tyre, and Tyre's gods are Baal and Astarte; his own inscriptions and his people's practice are not in doubt. Two centuries later a king of Israel marries a princess of Sidon called Jezebel, and what she brings with her burns through the northern kingdom for three generations.

Kings of that world habitually acknowledged the god of a neighbouring country as a courtesy, and some of that is certainly in this sentence.

What can be said is that the writer of Kings, who is merciless about Israelite kings, gives a foreigner an unqualified good line and lets it stand. It is a pattern the reader has met before — Uriah the Hittite, Ittai the Gittite, Obed-edom, the Ammonite who brought bedding to Mahanaim — and it will recur in this book with a widow at Zarephath and a Syrian general.

'"Now therefore command that cedars of Lebanon be cut for me... So Hiram sent to Solomon, saying, "I have heard the message that you have sent to me. I am ready to do all you desire in the matter of cedar and cypress timber."'

'"My servants shall bring it down to the sea from Lebanon, and I will make it into rafts to go by sea to the place you direct. And I will have them broken up there, and you shall receive it. And you shall meet my wishes by providing food for my household."'

The logistics are worth a sentence because they are how the thing was actually done.

Cedar was felled in the mountains, dragged to the coast, lashed into rafts, and floated down the Mediterranean by sea to a landing point — Chronicles names Joppa (2 Chron. 2:16) — and then hauled the forty miles up to Jerusalem overland. Every beam in the house of God came that way.

Hiram's price is food. Tyre was a trading city on a rocky coast with almost no agricultural land behind it, and it fed itself by importing. What Israel had that Tyre needed was grain and oil.

'So Hiram supplied Solomon with all the timber of cedar and cypress that he desired,'

'while Solomon gave Hiram 20,000 cors of wheat as food for his household, and 20,000 cors of beaten oil. Solomon gave this to Hiram year by year.'

Year by year. This is not a single purchase; it is a standing annual obligation for as long as the work goes on, and the wheat and oil have to come from somewhere, which is what the twelve districts of the previous chapter are for.

Beaten oil is the best grade — olives crushed by hand rather than pressed — and it is the quality specified for the lamps of the sanctuary (Ex. 27:20).

'And the LORD gave Solomon wisdom, as he promised him. And there was peace between Hiram and Solomon, and the two of them made a treaty.'

Note where the writer puts that sentence.

He has just described a shrewd and favourable trade agreement, negotiated at market rates, with the one supplier in the world who had what Israel needed — and his comment on it is the LORD gave Solomon wisdom, as he promised him.

Not Solomon negotiated well. The wisdom on display in a timber contract is the wisdom given in a dream at Gibeon, and the writer keeps saying so.

One more thing in the verse: as he promised him. The historian is checking the account. God said at Gibeon that he would give a wise and discerning mind, and here is the receipt.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: King Solomon drafted forced labor out of all Israel, and the draft numbered 30,000 men (v. 13). They go to Lebanon ten thousand a month in shifts, a month in Lebanon and two months at home, under Adoniram (v. 14). Solomon also had 70,000 burden-bearers and 80,000 stonecutters in the hill country, besides 3,300 chief officers over the work (vv. 15-16). Great costly stones are quarried for the foundation, and Solomon's builders and Hiram's and the men of Gebal prepare the timber and the stone (vv. 17-18).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the department the kingdom eventually breaks over. The one thing the northern tribes ask of Solomon's son is lighten the hard service of your father and his heavy yoke on us (12:4), and when he refuses they stone the man named in verse 14.
verseByVerse.examples: There is a real tension here that should be stated rather than smoothed: 9:22 says Solomon made no slaves of the people of Israel, and this verse says he drafted forced labour out of all Israel. The usual reconciliation is that the permanent gangs were Canaanite and the Israelite levy was rotational conscription rather than slavery. That is plausible, and the men of chapter 12 evidently did not experience the distinction as a large one.

verseByVerse.quote: King Solomon drafted forced labor out of all Israel, and the draft numbered 30,000 men. And he sent them to Lebanon, 10,000 a month in shifts. They would be a month in Lebanon and two months at home. Adoniram was in charge of the draft. Solomon also had 70,000 burden-bearers and 80,000 stonecutters in the hill country, besides Solomon's 3,300 chief officers who were over the work, who had charge of the people who carried on the work. At the king's command they quarried out great, costly stones in order to lay the foundation of the house with dressed stones. So Solomon's builders and Hiram's builders and the men of Gebal did the cutting and prepared the timber and the stone to build the house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'King Solomon drafted forced labor out of all Israel, and the draft numbered 30,000 men.'

Here is the sentence the kingdom eventually dies of.

The word is mas, and it means a corvée — compulsory unpaid labour owed to the crown. It is the same word used of what the Egyptians imposed on Israel in Exodus 1:11, where taskmasters were set over them to afflict them with heavy burdens.

That is not a small echo and the writer knows the vocabulary he is using.

'And he sent them to Lebanon, 10,000 a month in shifts. They would be a month in Lebanon and two months at home. Adoniram was in charge of the draft.'

The terms are humane by the standards of the age, and that should be said. One month away and two at home is a third of a man's time, not all of it; a farmer could still get a crop in. It is rotational conscription, not slavery.

The man in charge is the one from the cabinet list, and the reader has been told to keep his name. Adoniram was in charge of the draft.

Follow him to chapter 12. Solomon dies, and the northern tribes come to Rehoboam with a single request — not about religion, not about the succession, not about tribal rights: your father made our yoke heavy. Now therefore lighten the hard service of your father and his heavy yoke on us, and we will serve you (12:4).

He answers with the line about scorpions. And King Rehoboam sent Adoram, who was taskmaster over the forced labor, and all Israel stoned him to death with stones (12:18).

They killed the minister of labour, and the kingdom split, and it never came back together.

'Solomon also had 70,000 burden-bearers and 80,000 stonecutters in the hill country,'

'besides Solomon's 3,300 chief officers who were over the work, who had charge of the people who carried on the work.'

A hundred and fifty thousand labourers and three and a half thousand foremen.

Now here is a tension in the text that ought to be named rather than smoothed over, because an attentive reader will find it.

Four chapters from now the writer says this: but of the people of Israel Solomon made no slaves. They were the soldiers, they were his officials, his commanders, his captains, his chariot commanders and his horsemen (9:22). And the verses before it say the permanent labour gangs were drawn from the surviving Canaanite peoples of the land.

And this chapter says King Solomon drafted forced labor out of all Israel.

The usual reconciliation is a real one and it is probably right: two different arrangements are being described. The Canaanite population was in permanent bondage; the Israelite levy was rotational, temporary, and for the temple project specifically. The Hebrew even uses slightly different terms in the two passages.

That distinction is genuine and it is legal, and it is also the sort of distinction that looks much smaller from underneath.

Because the men who came to Rehoboam did not say your father enslaved us. They said your father made our yoke heavy, and they said it about a system that had been described in its own records as fair.

Two things ought to be held together here without either cancelling the other.

The work is glorious. This is the house of God going up, and the men quarrying stone in the hill country are building the place where the ark will rest and where Israel will meet God for four hundred years. Every one of them could tell his grandchildren what he had a hand in.

And it is being paid for by conscripted labour on a scale the country had never seen, administered by a department that did not exist under David, and the bill arrives at the end of Solomon's life and is presented to his son.

The writer states the numbers and does not comment. He has done this from the beginning of the book — the wedding to Egypt in 3:1, the forty thousand stalls in 4:26, the levy here — laying things down in sequence and trusting the reader to still be holding them in chapter 11.

'At the king's command they quarried out great, costly stones in order to lay the foundation of the house with dressed stones.'

Great, costly stones. The foundation is out of sight and it gets the best material, which is a thing worth noticing about how this building was made.

'So Solomon's builders and Hiram's builders and the men of Gebal did the cutting and prepared the timber and the stone to build the house.'

The last verse of the chapter lists three workforces, and two of them are foreign.

Solomon's men, Hiram's men, and the men of Gebal — which is Byblos, another Phoenician port up the coast, famous for stonework.

So the house of the LORD is quarried, dressed, felled and rafted by Israelites and Phoenicians working side by side, on a foreign king's timber, to a plan given to David by God, on ground bought from a Jebusite for fifty shekels of silver.

5.theology:
Two true reasons that are not the same (v. 3). Solomon says the wars prevented it; God said the blood disqualified him (1 Chron. 22:8; 28:3). The accounts touch, because the same wars produced the bloodshed — and they are not interchangeable, and a son writing to a Phoenician about a timber contract is not going to say that his father was refused a building permit by God on account of bloodshed. The writer records what was said and trusts the reader to hold the other half.

Rest is the condition (v. 4). The same word opened the covenant chapter — the LORD had given him rest from all his surrounding enemies (2 Sam. 7:1) — and rest is what prompted David to think about the tent at all. Solomon has been given it rather than won it: his father broke the Philistines from Geba to Gezer, destroyed a Syrian army twice, subdued Moab and Edom and Ammon; the son inherits neither adversary nor misfortune and builds in the quiet. Note too that he says the LORD my God twice, having said the LORD his God of David a verse earlier. He has taken possession of the relationship.

The warrant is a quotation (v. 5). As the LORD said to David my father, "Your son... shall build the house for my name" — which is 2 Samuel 7:13, spoken in a night vision before Solomon existed. David wanted to build and was told no, and told instead that God would build him a house. The temple is not a good idea being executed; it is a promise being kept.

Israel admits it cannot do this part (v. 6). There is no one among us who knows how to cut timber like the Sidonians. The Phoenicians supplied the whole eastern Mediterranean, and Egypt and later Assyria bought from them. So the house of the LORD is built out of foreign wood cut by foreign hands — and Solomon offers the going rate, such wages as you set, rather than asking for a gift or naming his own price.

A foreigner gets it right (v. 7). He blesses the LORD by the covenant name, credits God rather than Solomon with the wisdom, and calls Israel this great people — better theology than a great many Israelites managed. And it should not be turned into a conversion: Tyre's gods were Baal and Astarte, kings of that world habitually acknowledged a neighbour's god as a courtesy, and two centuries later a princess of Sidon called Jezebel burns through the northern kingdom for three generations. What can be said is that this writer, who is merciless about Israelite kings, gives a foreigner an unqualified good line — a pattern the reader has met in Uriah, Ittai, Obed-edom and the Ammonite at Mahanaim, and will meet again in a widow at Zarephath and a Syrian general.

How the timber actually travelled (vv. 8-9). Felled in the mountains, dragged to the coast, lashed into rafts, floated down the Mediterranean to a landing point — Chronicles names Joppa (2 Chron. 2:16) — and hauled forty miles up to Jerusalem. Every beam in the house of God came that way. And Hiram's price is food, because Tyre was a trading city on a rocky coast with no farmland: what Israel had that Tyre needed was grain and oil, year by year, which is a standing annual obligation that the twelve districts of chapter 4 exist to meet. The oil is beaten — the best grade, crushed by hand, the quality specified for the sanctuary lamps (Ex. 27:20).

Where the writer puts the credit (v. 12). He has just described a shrewd trade agreement at market rates with the one supplier in the world who had what Israel needed, and his comment is the LORD gave Solomon wisdom, as he promised him. Not that Solomon negotiated well. And as he promised him is the historian checking the account against Gibeon.

The word for the levy (v. 13). Mas is a corvée — compulsory unpaid labour owed to the crown — and it is the word used of what Egypt imposed on Israel, where taskmasters afflicted them with heavy burdens (Ex. 1:11). The writer knows the vocabulary he is using. And the terms are humane for the age: one month away and two at home is a third of a man's time, not all of it, and a farmer could still get a crop in.

The tension with 9:22, named rather than smoothed. Four chapters on: but of the people of Israel Solomon made no slaves (9:22), with the permanent gangs drawn from the surviving Canaanite peoples. Here: forced labor out of all Israel. The usual reconciliation is probably right — two arrangements, the Canaanite one permanent and the Israelite one rotational and project-specific, with slightly different terms in the Hebrew. The distinction is genuine and legal, and it is the sort of distinction that looks much smaller from underneath: the men who came to Rehoboam did not say your father enslaved us, they said your father made our yoke heavy (12:4) — about a system its own records described as fair.

Hold both. The work is glorious: this is the house of God going up, and the men quarrying in the hill country are building the place where the ark will rest and where Israel will meet God for four centuries, and every one of them could tell his grandchildren what he had a hand in. And it is paid for by conscription on a scale the country had never seen, run by a department that did not exist under David, and the bill is presented to Solomon's son. The writer states the numbers and comments on none of it — the wedding to Egypt at 3:1, the forty thousand stalls at 4:26, the levy here — laying things down in sequence and trusting the reader to still be holding them in chapter 11.

The foundation gets the best stone (v. 17). Great, costly stones, for the part nobody would ever see. And the last verse lists three workforces, two of them foreign: Solomon's men, Hiram's men, and the men of Gebal, which is Byblos. The house of the LORD is quarried and dressed and rafted by Israelites and Phoenicians side by side, on a foreign king's timber, to a promise given to David, on ground bought from a Jebusite for fifty shekels of silver.
5.examples:
Then: Cedar was felled in the mountains of Lebanon by Phoenician woodcutters, dragged to the sea, lashed into rafts, floated down the coast, broken up on a beach and hauled forty miles inland — and paid for with twenty thousand measures of wheat and the finest hand-crushed oil, every year, for as long as the building took.

Now: Two things. Solomon's version of why his father was excluded is the honest one to sit with: it was true, it was kinder than the truth God had given, and it was told to somebody who was never going to check. Most of the half-accounts people give of their families are exactly that shape — not lies, just the version that reflects better, offered where the fuller one would cost something. And the second is the levy. Everything about that project was good; the thing being built was the house of God, and the arrangement was legal and by the standards of the age humane. And the people carrying it experienced it as a yoke, and said so the moment the man who imposed it was dead. It is possible to build something genuinely magnificent on terms the builders would not have chosen, and to find out what they thought only when it is too late to ask.

6.text: <sup>1</sup>In the four hundred and eightieth year after the people of Israel came out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon's reign over Israel, in the month of Ziv, which is the second month, he began to build the house of the LORD.<sup>2</sup>The house that King Solomon built for the LORD was sixty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high.<sup>3</sup>The vestibule in front of the nave of the house was twenty cubits long, equal to the width of the house, and ten cubits deep in front of the house.<sup>4</sup>And he made for the house windows with recessed frames.<sup>5</sup>He also built a structure against the wall of the house, running around the walls of the house, both the nave and the inner sanctuary. And he made side chambers all around.<sup>6</sup>The lowest story was five cubits broad, the middle one was six cubits broad, and the third was seven cubits broad. For around the outside of the house he made offsets on the wall in order that the supporting beams should not be inserted into the walls of the house.<sup>7</sup>When the house was built, it was with stone prepared at the quarry, so that neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron was heard in the house while it was being built.<sup>8</sup>The entrance for the lowest story was on the south side of the house, and one went up by stairs to the middle story, and from the middle story to the third.<sup>9</sup>So he built the house and finished it, and he made the ceiling of the house of beams and planks of cedar.<sup>10</sup>He built the structure against the whole house, five cubits high, and it was joined to the house with timbers of cedar.<sup>11</sup>Now the word of the LORD came to Solomon,<sup>12</sup>"Concerning this house that you are building, if you will walk in my statutes and obey my rules and keep all my commandments and walk in them, then I will establish my word with you, which I spoke to David your father.<sup>13</sup>And I will dwell among the children of Israel and will not forsake my people Israel."<sup>14</sup>So Solomon built the house and finished it.<sup>15</sup>He lined the walls of the house on the inside with boards of cedar. From the floor of the house to the walls of the ceiling, he covered them on the inside with wood, and he covered the floor of the house with boards of cypress.<sup>16</sup>He built twenty cubits of the rear of the house with boards of cedar from the floor to the walls, and he built this within as an inner sanctuary, as the Most Holy Place.<sup>17</sup>The house, that is, the nave in front of the inner sanctuary, was forty cubits long.<sup>18</sup>The cedar within the house was carved in the form of gourds and open flowers. All was cedar; no stone was seen.<sup>19</sup>The inner sanctuary he prepared in the innermost part of the house, to set there the ark of the covenant of the LORD.<sup>20</sup>The inner sanctuary was twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and twenty cubits high, and he overlaid it with pure gold. He also overlaid an altar of cedar.<sup>21</sup>And Solomon overlaid the inside of the house with pure gold, and he drew chains of gold across, in front of the inner sanctuary, and overlaid it with gold.<sup>22</sup>And he overlaid the whole house with gold, until all the house was finished. Also the whole altar that belonged to the inner sanctuary he overlaid with gold.<sup>23</sup>In the inner sanctuary he made two cherubim of olivewood, each ten cubits high.<sup>24</sup>Five cubits was the length of one wing of the cherub, and five cubits the length of the other wing of the cherub; it was ten cubits from the tip of one wing to the tip of the other.<sup>25</sup>The other cherub also measured ten cubits; both cherubim had the same measure and the same form.<sup>26</sup>The height of one cherub was ten cubits, and so was that of the other cherub.<sup>27</sup>He put the cherubim in the innermost part of the house. And the wings of the cherubim were spread out so that a wing of one touched the one wall, and a wing of the other cherub touched the other wall; their other wings touched each other in the middle of the house.<sup>28</sup>And he overlaid the cherubim with gold.<sup>29</sup>Around all the walls of the house he carved engraved figures of cherubim and palm trees and open flowers, in the inner and outer rooms.<sup>30</sup>The floor of the house he overlaid with gold in the inner and outer rooms.<sup>31</sup>For the entrance to the inner sanctuary he made doors of olivewood; the lintel and the doorposts were five-sided.<sup>32</sup>He covered the two doors of olivewood with carvings of cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers. He overlaid them with gold and spread gold on the cherubim and on the palm trees.<sup>33</sup>So also he made for the entrance to the nave doorposts of olivewood, in the form of a square,<sup>34</sup>and two doors of cypress wood. The two leaves of the one door were folding, and the two leaves of the other door were folding.<sup>35</sup>On them he carved cherubim and palm trees and open flowers, and he overlaid them with gold evenly applied on the carved work.<sup>36</sup>He built the inner court with three courses of cut stone and one course of cedar beams.<sup>37</sup>In the fourth year the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid, in the month of Ziv.<sup>38</sup>And in the eleventh year, in the month of Bul, which is the eighth month, the house was finished in all its parts, and according to all its specifications. He was seven years in building it.
6.overview:
The writer dates the temple from the exodus — in the four hundred and eightieth year after the people of Israel came out of the land of Egypt — and not from a dynasty or a foreign king's reign, which is how the ancient world usually fixed a date. Israel's calendar runs from the night God brought them out of a country where they were slaves, and the temple is a chapter in that story rather than the start of a new one.

The proportions are the tabernacle doubled — Moses' tent was thirty cubits by ten by fifteen, and this is exactly twice that in all three dimensions. So what goes up is not a new idea: it is the tent Israel carried through the wilderness, built in stone and cedar and gold, and no longer portable. And every stone was finished at the quarry so that neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron was heard in the house while it was being built. That is not efficiency. The noise and violence of manufacture are kept away from the place where God will be met.

And then, in the middle of a building specification, between the side chambers and the cedar panelling, the narrative stops and God speaks. The placement is the message. Concerning this house that you are building — and then four clauses, every one of them about conduct and not one about the house. There is no if you build it well. A man in the fourth year of a seven-year project, watching a magnificent thing rise that God himself asked for, is in real danger of thinking the building secures something. God says otherwise while the walls are still going up. Three centuries later Jeremiah had to stand in the gate of this same house and shout at people chanting the temple of the LORD as though the words were a charm.

Inside, no stone is seen — every surface lined and carved with cherubim, palm trees and open flowers. Guardians and growing things. It is Eden remembered in cedar and gold, and the last cherubim the reader met were standing at the gate of a garden with a flaming sword. Seven years to build it, and the very next verse in the book gives the figure for his own house.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — No Hammer or Axe Was Heard
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the four hundred and eightieth year after the people of Israel came out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon's reign over Israel... he began to build the house of the LORD (v. 1). It is sixty cubits long, twenty wide and thirty high, with a vestibule across the front and narrow windows and a three-storey side structure of chambers built against the walls but not into them (vv. 2-6, 8-10). And a note about the method: when the house was built, it was with stone prepared at the quarry, so that neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron was heard in the house while it was being built (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The date is given from the exodus, not from a dynasty or a foreign king's reign. Israel's calendar runs from the night God brought them out, and the temple is dated by it — which says what the building is for before a single dimension is given.
verseByVerse.examples: And every stone was finished at the quarry so that no iron tool would be heard on the site. That is not efficiency; it is reverence, and it is the same instinct as the law about altars — if you make me an altar of stone... you shall not build it of hewn stones, for if you wield your tool on it you profane it (Ex. 20:25). The noise of manufacture is kept away from the place where God will be met.

verseByVerse.quote: In the four hundred and eightieth year after the people of Israel came out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon's reign over Israel, in the month of Ziv, which is the second month, he began to build the house of the LORD. The house that King Solomon built for the LORD was sixty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high. The vestibule in front of the nave of the house was twenty cubits long, equal to the width of the house, and ten cubits deep in front of the house. And he made for the house windows with recessed frames. He also built a structure against the wall of the house, running around the walls of the house, both the nave and the inner sanctuary. And he made side chambers all around. The lowest story was five cubits broad, the middle one was six cubits broad, and the third was seven cubits broad. For around the outside of the house he made offsets on the wall in order that the supporting beams should not be inserted into the walls of the house. When the house was built, it was with stone prepared at the quarry, so that neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron was heard in the house while it was being built. The entrance for the lowest story was on the south side of the house, and one went up by stairs to the middle story, and from the middle story to the third. So he built the house and finished it, and he made the ceiling of the house of beams and planks of cedar. He built the structure against the whole house, five cubits high, and it was joined to the house with timbers of cedar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'In the four hundred and eightieth year after the people of Israel came out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon's reign over Israel, in the month of Ziv, which is the second month, he began to build the house of the LORD.'

Look at how the writer dates this.

He could have dated it from the founding of the monarchy, or from David's capture of Jerusalem, or by the reign of a Phoenician or Egyptian king, which is how the ancient world usually fixed a date.

He dates it from the exodus.

In the four hundred and eightieth year after the people of Israel came out of the land of Egypt. That is the only date of that kind in the historical books, and it is the chronological spine of the entire Old Testament narrative — the fixed point from which everything else can be measured.

And it says what the building is for before a single dimension is given. Israel's calendar runs from the night God brought them out of a country where they were slaves. The temple is a chapter in that story, not the start of a new one; the house being built is for the God who did that.

There is a second thing in the same verse. The month is named twice — Ziv, which is the second month — because Ziv is an old Canaanite month-name that had gone out of use, and the writer glosses it for readers who no longer knew it. That small editorial habit tells you this account was written down a long time after the event and from records.

'The house that King Solomon built for the LORD was sixty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high.'

Roughly ninety feet by thirty by forty-five.

By the standards of the great temples of Egypt and Mesopotamia that is not large. Anyone who came from Thebes or Babylon would have found it modest. It was never meant to hold a congregation; Israel worshipped in the courts, and the building itself was the dwelling.

And the proportions are not invented. Set them against the tabernacle: the tent Moses made was thirty cubits by ten by fifteen. This is exactly double, in all three dimensions.

So what is going up is not a new idea. It is the tent Israel carried through the wilderness for forty years and set up at Shiloh and lost the ark from at Aphek, rebuilt at twice the size, in stone and cedar and gold, and no longer portable.

That last change is the significant one, and God has something to say about it in chapter 7 of 2 Samuel and again in the middle of this chapter.

'The vestibule in front of the nave of the house was twenty cubits long, equal to the width of the house, and ten cubits deep in front of the house.'

'And he made for the house windows with recessed frames.'

Narrow windows, wider on the inside than the outside — which lets light in and keeps weather and eyes out.

'He also built a structure against the wall of the house, running around the walls of the house, both the nave and the inner sanctuary. And he made side chambers all around.'

'The lowest story was five cubits broad, the middle one was six cubits broad, and the third was seven cubits broad. For around the outside of the house he made offsets on the wall in order that the supporting beams should not be inserted into the walls of the house.'

And this is a detail worth slowing down for, because it is doing something.

Three storeys of chambers are built all round the outside of the temple — storerooms and service rooms. And the builders went to deliberate trouble to make sure that not one beam of those chambers was set into the wall of the house itself. Instead the temple wall was stepped, narrowing as it rose, so that each floor of the side structure could rest on a ledge.

Nothing is cut into the sanctuary wall. Nothing is fastened to it. The house of God carries no holes.

It would have been far easier to socket the beams straight in. They designed round it.

'When the house was built, it was with stone prepared at the quarry, so that neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron was heard in the house while it was being built.'

And here is the sentence everybody remembers from this chapter.

Every stone was cut, squared and finished at the quarry in the hill country, then carried to the site and set in place. The whole enormous structure went up in something close to silence — no ring of iron on stone anywhere on the mountain.

Consider the labour that involves. Every block had to be measured before it left the quarry, and a mistake could not be corrected on site. Eighty thousand stonecutters were working in the hills to make that possible.

Why go to that trouble?

The law gives the instinct. When God gave Israel the rule for altars at Sinai he said: if you make me an altar of stone, you shall not build it of hewn stones, for if you wield your tool on it you profane it (Ex. 20:25). Iron on the stone of an altar profanes it.

Whatever the full reason — and the law does not explain itself — the effect is that the noise and violence of manufacture are kept away from the place where God will be met. The work is done somewhere else. What arrives at the site is finished.

And Peter takes the picture up and does something with it that no reader of this chapter could have predicted. He tells scattered Christians: as you come to him, a living stone rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen and precious, you yourselves like living stones are being built up as a spiritual house (1 Pet. 2:4-5).

Each stone shaped somewhere else, out of sight, and brought to the place already fitted for where it goes. That is what is happening to people, and the cutting is not done on the site.
