'The entrance for the lowest story was on the south side of the house, and one went up by stairs to the middle story, and from the middle story to the third.'

'So he built the house and finished it, and he made the ceiling of the house of beams and planks of cedar.'

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–13 — Concerning This House That You Are Building
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the middle of the specification, the narrative stops: now the word of the LORD came to Solomon, "Concerning this house that you are building, if you will walk in my statutes and obey my rules and keep all my commandments and walk in them, then I will establish my word with you, which I spoke to David your father. And I will dwell among the children of Israel and will not forsake my people Israel" (vv. 11-13).
verseByVerse.theology: The placement is the message. God interrupts a building account — between the side-chambers and the panelling — to say that the house is not what secures anything. The if is about walking in his statutes, not about the quality of the stonework.
verseByVerse.examples: And the promise at the end is the thing the whole building exists for, and it is not about a structure: I will dwell among the children of Israel and will not forsake my people. Not in this house — among the people. The temple was always the sign of that and never the cause of it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the word of the LORD came to Solomon, "Concerning this house that you are building, if you will walk in my statutes and obey my rules and keep all my commandments and walk in them, then I will establish my word with you, which I spoke to David your father. And I will dwell among the children of Israel and will not forsake my people Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now the word of the LORD came to Solomon,'

Stop here, because of where this verse is.

The writer has been giving a building specification. Dimensions, a vestibule, recessed windows, three storeys of side chambers with the beams resting on ledges rather than sunk into the wall, a cedar ceiling. He is in the middle of describing a construction site.

And he breaks off, mid-account, to record that God spoke.

Nothing in the surrounding verses prepares for it and nothing follows from it structurally; the narrative goes straight back to cedar boards in verse 15. The three verses sit in the middle of the masonry like a hand laid on somebody's arm.

That placement is the message.

'"Concerning this house that you are building, if you will walk in my statutes and obey my rules and keep all my commandments and walk in them, then I will establish my word with you, which I spoke to David your father."'

Read the first four words. Concerning this house that you are building.

God begins by naming the very thing Solomon is standing in the middle of — the project that has consumed a hundred and fifty thousand men, the finest timber in the world, and the wealth of a kingdom — and then says something about it that has nothing to do with building.

If you will walk in my statutes and obey my rules and keep all my commandments and walk in them.

Four clauses, and every one of them is about conduct. Not one is about the house.

There is no if you build it well. No if the gold is pure and the cedar the best. No if the proportions are right. The condition attached to the greatest building project in Israel's history is entirely about whether the man building it keeps the commandments.

And what is promised on that condition is not a good building. It is I will establish my word with you, which I spoke to David your father — the covenant of 2 Samuel 7, the throne, the house that means a dynasty and not a temple.

Now think about the temptation this is guarding against, because it is the reason God says it here rather than at the dedication.

A man in the fourth year of a seven-year project, watching a magnificent thing rise out of the ground that God himself asked for, is in real danger of a particular confusion: that the building is the relationship. That God will be secured by it. That a house this good must guarantee something.

God says it in the middle of the scaffolding, before the roof is on. The house does not secure anything. Your obedience is what the promise runs through.

Israel forgot this comprehensively, and Jeremiah had to stand in the gate of this very building three centuries later and shout at people who were chanting the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD as though the words were a charm — and tell them to go and look at Shiloh, where God had made his name dwell at first, and see what he did to it (Jer. 7:4, 12).

The warning was given while the walls were still going up.

'"And I will dwell among the children of Israel and will not forsake my people Israel."'

And here is the promise, and it is the sentence the whole building exists to serve.

Read it exactly. I will dwell among the children of Israel.

Not I will dwell in this house. Among the people.

That is what God has been saying since Sinai: let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst (Ex. 25:8). The tabernacle was never a residence; it was a sign that God had come to live in the middle of a camp. The temple is the same sign in stone.

And I will not forsake my people Israel is the other half, and it is the promise that outlasts the building. The house that Solomon is standing in will be looted by Shishak within a generation, stripped by later kings to pay tribute, defiled, and finally burned to the ground by Nebuchadnezzar's men.

And God does not forsake his people. He goes into exile with them, and Ezekiel sees him there by a canal in Babylon.

The whole line runs out to a sentence in John's Gospel that uses the tabernacle word: and the Word became flesh and dwelt among us — literally, pitched his tent among us — and we have seen his glory (John 1:14). And out further still to a voice at the end of the Bible: behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people (Rev. 21:3).

God dwelling with people is the thing. Every building in between is a sign of it, and the signs get destroyed, and the thing does not.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–30 — The Inner Sanctuary He Overlaid with Pure Gold
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Solomon builds and finishes it (v. 14), lines the walls with cedar boards from floor to ceiling and the floor with cypress (v. 15), and partitions off twenty cubits at the rear for the Most Holy Place (v. 16). The cedar within the house was carved in the form of gourds and open flowers. All was cedar; no stone was seen (v. 18). The inner sanctuary is prepared for the ark of the covenant (v. 19), twenty cubits in length, width and height, overlaid with pure gold, with an altar of cedar (vv. 20-22). So he overlaid the whole house with gold, until all the house was finished (v. 22). Two cherubim of olivewood, ten cubits high, stand in the inner sanctuary with their wings touching wall to wall and each other in the middle (vv. 23-28). The walls all round are carved with cherubim and palm trees and open flowers, inside and out, and the floor is overlaid with gold (vv. 29-30).
verseByVerse.theology: The dimensions are the tabernacle at double scale — Moses' tent was thirty cubits by ten by fifteen, and this is sixty by twenty by thirty. It is the tent Israel carried through the wilderness, built in stone and cedar and gold, and standing still.
verseByVerse.examples: And the Most Holy Place is a perfect cube, twenty by twenty by twenty. The only other perfect cube in Scripture is the city at the end of the Bible: its length and width and height are equal (Rev. 21:16) — a city with no temple in it, because the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb are its temple.

verseByVerse.quote: So Solomon built the house and finished it. He lined the walls of the house on the inside with boards of cedar. From the floor of the house to the walls of the ceiling, he covered them on the inside with wood, and he covered the floor of the house with boards of cypress. He built twenty cubits of the rear of the house with boards of cedar from the floor to the walls, and he built this within as an inner sanctuary, as the Most Holy Place. The house, that is, the nave in front of the inner sanctuary, was forty cubits long. The cedar within the house was carved in the form of gourds and open flowers. All was cedar; no stone was seen. The inner sanctuary he prepared in the innermost part of the house, to set there the ark of the covenant of the LORD. The inner sanctuary was twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and twenty cubits high, and he overlaid it with pure gold. He also overlaid an altar of cedar. And Solomon overlaid the inside of the house with pure gold, and he drew chains of gold across, in front of the inner sanctuary, and overlaid it with gold. And he overlaid the whole house with gold, until all the house was finished. Also the whole altar that belonged to the inner sanctuary he overlaid with gold. In the inner sanctuary he made two cherubim of olivewood, each ten cubits high. Five cubits was the length of one wing of the cherub, and five cubits the length of the other wing of the cherub; it was ten cubits from the tip of one wing to the tip of the other. The other cherub also measured ten cubits; both cherubim had the same measure and the same form. The height of one cherub was ten cubits, and so was that of the other cherub. He put the cherubim in the innermost part of the house. And the wings of the cherubim were spread out so that a wing of one touched the one wall, and a wing of the other cherub touched the other wall; their other wings touched each other in the middle of the house. And he overlaid the cherubim with gold. Around all the walls of the house he carved engraved figures of cherubim and palm trees and open flowers, in the inner and outer rooms. The floor of the house he overlaid with gold in the inner and outer rooms.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So Solomon built the house and finished it.'

'He lined the walls of the house on the inside with boards of cedar. From the floor of the house to the walls of the ceiling, he covered them on the inside with wood, and he covered the floor of the house with boards of cypress.'

'He built twenty cubits of the rear of the house with boards of cedar from the floor to the walls, and he built this within as an inner sanctuary, as the Most Holy Place.'

The rear third of the building is partitioned off, and this is the room the whole structure exists for.

Nothing about it is designed to be seen. It has no windows. Nobody goes in except the high priest, once a year, on the Day of Atonement, with blood.

'The house, that is, the nave in front of the inner sanctuary, was forty cubits long.'

'The cedar within the house was carved in the form of gourds and open flowers. All was cedar; no stone was seen.'

No stone was seen.

The whole interior is lined so that not one inch of the masonry is visible. Every surface a person could look at is worked wood, carved with gourds and flowers.

Think about what that means for the eighty thousand men in the hill country. They cut and squared and finished those stones to a tolerance that allowed the building to go up without a hammer being heard, and then the stones were covered over and nobody ever saw them again.

The care was not for the audience. It was for the God who would be in the room.

'The inner sanctuary he prepared in the innermost part of the house, to set there the ark of the covenant of the LORD.'

And there is what all of this is for: a box.

The gold and the cedar and the seven years and the hundred and fifty thousand men are to make a room to put the ark in — the chest Moses had made in the wilderness, with the tablets of the covenant inside it and the mercy seat on top, and the two cherubim of hammered gold where God said there I will meet with you (Ex. 25:22).

The same chest the Philistines captured at Aphek. The same one that came home on a cart pulled by two cows. The one that stood in a private house at Kiriath-jearim for twenty years while nobody thought about it, and killed a man at a threshing floor, and blessed a Gittite's household for three months, and came into Jerusalem with a king dancing in front of it in a linen ephod.

It has been in a tent since David pitched one for it. Now it gets a room.

'The inner sanctuary was twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and twenty cubits high, and he overlaid it with pure gold. He also overlaid an altar of cedar.'

Twenty by twenty by twenty. A perfect cube.

That is deliberate, and there is only one other perfect cube in Scripture, and it is at the far end of the Bible. When John is shown the holy city coming down out of heaven, the angel measures it: the city lies foursquare, its length the same as its width... its length and width and height are equal (Rev. 21:16).

The New Jerusalem is shaped like the Most Holy Place. And the thing John notices about that city is what is missing from it: and I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb (Rev. 21:22).

The room where one man went once a year becomes the shape of a city where everybody lives.

'And Solomon overlaid the inside of the house with pure gold, and he drew chains of gold across, in front of the inner sanctuary, and overlaid it with gold.'

'And he overlaid the whole house with gold, until all the house was finished. Also the whole altar that belonged to the inner sanctuary he overlaid with gold.'

Gold over everything, and the writer says it three times in three verses because the accumulation is the effect.

'In the inner sanctuary he made two cherubim of olivewood, each ten cubits high.'

'Five cubits was the length of one wing of the cherub, and five cubits the length of the other wing of the cherub; it was ten cubits from the tip of one wing to the tip of the other.'

Two figures, fifteen feet high, with a fifteen-foot wingspan each.

'The other cherub also measured ten cubits; both cherubim had the same measure and the same form.'

'And he put the cherubim in the innermost part of the house. And the wings of the cherubim were spread out so that a wing of one touched the one wall, and a wing of the other cherub touched the other wall; their other wings touched each other in the middle of the house.'

Wall to wall. The four wings span the entire thirty feet of the room, meeting in the centre, over the place where the ark will stand.

Now think about where the reader has met cherubim before.

The first time is at the end of Genesis 3. A man and a woman are driven out of a garden, and God placed the cherubim and a flaming sword that turned every way to guard the way to the tree of life (Gen. 3:24). Cherubim are what stand between people and the presence of God, with a sword, to keep them out.

And here are two of them, fifteen feet high, standing over the exact place where God has promised to meet his people.

The guards are still there. The sword is not mentioned.

'And he overlaid the cherubim with gold.'

'Around all the walls of the house he carved engraved figures of cherubim and palm trees and open flowers, in the inner and outer rooms.'

And the same three things are carved on every surface of the building: cherubim, palm trees, open flowers.

Guardians and growing things.

Whoever designed this room wanted a person standing in it to be reminded of a garden with something watching over it. Palm trees and flowers in a stone box, and winged figures among them, forty feet underground in the imagination even though they are on a hilltop.

It is Eden, remembered in cedar and gold, in a building whose innermost room nobody may enter.

'The floor of the house he overlaid with gold in the inner and outer rooms.'

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Doors of olivewood for the inner sanctuary, carved with cherubim and palm trees and open flowers and overlaid with gold (vv. 31-32); doorposts and doors of cypress for the nave (vv. 33-35); and an inner court of three courses of cut stone and one of cedar beams (v. 36). In the fourth year the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid, in the month of Ziv. And in the eleventh year, in the month of Bul, which is the eighth month, the house was finished in all its parts, and according to all its specifications. He was seven years in building it (vv. 37-38).
verseByVerse.theology: The same three motifs run through every surface in the building: cherubim, palm trees and open flowers. Guardians, and growing things. Whoever designed this room wanted people standing in it to think of a garden with something watching over it.
verseByVerse.examples: He was seven years in building it. Hold that number for one verse, because the next chapter opens with the length of time he spent on his own house.

verseByVerse.quote: For the entrance to the inner sanctuary he made doors of olivewood; the lintel and the doorposts were five-sided. He covered the two doors of olivewood with carvings of cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers. He overlaid them with gold and spread gold on the cherubim and on the palm trees. So also he made for the entrance to the nave doorposts of olivewood, in the form of a square, and two doors of cypress wood. The two leaves of the one door were folding, and the two leaves of the other door were folding. On them he carved cherubim and palm trees and open flowers, and he overlaid them with gold evenly applied on the carved work. He built the inner court with three courses of cut stone and one course of cedar beams. In the fourth year the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid, in the month of Ziv. And in the eleventh year, in the month of Bul, which is the eighth month, the house was finished in all its parts, and according to all its specifications. He was seven years in building it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'For the entrance to the inner sanctuary he made doors of olivewood; the lintel and the doorposts were five-sided.'

'He covered the two doors of olivewood with carvings of cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers. He overlaid them with gold and spread gold on the cherubim and on the palm trees.'

The same three motifs again, this time on the doors of the Most Holy Place.

Olivewood for the doors and the cherubim inside, cedar for the walls, cypress for the floor and the outer doors. Every material in the building is a living thing that grew and was cut down.

'So also he made for the entrance to the nave doorposts of olivewood, in the form of a square, and two doors of cypress wood.'

'The two leaves of the one door were folding, and the two leaves of the other door were folding. On them he carved cherubim and palm trees and open flowers, and he overlaid them with gold evenly applied upon the carved work.'

'He built the inner court with three courses of cut stone and one course of cedar beams.'

'In the fourth year the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid, in the month of Ziv.'

'And in the eleventh year, in the month of Bul, which is the eighth month, the house was finished in all its parts, and according to all its specifications. He was seven years in building it.'

The last verse gives the figure, and it is the point of the whole chapter's ending.

He was seven years in building it.

Seven years, which in Hebrew is not merely a duration but a number that means completeness. The house of God took a full and finished span of time.

Note also according to all its specifications. The Hebrew is closer to according to all its plans, and Chronicles tells us where the plans came from: David gave Solomon the pattern for all of it — the porch, the houses, the treasuries, the courts, the chambers — and said, all this he made clear to me in writing from the hand of the LORD (1 Chron. 28:11-19). Which is what Moses was told about the tabernacle: see that you make them after the pattern for them, which is being shown you on the mountain (Ex. 25:40).

Solomon did not design this building. He built to a drawing.

And now hold the number seven for exactly one verse, because the next sentence in the book is this: Solomon was building his own house thirteen years, and he finished his entire house (7:1).

Seven years for the house of God. Thirteen for his own.

The writer sets them in consecutive verses, does not remark on the difference, and goes on to describe the palace at greater length than he described the temple.

He has been doing this since chapter 3, and by now a reader ought to be able to feel it coming.

6.theology:
Dated from the exodus (v. 1). The only date of its kind in the historical books, and the chronological spine of the Old Testament narrative. It says what the building is for before a dimension is given: the house is for the God who brought slaves out of Egypt. Note too that the month is glossed — Ziv, which is the second month — because the old Canaanite name had gone out of use, which tells you this account was written from records a long time afterwards.

The tabernacle at double scale (v. 2). Thirty by ten by fifteen becomes sixty by twenty by thirty. Not large by the standards of Thebes or Babylon, and never meant to hold a congregation — Israel worshipped in the courts and the building was the dwelling. What has changed is that it no longer moves, and God has something to say about that in 2 Samuel 7 and again in the middle of this chapter.

Nothing cut into the sanctuary wall (v. 6). Three storeys of chambers all round the outside, and the builders took deliberate trouble to ensure no beam was set into the temple wall itself: the wall was stepped, narrowing as it rose, so each floor could rest on a ledge. It would have been far easier to socket the beams straight in. They designed round it. The house of God carries no holes.

Silence on the mountain (v. 7). Every block measured, cut and finished at the quarry, where a mistake could not be corrected on site — which is what eighty thousand stonecutters in the hill country were for. The instinct is the law's: if you make me an altar of stone, you shall not build it of hewn stones, for if you wield your tool on it you profane it (Ex. 20:25). And Peter takes the picture somewhere no reader of this chapter could have predicted: you yourselves like living stones are being built up as a spiritual house (1 Pet. 2:4-5). Each stone shaped somewhere else, out of sight, and brought to the site already fitted for its place. The cutting is not done on the site.

Where God interrupts (vv. 11-13). Mid-specification, with nothing before it to prepare for it and nothing structurally following — the narrative goes straight back to cedar boards. Three verses laid in the middle of the masonry like a hand on somebody's arm. And concerning this house that you are building names the very project consuming a hundred and fifty thousand men and the wealth of a kingdom, and then says something about it that has nothing to do with building.

Four clauses, none about the house (v. 12). Walk in my statutes, obey my rules, keep all my commandments, walk in them. No if you build it well, no if the gold is pure. And what is promised on that condition is not a good building but my word... which I spoke to David your father — the covenant of 2 Samuel 7. This is guarding against a specific confusion: that the building is the relationship, that God is secured by it, that a house this good must guarantee something. Israel forgot it comprehensively, and Jeremiah stood in the gate of this building shouting at people who chanted the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD as a charm, and told them to go and look at Shiloh (Jer. 7:4, 12).

Among, not in (v. 13). I will dwell among the children of Israel — not in this house. That is what God has said since Sinai: let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst (Ex. 25:8). The tabernacle was never a residence but a sign that God had come to live in the middle of a camp, and the temple is the same sign in stone. And I will not forsake my people Israel outlasts the building: this house is looted by Shishak within a generation, stripped by later kings for tribute, and finally burned by Nebuchadnezzar's men — and God goes into exile with his people, and Ezekiel sees him there by a canal in Babylon. The line runs out to John's tabernacle word, the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14), and to behold, the dwelling place of God is with man (Rev. 21:3). God dwelling with people is the thing; every building between is a sign, the signs get destroyed, and the thing does not.

No stone was seen (v. 18). Every inch of masonry lined over, so that stones finished to a tolerance that let the building rise without a hammer being heard were covered and never looked at again. The care was not for an audience. It was for the God who would be in the room.

All of it for a box (v. 19). The gold, the cedar, the seven years and the hundred and fifty thousand men are to make a room for the ark — the chest Moses made in the wilderness, with the tablets inside and the mercy seat on top, where God said there I will meet with you (Ex. 25:22). The same chest the Philistines captured at Aphek, that came home on a cart pulled by two cows, that stood in a private house for twenty years while nobody thought about it, that killed a man at a threshing floor and blessed a Gittite's household for three months, and came into Jerusalem with a king dancing in front of it in a linen ephod.

A perfect cube (v. 20). Twenty by twenty by twenty, and the only other one in Scripture is at the far end of the Bible: its length and width and height are equal (Rev. 21:16). The New Jerusalem is shaped like the Most Holy Place — and what John notices about that city is what is missing: I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb (Rev. 21:22). The room one man entered once a year becomes the shape of a city where everybody lives.

The guards are still there (vv. 23-27). Two figures fifteen feet high, wings spanning the room wall to wall and meeting over the place where the ark will stand. The reader last met cherubim at the end of Genesis 3, where God placed the cherubim and a flaming sword that turned every way to guard the way to the tree of life (Gen. 3:24) — what stands between people and God's presence, with a sword, to keep them out. Here they stand over the exact place where God has promised to meet his people, and the sword is not mentioned.

Eden in cedar and gold (v. 29). The same three motifs on every surface of the building and on both sets of doors: cherubim, palm trees, open flowers. Guardians and growing things. Whoever designed this room wanted a person standing in it to think of a garden with something watching over it. And every material in the place — olivewood, cedar, cypress — is a living thing that grew and was cut down.

He built to a drawing (v. 38). According to all its specifications is nearer according to all its plans, and Chronicles says where they came from: David gave Solomon the pattern for everything and said all this he made clear to me in writing from the hand of the LORD (1 Chron. 28:11-19) — which is what Moses was told about the tabernacle (Ex. 25:40). Solomon did not design this building.

Seven years, and hold the number. A full and finished span. And the very next sentence in the book is Solomon was building his own house thirteen years (7:1). The writer sets them in consecutive verses, remarks on nothing, and then describes the palace at greater length than he described the temple.
6.examples:
Then: A building the size of a large barn went up on a hilltop over seven years without one blow of an iron tool being heard on the site — every stone measured, cut and finished miles away in the hill country and carried up already fitted — and when it was done, every one of those stones was panelled over in cedar so that nobody ever saw them again.

Now: Three things. God's interruption in verses 11-13 is the one to carry, because the confusion it guards against is permanent: the condition attached to the greatest building project in Israel's history had nothing whatever to do with the building. It is very easy to mistake the thing you are doing for God for your standing with God, and the more magnificent the thing, the easier it gets. Second, the covered stones. Work done to a standard nobody will ever inspect, for an audience of one, is not wasted — it is most of what the Christian life actually consists of. And third, Peter's use of the quarry: the shaping happens off-site, out of sight, before the stone is set in place. If your life feels like being worked on in a noisy place a long way from anything that looks finished, that is where the cutting is supposed to happen.

7.text: <sup>1</sup>Solomon was building his own house thirteen years, and he finished his entire house.<sup>2</sup>He built the House of the Forest of Lebanon. Its length was a hundred cubits and its breadth fifty cubits and its height thirty cubits, and it was built on four rows of cedar pillars, with cedar beams on the pillars.<sup>3</sup>And it was covered with cedar above the chambers that were on the forty-five pillars, fifteen in each row.<sup>4</sup>There were window frames in three rows, and window opposite window in three tiers.<sup>5</sup>All the doorways and windows had square frames, and window was opposite window in three tiers.<sup>6</sup>And he made the Hall of Pillars; its length was fifty cubits, and its breadth thirty cubits. There was a porch in front with pillars, and a canopy in front of them.<sup>7</sup>And he made the Hall of the Throne where he was to pronounce judgment, even the Hall of Judgment. It was finished with cedar from floor to rafters.<sup>8</sup>His own house where he was to dwell, in the other court at the back of the hall, was of like workmanship. Solomon also made a house like this hall for Pharaoh's daughter whom he had taken in marriage.<sup>9</sup>All these were made of costly stones, cut according to measure, sawed with saws, back and front, even from the foundation to the coping, and from the outside to the great court.<sup>10</sup>The foundation was of costly stones, huge stones, stones of eight and ten cubits.<sup>11</sup>And above were costly stones, cut according to measurement, and cedar.<sup>12</sup>The great court had three courses of cut stone all around, and a course of cedar beams; so had the inner court of the house of the LORD and the vestibule of the house.<sup>13</sup>And King Solomon sent and brought Hiram from Tyre.<sup>14</sup>He was the son of a widow of the tribe of Naphtali, and his father was a man of Tyre, a worker in bronze. And he was full of wisdom, understanding, and skill for making any work in bronze. He came to King Solomon and did all his work.<sup>15</sup>He cast two pillars of bronze. Eighteen cubits was the height of one pillar, and a line of twelve cubits measured its circumference. It was hollow, and its thickness was four fingers. The second pillar was the same.<sup>16</sup>He also made two capitals of cast bronze to set on the tops of the pillars. The height of the one capital was five cubits, and the height of the other capital was five cubits.<sup>17</sup>There were lattices of checker work with wreaths of chain work for the capitals on the tops of the pillars, a lattice for the one capital and a lattice for the other capital.<sup>18</sup>Likewise he made pomegranates in two rows around the one latticework to cover the capital that was on the top of the pillar, and he did the same with the other capital.<sup>19</sup>Now the capitals that were on the tops of the pillars in the vestibule were of lily-work, four cubits.<sup>20</sup>The capitals were on the two pillars and also above the rounded projection which was beside the latticework. There were two hundred pomegranates in two rows all around, and so with the other capital.<sup>21</sup>He set up the pillars at the vestibule of the temple. He set up the pillar on the south and called its name Jachin, and he set up the pillar on the north and called its name Boaz.<sup>22</sup>And on the tops of the pillars was lily-work. Thus the work of the pillars was finished.<sup>23</sup>Then he made the sea of cast metal. It was round, ten cubits from brim to brim, and five cubits high, and a line of thirty cubits measured its circumference.<sup>24</sup>Under its brim were gourds, for ten cubits, compassing the sea all around. The gourds were in two rows, cast with it when it was cast.<sup>25</sup>It stood on twelve oxen, three facing north, three facing west, three facing south, and three facing east. The sea was set on them, and all their rear parts were inward.<sup>26</sup>Its thickness was a handbreadth, and its brim was made like the brim of a cup, like the flower of a lily. It held two thousand baths.<sup>27</sup>He also made the ten stands of bronze. Each stand was four cubits long, four cubits wide, and three cubits high.<sup>28</sup>This was the construction of the stands: they had panels, and the panels were set in the frames,<sup>29</sup>and on the panels that were set in the frames were lions, oxen, and cherubim. On the frames, both above and below the lions and oxen, there were wreaths of beveled work.<sup>30</sup>Moreover, each stand had four bronze wheels and axles of bronze, and at the four corners were supports for a basin. The supports were cast with wreaths at the side of each.<sup>31</sup>Its opening was within a crown that projected upward one cubit. Its opening was round, as a pedestal is made, a cubit and a half deep. At its opening there were carvings, and its panels were square, not round.<sup>32</sup>And the four wheels were underneath the panels. The axles of the wheels were of one piece with the stands, and the height of a wheel was a cubit and a half.<sup>33</sup>The wheels were made like a chariot wheel; their axles, their rims, their spokes, and their hubs were all cast.<sup>34</sup>There were four supports at the four corners of each stand. The supports were of one piece with the stands.<sup>35</sup>And on the top of the stand there was a round band half a cubit high; and on the top of the stand its stays and its panels were of one piece with it.<sup>36</sup>And on the surfaces of its stays and on its panels, he carved cherubim, lions, and palm trees, according to the space of each, with wreaths all around.<sup>37</sup>After this manner he made the ten stands. All of them were cast alike, of the same measure and the same form.<sup>38</sup>And he made ten basins of bronze. Each basin held forty baths, each basin measured four cubits, and there was a basin for each of the ten stands.<sup>39</sup>And he set the stands, five on the south side of the house, and five on the north side of the house. And he set the sea at the southeast corner of the house.<sup>40</sup>Hiram also made the pots, the shovels, and the basins. So Hiram finished all the work that he did for King Solomon on the house of the LORD:<sup>41</sup>the two pillars, the two bowls of the capitals that were on the tops of the pillars, and the two latticeworks to cover the two bowls of the capitals that were on the tops of the pillars;<sup>42</sup>and the four hundred pomegranates for the two latticeworks, two rows of pomegranates for each latticework, to cover the two bowls of the capitals that were on the pillars;<sup>43</sup>the ten stands, and the ten basins on the stands;<sup>44</sup>and the one sea, and the twelve oxen underneath the sea.<sup>45</sup>Now the pots, the shovels, and the basins, all these vessels in the house of the LORD, which Hiram made for King Solomon, were of burnished bronze.<sup>46</sup>In the plain of the Jordan the king cast them, in the clay ground between Succoth and Zarethan.<sup>47</sup>And Solomon left all the vessels unweighed, because there were so many of them; the weight of the bronze was not ascertained.<sup>48</sup>So Solomon made all the vessels that were in the house of the LORD: the golden altar, the golden table for the bread of the Presence,<sup>49</sup>the lampstands of pure gold, five on the south side and five on the north, before the inner sanctuary; the flowers, the lamps, and the tongs, of gold;<sup>50</sup>the cups, snuffers, basins, dishes for incense, and fire pans, of pure gold; and the sockets of gold, for the doors of the innermost part of the house, the Most Holy Place, and for the doors of the nave of the temple.<sup>51</sup>Thus all the work that King Solomon did on the house of the LORD was finished. And Solomon brought in the things that David his father had dedicated, the silver, the gold, and the vessels, and stored them in the treasuries of the house of the LORD.
7.overview:
The previous sentence in the book was he was seven years in building it, about the house of the LORD. This one is thirteen, about his own. The writer sets the two figures in consecutive verses, with no chapter break in the Hebrew and no comment of any kind — and then describes the palace complex at greater length and in more admiring detail than he described the temple.

Things can be said in mitigation, and should be. The complex is several buildings — an armoury, a colonnade, a courtroom, two residences — where the temple is one modest structure, and the projects overlap. Nobody in Israel would have thought thirteen years unreasonable. And the figures are still seven and thirteen, and the writer still put them next to each other.

One room in the palace deserves a moment: the Hall of the Throne where he was to pronounce judgment. The man who asked for a hearing heart has built a courtroom, panelled in cedar from floor to rafters. It is right that a king who takes justice seriously should have somewhere proper to hear cases — and a hall is not a hearing. What Absalom found at the gate a generation earlier was not a shortage of buildings.

Then the bronze, cast by a widow's son from Naphtali with a Tyrian father, described in the exact words used of Bezalel, whom God filled with his Spirit to build the tabernacle. And two pillars at the door, twenty-seven feet high, free-standing and holding nothing up, whose entire function is to say a sentence to everyone who walks between them: Jachin, he shall establish; Boaz, in him is strength.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Solomon was building his own house thirteen years, and he finished his entire house (v. 1). The House of the Forest of Lebanon is a hundred cubits by fifty by thirty, on four rows of cedar pillars (vv. 2-5); then a Hall of Pillars, and a Hall of the Throne where he was to pronounce judgment, even the Hall of Judgment (vv. 6-7); then his own dwelling in another court, and he made a house like this hall for Pharaoh's daughter whom he had taken as his wife (v. 8). All of it is costly stone, sawn to measure inside and out, from the foundation to the coping and from the outside to the great court (vv. 9-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Seven years for the house of the LORD; thirteen for his own. The writer puts the two figures in consecutive sentences and does not remark on the difference — and then describes the palace complex at greater length than he described the temple.
verseByVerse.examples: And the daughter of Pharaoh gets a house of her own, named as such. She entered the story in 3:1, before Gibeon and before the temple; she is named first in the list of the women who turn his heart in 11:1. The writer keeps mentioning her and never comments.

verseByVerse.quote: Solomon was building his own house thirteen years, and he finished his entire house. He built the House of the Forest of Lebanon. Its length was a hundred cubits and its breadth fifty cubits and its height thirty cubits, and it was built on four rows of cedar pillars, with cedar beams on the pillars. And it was covered with cedar above the chambers that were on the forty-five pillars, fifteen in each row. There were window frames in three rows, and window opposite window in three tiers. All the doorways and windows had square frames, and window was opposite window in three tiers. And he made the Hall of Pillars; its length was fifty cubits, and its breadth thirty cubits. There was a porch in front with pillars, and a canopy in front of them. And he made the Hall of the Throne where he was to pronounce judgment, even the Hall of Judgment. It was finished with cedar from floor to rafters. His own house where he was to dwell, in the other court at the back of the hall, was of like workmanship. Solomon also made a house like this hall for Pharaoh's daughter whom he had taken in marriage. All these were made of costly stones, cut according to measure, sawed with saws, back and front, even from the foundation to the coping, and from the outside to the great court. The foundation was of costly stones, huge stones, stones of eight and ten cubits. And above were costly stones, cut according to measurement, and cedar. The great court had three courses of cut stone all around, and a course of cedar beams; so had the inner court of the house of the LORD and the vestibule of the house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Solomon was building his own house thirteen years, and he finished his entire house.'

The previous sentence in the book was he was seven years in building it, about the house of the LORD.

This one is thirteen.

The writer sets the two figures in consecutive verses, with no chapter break in the Hebrew and no comment of any kind. He does not say it was too long. He does not say Solomon loved his own comfort. He gives a seven and then a thirteen and moves on to the specifications.

Then he does something else, which is harder to miss the more carefully you read. He describes the palace complex at greater length and in more admiring detail than he described the temple.

Some things can fairly be said in mitigation. The palace complex is much bigger — it is several buildings, including an armoury, a colonnade, a courtroom, a residence and a second residence — where the temple is one modest structure. And the two projects overlap; the twenty years of 9:10 covers both. Nobody in Israel would have thought thirteen years unreasonable for a royal quarter.

The figures are still seven and thirteen, and the writer still put them next to each other.

'He built the House of the Forest of Lebanon. Its length was a hundred cubits and its breadth fifty cubits and its height thirty cubits, and it was built on four rows of cedar pillars, with cedar beams on the pillars.'

A hundred and fifty feet by seventy-five by forty-five, which makes it more than four times the floor area of the temple.

It is called the House of the Forest of Lebanon because of the forty-five cedar pillars standing in rows inside it — a man walking through it was walking through trees. Chapter 10 tells us what it was for: three hundred shields of beaten gold were kept there (10:17). It is an armoury and a treasury and a very large statement.

'And it was covered with cedar above the chambers that were on the forty-five pillars, fifteen in each row.'

'There were window frames in three rows, and window opposite window in three tiers.'

'All the doorways and windows had square frames, and window was opposite window in three tiers.'

'And he made the Hall of Pillars; its length was fifty cubits, and its breadth thirty cubits. There was a porch in front with pillars, and a canopy in front of them.'

'And he made the Hall of the Throne where he was to pronounce judgment, even the Hall of Judgment. It was finished with cedar from floor to rafters.'

One room in this complex deserves a moment.

The Hall of the Throne where he was to pronounce judgment, even the Hall of Judgment.

A purpose-built courtroom. The man who asked at Gibeon for a hearing heart to govern your people, that I may discern between good and evil has built a room for doing it in, panelled in cedar from floor to rafters.

And there is something to be held on both sides of that. It is right that a king who takes justice seriously should have somewhere proper to hear cases; that is 2 Samuel 8:15 given an address.

And a hall is not a hearing. Two prostitutes with no standing walked in front of this man in chapter 3 and got a verdict. What Absalom found at the gate a generation earlier was not a shortage of buildings; it was that there is no man designated by the king to hear you (2 Sam. 15:3).

The room is not the thing. It is the same point God made in the middle of the temple site one chapter ago.

'His own house where he was to dwell, in the other court back of the hall, was of like workmanship. Solomon also made a house like this hall for Pharaoh's daughter whom he had taken as his wife.'

There she is again.

She arrived in 3:1, in the first sentence of the reign after the executions, before Gibeon and before the temple. She gets a house of her own here, built to the same standard as the Hall of Judgment. Chapter 9 records that Solomon moved her out of the city of David, on the grounds that the places where the ark of the LORD has come are holy (9:24).

And chapter 11 opens: now King Solomon loved many foreign women, along with the daughter of Pharaoh (11:1).

Four mentions across nine chapters, each one flat and factual, and no comment attached to any of them. The writer is doing what he has done since the first chapter: putting things down in order and trusting the reader to be holding them when the account comes due.

'All these were made of costly stones, cut according to measure, sawed with saws, back and front, even from the foundation to the coping, and from the outside to the great court.'

'The foundation was of costly stones, huge stones, stones of eight and ten cubits.'

'And above were costly stones, cut according to measurement, and cedar.'

'The great court had three courses of cut stone all around, and a course of cedar beams; so had the inner court of the house of the LORD and the vestibule of the house.'

The last verse of the section is the one that quietly joins the two building projects together.

The great court of the palace is built to the same specification as the inner court of the temple: three courses of cut stone and a course of cedar beams. Same materials, same method, same pattern.

The house of God and the house of the king are going up on the same hill, out of the same quarry, by the same workforce, to the same standard.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–22 — He Shall Establish; In Him Is Strength
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Solomon sends for Hiram from Tyre — the son of a widow of the tribe of Naphtali, and his father was a man of Tyre, a worker in bronze. And he was full of wisdom, understanding, and skill for making any work in bronze (vv. 13-14). He casts two bronze pillars, eighteen cubits high and twelve in circumference, hollow, with capitals of five cubits and nets of checker work and two rows of pomegranates each (vv. 15-20). He set up the pillars at the vestibule of the temple. He set up the pillar on the south and called its name Jachin, and he set up the pillar on the north and called its name Boaz (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: The craftsman is half-Israelite — a widow's son from Naphtali by a Tyrian father — and the description of him is the description of Bezalel, whom God filled with his Spirit with ability and intelligence, with knowledge and all craftsmanship to build the tabernacle (Ex. 31:1-5). Skill in metal is treated by Scripture as a gift of God, twice, by name.
verseByVerse.examples: And the two pillars are a sentence. Jachin means he shall establish; Boaz means something like in him is strength. They stand at the door, twenty-seven feet high, free of the building — they hold nothing up. Their whole function is to say something as a person walks in.

verseByVerse.quote: And King Solomon sent and brought Hiram from Tyre. He was the son of a widow of the tribe of Naphtali, and his father was a man of Tyre, a worker in bronze. And he was full of wisdom, understanding, and skill for making any work in bronze. He came to King Solomon and did all his work. He cast two pillars of bronze. Eighteen cubits was the height of one pillar, and a line of twelve cubits measured its circumference. It was hollow, and its thickness was four fingers. The second pillar was the same. He also made two capitals of cast bronze to set on the tops of the pillars. The height of the one capital was five cubits, and the height of the other capital was five cubits. There were lattices of checker work with wreaths of chain work for the capitals on the tops of the pillars, a lattice for the one capital and a lattice for the other capital. Likewise he made pomegranates in two rows around the one latticework to cover the capital that was on the top of the pillar, and he did the same with the other capital. Now the capitals that were on the tops of the pillars in the vestibule were of lily-work, four cubits. The capitals were on the two pillars and also above the rounded projection which was beside the latticework. There were two hundred pomegranates in two rows all around, and so with the other capital. He set up the pillars at the vestibule of the temple. He set up the pillar on the south and called its name Jachin, and he set up the pillar on the north and called its name Boaz. And on the tops of the pillars was lily-work. Thus the work of the pillars was finished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And King Solomon sent and brought Hiram from Tyre.'

This is a different man from the king of the same name, and the writer immediately tells us who he is.

'He was the son of a widow of the tribe of Naphtali, and his father was a man of Tyre, a worker in bronze. And he was full of wisdom, understanding, and skill for making any work in bronze. He came to King Solomon and did all his work.'

Take the description apart, because there is a great deal in one verse.

He is the son of a widow of the tribe of Naphtali. His mother was an Israelite from a northern tribe, and she is a widow, and her son is the finest bronze-worker in the region. His father was a Tyrian.

So the man who casts every piece of bronze in the house of the LORD is half a foreigner, brought in from a Phoenician port, and the son of a woman with no husband.

The book keeps doing this. The timber is foreign, the stonemasons of Gebal are foreign, and now the metalwork.

Then the phrase a reader of the Pentateuch will recognise instantly: he was full of wisdom, understanding, and skill.

Go back to Exodus. God is giving Moses the instructions for the tabernacle, and he names the man who will make it: see, I have called by name Bezalel the son of Uri... and I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with ability and intelligence, with knowledge and all craftsmanship, to devise artistic designs, to work in gold, silver, and bronze (Ex. 31:2-4).

The same three words, in the same order, of the same kind of work.

That correspondence is deliberate, and it says something Scripture says in very few places and means every time. Skill in a craft is a gift of God. Not a natural talent that God happens to tolerate, and not a lesser thing than teaching or prophesying — the ability to make a beautiful object out of metal is listed in Exodus as a filling of the Spirit of God, and the only two men in the Bible described this way are both metalworkers.

A widow's son from Naphtali, who learned his trade in a Phoenician foundry, is filled with wisdom and understanding and skill, and he casts the pillars of the house of God.

'He cast two pillars of bronze. Eighteen cubits was the height of one pillar, and a line of twelve cubits measured its circumference. It was hollow, and its thickness was four fingers.'

Twenty-seven feet high and about six feet across, hollow, with walls three inches thick.

Casting an object that size in bronze in the tenth century before Christ is a serious technical achievement, and verse 46 tells us where it was done: out in the Jordan valley, in the clay ground, where there was earth suitable for the moulds.

'He also made two capitals of cast bronze to set on the tops of the pillars. The height of the one capital was five cubits, and the height of the other capital was five cubits.'

'There were lattice works of checker work with wreaths of chain work for the capitals on the tops of the pillars, a lattice work for the one capital and a lattice work for the other capital.'

'Likewise he made pomegranates in two rows around the one latticework to cover the capital that was on the top of the pillar, and he did the same with the other capital.'

'Now the capitals that were on the tops of the pillars in the vestibule were of lily-work, four cubits.'

Lilies and pomegranates, seven and a half feet of them on the top of each pillar.

The temple interior was carved with palm trees and open flowers, and the great bronze basin has lilies at the brim, and here are pomegranates and lily-work in cast metal. Everything decorative in this building is a growing thing.

'Then he set up the pillars at the vestibule of the temple. He set up the pillar on the south and called its name Jachin, and he set up the pillar on the north and called its name Boaz.'

Here is the thing to carry out of this chapter.

The two pillars have names, and the names are a sentence.

Jachin means he shall establish. Boaz is harder, and the most widely accepted sense is in him is strength.

Read them together and you get the confession of the whole building: he shall establish; in him is strength.

Not Solomon shall establish. Not in this house is strength. He, and him.

Now the detail that makes it: the pillars are free-standing.

They are not part of the structure. They hold up no roof and support no beam; they stand in front of the vestibule, one either side of the door, carrying nothing at all.

Which means their entire function is to say something. Every priest going in to serve, and every Israelite coming up to the courts, walked between two enormous bronze columns whose only purpose was to declare that God establishes and that strength belongs to him.

Two hundred years later a king of Judah will strip the gold off the doors of this house to pay tribute to Assyria. Three hundred years after that, when Nebuchadnezzar's men come, the writer of Kings records what they did with these pillars: and the pillars of bronze that were in the house of the LORD... the Chaldeans broke in pieces and carried the bronze to Babylon (2 Kings 25:13).

They broke up he shall establish and carried it away in pieces.

The sentence was still true, which is what the rest of the Old Testament is about.

'And on the tops of the pillars was lily-work. Thus the work of the pillars was finished.'

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–39 — The Sea of Cast Metal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then he made the sea of cast metal. It was round, ten cubits from brim to brim, and five cubits high, and a line of thirty cubits measured its circumference (v. 23), with gourds beneath the brim (v. 24). It stood on twelve oxen, three facing north, three facing west, three facing south, and three facing east. The sea was set on them, and all their rear parts were inward (v. 25). Its brim was like the brim of a cup, like the flower of a lily, and it held two thousand baths (v. 26). Then ten bronze stands on wheels, with panels of lions, oxen and cherubim (vv. 27-37), and ten basins on them, five on the south side of the house and five on the north, with the sea on the south-east corner (vv. 38-39).
verseByVerse.theology: The sea is the laver of the tabernacle at enormous scale — the basin between the tent and the altar where Aaron and his sons washed their hands and feet lest they die (Ex. 30:18-21). Chronicles says plainly what this one was for: the sea was for the priests to wash in (2 Chron. 4:6).
verseByVerse.examples: Twelve oxen carry it, three to each point of the compass, with their backs to the centre. Twelve is the number of the tribes, and the four directions are the whole earth, and the thing they are holding up is water for washing.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he made the sea of cast metal. It was round, ten cubits from brim to brim, and five cubits high, and a line of thirty cubits measured its circumference. Under its brim were gourds, for ten cubits, compassing the sea all around. The gourds were in two rows, cast with it when it was cast. It stood on twelve oxen, three facing north, three facing west, three facing south, and three facing east. The sea was set on them, and all their rear parts were inward. Its thickness was a handbreadth, and its brim was made like the brim of a cup, like the flower of a lily. It held two thousand baths. He also made the ten stands of bronze. Each stand was four cubits long, four cubits wide, and three cubits high. This was the construction of the stands: they had panels, and the panels were set in the frames, and on the panels that were set in the frames were lions, oxen, and cherubim. On the frames, both above and below the lions and oxen, there were wreaths of beveled work. Moreover, each stand had four bronze wheels and axles of bronze, and at the four corners were supports for a basin. The supports were cast with wreaths at the side of each. Its opening was within a crown that projected upward one cubit. Its opening was round, as a pedestal is made, a cubit and a half deep. At its opening there were carvings, and its panels were square, not round. And the four wheels were underneath the panels. The axles of the wheels were of one piece with the stands, and the height of a wheel was a cubit and a half. The wheels were made like a chariot wheel; their axles, their rims, their spokes, and their hubs were all cast. There were four supports at the four corners of each stand. The supports were of one piece with the stands. And on the top of the stand there was a round band half a cubit high; and on the top of the stand its stays and its panels were of one piece with it. And on the surfaces of its stays and on its panels, he carved cherubim, lions, and palm trees, according to the space of each, with wreaths all around. After this manner he made the ten stands. All of them were cast alike, of the same measure and the same form. And he made ten basins of bronze. Each basin held forty baths, each basin measured four cubits, and there was a basin for each of the ten stands. And he set the stands, five on the south side of the house, and five on the north side of the house. And he set the sea at the southeast corner of the house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then he made the sea of cast metal. It was round, ten cubits from brim to brim, and five cubits high, and a line of thirty cubits measured its circumference.'

A bronze basin fifteen feet across and seven and a half feet deep, cast in one piece.

It is called the sea, which is not a technical term but a description of the impression it made. Nobody had seen that much standing water in a vessel.

(The measurements have generated a good deal of unnecessary argument about the ratio of circumference to diameter. The figures are round numbers to the nearest cubit in an account describing a physical object, and the brim was like the flower of a lily, so it flared. There is nothing here that needs defending.)

'Under its brim were gourds, for ten cubits, compassing the sea all around. The gourds were in two rows, cast with it when it was cast.'

'It stood on twelve oxen, three facing north, three facing west, three facing south, and three facing east. The sea was set on them, and all their rear parts were inward.'

Twelve bronze oxen carrying it, in four groups of three, facing outward to the four points of the compass.

Twelve is the tribes. The four directions are the whole earth. And what the twelve are holding up, facing outward toward everything, is a great mass of water for washing.

'Its thickness was a handbreadth, and its brim was made like the brim of a cup, like the flower of a lily. It held two thousand baths.'

Something in the order of ten thousand gallons.

Chronicles tells us what it was for, plainly: the sea was for the priests to wash in (2 Chron. 4:6).

Which sends the reader back to Exodus, and to a small basin and a hard sentence. God told Moses to make a bronze laver and set it between the tent of meeting and the altar and put water in it, with which Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands and their feet. When they go into the tent of meeting, or when they come near the altar to minister... they shall wash with water, so that they may not die (Ex. 30:18-21).

So that they may not die.

A man who is going to handle holy things does not simply walk up. He washes first, and the law attaches the penalty in as many words. And when Israel builds the permanent house, the little laver becomes ten thousand gallons standing on twelve oxen.

There is a great deal of blood in this building and there is also a great deal of water, and both of them are there because people cannot come near God as they are.

'He also made the ten stands of bronze. Each stand was four cubits long, four cubits wide, and three cubits high.'

'This was the construction of the stands: they had panels, and the panels were set in the frames,'

'and on the panels that were set in the frames were lions, oxen, and cherubim.'

Ten wheeled trolleys, six feet square, with panels showing lions, oxen and cherubim.

The writer spends eleven verses on the engineering of these things — the frames, the axles, the wheels, the hubs and spokes and rims, the wreaths on the supports — in more mechanical detail than he gave for anything in the temple itself.

'Upon the frames there was a round band half a cubit high; and on the top of the stand its supports and its panels were of one piece with it.'

'And on the surfaces of its stays and on its panels, he carved cherubim, lions, and palm trees, according to the space of each, with wreaths all around.'

'After this manner he made the ten stands. All of them were cast alike, of the same measure and the same form.'

'And he made ten basins of bronze. Each basin held forty baths, each basin measured four cubits, and there was a basin for each of the ten stands.'

Ten basins of about two hundred gallons each, on wheels, so that water could be moved about the court.

Chronicles again supplies the use, and the division of labour is exact: in these they were to rinse off what was used for the burnt offering, and the sea was for the priests to wash in (2 Chron. 4:6).

The great sea is for the men. The ten wheeled basins are for the equipment.

'And he set the stands, five on the south side of the house, and five on the north side of the house. And he set the sea at the southeast corner of the house.'

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 40–51 — The Weight of the Bronze Was Not Ascertained
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hiram finishes the pots and shovels and basins and all the work he did for King Solomon on the house of the LORD, and the writer lists it (vv. 40-45). It was cast in the plain of the Jordan in the clay ground between Succoth and Zarethan (v. 46). And Solomon left all the vessels unweighed, because there were so many of them; the weight of the bronze was not ascertained (v. 47). Then the gold furnishings: the golden altar, the table for the bread of the Presence, the lampstands of pure gold, the flowers and lamps and tongs, the cups and snuffers and basins and dishes and fire pans, and the sockets of the doors (vv. 48-50). Thus all the work that King Solomon did on the house of the LORD was finished. And Solomon brought in the things that David his father had dedicated, the silver, the gold, and the vessels, and stored them in the treasuries of the house of the LORD (v. 51).
verseByVerse.theology: One measurement was never taken. Everything else in these two chapters is given to the cubit, and the bronze was simply too much to weigh — which is a small note about a reign that will shortly stop counting other things too.
verseByVerse.examples: And the chapter ends by bringing in what David dedicated: the tribute of Edom and Moab and Ammon and Amalek and Hadadezer, set apart for the LORD by a man who was told he could not build (2 Sam. 8:11-12). He funded it for twenty years and never saw a stone laid, and here his silver goes into the treasuries of the finished house.

verseByVerse.quote: Hiram also made the pots, the shovels, and the basins. So Hiram finished all the work that he did for King Solomon on the house of the LORD: the two pillars, the two bowls of the capitals that were on the tops of the pillars, and the two latticeworks to cover the two bowls of the capitals that were on the tops of the pillars; and the four hundred pomegranates for the two latticeworks, two rows of pomegranates for each latticework, to cover the two bowls of the capitals that were on the pillars; the ten stands, and the ten basins on the stands; and the one sea, and the twelve oxen underneath the sea. Now the pots, the shovels, and the basins, all these vessels in the house of the LORD, which Hiram made for King Solomon, were of burnished bronze. In the plain of the Jordan the king cast them, in the clay ground between Succoth and Zarethan. And Solomon left all the vessels unweighed, because there were so many of them; the weight of the bronze was not ascertained. So Solomon made all the vessels that were in the house of the LORD: the golden altar, the golden table for the bread of the Presence, the lampstands of pure gold, five on the south side and five on the north, before the inner sanctuary; the flowers, the lamps, and the tongs, of gold; the cups, snuffers, basins, dishes for incense, and fire pans, of pure gold; and the sockets of gold, for the doors of the innermost part of the house, the Most Holy Place, and for the doors of the nave of the temple. Thus all the work that King Solomon did on the house of the LORD was finished. And Solomon brought in the things that David his father had dedicated, the silver, the gold, and the vessels, and stored them in the treasuries of the house of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Hiram also made the pots, the shovels, and the basins. So Hiram finished all the work that he did for King Solomon on the house of the LORD:'

The list that follows is an inventory. Read it as one.

'the two pillars, the two bowls of the capitals that were on the tops of the pillars, and the two latticeworks to cover the two bowls of the capitals that were on the tops of the pillars;'

'and the four hundred pomegranates for the two latticeworks, two rows of pomegranates for each latticework, to cover the two bowls of the capitals that were on the tops of the pillars;'

'the ten stands, and the ten basins on the stands;'

'and the one sea, and the twelve oxen underneath the sea.'

'Now the pots, the shovels, and the basins, all these vessels in the house of the LORD, which Hiram made for King Solomon, were of burnished bronze.'

Pots and shovels.

Set that beside the pillars and the sea. The same craftsman who cast a twenty-seven-foot column and a ten-thousand-gallon basin also made the pots for carrying ash and the shovels for clearing the altar, and the writer lists them in the same sentence as the pillars.

There was a great deal of ordinary work in that building. Somebody had to shovel out a fire that never went out.

'In the plain of the Jordan the king cast them, in the clay ground between Succoth and Zarethan.'

Here is the one glimpse of how it was actually done.

The casting happened forty miles away, down in the Jordan valley, because that is where the right clay was. Everything in these chapters was made somewhere else and brought: the stone finished in the hill country, the cedar rafted down the coast from Lebanon, the bronze cast in the mud of the Jordan plain.

Nothing was manufactured on the mountain.

'And Solomon left all the vessels unweighed, because there were so many of them; the weight of the bronze was not ascertained.'

Here is a small sentence with a long shadow.

Everything in these two chapters has been measured. Cubits of length and breadth and height, the thickness of the bronze in handbreadths, the capacity of the sea in baths, four hundred pomegranates counted, ten stands of the same measure and the same form.

And the bronze was not weighed, because there was too much of it.

Read plainly, it is a note about scale, and that is probably all the writer intends by it.

It is also the first thing in this reign that was too big to count, and it is not the last. In three chapters the gold coming in yearly will be six hundred and sixty-six talents; the silver will be as common in Jerusalem as stone (10:27); there will be seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines. A reign that begins by measuring everything to the cubit ends with quantities nobody bothers to total.

'So Solomon made all the vessels that were in the house of the LORD: the golden altar, the golden table for the bread of the Presence,'

'the lampstands of pure gold, five on the south side and five on the north, before the inner sanctuary; the flowers, the lamps, and the tongs, of gold;'

'the cups, snuffers, basins, dishes for incense, and fire pans, of pure gold; and the sockets of gold, for the doors of the innermost part of the house, the Most Holy Place, and for the doors of the nave of the temple.'

The furniture of the tabernacle, in gold, at scale — and note the lampstands. Moses had one, with seven lamps. Solomon has ten.

Even the door sockets are gold. The hinge-pivots, in the floor, that nobody would ever see.

'Thus all the work that King Solomon did on the house of the LORD was finished.'

'And Solomon brought in the things that David his father had dedicated, the silver, the gold, and the vessels, and stored them in the treasuries of the house of the LORD.'

The last verse of the building account belongs to a man who has been dead for eleven years.

Go back and find what those dedicated things are. They are listed in 2 Samuel 8: the tribute of Toi of Hamath, and the plunder of Edom and Moab and Ammon and the Philistines and Amalek and the whole treasury of Hadadezer of Zobah — these also King David dedicated to the LORD, together with the silver and gold that he dedicated from all the nations he subdued (2 Sam. 8:11-12).

He could not build. He was told plainly why: you have shed much blood and have waged great wars (1 Chron. 22:8). And what he did about it, for the rest of his working life, was win wars and hand every penny of the proceeds to a project he was forbidden to work on, and lay up gold and silver and bronze and iron beyond weighing, and give his own personal fortune to it at the end, and die before the foundations went in (1 Chron. 22:14; 29:2-5).

The house is finished, and the last thing carried into it is his.

7.theology:
Seven and thirteen (v. 1). Consecutive sentences, no comment, and then a longer and warmer description of the palace than of the temple. The mitigations are real — a whole royal quarter against one modest building, overlapping timelines — and the writer still chose to put the numbers side by side and let them sit there.

The House of the Forest of Lebanon (v. 2). Four times the floor area of the temple, named for the forty-five cedar pillars standing inside it so that walking through was like walking through trees. Chapter 10 says what it held: three hundred shields of beaten gold (10:17). An armoury, a treasury, and a very large statement.

A room for judgment (v. 7). The man who asked at Gibeon for a hearing heart to govern your people, that I may discern between good and evil builds a courtroom for it, cedar from floor to rafters. Hold both sides: it is right that justice should have a proper address, and that is 2 Samuel 8:15 given a building. And a hall is not a hearing — two prostitutes with no standing got a verdict from this man in chapter 3, and what Absalom exploited at the gate was not a shortage of rooms but there is no man designated by the king to hear you (2 Sam. 15:3). The room is not the thing, which is exactly what God said in the middle of the temple site one chapter ago.

Pharaoh's daughter, fourth mention (v. 8). She arrived at 3:1, in the first sentence of the reign after the executions, before Gibeon and before the temple. Here she gets a house built to the standard of the Hall of Judgment. At 9:24 Solomon moves her out of the city of David because the places the ark has come are holy. And 11:1: King Solomon loved many foreign women, along with the daughter of Pharaoh. Four flat factual mentions across nine chapters with no comment attached to any of them.

Same quarry, same standard (v. 12). The great court of the palace is built to the specification of the inner court of the temple — three courses of cut stone and a course of cedar beams. The house of God and the house of the king go up on the same hill, from the same quarry, by the same workforce.

Bezalel's words, used again (v. 14). Full of wisdom, understanding, and skill is the description of the man God named to build the tabernacle: I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with ability and intelligence, with knowledge and all craftsmanship, to work in gold, silver, and bronze (Ex. 31:2-4). Same three words, same order, same kind of work. Scripture says this in very few places and means it every time: skill in a craft is a gift of God, not a natural talent he tolerates and not a lesser thing than teaching or prophesying. The only two men in the Bible described this way are both metalworkers — and this one is half foreign, brought from a Phoenician port, the son of a woman with no husband.

The pillars are a sentence, and they hold nothing up (v. 21). Jachin is he shall establish; Boaz is most likely in him is strength. Not Solomon shall establish, and not in this house is strength — he, and him. And they are free-standing: no roof rests on them, no beam, nothing. Their whole function is to declare something to every priest going in to serve and every Israelite coming up to the courts. Three and a half centuries later the Chaldeans broke in pieces these pillars and carried the bronze to Babylon (2 Kings 25:13). They broke up he shall establish and carted it away, and the sentence was still true, which is what the rest of the Old Testament is about.

So that they may not die (vv. 23-26). The sea is the laver of Exodus at enormous scale — the basin between the tent and the altar where Aaron and his sons washed hands and feet, and the law attaches the penalty in as many words: they shall wash with water, so that they may not die (Ex. 30:18-21). Chronicles says this one was for the priests to wash in (2 Chron. 4:6). A man handling holy things does not simply walk up. There is a great deal of blood in this building and a great deal of water, and both are there because people cannot come near God as they are. And twelve oxen carry it, in fours facing every point of the compass — the tribes, facing the whole earth, holding up water for washing.

The one measurement nobody took (v. 47). Everything else in these two chapters is given to the cubit: lengths, breadths, heights, the thickness of the bronze in handbreadths, the capacity in baths, four hundred pomegranates counted. And the bronze was left unweighed because there was too much of it. Read plainly it is a note about scale, and that is probably all the writer intends — and it is the first thing in this reign too big to count, and not the last. Within three chapters the gold arriving yearly is six hundred and sixty-six talents, silver is as common in Jerusalem as stone (10:27), and there are seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines. A reign that began measuring everything to the cubit ends with quantities nobody bothers to total.

Nothing was made on the mountain (v. 46). The bronze was cast forty miles away in the clay ground of the Jordan plain, because that is where the right earth for moulds was. Stone finished in the hill country, cedar rafted down from Lebanon, bronze cast in the mud of the valley. And the same craftsman who cast a twenty-seven-foot pillar made the pots for carrying ash and the shovels for clearing the altar, listed in the same sentence. Somebody had to shovel out a fire that never went out.

The last thing carried in belongs to a dead man (v. 51). David's dedicated things are the tribute of Toi and the plunder of Edom, Moab, Ammon, the Philistines, Amalek and the whole treasury of Hadadezer — set apart for the LORD by a man who had been told you have shed much blood... you shall not build a house to my name (1 Chron. 22:8). What he did about that refusal, for the rest of his working life, was win wars and hand every penny to a project he was forbidden to work on, lay up metal beyond weighing, give his own fortune at the end, and die before the foundations went in (1 Chron. 22:14; 29:2-5). The house is finished, and the last thing carried into it is his.
7.examples:
Then: Two hollow bronze columns twenty-seven feet high were cast in the mud of the Jordan valley, hauled forty miles up to Jerusalem, and stood one on either side of the temple door holding up absolutely nothing — because their entire purpose was to say, to everyone who walked between them, that God establishes and that the strength is his.

Now: Three things. Verse 1 is the writer's method at its purest: he does not accuse Solomon of anything, he puts a seven and a thirteen in consecutive sentences, and anybody honest can do the arithmetic on their own life with the same two columns. Second, Hiram the craftsman, because Scripture says something here it says almost nowhere else: the ability to make something beautiful out of metal is described in the same words as the filling of the Spirit of God. Skill in a trade is a gift, and the man who had it most was half a foreigner and a widow's son. And third, the pillars. They carried no weight and were broken up and carted to Babylon in the end, and what they said was true the whole time and stayed true after they were gone.

8.overview:
Everything in the last three chapters has been building toward moving one object half a mile uphill. And the week Solomon chooses is the Feast of Booths — the week Israel lived in shelters made of branches to remember that their fathers had no houses and God travelled with them. That is the week he moves God into a permanent building. The tent of meeting comes up too, and is stored: four hundred and eighty years of portable worship end in one verse.

Then the writer tells us what all of it was for. Seven years, a hundred and fifty thousand labourers, cedar rafted down a coast, stone finished at the quarry so no iron would be heard, gold over every surface until no stone could be seen — to make a room, for a box, containing two pieces of stone. And he names them: the tablets Moses put there at Horeb, when they came out of the land of Egypt. The centre of the most expensive building in Israel's history is a copy of the terms on which God bound himself to a company of runaway slaves.

It works. The cloud fills the house and the priests cannot stand to minister, exactly as at the tabernacle four hundred and eighty years earlier. A room full of trained men walk out into the courtyard because there is nothing they can do in there.

And then the sentence the book turns on, spoken by the man who built the building, on the day he dedicated it, with the glory of God visibly inside: but will God indeed dwell on the earth? Behold, heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house that I have built! Nobody made him say it. The assembly would have been perfectly satisfied with verse 13.
