He corrects himself, out loud, in public, fourteen verses later — and then kneels down and prays the longest prayer in the Old Testament, and every one of its seven petitions is about sin, and the refrain is hear in heaven... and forgive.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Glory of the LORD Filled the House
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Solomon assembles the elders and heads of tribes to bring up the ark from Zion, at the feast in the seventh month (vv. 1-2). The priests carry it — the ark, the tent of meeting and all the holy vessels — with sacrifices beyond counting (vv. 3-5). They set it in the inner sanctuary beneath the wings of the cherubim, and the poles are so long their ends can be seen from the Holy Place (vv. 6-8). There was nothing in the ark except the two tablets of stone that Moses put there at Horeb, where the LORD made a covenant with the people of Israel, when they came out of the land of Egypt (v. 9). And when the priests came out of the Holy Place, a cloud filled the house of the LORD, so that the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD (vv. 10-11). Then Solomon: the LORD has said that he would dwell in thick darkness. I have indeed built you an exalted house, a place for you to dwell in forever (vv. 12-13).
verseByVerse.theology: It works. The same thing happened when Moses finished the tabernacle — Moses was not able to enter the tent of meeting because the cloud settled on it, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle (Ex. 40:35). The priests have to walk out of the building because God has come into it.
verseByVerse.examples: And note what is in the ark: two stone tablets and nothing else. Not the gold and not the cherubim above it — inside the box is a copy of the covenant God made with slaves he had brought out of Egypt. That is what the whole house was built to hold.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Solomon assembled the elders of Israel and all the heads of the tribes, the leaders of the fathers' houses of the people of Israel, before King Solomon in Jerusalem, to bring up the ark of the covenant of the LORD out of the city of David, which is Zion. And all the men of Israel assembled to King Solomon at the feast in the month Ethanim, which is the seventh month. And all the elders of Israel came, and the priests took up the ark. And they brought up the ark of the LORD, the tent of meeting, and all the holy vessels that were in the tent; the priests and the Levites brought them up. And King Solomon and all the congregation of Israel, who had assembled before him, were with him before the ark, sacrificing so many sheep and oxen that they could not be counted or numbered. Then the priests brought the ark of the covenant of the LORD to its place in the inner sanctuary of the house, in the Most Holy Place, underneath the wings of the cherubim. For the cherubim spread out their wings over the place of the ark, so that the cherubim overshadowed the ark and its poles. And the poles were so long that the ends of the poles were seen from the Holy Place before the inner sanctuary; but they could not be seen from outside. And they are there to this day. There was nothing in the ark except the two tablets of stone that Moses put there at Horeb, where the LORD made a covenant with the people of Israel, when they came out of the land of Egypt. And when the priests came out of the Holy Place, a cloud filled the house of the LORD, so that the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD. Then Solomon said, "The LORD has said that he would dwell in thick darkness. I have indeed built you an exalted house, a place for you to dwell in forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Solomon assembled the elders of Israel and all the heads of the tribes, the leaders of the fathers' houses of the people of Israel, before King Solomon in Jerusalem, to bring up the ark of the covenant of the LORD out of the city of David, which is Zion.'

Everything in the last three chapters has been building toward moving one object about half a mile uphill.

The ark has been in the tent David pitched for it since 2 Samuel 6 — since the second attempt, after Uzzah, when it was carried properly on poles on Levites' shoulders and a king danced in front of it in a linen ephod.

'And all the men of Israel assembled to King Solomon at the feast in the month Ethanim, which is the seventh month.'

The seventh month is Tishri, and the feast is Booths — the week when Israel lived in shelters made of branches to remember that their fathers had no houses at all, and God travelled with them.

That is the week Solomon chooses to move God into a permanent building.

'And all the elders of Israel came, and the priests took up the ark.'

'And they brought up the ark of the LORD, the tent of meeting, and all the holy vessels that were in the tent; the priests and the Levites brought them up.'

The tent comes too, and this is the end of something.

The tent of meeting is the tabernacle — the structure Moses made at Sinai to a pattern God showed him, carried through forty years of wilderness, set up at Shiloh, and standing at Gibeon in Solomon's own day. It is brought up and stored.

Four hundred and eighty years of portable worship end in this verse.

'And King Solomon and all the congregation of Israel, who had assembled before him, were with him before the ark, sacrificing so many sheep and oxen that they could not be counted or numbered.'

'Then the priests brought the ark of the covenant of the LORD to its place in the inner sanctuary of the house, in the Most Holy Place, underneath the wings of the cherubim.'

'For the cherubim spread out their wings over the place of the ark, so that the cherubim overshadowed the ark and its poles.'

The two olivewood figures from chapter 6, fifteen feet high with their wings meeting in the middle of the room, are standing over it.

Note what is now in that room: two sets of cherubim. The great olivewood ones Solomon made, and the small hammered-gold ones on the mercy seat that Moses made, where God said there I will meet with you (Ex. 25:22).

'And the poles were so long that the ends of the poles were seen from the Holy Place before the inner sanctuary; but they could not be seen from outside. And they are there to this day.'

The poles stay in.

The law required it: the poles shall remain in the rings of the ark; they shall not be taken from it (Ex. 25:15). They were never removed, ever, so that the ark could always be lifted and never handled — which is the law a cart made it impossible to keep, and a man died at a threshing floor because of it.

Now the ark has arrived at the place it will stay for four hundred years. And the poles stay in.

God is settling into a stone house and the carrying poles are left where they are, and their ends can be seen sticking out from inside the Holy Place, which is presumably why the writer mentions it at all. A priest standing in the outer room could see them.

He is not tied to the building.

'There was nothing in the ark except the two tablets of stone that Moses put there at Horeb, where the LORD made a covenant with the people of Israel, when they came out of the land of Egypt.'

Here is what all of it was for.

Seven years of building. A hundred and fifty thousand labourers. Cedar from Lebanon rafted down a coast, stone finished at the quarry so no iron would be heard on the mountain, gold over every surface until no stone was seen, two bronze pillars twenty-seven feet high, a basin holding ten thousand gallons on twelve oxen.

To make a room, for a box, containing two pieces of stone.

And the writer tells us exactly what the stones are and when they were cut: the tablets Moses put there at Horeb, where the LORD made a covenant with the people of Israel, when they came out of the land of Egypt.

The centre of the most expensive building in Israel's history is a copy of the terms on which God bound himself to a company of runaway slaves.

One note on the contents, since readers ask. Hebrews describes the tabernacle as having in the ark a golden urn holding the manna, and Aaron's staff that budded, and the tablets of the covenant (Heb. 9:4). Exodus and Numbers record the jar and the rod being placed before the testimony (Ex. 16:34; Num. 17:10), which may mean in front of the ark rather than inside it, and in any case this verse describes the situation four centuries later. What is certain is what Kings says: by Solomon's day there were two stone tablets in that box and nothing else.

'And when the priests came out of the Holy Place, a cloud filled the house of the LORD,'

'so that the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD.'

It works.

The priests set the ark in place, walk out of the inner room, and the building fills with cloud until they cannot do their jobs. They have to leave.

Now go back four hundred and eighty years. Moses finished the tabernacle in the wilderness, set up everything exactly as he had been told, and: then the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle. And Moses was not able to enter the tent of meeting because the cloud settled on it, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle (Ex. 40:34-35).

The same thing, in the same words, at the completion of the same design at twice the scale.

God has done what he did before. He has come into the building.

And the effect on the professionals is that they cannot work. Sit with that, because it is not how anybody plans a dedication. The priests have spent their lives learning a liturgy and the moment the glory arrives the liturgy stops, and a room full of trained men walk out into the courtyard because there is nothing they can do in there.

'Then Solomon said, "The LORD has said that he would dwell in thick darkness."'

The room has no windows, and the cloud is in it, and the king says the darkness is the point.

God said at Sinai that he would come in a thick cloud (Ex. 19:9), and Moses drew near to the thick darkness where God was (Ex. 20:21). The dark is not the absence of God in that room. It is where he is.

'"I have indeed built you an exalted house, a place for you to dwell in forever."'

Solomon's first sentence about his own work is a proud one, and he is about to correct it himself fourteen verses later.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–27 — Will God Indeed Dwell on the Earth?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Solomon turns and blesses the assembly, and rehearses the promise: God chose no city for a house but chose David, and told him that his son would build it (vv. 15-19). Now the LORD has fulfilled his promise that he made (v. 20). He sets a place for the ark, in which is the covenant of the LORD that he made with our fathers, when he brought them out of the land of Egypt (v. 21). Then, standing before the altar with hands spread to heaven: O LORD, God of Israel, there is no God like you, in heaven above or on earth beneath, keeping covenant and showing steadfast love to your servants who walk before you with all their heart (vv. 22-23). He holds God to the covenant with David (vv. 24-26). And then the question: but will God indeed dwell on the earth? Behold, heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house that I have built! (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: He has just spent seven years and the wealth of a kingdom on this building, and on the day he dedicates it he says out loud that it cannot possibly do what it was built for. Nobody made him say that.
verseByVerse.examples: And note where he stands in verse 22 — not on a platform but before the altar, with his hands open toward heaven. Verse 54 says he had been kneeling. The king of Israel dedicates the greatest building in his kingdom on his knees in the courtyard.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king turned around and blessed all the assembly of Israel, while all the assembly of Israel stood. And he said, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who with his hand has fulfilled what he promised with his mouth to David my father, saying, 'Since the day that I brought my people Israel out of Egypt, I chose no city out of all the tribes of Israel in which to build a house, that my name might be there. But I chose David to be over my people Israel.' Now it was in the heart of David my father to build a house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel. But the LORD said to David my father, 'Whereas it was in your heart to build a house for my name, you did well that it was in your heart. Nevertheless, you shall not build the house, but your son who shall be born to you shall build the house for my name.' Now the LORD has fulfilled his promise that he made. For I have risen in the place of David my father, and sit on the throne of Israel, as the LORD promised, and I have built the house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel. And there I have provided a place for the ark, in which is the covenant of the LORD that he made with our fathers, when he brought them out of the land of Egypt." Then Solomon stood before the altar of the LORD in the presence of all the assembly of Israel and spread out his hands toward heaven, and said, "O LORD, God of Israel, there is no God like you, in heaven above or on earth beneath, keeping covenant and showing steadfast love to your servants who walk before you with all their heart; you have kept with your servant David my father what you declared to him. You spoke with your mouth, and with your hand have fulfilled it this day. Now therefore, O LORD, God of Israel, keep for your servant David my father what you have promised him, saying, 'You shall not lack a man to sit before me on the throne of Israel, if only your sons pay close attention to their way, to walk before me as you have walked before me.' Now therefore, O God of Israel, let your word be confirmed, which you have spoken to your servant David my father. "But will God indeed dwell on the earth? Behold, heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house that I have built!
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then the king turned around and blessed all the assembly of Israel, while all the assembly of Israel stood.'

'And he said, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who with his hand has fulfilled what he promised with his mouth to David my father, saying,"'

He begins with a promise being kept, and the phrasing is exact: what he promised with his mouth, done with his hand.

'"'Since the day that I brought my people Israel out of Egypt, I chose no city out of all the tribes of Israel in which to build a house, that my name might be there. But I chose David to be over my people Israel.'"'

Look at what God says he chose.

Not a city. Not a site. For four hundred and eighty years, from the exodus to this morning, God picked no place at all for a house.

What he chose was a man.

That is the answer to the whole question of chapter 6 stated from the other direction. God's interest was never in real estate. He selected a shepherd out of a field in Bethlehem and made promises to him, and the building is downstream of that.

'"Now it was in the heart of David my father to build a house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel."'

'"But the LORD said to David my father, 'Whereas it was in your heart to build a house for my name, you did well that it was in your heart.'"'

Here is one of the kindest sentences in the Old Testament, and it is easy to read past.

You did well that it was in your heart.

David wanted to build the temple and was refused. He never laid a stone of it; he was told no, and told why, and died eleven years before this morning.

And God says: it was good that you wanted to.

The desire is commended even though the project was denied. That is not a consolation prize and it is not politeness. God is saying that the wanting itself was right and that he saw it and valued it.

Anybody who has had a genuine desire to do something for God and been prevented — by health, by circumstance, by other people's decisions, by simply being the wrong person for it — is looking at the verse that speaks to it. The thing was refused. The wanting was not wasted.

'"Nevertheless, you shall not build the house, but your son who shall be born to you shall build the house for my name."'

'"Now the LORD has fulfilled his promise that he made. For I have risen in the place of David my father, and sit on the throne of Israel, as the LORD promised, and I have built the house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel."'

'"And there I have provided a place for the ark, in which is the covenant of the LORD that he made with our fathers, when he brought them out of the land of Egypt."'

Twice in four verses he grounds all of this in the exodus. The covenant in the box was made with people coming out of Egypt, and the building exists to house it.

'Then Solomon stood before the altar of the LORD in the presence of all the assembly of Israel and spread out his hands toward heaven,'

Note where he is standing and what he does with his hands.

Not on a platform, not on a throne, not in the building — before the altar, in the courtyard, in front of everybody, with his hands open and lifted.

And verse 54 will tell us something this verse does not: he was on his knees. He arose from before the altar of the LORD, where he had knelt with hands outstretched toward heaven.

The richest man in the world, on the greatest day of his reign, dedicates the building he spent seven years on from his knees in a courtyard with his hands empty and open.

'and said, "O LORD, God of Israel, there is no God like you, in heaven above or on earth beneath, keeping covenant and showing steadfast love to your servants who walk before you with all their heart;"'

The prayer opens where every good prayer in Scripture opens: with who God is.

And the thing he singles out is not power or majesty. Keeping covenant and showing steadfast love — God's distinguishing characteristic, in the mouth of a man dedicating a temple, is that he keeps his promises.

'"you have kept with your servant David my father what you declared to him. You spoke with your mouth, and with your hand have fulfilled it this day."'

'"Now therefore, O LORD, God of Israel, keep for your servant David my father what you have promised him, saying, 'You shall not lack a man to sit before me on the throne of Israel, if only your sons pay close attention to their way, to walk before me as you have walked before me.'"'

'"Now therefore, O God of Israel, let your word be confirmed, which you have spoken to your servant David my father."'

He prays the promise back, which is exactly what his father did in the same situation.

When Nathan brought the covenant to David, David went in and sat before the LORD and said do as you have spoken, and gave his reason: you have made this revelation to your servant... therefore your servant has found courage to pray this prayer to you (2 Sam. 7:25-27).

Solomon does the same thing. Let your word be confirmed. He is not informing God of anything. He is taking him at his word in his hearing.

'"But will God indeed dwell on the earth? Behold, heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house that I have built!"'

Here is the sentence, and it is the theological centre of the entire book.

Consider who says it and when.

The man speaking has just finished seven years of work. He has conscripted thirty thousand Israelites in monthly shifts and employed a hundred and fifty thousand labourers. He has imported the finest timber in the world and paid for it with twenty thousand measures of wheat a year. He has had every stone finished at the quarry so that no iron would ring on the mountain. He has covered every surface with gold until no stone could be seen, and cast two pillars twenty-seven feet high, and made a basin holding ten thousand gallons.

He is standing in front of it, on the day of its dedication, with the glory of God visibly inside it and the entire nation watching.

And he says: this cannot possibly hold you.

Will God indeed dwell on the earth? The question is genuine. Not will God dwell in this building — will God dwell on the earth at all? Is such a thing even a category?

Behold, heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you. The sky will not hold him. The sky beyond the sky will not hold him. There is no volume of anything anywhere that is large enough.

How much less this house that I have built. And then he adds the four words that make the sentence what it is: that I have built. He does not distance himself from it. He names it as his own work and says his own work is not adequate to the purpose, on the day the work was finished.

Nobody made him say this. There was no prophet standing there to correct him. The assembly would have been perfectly satisfied with verse 13 — I have indeed built you an exalted house, a place for you to dwell in forever — and he corrects it himself fourteen verses later, out loud, in public.

That is what a hearing heart looks like when it has been used for seven years. He has thought about what he is doing, and the more magnificent it got the clearer it became that it could not do the one thing it was for.

And the sentence has a long life ahead of it.

Isaiah picks it up and gives it as God's own words: heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool; what is the house that you would build for me?... All these things my hand has made... But this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word (Isa. 66:1-2).

And Stephen quotes Solomon almost directly, standing in front of the council that was about to stone him for speaking against the temple: yet the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands (Acts 7:48). And Paul, standing on the Areopagus in a city full of temples: the God who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in temples made by man (Acts 17:24).

The best thing anybody has ever said about the limits of religious buildings was said by the man who built the best one, on the day he opened it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–40 — Hear in Heaven, and Forgive
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prayer proper begins: that your eyes may be open night and day toward this house... and listen to the plea of your servant and of your people Israel (vv. 28-30). Then seven petitions, each turning on the same refrain. When a man swears an oath at this altar — then hear in heaven and act and judge your servants (vv. 31-32). When Israel is defeated because they have sinned and they turn and confess — then hear in heaven and forgive the sin of your people (vv. 33-34). When the heavens are shut up and there is no rain (vv. 35-36). When there is famine, blight, mildew, locust, siege, whatever plague, whatever sickness there is — whatever prayer, whatever plea is made by any man or by all your people Israel, each knowing the affliction of his own heart (vv. 37-40). When a foreigner comes from a far country for the sake of the name (vv. 41-43). When the people go out to battle (vv. 44-45).
verseByVerse.theology: Every one of the seven is about sin and its consequences. Not one asks for prosperity, victory, long life, or a secure throne — the things the king could have asked for at Gibeon and did not. And the refrain is hear in heaven... and forgive.
verseByVerse.examples: Each knowing the affliction of his own heart (v. 38) is the most personal clause in the prayer. In a national dedication with the whole assembly present, he asks God to hear the man who knows what is wrong with him and cannot say it to anybody.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet have regard to the prayer of your servant and to his plea, O LORD my God, listening to the cry and to the prayer that your servant prays before you this day, that your eyes may be open night and day toward this house, the place of which you have said, 'My name shall be there,' that you may listen to the prayer that your servant offers toward this place. And listen to the plea of your servant and of your people Israel, when they pray toward this place. And listen in heaven your dwelling place, and when you hear, forgive. "If a man sins against his neighbor and is made to take an oath and comes and swears his oath before your altar in this house, then hear in heaven and act and judge your servants, condemning the guilty by bringing his conduct on his own head, and vindicating the righteous by rewarding him according to his righteousness. "When your people Israel are defeated before the enemy because they have sinned against you, and if they turn again to you and acknowledge your name and pray and plead with you in this house, then hear in heaven and forgive the sin of your people Israel and bring them again to the land that you gave to their fathers. "When heaven is shut up and there is no rain because they have sinned against you, if they pray toward this place and acknowledge your name and turn from their sin, when you afflict them, then hear in heaven and forgive the sin of your servants, your people Israel, when you teach them the good way in which they should walk, and grant rain upon your land, which you have given to your people as an inheritance. "If there is famine in the land, if there is pestilence or blight or mildew or locust or caterpillar, if their enemy besieges them in the land at their gates, whatever plague, whatever sickness there is, whatever prayer, whatever plea is made by any man or by all your people Israel, each knowing the affliction of his own heart and stretching out his hands toward this house, then hear in heaven your dwelling place and forgive and act and render to each whose heart you know, according to all his ways (for you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind), that they may fear you all the days that they live in the land that you gave to our fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'"Yet have regard to the prayer of your servant and to his plea, O LORD my God, listening to the cry and to the prayer that your servant prays before you this day,"'

Yet.

That single word is the turn. He has just said the building cannot contain God — and now he asks God to pay attention to it anyway.

He is not being inconsistent. He is holding two things that both need holding: God is not contained by any building, and God has chosen to make himself available at a particular place to people who cannot come to heaven.

'"that your eyes may be open night and day toward this house, the place of which you have said, 'My name shall be there,' that you may listen to the prayer that your servant offers toward this place."'

Here is what the temple actually is, in the phrase Solomon uses six times in this prayer.

My name shall be there.

Not I shall be there, as though God were resident in a room like a householder. His name — his reputation, his self-disclosure, the way he has made himself known and findable. The house is where God has put his name so that people know where to turn.

Which is why every petition that follows is about praying toward this place, not in it. Almost nobody in Israel could get to Jerusalem often, and the exiles of verse 46 will not be able to get there at all.

'"And listen to the plea of your servant and of your people Israel, when they pray toward this place. And listen in heaven your dwelling place, and when you hear, forgive."'

Listen in heaven your dwelling place.

He has just built God a dwelling place and he does not call it that. Heaven is God's dwelling place; the house on the hill is where you face when you speak.

And then the word the whole prayer runs on, arriving for the first time: forgive.

'"If a man sins against his neighbor and is made to take an oath and comes and swears his oath before your altar in this house, then hear in heaven and act and judge your servants, condemning the guilty by bringing his conduct on his own head, and vindicating the righteous by rewarding him according to his righteousness."'

The first petition, and it is about a lawsuit with no evidence.

This is the case that cannot be settled in court: one man's word against another's, so the accused is put on oath at the altar. Solomon asks God to be the court of last resort where human justice runs out.

Which is a thing he knows about. Two women stood in front of him with a baby and no witnesses.

The procedure behind this petition is in the law. Where property was in dispute and there was no proof either way, an oath by the LORD shall be between them both to see whether or not he has put his hand to his neighbour's property. The owner shall accept the oath, and he shall not make restitution (Ex. 22:11). The oath ends the case, because there is nothing else to end it with.

Which means the whole thing rests on the man swearing believing that God is listening. Take that away and the oath is a formula, and the guilty man simply says the words and walks out with his neighbour's ox.

And note what Solomon asks for. Not mercy — this is the one petition in the seven with no forgive in it. He asks God to condemn the guilty by bringing his conduct on his own head, and vindicate the righteous by rewarding him according to his righteousness.

Both halves matter. There is a man in that scenario who has been wronged and has no way to prove it, and the prayer is that he should be publicly cleared. Every court in the world produces people who were right and could not show it, and the first thing Solomon asks of the new temple is that God be the place where that is finally sorted out.

'"When your people Israel are defeated before the enemy because they have sinned against you, and if they turn again to you and acknowledge your name and pray and plead with you in this house, then hear in heaven and forgive the sin of your people Israel and bring them again to the land that you gave to their fathers."'

The second, and now the pattern of all seven is established.

Watch the shape: a disaster, and the disaster is because they have sinned, and then turning and praying, and then hear in heaven and forgive.

Solomon is not asking God to keep trouble away from Israel. He is assuming trouble, assuming that much of it will be deserved, and asking that there be a way back from it.

That is a striking thing to build into a dedication. The obvious prayer for a new national sanctuary is that the nation should prosper. What he asks for is a road back from disasters that have not happened yet and will be their own fault.

And the specific request at the end of it is territorial: bring them again to the land that you gave to their fathers. Defeat in the ancient world meant deportation — populations moved, land lost, families broken up across an empire. He is asking that the losing of the land not be final.

Which is exactly the ground the seventh petition will stand on, thirteen verses later, when the loss is total.

'"When heaven is shut up and there is no rain because they have sinned against you, if they pray toward this place and acknowledge your name and turn from their sin, when you afflict them,"'

'"then hear in heaven and forgive the sin of your servants, your people Israel, when you teach them the good way in which they should walk, and grant rain upon your land, which you have given to your people as an inheritance."'

The third: drought. And note the clause slipped into the middle of it — when you teach them the good way in which they should walk.

The affliction is teaching. He is asking that a shut sky do its work.

Elijah is going to stand in front of a king in chapter 17 and shut the sky for three and a half years, and this petition is what he is standing on.

The theology of it comes straight out of Deuteronomy, and every Israelite farmer knew it. Rain in that country is not a weather event; it is the covenant made visible. If you will indeed obey my commandments... he will give the rain for your land in its season — and the warning attached: then the anger of the LORD will be kindled against you, and he will shut up the heavens, so that there will be no rain (Deut. 11:13-17).

So a dry sky was a sermon. A nation that had gone after other gods for the very reason that they were thought to control the weather would find the weather stopped.

And the clause in the middle is what makes the petition Christian rather than merely transactional: when you teach them the good way in which they should walk. The drought is not simply a penalty being served. It is instruction, and Solomon asks that it work — that the affliction actually teach the thing it was sent to teach, so that it need not be repeated.

Anybody who has been in a long dry season of their own can pray verse 36 as it stands. Not take this away first, but teach me the good way in which I should walk, and then the rain.

'"If there is famine in the land, if there is pestilence or blight or mildew or locust or caterpillar, if their enemy besieges them in the land at their gates, whatever plague, whatever sickness there is,"'

The fourth petition, and he simply lists everything that can go wrong.

Famine, plague, blight, mildew, locusts, caterpillar, siege — and then, because no list is complete, whatever plague, whatever sickness there is.

'"whatever prayer, whatever plea is made by any man or by all your people Israel, each knowing the affliction of his own heart and stretching out his hands toward this house,"'

Here is the most personal clause in the whole prayer, and it is the one to stop on.

Each knowing the affliction of his own heart.

Solomon is standing in front of the entire nation on the greatest public occasion of his reign, with twenty-two thousand oxen about to be sacrificed, and he stops and asks God to hear the individual man who knows what is wrong with him.

The phrase is literally about a man knowing the plague of his own heart. It is the same word he just used for the diseases and the locusts, turned inward.

Every other petition in this prayer is corporate: when the people are defeated, when the land has no rain, when they go out to battle. This one is any man, alone, who knows something about himself that nobody else in that crowd knows, and stretches out his hands.

Whatever else the temple was for, it was for him.

'"then hear in heaven your dwelling place and forgive and act and render to each whose heart you know, according to all his ways (for you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind),"'

The parenthesis is the reason it works.

You, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind.

The man knows the affliction of his own heart. God knows it too, and God is the only one who does.

That is why the prayer can be made without words that anybody else hears, and why the judgment asked for is exact — render to each whose heart you know. Nobody is being processed in a group.

'"that they may fear you all the days that they live in the land that you gave to our fathers."'

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–53 — The Foreigner, and the Far Country
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Likewise, when a foreigner, who is not of your people Israel, comes from a far country for your name's sake — for they shall hear of your great name and your mighty hand and your outstretched arm — when he comes and prays toward this house, hear in heaven your dwelling place and do according to all for which the foreigner calls to you, in order that all the peoples of the earth may know your name and fear you, as do your people Israel (vv. 41-43). And the last petition looks past everything: if they sin against you — for there is no one who does not sin — and you are angry with them and give them to an enemy, so that they are carried away captive to the land of the enemy, far off or near, yet if they turn their heart in the land to which they have been carried captive, and repent and plead with you... then hear in heaven your dwelling place their prayer and their plea, and maintain their cause and forgive your people (vv. 46-50).
verseByVerse.theology: The foreigner's petition is unconditional in a way none of Israel's are. For Israel the asking turns on repentance and confession; for the man from a far country it is do according to all for which the foreigner calls to you — and the reason given is missionary: in order that all the peoples of the earth may know your name.
verseByVerse.examples: And the seventh petition foresees the exile three and a half centuries before it happened. The book of Kings was compiled in that exile, and its first readers were captives in Babylon reading a prayer that had already asked God to hear them there.

verseByVerse.quote: "Likewise, when a foreigner, who is not of your people Israel, comes from a far country for your name's sake (for they shall hear of your great name and your mighty hand, and of your outstretched arm), when he comes and prays toward this house, hear in heaven your dwelling place and do according to all for which the foreigner calls to you, in order that all the peoples of the earth may know your name and fear you, as do your people Israel, and that they may know that this house that I have built is called by your name. "If your people go out to battle against their enemy, by whatever way you shall send them, and they pray to the LORD toward the city that you have chosen and the house that I have built for your name, then hear in heaven their prayer and their plea, and maintain their cause. "If they sin against you— for there is no one who does not sin—and you are angry with them and give them to an enemy, so that they are carried away captive to the land of the enemy, far off or near, yet if they turn their heart in the land to which they have been carried captive, and repent and plead with you in the land of their captors, saying, 'We have sinned and have acted perversely and wickedly,' if they repent with all their heart and with all their soul in the land of their enemies, who carried them captive, and pray to you toward their land, which you gave to their fathers, the city that you have chosen, and the house that I have built for your name, then hear in heaven your dwelling place their prayer and their plea, and maintain their cause and forgive your people who have sinned against you, and all their transgressions that they have committed against you, and grant them compassion in the sight of those who carried them captive, that they may have compassion on them (for they are your people, and your heritage, which you brought out of Egypt, from the midst of the iron furnace). Let your eyes be open to the plea of your servant and to the plea of your people Israel, giving ear to them whenever they call to you. For you separated them from among all the peoples of the earth to be your heritage, as you declared through Moses your servant, when you brought our fathers out of Egypt, O Lord GOD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'"Likewise, when a foreigner, who is not of your people Israel, comes from a far country for your name's sake"'

The fifth petition is about somebody who has no covenant, no claim, no inheritance in the land, and no business being there at all.

'"(for they shall hear of your great name and your mighty hand, and of your outstretched arm), when he comes and prays toward this house,"'

Note what draws him: a reputation.

They shall hear of your great name and your mighty hand and your outstretched arm. Those are exodus words — the phrases Deuteronomy uses over and over for what God did in Egypt. What reaches a foreigner in a far country is the story of God rescuing slaves.

'"hear in heaven your dwelling place and do according to all for which the foreigner calls to you,"'

Now read that against every other petition in this prayer, because the difference is startling.

For Israel, the asking has conditions. If they turn again to you and acknowledge your name. If they pray toward this place and turn from their sin. If they repent with all their mind and with all their heart. Every petition for God's own people runs through repentance.

For the foreigner: do according to all for which the foreigner calls to you.

All. No conditions attached, no repentance specified, no requirement that he become an Israelite first. A man arrives from a far country having heard something about the God of Israel, faces a building, and asks — and Solomon asks God to give him everything he asks for.

'"in order that all the peoples of the earth may know your name and fear you, as do your people Israel, and that they may know that this house that I have built is called by your name."'

The reason given is missionary.

In order that all the peoples of the earth may know your name.

This is not a footnote about hospitality. In the middle of the dedication of Israel's national sanctuary, on the day it became the one place on earth where Israel's God had put his name, the king asks God to answer foreigners generously specifically so that the whole world will hear about him.

The temple was never meant to be a wall. Isaiah says it in as many words, quoting God about foreigners who join themselves to the LORD: these I will bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer... for my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples (Isa. 56:6-7).

And a thousand years later a man walked into the outer court of the rebuilt temple — the court of the Gentiles, the one place a foreigner could stand — and found it full of money changers and cattle, and threw them out, and said: is it not written, "My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations"? But you have made it a den of robbers (Mark 11:17).

They had filled the only room a foreigner could pray in with livestock.

Solomon asked God to hear that man on the day the building opened.

'"If your people go out to battle against their enemy, by whatever way you shall send them, and they pray to the LORD toward the city that you have chosen and the house that I have built for your name,"'

'"then hear in heaven their prayer and their plea, and maintain their cause."'

The sixth, and it is the shortest, and it is the only one of the seven that does not mention sin.

Notice that, after five petitions that all did. Israel goes out to fight, and there is no suggestion that the war is a judgment or that anybody has done anything wrong. Sometimes trouble is simply trouble.

And look at the qualification he attaches: by whatever way you shall send them.

He is not asking God to bless whatever war Israel decides to fight. The petition covers armies God has sent, and it quietly excludes the rest — which is a good deal more restraint than most national prayers manage, and it is being prayed by a king with twelve thousand horsemen and forty thousand stalls.

The request itself is two words in effect: maintain their cause. Not give them victory. Take up their case, see that right is done. It is the same phrase he uses for the exiles in verse 49, and it is what a man asks for when he trusts the judge more than he trusts the verdict he wants.

'"If they sin against you — for there is no one who does not sin — and you are angry with them and give them to an enemy, so that they are carried away captive to the land of the enemy, far off or near,"'

Now the seventh petition, and it looks further ahead than any prayer in the Old Testament.

First, the parenthesis, and it should not be hurried: for there is no one who does not sin.

He puts it in as a matter of course, in the middle of a sentence, as a fact so obvious it needs no argument. Not most people. Not people who have not been properly taught. Nobody. Paul will build a chapter of Romans on that proposition and quote the Old Testament repeatedly to establish it, and here it is, stated in passing at a temple dedication.

And then the scenario: defeat, captivity, deportation to the land of the enemy.

'"yet if they turn their heart in the land to which they have been carried captive, and repent and plead with you in the land of their captors, saying, 'We have sinned and have acted perversely and wickedly,'"'

'"if they repent with all their mind and with all their heart in the land of their enemies, who carried them captive, and pray to you toward their land, which you gave to their fathers, the city that you have chosen, and the house that I have built for your name,"'

'"then hear in heaven your dwelling place their prayer and their plea, and maintain their cause"'

'"and forgive your people who have sinned against you, and all their transgressions that they have committed against you, and grant them compassion in the sight of those who carried them captive, that they may have compassion on them"'

Now stop and think about who first read this.

The books of Kings were compiled during the exile in Babylon. The last thing recorded in them is a Judean king eating at a Babylonian table (2 Kings 25:27-30). The people who first read this account of the temple were people who had watched that temple burn.

And what they found, in the record of the day it opened, was a prayer that had already asked God to hear them where they were.

In the land of their captors. In the land of their enemies, who carried them captive. Solomon says it three times, three and a half centuries before it happened.

A man in Babylon reading this could put his finger on the sentence and know that on the greatest day in Israel's history somebody had prayed for him by name — not for the nation in the abstract, but for the specific situation of an Israelite far from a ruined city, facing the wrong direction, with nothing left to bring.

Notice what the prayer asks for on his behalf. Not a return, in the first instance. Grant them compassion in the sight of those who carried them captive. Make their captors kind to them.

That is the smaller, humbler request underneath the large one, and it is the one that got answered first. Daniel in a Babylonian court. Nehemiah as cupbearer to a Persian king. Esther. Every one of them a case of God granting his people compassion in the sight of those who held them.

'"(for they are your people, and your heritage, which you brought out of Egypt, from the midst of the iron furnace)."'

'"Let your eyes be open to the plea of your servant and to the plea of your people Israel, giving ear to them whenever they call to you."'

'"For you separated them from among all the peoples of the earth to be your heritage, as you declared through Moses your servant, when you brought our fathers out of Egypt, O Lord GOD."'

The prayer ends where it has gone six times already: Egypt.

The iron furnace. That is Deuteronomy's phrase for the slavery (Deut. 4:20). Standing in the most beautiful building in the world, in the richest reign in Israel's history, the king's final argument for why God should hear his people is that he brought them out of a smelting furnace.

The claim is never merit. It is always the exodus.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 54–66 — Not One Word Has Failed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Solomon rises from before the altar of the LORD, where he had knelt with hands outstretched toward heaven, and blesses the assembly (vv. 54-55). Blessed be the LORD who has given rest to his people Israel, according to all that he promised. Not one word has failed of all his good promise, which he spoke by Moses his servant (v. 56). He asks that God incline their hearts to walk in his ways (vv. 57-58), and that his cause be maintained day by day that all the peoples of the earth may know that the LORD is God; there is no other (vv. 59-60). Let your heart therefore be wholly true to the LORD our God, walking in his statutes and keeping his commandments, as at this day (v. 61). Then twenty-two thousand oxen and a hundred and twenty thousand sheep, a feast of seven days and seven more, and on the eighth day he sends the people away, joyful and glad of heart for all the goodness that the LORD had shown to David his servant and to Israel his people (vv. 62-66).
verseByVerse.theology: Not one word has failed of all his good promise. That is Joshua's claim (Josh. 21:45; 23:14) restated at the high-water mark of the whole story, by a man standing in a finished temple with the glory of God inside it.
verseByVerse.examples: And the last word of his benediction is shalem — whole, complete, undivided — the root of his own name. Let your heart therefore be wholly true to the LORD our God. Chapter 11 says of him: his heart was not wholly true to the LORD his God, as was the heart of David his father (11:4). He is measured by the word of his own blessing.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as Solomon finished offering all this prayer and plea to the LORD, he arose from before the altar of the LORD, where he had knelt with hands outstretched toward heaven. And he stood and blessed all the assembly of Israel with a loud voice, saying, "Blessed be the LORD who has given rest to his people Israel, according to all that he promised. Not one word has failed of all his good promise, which he spoke by Moses his servant. The LORD our God be with us, as he was with our fathers. May he not leave us or forsake us, that he may incline our hearts to him, to walk in all his ways and to keep his commandments, his statutes, and his rules, which he commanded our fathers. Let these words of mine, with which I have pleaded before the LORD, be near to the LORD our God day and night, and may he maintain the cause of his servant and the cause of his people Israel, as each day requires, that all the peoples of the earth may know that the LORD is God; there is no other. Let your heart therefore be wholly true to the LORD our God, walking in his statutes and keeping his commandments, as at this day." Then the king, and all Israel with him, offered sacrifice before the LORD. Solomon offered as peace offerings to the LORD 22,000 oxen and 120,000 sheep. So the king and all the people of Israel dedicated the house of the LORD. The same day the king consecrated the middle of the court that was before the house of the LORD, for there he offered the burnt offering and the grain offering and the fat pieces of the peace offerings, because the bronze altar that was before the LORD was too small to receive the burnt offering and the grain offering and the fat pieces of the peace offerings. So Solomon held the feast at that time, and all Israel with him, a great assembly, from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of Egypt, before the LORD our God, seven days. On the eighth day he sent the people away, and they blessed the king and went to their homes joyful and glad of heart for all the goodness that the LORD had shown to David his servant and to Israel his people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now as Solomon finished offering all this prayer and plea to the LORD, he arose from before the altar of the LORD, where he had knelt with hands outstretched toward heaven.'

Now we are told what he had been doing for the last twenty-six verses.

He was on his knees.

Verse 22 said he stood before the altar and spread out his hands. It did not say this. The writer holds it back until the prayer is over, and then mentions it in passing as the king gets up.

The wealthiest monarch in the world, on the day of the greatest achievement of his reign, prayed the longest prayer in the Old Testament from his knees in a courtyard, in front of the whole nation, with his hands open and empty.

'And he stood and blessed all the assembly of Israel with a loud voice, saying,'

'"Blessed be the LORD who has given rest to his people Israel, according to all that he promised. Not one word has failed of all his good promise, which he spoke by Moses his servant."'

Here is the verdict on the whole story so far.

Not one word has failed of all his good promise.

Joshua said this twice at the end of the conquest — not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed; all came to pass (Josh. 21:45), and again in his farewell: not one word of all the good things that the LORD your God promised concerning you has failed (Josh. 23:14).

Now Solomon says it again, from a finished temple, at the widest borders Israel ever held, with the glory of God in the building behind him.

Count what is behind that sentence. A promise to a childless man in Ur about offspring like the sand. A promise about a land, made to a man who owned one field in it, and that a grave. Four hundred years of slavery, and a bush that would not burn up, and a night with blood on the doorposts. Forty years of wandering with a tent. Judges, and a period when everyone did what was right in his own eyes. A boy with a sling. A man in a cave. A promise in a night vision about a son who would build a house.

All of it, and not one word has failed.

'"The LORD our God be with us, as he was with our fathers. May he not leave us or forsake us,"'

'"that he may incline our hearts to him, to walk in all his ways and to keep his commandments, his statutes, and his rules, which he commanded our fathers."'

This is the most theologically acute request in the chapter.

That he may incline our hearts to him.

He does not ask God to help them keep the commandments. He asks God to bend their hearts toward himself in the first place.

Solomon has understood something about people that a man could easily miss on a day like this. The problem is not information — they have the law, and it has just been read and the covenant is in a box thirty feet away. The problem is that the heart does not lean the right way on its own, and if God does not tilt it, nothing else will help.

It is the prayer of Jeremiah's new covenant, three hundred years early: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts (Jer. 31:33). And of Ezekiel's: I will give you a new heart... and I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes (Ezek. 36:26-27).

A reader who knows chapter 11 will feel the weight of it. Solomon prays that God would incline the hearts of Israel — and the sentence recorded about him at the end is his wives turned away his heart after other gods (11:4).

He asked for the one thing he needed most and did not receive it, or did not keep it.

'"Let these words of mine, with which I have pleaded before the LORD, be near to the LORD our God day and night, and may he maintain the cause of his servant and the cause of his people Israel, as each day requires,"'

'"that all the peoples of the earth may know that the LORD is God; there is no other."'

The foreigner again. That is the second time in this prayer that the horizon opens to the whole world, and the phrase is Deuteronomy's great confession: the LORD is God; there is no other (Deut. 4:35, 39).

'"Let your heart therefore be wholly true to the LORD our God, walking in his statutes and keeping his commandments, as at this day."'

The last word of the benediction is the word he will be measured by.

Wholly true is shalem — whole, complete, undivided, at peace. It is the root of his own name.

He tells the nation that their hearts must be shalem toward God: not partly, not mostly, not on the main points. Undivided.

And here is what the writer records about him at the end of his life: for when Solomon was old his wives turned away his heart after other gods, and his heart was not wholly true to the LORD his God, as was the heart of David his father (11:4).

Not shalem. The exact word of his own blessing, negated, and applied to him.

The writer does not point it out. He has never pointed anything out. He puts the word in Solomon's mouth in chapter 8 and takes it away from him in chapter 11, and leaves the reader to lay the two verses side by side.

'Then the king, and all Israel with him, offered sacrifice before the LORD.'

'Solomon offered as peace offerings to the LORD 22,000 oxen and 120,000 sheep. So the king and all the people of Israel dedicated the house of the LORD.'

The numbers are enormous and the kind of offering matters.

These are peace offerings, which are the sacrifices that get eaten. A burnt offering is entirely consumed; a peace offering is shared, with a portion burned and the rest given back to the worshipper as a meal.

So a hundred and forty-two thousand animals means a national feast on a scale no one there had ever seen. This is not slaughter for its own sake. It is dinner for everybody in the country who came, for two weeks.

'The same day the king consecrated the middle of the court that was before the house of the LORD, because there he offered the burnt offering and the grain offering and the fat pieces of the peace offerings, because the bronze altar that was before the LORD was too small to receive the burnt offering and the grain offering and the fat pieces of the peace offerings.'

The altar was too small.

They had to consecrate the middle of the courtyard as an overflow, because there was more coming than the equipment could handle.

'So Solomon held the feast at that time, and all Israel with him, a great assembly, from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of Egypt, before the LORD our God, seven days.'

From Lebo-hamath to the Brook of Egypt. The full extent of the land, north to south. Every part of the country is represented.

'On the eighth day he sent the people away, and they blessed the king and went to their homes joyful and glad of heart for all the goodness that the LORD had shown to David his servant and to Israel his people.'

This is the last verse of the high-water mark. Read it slowly, because nothing in the rest of the Old Testament is like it.

The whole nation goes home.

They are joyful and glad of heart, and the writer says what about — not about the building, not about the king, not about the empire or the wealth. About all the goodness that the LORD had shown to David his servant and to Israel his people.

The ark is in its place. The glory has filled the house. Not one word of God's promise has failed. The borders run from the Euphrates to Egypt, every man sits under his own vine and fig tree, and a hundred and forty-two thousand animals have been eaten in a fortnight by people who came from every corner of the country.

This is as good as it ever gets.

Three chapters from now the same writer will record that Solomon's heart was not whole, that God raised up adversaries against him, and that a prophet met a young official on a road outside Jerusalem and tore a new cloak into twelve pieces.

But not yet. On this day the people went home glad.

8.theology:
The week he chose (v. 2). The seventh month is Tishri and the feast is Booths, when Israel lived in shelters of branches to remember that their fathers had no houses at all and God went with them. That is the week Solomon moves God into stone.

The end of portable worship (v. 4). The tent of meeting — made at Sinai to a pattern God showed Moses, carried forty years, set up at Shiloh, standing at Gibeon in Solomon's own day — is brought up and stored.

The poles stay in (v. 8). The law required it: the poles shall remain in the rings of the ark; they shall not be taken from it (Ex. 25:15), so that it could always be lifted and never handled — the law a cart made it impossible to keep, and a man died at a threshing floor for it. The ark has now arrived where it will stay for four centuries, and the carrying poles are left in, their ends visible from the Holy Place, which is presumably why the writer mentions it. He is not tied to the building.

Two stones and nothing else (v. 9). That is what the seven years and the hundred and fifty thousand men produced a room for. And the writer says when they were cut and why: at Horeb, when they came out of the land of Egypt. (On the contents: Hebrews describes the tabernacle ark as holding the jar of manna and Aaron's staff as well (Heb. 9:4), while Exodus and Numbers have those placed before the testimony (Ex. 16:34; Num. 17:10), which may mean in front of it. Either way this verse describes the situation four centuries later, and what Kings says is that by Solomon's day there were two tablets in that box and nothing else.)

The liturgy stops (vv. 10-11). Moses finished the tabernacle and was not able to enter the tent of meeting because the cloud settled on it, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle (Ex. 40:34-35). The same thing, in the same words, at twice the scale. And the effect on the professionals is that they cannot work: men who have spent their lives learning a liturgy walk out into the courtyard the moment the glory arrives, because there is nothing they can do in there. And the room has no windows, and Solomon says the darkness is the point — God said he would come in a thick cloud (Ex. 19:9), and Moses drew near to the thick darkness where God was (Ex. 20:21).

God chose a man, not a place (v. 16). I chose no city out of all the tribes of Israel in which to build a house... but I chose David. For four hundred and eighty years God picked no site at all. What he chose was a person, and the building is downstream of that.

You did well that it was in your heart (v. 18). One of the kindest sentences in the Old Testament, and easy to read past. David wanted to build and was refused, laid not one stone of it, and died eleven years before this morning — and God says the wanting was good. That is not a consolation prize and it is not politeness. Anybody who has had a genuine desire to do something for God and been prevented, by health or circumstance or other people's decisions or simply being the wrong person, is looking at the verse for it. The thing was refused; the wanting was not wasted.

He prays the promise back (v. 26). Let your word be confirmed is exactly what his father did in the same situation — do as you have spoken, because you have made this revelation to your servant... therefore your servant has found courage to pray this prayer (2 Sam. 7:25-27). Not informing God of anything: taking him at his word in his hearing.

Verse 27, and who says it. Seven years of work, thirty thousand conscripted in shifts and a hundred and fifty thousand labourers, the finest timber in the world, every stone finished at the quarry, gold over every surface, two pillars twenty-seven feet high, ten thousand gallons of water on twelve bronze oxen — and he is standing in front of it on the day of its dedication with the glory of God visibly inside and the nation watching, and he says it cannot possibly hold him. Will God indeed dwell on the earth? is a genuine question, and not about this building: will God dwell on the earth at all? And then the four words that make the sentence — this house that I have built. He does not distance himself from it; he names it as his own work and says his own work is inadequate to its purpose, on the day it was finished. That is what a hearing heart looks like after seven years of use: the more magnificent it got, the clearer it became that it could not do the one thing it was for.

And the sentence has a long life. Isaiah gives it back as God's own words — heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool; what is the house that you would build for me?... But this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit (Isa. 66:1-2). Stephen quotes it in front of the council about to stone him: the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands (Acts 7:48). Paul says it on the Areopagus in a city full of temples (Acts 17:24). The best thing ever said about the limits of religious buildings was said by the man who built the best one, on the day he opened it.

Yet (v. 28). One word, and it is the turn. The building cannot contain God, and God has chosen to make himself available at a particular place to people who cannot come to heaven. Both need holding. And the phrase Solomon uses six times is my name shall be there — not I shall be there as though God were resident in a room, but his name, his self-disclosure, the way he has made himself findable. Which is why every petition is about praying toward the place, not in it: almost nobody in Israel could get to Jerusalem often, and the exiles of verse 46 cannot get there at all. He has just built God a dwelling place and does not call it one — listen in heaven your dwelling place.

Seven petitions, and every one is about sin (vv. 31-53). A lawsuit with no evidence; defeat; drought; famine and plague and siege; the foreigner; battle; and exile. Not one asks for prosperity, victory, long life or a secure throne — the things he could have asked for at Gibeon and did not. The shape is always the same: a disaster, because they have sinned, then turning, then hear in heaven and forgive. He is not asking God to keep trouble away. He assumes trouble, assumes much of it deserved, and asks that there be a way back. Note also the clause inside the drought petition — when you teach them the good way in which they should walk: the affliction is teaching, and Elijah stands on this petition when he shuts the sky in chapter 17.

Each knowing the affliction of his own heart (v. 38). The most personal clause in the prayer, and it is literally about a man knowing the plague of his own heart — the same word used of the locusts and the mildew, turned inward. Every other petition is corporate; this one is any man, alone, who knows something about himself nobody else in that enormous crowd knows, stretching out his hands. And the parenthesis is why it works: you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind. The man knows the affliction of his own heart, and God knows it too, and God is the only one who does — so the prayer needs no words anybody else hears, and the answer is exact: render to each whose heart you know. Nobody is processed in a group.

The foreigner, and the difference (vv. 41-43). Every petition for Israel runs through repentance — if they turn, if they repent with all their heart. For the foreigner: do according to all for which the foreigner calls to you. All. No conditions, no requirement that he become an Israelite first. And what drew him is exodus vocabulary — your great name and your mighty hand and your outstretched arm, the phrases Deuteronomy uses for Egypt. What reaches a foreigner in a far country is the story of God rescuing slaves. The reason given is missionary: in order that all the peoples of the earth may know your name. The temple was never meant to be a wall — my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples (Isa. 56:7). And a thousand years later a man walked into the one court a foreigner could stand in, found it full of money changers and cattle, and threw them out quoting that verse (Mark 11:17). They had filled the only room a foreigner could pray in with livestock, and Solomon had asked God to hear that man on the day the building opened.

There is no one who does not sin (v. 46). Put in as a parenthesis, mid-sentence, as a fact too obvious to argue. Not most people, not the badly taught — nobody. Paul builds a chapter of Romans on that proposition with a string of citations; here it is, stated in passing at a temple dedication.

The seventh petition, and who first read it (vv. 46-50). Kings was compiled during the exile; the last thing recorded in it is a Judean king eating at a Babylonian table (2 Kings 25:27-30). The people who first read this account of the temple had watched that temple burn — and what they found in the record of its opening was a prayer that had already asked God to hear them where they were. In the land of their captors, three times, three and a half centuries early. A man in Babylon could put his finger on the sentence and know that on the greatest day in Israel's history somebody prayed for his exact situation.

And notice what is asked on his behalf: not a return, in the first instance, but grant them compassion in the sight of those who carried them captive. Make their captors kind to them — which is the request that got answered first, in Daniel in a Babylonian court, Nehemiah as cupbearer to a Persian king, and Esther. And the prayer ends where it has gone six times: the iron furnace (Deut. 4:20). Standing in the most beautiful building in the world, the king's final argument for why God should hear his people is that he brought them out of a smelting furnace. The claim is never merit. It is always the exodus.

He was on his knees (v. 54). Verse 22 said he stood and spread out his hands; the writer holds this back until the prayer is over and mentions it in passing as the king gets up. The wealthiest monarch in the world prayed the longest prayer in the Old Testament from his knees in a courtyard, in front of the nation, with his hands open and empty.

Not one word has failed (v. 56). Joshua said it twice at the end of the conquest (Josh. 21:45; 23:14), and Solomon says it again from a finished temple at the widest borders Israel ever held. Count what stands behind it: a promise to a childless man in Ur about offspring like the sand; a promise about a land, to a man who owned one field in it and that a grave; four hundred years of slavery, a bush that would not burn up, blood on doorposts; forty years of wandering with a tent; judges, and a period when everyone did what was right in his own eyes; a boy with a sling; a man in a cave; a night vision about a son who would build a house.

Incline our hearts (v. 58). The most theologically acute request in the chapter. He does not ask for help keeping the commandments; he asks God to bend their hearts toward himself in the first place. The problem is not information — they have the law, and the covenant is in a box thirty feet away. The heart does not lean the right way on its own, and if God does not tilt it nothing else will help. It is Jeremiah's new covenant three centuries early (Jer. 31:33) and Ezekiel's new heart (Ezek. 36:26-27). And a reader who knows chapter 11 feels the weight: he prayed that God would incline Israel's hearts, and what is recorded of him at the end is his wives turned away his heart after other gods.

The word he is measured by (v. 61). Wholly true is shalem — whole, complete, undivided — the root of his own name. He tells the nation their hearts must be undivided: not partly, not mostly, not on the main points. And the writer's verdict on him is his heart was not wholly true to the LORD his God, as was the heart of David his father (11:4). The exact word of his own blessing, negated and applied to him. The writer does not point it out; he puts the word in Solomon's mouth in chapter 8, takes it away in chapter 11, and leaves the reader to set the two verses side by side.

Peace offerings, which are eaten (v. 63). Twenty-two thousand oxen and a hundred and twenty thousand sheep — and a peace offering is shared, a portion burned and the rest given back to the worshipper as a meal. This is not slaughter for its own sake; it is dinner for everybody in the country who came, for a fortnight. And the bronze altar was too small, so they had to consecrate the middle of the courtyard as overflow: there was more coming than the equipment could handle.

This is as good as it ever gets (v. 66). The whole nation goes home joyful and glad of heart, and the writer says what about — not the building, not the king, not the empire: all the goodness that the LORD had shown to David his servant and to Israel his people. The ark is in its place, the glory has filled the house, not one word has failed, the borders run from the Euphrates to Egypt, every man sits under his own vine. Three chapters on, the same writer records that Solomon's heart was not whole, that God raised up adversaries, and that a prophet tore a new cloak into twelve pieces on a road outside Jerusalem. But not yet. On this day the people went home glad.
8.examples:
Then: The richest king on earth finished the most expensive building in his nation's history, watched the glory of God fill it so completely that the priests had to walk out of the room — and then knelt down in the courtyard in front of the whole country and said out loud that the thing he had just spent seven years building could not possibly hold the God it was built for.

Now: Three things. Verse 27 is the one to take away, and its power is who said it and when. It is easy to be humble about somebody else's achievement; Solomon said his own finest work was inadequate on the day it was finished, with everyone watching and nobody requiring it of him. Second, verse 38: in the middle of a national occasion with a hundred and forty thousand animals being offered, the prayer stops for the one man who knows the affliction of his own heart and cannot say it to anybody. If you are that person, the temple was for you, and the reason it works is the parenthesis — God alone knows the hearts of all the children of mankind. And third, verse 58, which is the honest request. He did not ask for help obeying. He asked God to incline their hearts, because the heart does not lean the right way on its own — and the man who prayed it had his own heart turned away in the end, which is why it is the prayer to keep praying.

9.text: <sup>1</sup>As soon as Solomon had finished building the house of the LORD and the king's house and all that Solomon desired to build,<sup>2</sup>the LORD appeared to Solomon a second time, as he had appeared to him at Gibeon.<sup>3</sup>And the LORD said to him, "I have heard your prayer and your plea, which you have made before me. I have consecrated this house that you have built, by putting my name there forever. My eyes and my heart will be there for all time.<sup>4</sup>And as for you, if you will walk before me, as David your father walked, with integrity of heart and uprightness, doing according to all that I have commanded you, and keeping my statutes and my rules,<sup>5</sup>then I will establish your royal throne over Israel forever, as I promised David your father, saying, 'You shall not lack a man on the throne of Israel.'<sup>6</sup>But if you turn aside from following me, you or your children, and do not keep my commandments and my statutes that I have set before you, but go and serve other gods and worship them,<sup>7</sup>then I will cut off Israel from the land that I have given them, and the house that I have consecrated for my name I will cast out of my sight, and Israel will become a proverb and a byword among all peoples.<sup>8</sup>And this house will become a heap of ruins. Everyone passing by it will be astonished and will hiss, and they will say, 'Why has the LORD done thus to this land and to this house?'<sup>9</sup>Then they will say, 'Because they abandoned the LORD their God who brought their fathers out of the land of Egypt and laid hold on other gods and worshiped them and served them. Therefore the LORD has brought all this disaster on them.'"<sup>10</sup>At the end of twenty years, in which Solomon had built the two houses, the house of the LORD and the king's house,<sup>11</sup>and Hiram king of Tyre had supplied Solomon with cedar and cypress timber and gold, as much as he desired, King Solomon gave to Hiram twenty cities in the land of Galilee.<sup>12</sup>But when Hiram came from Tyre to see the cities that Solomon had given him, they did not please him.<sup>13</sup>Therefore he said, "What kind of cities are these that you have given me, my brother?" So they are called the land of Cabul to this day.<sup>14</sup>Hiram had sent to the king 120 talents of gold.<sup>15</sup>And this is the account of the forced labor that King Solomon drafted to build the house of the LORD and his own house and the Millo and the wall of Jerusalem and Hazor and Megiddo and Gezer<sup>16</sup>(Pharaoh king of Egypt had gone up and captured Gezer and burned it with fire, and had killed the Canaanites who lived in the city, and had given it as dowry to his daughter, Solomon's wife;<sup>17</sup>so Solomon rebuilt Gezer) and Lower Beth-horon<sup>18</sup>and Baalath and Tamar in the wilderness, in the land of Judah,<sup>19</sup>and all the store cities that Solomon had, and the cities for his chariots, and the cities for his horsemen, and whatever Solomon desired to build in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and in all the land of his dominion.<sup>20</sup>All the people who were left of the Amorites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, who were not of the people of Israel—<sup>21</sup>their descendants who were left after them in the land, whom the people of Israel were unable to devote to destruction — these Solomon drafted to be slaves, and so they are to this day.<sup>22</sup>But of the people of Israel Solomon made no slaves. They were the soldiers, they were his officials, his commanders, his captains, his chariot commanders and his horsemen.<sup>23</sup>These were the chief officers who were over Solomon's work: 550 who had charge of the people who carried on the work.<sup>24</sup>But Pharaoh's daughter went up from the city of David to her own house that Solomon had built for her. Then he built the Millo.<sup>25</sup>Three times a year Solomon used to offer up burnt offerings and peace offerings on the altar that he built to the LORD, making offerings with it before the LORD. So he finished the house.<sup>26</sup>King Solomon built a fleet of ships at Ezion-geber, which is near Eloth on the shore of the Red Sea, in the land of Edom.<sup>27</sup>And Hiram sent with the fleet his servants, seamen who were familiar with the sea, together with the servants of Solomon.<sup>28</sup>And they went to Ophir and brought from there gold, 420 talents, and they brought it to King Solomon.
9.overview:
God appears a second time, and the writer says so explicitly and points back to Gibeon. That is not a stylistic detail: two chapters from now the charge against Solomon is aggravated by this exact fact — the LORD was angry with Solomon, because his heart had turned away from the LORD, the God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice (11:9).

What he says first is the answer to chapter 8, granted in the words it was asked in — and then more than was asked. Solomon prayed that God's eyes be open toward the house night and day. God says my eyes and my heart will be there for all time. Nobody asked for his heart. The word is lev, the same word Solomon used when he asked for a hearing heart and the same word chapter 11 uses against him. God's attention and his affection will both be fixed on that building, permanently — which means that when it is looted, stripped, defiled and finally burned, his heart is in it the whole time.

And then, to the man in the year he finished it, God says the house will become a heap of ruins. Read the two sentences four verses apart: my eyes and my heart will be there for all time, and I will cast it out of my sight. That is the whole theology of the temple, stated by God in the harshest available form.

The question in verse 8 is not theoretical. The people who first read this book had watched Nebuchadnezzar's men burn that house, and their question was not whether God was angry but whether he was finished or defeated — and they found their own question in the middle of the temple account, four centuries early, already answered. Not that God failed and not that Babylon's gods were stronger, which is what any other nation would have concluded: because they abandoned the LORD their God who brought their fathers out of the land of Egypt.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — My Eyes and My Heart Will Be There
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When Solomon has finished the house of the LORD and his own house, the LORD appeared to Solomon a second time, as he had appeared to him at Gibeon (vv. 1-2). I have heard your prayer and your plea, which you have made before me. I have consecrated this house that you have built, by putting my name there forever.
