My eyes and my heart will be there for all time (v. 3). Then the condition: if you walk before me as David did, I will establish your royal throne over Israel forever (vv. 4-5). But if you turn aside from following me, you or your children, and do not keep my commandments... and go and serve other gods and worship them, then I will cut off Israel from the land that I have given them, and the house that I have consecrated for my name I will cast out of my sight (vv. 6-7). And this house will become a heap of ruins. Everyone passing by it will be astonished and will hiss, and they will say, "Why has the LORD done thus to this land and to this house?" (v. 8). And the answer: because they abandoned the LORD their God who brought their fathers out of the land of Egypt (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the answer to chapter 8. Solomon asked that God's eyes be open toward the house night and day (8:29), and God says my eyes and my heart will be there for all time — which is more than was asked, because nobody asked for his heart.
verseByVerse.examples: And in the same breath, to the man in the year he finished it, God says the building will become a heap of ruins. The question in verse 8 is the question the first readers of this book were asking in Babylon, standing in the ash of it. Verse 9 is the answer, and the whole of Kings is the long working out of that answer.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as Solomon had finished building the house of the LORD and the king's house and all that Solomon desired to build, the LORD appeared to Solomon a second time, as he had appeared to him at Gibeon. And the LORD said to him, "I have heard your prayer and your plea, which you have made before me. I have consecrated this house that you have built, by putting my name there forever. My eyes and my heart will be there for all time. And as for you, if you will walk before me, as David your father walked, with integrity of heart and uprightness, doing according to all that I have commanded you, and keeping my statutes and my rules, then I will establish your royal throne over Israel forever, as I promised David your father, saying, 'You shall not lack a man on the throne of Israel.' But if you turn aside from following me, you or your children, and do not keep my commandments and my statutes that I have set before you, but go and serve other gods and worship them, then I will cut off Israel from the land that I have given them, and the house that I have consecrated for my name I will cast out of my sight, and Israel will become a proverb and a byword among all peoples. And this house will become a heap of ruins. Everyone passing by it will be astonished and will hiss, and they will say, 'Why has the LORD done thus to this land and to this house?' Then they will say, 'Because they abandoned the LORD their God who brought their fathers out of the land of Egypt and laid hold on other gods and worshiped them and served them. Therefore the LORD has brought all this disaster on them.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'As soon as Solomon had finished building the house of the LORD and the king's house and all that Solomon desired to build,'

Note the third item in that list.

The house of the LORD, the king's house, and all that Solomon desired to build. The writer has been keeping a running account and he keeps adding to it without comment.

'the LORD appeared to Solomon a second time, as he had appeared to him at Gibeon.'

A second time.

The writer says so explicitly and points back to Gibeon, and it is not a stylistic detail. Two chapters from now, when the account of the reign comes due, this exact fact is what makes the charge so heavy: and the LORD was angry with Solomon, because his heart had turned away from the LORD, the God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice (11:9).

God does not appear twice to many people. Abraham, Moses, Jacob — and this man, once as a young king who asked for a hearing heart, and once here.

'And the LORD said to him, "I have heard your prayer and your plea, which you have made before me. I have consecrated this house that you have built, by putting my name there forever. My eyes and my heart will be there for all time."'

This is the answer to chapter 8, and it should be read with that prayer open beside it.

Solomon asked: that your eyes may be open night and day toward this house, the place of which you have said, "My name shall be there" (8:29).

God says: I have consecrated this house that you have built, by putting my name there forever. Granted, in the words it was asked in.

Then something nobody asked for.

My eyes and my heart will be there for all time.

Solomon asked for the eyes. God adds the heart.

That is a remarkable thing for God to say about a building, and the urge to soften it into a figure of speech should be resisted. The word is lev, the same word Solomon used when he asked for a hearing heart, and the same word that will be used against him in chapter 11. God is saying that his attention and his affection will both be fixed on that place, permanently.

Consider what that means for what follows. When the building is looted by Shishak within a generation, stripped by Ahaz and Hezekiah to pay tribute, defiled by Manasseh, and finally burned by Nebuchadnezzar's men — God's heart is in it the whole time.

He is not indifferent to the destruction of his own house. He says so before he threatens it.

'"And as for you, if you will walk before me, as David your father walked, with integrity of heart and uprightness, doing according to all that I have commanded you, and keeping my statutes and my rules,"'

'"then I will establish your royal throne over Israel forever, as I promised David your father, saying, 'You shall not lack a man on the throne of Israel.'"'

The standard given is his father, and the terms are the conditional half of the covenant — the same half David quoted to him on his deathbed (2:4).

Note the phrase for what David had: integrity of heart and uprightness. Integrity is tom, which means wholeness, undividedness. It is very close to the shalem Solomon used in his own benediction, and it is what 11:4 will say he did not have.

'"But if you turn aside from following me, you or your children, and do not keep my commandments and my statutes that I have set before you, but go and serve other gods and worship them,"'

There is the sin named in advance, and it is exactly the one he commits.

Not injustice. Not cruelty. Not pride. Go and serve other gods and worship them.

Chapter 11 opens with seven hundred wives, and closes the account with Solomon went after Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, and after Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites (11:5).

He was told the precise thing to avoid, twice, by God in person.

'"then I will cut off Israel from the land that I have given them, and the house that I have consecrated for my name I will cast out of my sight, and Israel will become a proverb and a byword among all peoples."'

Now God says what he will do to the building he has just put his heart in.

The house that I have consecrated for my name I will cast out of my sight.

Read those two sentences together, because they are four verses apart and they are the whole theology of the temple. My eyes and my heart will be there for all time. And: I will cast it out of my sight.

The building is not the guarantee. God said it in the middle of the scaffolding in chapter 6, and Solomon said it himself on dedication day in chapter 8, and here God says it a third time in the harshest available form: a house I have consecrated, with my name on it and my heart in it, will go if you go after other gods.

'"And this house will become a heap of ruins. Everyone passing by it will be astonished and will hiss, and they will say, 'Why has the LORD done thus to this land and to this house?'"'

Stop here, because of who first read this sentence.

The books of Kings were put together during the exile in Babylon. The people holding this scroll had seen it happen. Nebuchadnezzar's men burned the house of the LORD and the king's house and every great house in Jerusalem, and broke up the bronze pillars and carried the metal away, and the men of Judah were marched off in chains (2 Kings 25:9-13).

And those people had a question, and it is not a theoretical one. Their whole national theology said that this God had chosen Zion and put his name there and would defend it. So when it burned, the question was not is God angry. It was is God finished, or is he defeated?

Here is that question, put into the mouth of a passer-by, four hundred years before it happened, in a word spoken to the man who laid the foundations.

Why has the LORD done thus to this land and to this house?

The exiles found their own question in the middle of the account of the temple's dedication, and they found it already answered.

'"Then they will say, 'Because they abandoned the LORD their God who brought their fathers out of the land of Egypt and laid hold on other gods and worshiped them and served them. Therefore the LORD has brought all this disaster on them.'"'

There is the answer, and it is the thesis of both books of Kings.

Everything from here to the end of 2 Kings is the working out of this one sentence. Chapter after chapter of kings who did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and prophets sent and ignored, and high places not taken away, and finally the armies from the north.

The point of the answer is what it rules out.

It was not that God failed. It was not that Babylon's gods were stronger, which is what any other nation in the ancient world would have concluded from the same evidence, and which is why the writer puts the answer in the mouth of foreign passers-by.

It was that the people abandoned the God who brought their fathers out of the land of Egypt.

The exodus again, at the end of the sentence, exactly where Solomon kept putting it in chapter 8. The charge is not that Israel broke rules. It is that they walked away from the God who had come and got them out of a furnace.

There is a mercy inside the shape of it that is easy to miss. A God who has been defeated cannot help you. A God who has judged you can. If the ruin is God's own doing and for a stated reason, then repentance is a live option and there is somebody to repent to — which is exactly what Solomon asked for in the seventh petition, and exactly what a man in Babylon needed to know.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the end of twenty years of building, Solomon gives Hiram twenty cities in Galilee for the timber and gold he had supplied (vv. 10-11). But when Hiram came from Tyre to see the cities that Solomon had given him, they did not please him. Therefore he said, "What kind of cities are these that you have given me, my brother?" So they are called the land of Cabul to this day (vv. 12-13). He had sent a hundred and twenty talents of gold (v. 14). Then the account of the levy for the Millo, the wall of Jerusalem, Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer — Pharaoh king of Egypt had gone up and captured Gezer and burned it with fire, and had killed the Canaanites who lived in the city, and had given it as dowry to his daughter, Solomon's wife (vv. 15-16) — and the store cities and chariot cities he built (vv. 17-19).
verseByVerse.theology: The sour note is recorded and left there. Hiram loved David, blessed the LORD, supplied every beam in the temple and a hundred and twenty talents of gold — and at the settlement he looks at what he has been given and says what kind of cities are these? The name stuck.
verseByVerse.examples: And Gezer arrives as a wedding present. An Egyptian army burned an Israelite town, killed its people, and handed it to Solomon as a dowry. That is the marriage of 3:1 delivering territory, and it is the second thing the law warned about — not merely a foreign wife but a return of dealings with Egypt.

verseByVerse.quote: At the end of twenty years, in which Solomon had built the two houses, the house of the LORD and the king's house, and Hiram king of Tyre had supplied Solomon with cedar and cypress timber and gold, as much as he desired, King Solomon gave to Hiram twenty cities in the land of Galilee. But when Hiram came from Tyre to see the cities that Solomon had given him, they did not please him. Therefore he said, "What kind of cities are these that you have given me, my brother?" So they are called the land of Cabul to this day. Hiram had sent to the king 120 talents of gold. And this is the account of the forced labor that King Solomon drafted to build the house of the LORD and his own house and the Millo and the wall of Jerusalem and Hazor and Megiddo and Gezer (Pharaoh king of Egypt had gone up and captured Gezer and burned it with fire, and had killed the Canaanites who lived in the city, and had given it as dowry to his daughter, Solomon's wife; so Solomon rebuilt Gezer) and Lower Beth-horon and Baalath and Tamar in the wilderness, in the land of Judah, and all the store cities that Solomon had, and the cities for his chariots, and the cities for his horsemen, and whatever Solomon desired to build in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and in all the land of his dominion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'At the end of twenty years, in which Solomon had built the two houses, the house of the LORD and the king's house,'

Twenty years. Seven on the temple and thirteen on the palace, and the writer adds them up for us.

'and Hiram king of Tyre had supplied Solomon with cedar and cypress timber and gold, as much as he desired, King Solomon gave to Hiram twenty cities in the land of Galilee.'

The settlement, and it is territory rather than money.

That is worth a moment on its own. The land of Israel was not the crown's to sell. It was allotted by lot under Joshua, tribe by tribe and family by family, as each household's portion of what God had promised Abraham, and the law made permanent alienation nearly impossible — the land shall not be sold in perpetuity, for the land is mine. For you are strangers and sojourners with me (Lev. 25:23).

Solomon hands over twenty towns of it to pay a bill.

'But when Hiram came from Tyre to see the cities that Solomon had given him, they did not please him.'

He comes to look at them, and he does not like what he sees.

'Therefore he said, "What kind of cities are these that you have given me, my brother?" So they are called the land of Cabul to this day.'

Here is a small sour scene set down in the middle of the glory, and the writer does nothing with it at all.

Hiram has been the best friend Israel had. He loved David and sent him cedar unasked. He blessed the LORD by name and credited him with Solomon's wisdom. He supplied every beam in the house of God, sent his own craftsmen, and shipped a hundred and twenty talents of gold on top.

And when the account is settled he is given twenty towns in Galilee, and he travels down to inspect them, and asks a question with an edge on it: what kind of cities are these that you have given me, my brother?

The word brother is treaty language between allied kings, and here it is doing the work that word does when a business relationship has just soured.

He named the district. Cabul is close to a Hebrew phrase meaning something like as nothing or good for nothing, and whatever the precise derivation, the name is an insult and it stuck. The writer says to this day, which means people were still calling that stretch of Galilee by a Phoenician king's rude remark centuries later.

Chronicles records the transaction the other way round, with Hiram giving cities to Solomon (2 Chron. 8:2); the likeliest reading is that they were returned and rebuilt after this exchange.

What it leaves behind is smaller than a doctrine and true to life. The most generous foreign friendship in Israel's history ends its recorded dealings with a disappointed man looking at what he has been paid and asking what kind of cities these are.

'Hiram had sent to the king 120 talents of gold.'

'And this is the account of the forced labor that King Solomon drafted to build the house of the LORD and his own house and the Millo and the wall of Jerusalem and Hazor and Megiddo and Gezer'

The list keeps growing. It began with the house of the LORD and it now includes fortifications and three major cities and the Millo, which was some kind of earthwork or terracing on the Jerusalem ridge.

'(Pharaoh king of Egypt had gone up and captured Gezer and burned it with fire, and had killed the Canaanites who lived in the city, and had given it as dowry to his daughter, Solomon's wife;'

Now read that parenthesis carefully, because a great deal is in it.

An Egyptian army came up into the land, took an Israelite border town, burned it, and killed the population. Then Pharaoh gave the site to his daughter as a wedding present, and she brought it to Solomon.

Gezer was in the territory allotted to Ephraim (Josh. 16:3), and it had never been properly taken; Judges records that the Canaanites lived on in it (Judg. 1:29). So the town had been a standing failure of the conquest for three hundred years, and it is now handed to Israel by a foreign power that solved the problem for them.

Which sounds like a gift, and the writer states it flatly, and there are two things underneath it that he does not state.

The first is that Egypt has just conducted a military operation inside the land of promise and been thanked for it.

The second is the marriage. This is what the alliance of 3:1 actually produced — territory, a burned town, and an obligation. The law's warning about a king and Egypt was not superstition about a country; it was that the deal always costs more than the goods.

'so Solomon rebuilt Gezer) and Lower Beth-horon,'

'and Baalath and Tamar in the wilderness, in the land of Judah,'

'and all the store cities that Solomon had, and the cities for his chariots, and the cities for his horsemen, and whatever Solomon desired to build in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and in all the land of his dominion.'

The cities for his chariots, and the cities for his horsemen.

The forty thousand stalls of 4:26 have to be somewhere, and here are the towns built to hold them. Archaeologists have found the stabling at Megiddo, which is named two verses earlier.

The phrase at the end of the verse is the one the writer keeps using and never comments on: whatever Solomon desired to build. It appeared in verse 1 as well. Three times now the account of a reign that began by asking God for a hearing heart has been summarised as a list of what the king wanted.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The surviving Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites are put to permanent forced labour (vv. 20-21). But of the people of Israel Solomon made no slaves. They were the soldiers, they were his officials, his commanders, his captains, his chariot commanders and his horsemen (v. 22). Five hundred and fifty chief officers had charge of the work (v. 23). But Pharaoh's daughter went up from the city of David to her own house that Solomon had built for her. Then he built the Millo (v. 24). Three times a year he offers on the altar he built (v. 25). And a fleet is built at Ezion-geber on the Red Sea; Hiram sends seamen who know the sea, and they bring back four hundred and twenty talents of gold from Ophir (vv. 26-28).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 22 says plainly that Solomon made no slaves of Israelites, and 5:13 says he drafted forced labour out of all Israel. Two arrangements are being described — the Canaanite one permanent, the Israelite one rotational — and the men of chapter 12 did not experience the distinction as a large one.
verseByVerse.examples: And Pharaoh's daughter is moved out of the city of David. Chronicles gives the reason in Solomon's own words: my wife shall not live in the house of David king of Israel, for the places to which the ark of the LORD has come are holy (2 Chron. 8:11). It is a genuine scruple about holiness, carefully applied — and it does not touch the marriage.

verseByVerse.quote: All the people who were left of the Amorites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, who were not of the people of Israel— their descendants who were left after them in the land, whom the people of Israel were unable to devote to destruction — these Solomon drafted to be slaves, and so they are to this day. But of the people of Israel Solomon made no slaves. They were the soldiers, they were his officials, his commanders, his captains, his chariot commanders and his horsemen. These were the chief officers who were over Solomon's work: 550 who had charge of the people who carried on the work. But Pharaoh's daughter went up from the city of David to her own house that Solomon had built for her. Then he built the Millo. Three times a year Solomon used to offer up burnt offerings and peace offerings on the altar that he built to the LORD, making offerings with it before the LORD. So he finished the house. King Solomon built a fleet of ships at Ezion-geber, which is near Eloth on the shore of the Red Sea, in the land of Edom. And Hiram sent with the fleet his servants, seamen who were familiar with the sea, together with the servants of Solomon. And they went to Ophir and brought from there gold, 420 talents, and they brought it to King Solomon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'All the people who were left of the Amorites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, who were not of the people of Israel —'

'their descendants who were left after them in the land, whom the people of Israel were unable to devote to destruction — these Solomon drafted to be slaves, and so they are to this day.'

The permanent labour force is drawn from the peoples Israel never drove out.

The phrase whom the people of Israel were unable to devote to destruction is the writer reaching back to Joshua and Judges. The conquest was never completed; the book of Judges opens with a long list of what each tribe failed to take, and God said at Bochim they shall become thorns in your sides, and their gods shall be a snare to you (Judg. 2:3).

Two chapters from now, Solomon is worshipping their gods.

'But of the people of Israel Solomon made no slaves. They were the soldiers, they were his officials, his commanders, his captains, his chariot commanders and his horsemen.'

Here is the verse that sits against 5:13, and both should be stated.

This one says Solomon made no slaves of Israelites, and lists what they were instead: soldiers, officials, commanders, captains, chariot commanders, horsemen.

Chapter 5 said: King Solomon drafted forced labor out of all Israel, and the draft numbered 30,000 men, sent to Lebanon ten thousand a month in shifts.

The reconciliation is a real one. Two different arrangements are being described — a permanent Canaanite bondage and a rotational Israelite levy for a specific project — and the Hebrew uses somewhat different terms. Legally the distinction holds.

And it should be said, again, that the men who came to Rehoboam three chapters from now did not experience it as a large distinction. Their word for it was yoke.

'These were the chief officers who were over Solomon's work: 550 who had charge of the people who carried on the work.'

'But Pharaoh's daughter went up from the city of David to her own house that Solomon had built for her. Then he built the Millo.'

Here is a genuine scruple, carefully applied, and it deserves to be taken seriously.

The reason is given in Chronicles, in Solomon's own words: my wife shall not live in the house of David king of Israel, for the places to which the ark of the LORD has come are holy (2 Chron. 8:11).

He has thought about it. The ark came into the city of David; the ground it touched is holy; and a woman who worships the gods of Egypt should not be living on it. So he builds her a house elsewhere and moves her out.

That is not hypocrisy and it is not nothing. It is a man taking holiness seriously enough to rearrange his household over it.

It does not touch the marriage.

He has correctly identified that there is a problem with a foreign wife and the holiness of God, and he has solved it by moving her to a different postcode. The law's concern was never the address. You shall not intermarry with them... for they would turn away your sons from following me, to serve other gods (Deut. 7:3-4). The danger was in the house, not in the neighbourhood.

It is a very recognisable kind of care: real, thought about, sincerely costly, and aimed slightly to one side of the actual problem. And chapter 11 says exactly what happened.

'Three times a year Solomon used to offer up burnt offerings and peace offerings on the altar that he built to the LORD, making offerings with it before the LORD. So he finished the house.'

Three times a year is the requirement of the law — Unleavened Bread, Weeks, and Booths, the three pilgrim feasts when all Israel's males were to appear before the LORD (Deut. 16:16).

He keeps them.

'King Solomon built a fleet of ships at Ezion-geber, which is near Eloth on the shore of the Red Sea, in the land of Edom.'

'And Hiram sent with the fleet his servants, seamen who were familiar with the sea, together with the servants of Solomon.'

Israel builds ships and has to borrow sailors.

The same pattern as the timber: the fleet is Solomon's, the port is on the Red Sea in territory his father conquered, and the men who can actually handle a ship come from Tyre. The Phoenicians were the great sailors of the ancient world, and Israel was not a seafaring people.

Note also that Hiram, having just complained about his twenty cities, sends his crews anyway. The alliance survives the argument.

'And they went to Ophir and brought from there gold, 420 talents, and they brought it to King Solomon.'

Ophir is somewhere down the Red Sea — Arabia, or Africa, or further; nobody knows, and it became a byword for the finest gold. Job speaks of it, and a psalm has the queen standing in gold of Ophir.

Four hundred and twenty talents is something in the order of fifteen tons.

The chapter that began with God saying my eyes and my heart will be there for all time ends with a shipment of gold, and the next chapter is about what came in yearly.

9.theology:
A second time (v. 2). God does not appear twice to many people — Abraham, Jacob, Moses, and this man: once as a young king who asked for a hearing heart, and once here. The writer records it because 11:9 will make it the aggravation.

More than was asked (v. 3). Solomon prayed that your eyes may be open night and day toward this house (8:29), and God grants it in the same words and adds the heart. Resist softening it into a figure of speech: the word is lev, and God is saying his attention and his affection will both be fixed there permanently. He is not indifferent to the destruction of his own house — he says so before he threatens it.

The sin named in advance (v. 6). Not injustice, not cruelty, not pride: go and serve other gods and worship them. Chapter 11 opens with seven hundred wives and closes with Solomon went after Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, and after Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites (11:5). He was told the precise thing to avoid, twice, by God in person. And the standard held up is his father's integrity of heart — tom, wholeness, undividedness, very close to the shalem of Solomon's own benediction and to what 11:4 says he lacked.

Four verses apart (vv. 3, 7). My eyes and my heart will be there for all time, and the house that I have consecrated for my name I will cast out of my sight. The building is not the guarantee. God said it in the middle of the scaffolding in chapter 6, Solomon said it himself on dedication day in chapter 8, and here God says it a third time in the harshest form available: a house with my name on it and my heart in it will go if you go after other gods.

The exiles' own question, four centuries early (v. 8). Kings was compiled in Babylon by people who had seen the house burned and the bronze pillars broken up and carried away (2 Kings 25:9-13). Their whole national theology said God had chosen Zion and put his name there, so the question was not is God angry but is God finished, or defeated? And here is that question in the mouth of a passer-by, spoken to the man who laid the foundations.

The thesis of both books (v. 9). Everything from here to the end of 2 Kings works out this one sentence — kings who did evil, prophets sent and ignored, high places not taken away, and finally the armies from the north. And the point of the answer is what it rules out: not that God failed, and not that Babylon's gods were stronger, which is what any other nation in that world would have concluded from the same evidence, which is why the writer puts the answer in foreign mouths. The charge is not that Israel broke rules but that they walked away from the God who brought their fathers out of the land of Egypt. And there is a mercy in the shape of it: a God who has been defeated cannot help you, and a God who has judged you can. If the ruin is his own doing and for a stated reason, repentance is live and there is somebody to repent to — which is exactly what the seventh petition asked for.

Cabul (vv. 12-13). The settlement is paid in territory, and the land was not the crown's to sell: it was allotted by lot under Joshua as each household's portion of the promise, and the land shall not be sold in perpetuity, for the land is mine (Lev. 25:23). And the best friend Israel had — who loved David, sent cedar unasked, blessed the LORD by name, supplied every beam and a hundred and twenty talents of gold — travels down to look at his payment and asks what kind of cities are these that you have given me, my brother? The word brother is treaty language, doing what that word does when a relationship has soured. The name he gave the district sounds like a Hebrew phrase for as nothing, and it stuck: people were still calling that part of Galilee by a Phoenician's rude remark centuries later. (Chronicles has the cities going the other way at 2 Chron. 8:2; likeliest they were returned and rebuilt.)

Gezer as a wedding present (v. 16). An Egyptian army came into the land of promise, burned an Israelite border town, killed the population, and handed the site to Solomon as a dowry. Gezer was allotted to Ephraim (Josh. 16:3) and had never been properly taken (Judg. 1:29) — a three-hundred-year failure of the conquest, solved for Israel by a foreign power and thanked for. That is what the alliance of 3:1 actually produced: territory, a burned town, and an obligation. The law's warning about a king and Egypt was not superstition about a country; it was that the deal always costs more than the goods.

Thorns in your sides (vv. 20-21). The permanent labour force is drawn from the peoples Israel never drove out — and the phrase whom the people of Israel were unable to devote to destruction reaches back to Judges, which opens with a list of what each tribe failed to take, and to God's word at Bochim: they shall become thorns in your sides, and their gods shall be a snare to you (Judg. 2:3). Two chapters from now Solomon is worshipping those gods.

Verse 22 against 5:13. Here, no slaves of Israel, and a list of what they were instead. There, forced labor out of all Israel, thirty thousand in monthly shifts. Two arrangements, permanent and rotational, with different terms in the Hebrew; legally the distinction holds. And the men who came to Rehoboam three chapters from now had one word for it, and the word was yoke.

A real scruple, aimed slightly to one side (v. 24). Chronicles gives his reasoning: my wife shall not live in the house of David king of Israel, for the places to which the ark of the LORD has come are holy (2 Chron. 8:11). He has thought about it and rearranged his household over it, and that is neither hypocrisy nor nothing. And it does not touch the marriage. He identified correctly that there was a problem between a foreign wife and the holiness of God, and solved it by moving her to a different address — when the law's concern was never the address: they would turn away your sons from following me (Deut. 7:3-4). The danger was in the house, not the neighbourhood. It is a very recognisable kind of care: real, considered, genuinely costly, and aimed just past the actual problem.

Whatever Solomon desired to build (vv. 1, 19). Twice in one chapter, and the list keeps growing — the house of the LORD, the king's house, the Millo, the wall, Hazor, Megiddo, Gezer, store cities, and the cities for his chariots and horsemen, which is where the forty thousand stalls of 4:26 were kept. A reign that began by asking God for a hearing heart is now summarised as a list of what the king wanted.
9.examples:
Then: In the year the temple was finished, God appeared to the man who had built it and said that his eyes and his heart would be in that house for all time — and four verses later, that if Israel went after other gods he would cast it out of his sight and leave it a heap of ruins that passers-by would ask questions about. Four centuries later, people standing in the ash of it read that paragraph and found their own question written down in it.

Now: Three things. Verse 3 and verse 7 belong together and neither survives alone: God is not detached about the things he gives, and he will not be held hostage by them either. Second, verse 9 is the answer to the hardest question anybody asks in a catastrophe — and notice the mercy hidden in it. A God who has been defeated cannot help you. A God who has judged you can, and there is somebody to go back to. And third, verse 24, which is the uncomfortable one: Solomon took holiness seriously enough to move his wife out of a whole district over it, and the danger was never the district. Real scruple, real cost, aimed a few degrees off the actual problem — and chapter 11 records exactly what that was worth.

10.overview:
What she heard about was not the gold. It was the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD — which is precisely what Solomon had asked for at the dedication, that God would answer the foreigner in order that all the peoples of the earth may know your name (8:43). Sheba is most probably in south-west Arabia: something like fifteen hundred miles of desert each way, by camel, months of travelling, on the strength of a report. And she came to test him — the word is riddles, and testing a foreign king's wisdom with them was a recognised contest. She is not a tourist; she has come to find out whether it is true, and she says so: I did not believe the reports until I came.

Read the list of what she saw in the order she saw it: the wisdom, the house, the table, the seating of the officials, the servants and their clothing, the cupbearers — and last, climactically, his burnt offerings that he offered at the house of the LORD. The thing that finished her was the worship. And the writer's phrase for the effect is physical: there was no more breath in her.

Then verse 9, which is the finest thing said in the chapter, and a pagan queen says it. She gets three things right that Israel keeps forgetting: the LORD did this and delighted in you; he did it because the LORD loved Israel, so the king is a gift to the nation and not the reverse; and the throne exists that you may execute justice and righteousness. She names the purpose of the office — the first person to do so since 2 Samuel 8:15 — and she is a foreigner who has been in the country a few weeks.

And then the inventory. Every item is glorious and the writer stages it in tones of wonder: six hundred and sixty-six talents of gold in a year, five hundred golden shields, an ivory throne with twelve lions, silver not counted as anything, ships bringing apes and peacocks. And the law about Israel's kings had three prohibitions, and this chapter contains all three of them described as achievements — horses, Egypt, and silver and gold beyond counting. One is left, and it is the only one with a reason attached, and it is the first verse of chapter 11.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Half Was Not Told Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The queen of Sheba hears of Solomon's fame concerning the name of the LORD and comes to test him with hard questions, with a very great retinue, camels bearing spices and gold and precious stones (vv. 1-2). And Solomon answered all her questions; there was nothing hidden from the king that he could not explain to her (v. 3). She sees the wisdom, the house, the food of his table, his officials, his servants and their clothing, his cupbearers and his burnt offerings, and there was no more breath in her (vv. 4-5). The report was true that I heard in my own land of your words and of your wisdom, but I did not believe the reports until I came and my own eyes had seen it. And behold, the half was not told me (vv. 6-7). Then the blessing: blessed be the LORD your God, who has delighted in you and set you on the throne of Israel! Because the LORD loved Israel forever, he has made you king, that you may execute justice and righteousness (v. 9). She gives a hundred and twenty talents of gold and spices in unmatched quantity (v. 10), and he gives her all she desired (vv. 11-13).
verseByVerse.theology: She came a very long way on a rumour, and the rumour was not about the gold. It was the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD. What reached the ends of the earth was something about God.
verseByVerse.examples: And verse 9 is the finest thing said in this chapter, and a pagan queen says it. She gets three things right that Israel keeps forgetting: the LORD did this, he did it because he loved Israel, and the throne exists that you may execute justice and righteousness. That is the purpose of the office, named accurately, by a foreigner.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD, she came to test him with hard questions. She came to Jerusalem with a very great retinue, with camels bearing spices and very much gold and precious stones. And when she came to Solomon, she told him all that was on her mind. And Solomon answered all her questions; there was nothing hidden from the king that he could not explain to her. And when the queen of Sheba had seen all the wisdom of Solomon, the house that he had built, the food of his table, the seating of his officials, and the attendance of his servants, their clothing, his cupbearers, and his burnt offerings that he offered at the house of the LORD, there was no more breath in her. And she said to the king, "The report was true that I heard in my own land of your words and of your wisdom, but I did not believe the reports until I came and my own eyes had seen it. And behold, the half was not told me. Your wisdom and prosperity surpass the report that I heard. Happy are your men! Happy are your servants, who continually stand before you and hear your wisdom! Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delighted in you and set you on the throne of Israel! Because the LORD loved Israel forever, he has made you king, that you may execute justice and righteousness." Then she gave the king 120 talents of gold, and a very great quantity of spices and precious stones. Never again came such an abundance of spices as these that the queen of Sheba gave to King Solomon. Moreover, the fleet of Hiram, which brought gold from Ophir, brought from Ophir a very great amount of almug wood and precious stones. And the king made of the almug wood supports for the house of the LORD and for the king's house, also lyres and harps for the singers. No such almug wood has come or been seen to this day. And King Solomon gave to the queen of Sheba all that she desired, whatever she asked besides what was given her by the bounty of King Solomon. So she turned and went back to her own land with her servants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now when the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD, she came to test him with hard questions.'

Note what she heard about.

Not his wealth in the first instance, and not even his wisdom on its own: the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD.

What travelled to the ends of the earth was something about God. That is precisely what Solomon asked for at the dedication — that God would hear the foreigner in order that all the peoples of the earth may know your name (8:43) — and here is a foreigner arriving because she has heard the name.

Sheba is most probably in south-west Arabia, in the region of modern Yemen. That is a journey of something like fifteen hundred miles across desert, each way, by camel. Months of travelling, at enormous expense, on the strength of a report.

She comes to test him with hard questions. She is not a tourist. The word is riddles — the same word used of Samson's riddle at his wedding feast — and testing a foreign king's wisdom with them was a recognised diplomatic contest. She has come to find out whether the reports are true.

'She came to Jerusalem with a very great retinue, with camels bearing spices and very much gold and precious stones. And when she came to Solomon, she told him all that was on her mind.'

All that was on her mind. The Hebrew is all that was in her heart.

She had brought riddles, and she ended up telling him everything she was carrying. That is what happens when somebody turns out to be worth talking to.

'And Solomon answered all her questions; there was nothing hidden from the king that he could not explain to her.'

'And when the queen of Sheba had seen all the wisdom of Solomon, the house that he had built,'

'the food of his table, the seating of his officials, and the attendance of his servants, their clothing, his cupbearers, and his burnt offerings that he offered at the house of the LORD, there was no more breath in her.'

Read the list in the order she saw it.

The wisdom first. Then the house, the table, the seating of the officials, the servants and their clothing, the cupbearers — and last, and climactically, his burnt offerings that he offered at the house of the LORD.

The thing that finished her was the worship.

And the writer's phrase for the effect is physical: there was no more breath in her. It knocked the wind out of her.

'And she said to the king, "The report was true that I heard in my own land of your words and of your wisdom,"'

'"but I did not believe the reports until I came and my own eyes had seen it. And behold, the half was not told me. Your wisdom and prosperity surpass the report that I heard."'

She is honest about her own scepticism, which is why the testimony counts for something.

I did not believe the reports until I came. She did not take it on trust. She crossed fifteen hundred miles of desert to check, and what she found exceeded what she had refused to believe.

'"Happy are your men! Happy are your servants, who continually stand before you and hear your wisdom!"'

She envies the servants.

Not the king — the men who get to stand in the room every day and listen. She has had a few weeks of it and she can see what a lifetime of it would be worth.

'"Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delighted in you and set you on the throne of Israel! Because the LORD loved Israel forever, he has made you king, that you may execute justice and righteousness."'

Here is the finest thing said in this chapter, and a pagan queen says it.

Take the three things she gets right, because they are three things Israel keeps forgetting.

First: blessed be the LORD your God, who has delighted in you and set you on the throne. She does not congratulate Solomon on his achievements. She credits God, and she uses a warm word — delighted in you. Everything she has just been shown, she attributes to God's pleasure in this man.

Second: because the LORD loved Israel forever, he has made you king.

That is a remarkable piece of theology from a foreigner. She has worked out that the king is a gift to the nation and not the other way round — that Solomon exists because God loves Israel. It is exactly what David knew at his best: the LORD had established him king over Israel, and that he had exalted his kingdom for the sake of his people Israel (2 Sam. 5:12).

Third, and this is the one that lands hardest: that you may execute justice and righteousness.

She names the purpose of the throne. Not glory, not building, not wealth, not empire. The office exists so that right is done for people.

And she is the first person to say it since 2 Samuel 8:15, and she is not an Israelite, and she has been in the country a few weeks.

There is something uncomfortable in that and it is meant to be felt. The visitor from fifteen hundred miles away has looked at all of it — the gold, the table, the servants in their clothing, the House of the Forest of Lebanon — and identified the actual point of the thing better than the people living in it.

Hold verse 9 for two chapters. When the north comes to Rehoboam, what they ask for is relief from a yoke, and what they get is scorpions.

'Then she gave the king 120 talents of gold, and a very great quantity of spices and precious stones. Never again came such an abundance of spices as these that the queen of Sheba gave to King Solomon.'

'Moreover, the fleet of Hiram, which brought gold from Ophir, brought from Ophir a very great amount of almug wood and precious stones.'

'And the king made of the almug wood supports for the house of the LORD and for the king's house, also lyres and harps for the singers. No such almug wood has come or been seen to this day.'

Lyres and harps for the singers, made of a wood nobody has seen since.

'And King Solomon gave to the queen of Sheba all that she desired, whatever she asked besides what was given her by the bounty of King Solomon. So she turned and went back to her own land with her servants.'

She goes home.

The writer does not tell us what she did with any of it, and there is no record of her worshipping the LORD or of Sheba turning to him. She came, she saw, she blessed God, and she went back across the desert.

And a thousand years later the Lord Jesus brought her up in an argument. Some scribes and Pharisees had asked him for a sign, and he said this:

The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here (Matt. 12:42).

She will stand up at the judgment and her existence will be the case against them.

She had no Scriptures, no covenant, no prophets, and no invitation. What she had was a rumour about the name of a God she did not worship, and she crossed a desert on the strength of it because she wanted to know whether it was true.

The men he was speaking to were standing in front of the wisdom of God in a body, in the street, asking him to do a trick first.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–25 — Silver Was Not Considered as Anything
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now the weight of gold that came to Solomon in one year was 666 talents of gold, besides the traders and the kings of Arabia and the governors (vv. 14-15). He makes two hundred large shields and three hundred smaller ones of beaten gold and puts them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon (vv. 16-17). The great ivory throne overlaid with gold has six steps, a rounded top, armrests with lions beside them, and twelve lions on the steps — nothing like it was ever made for any kingdom (vv. 18-20). All King Solomon's drinking vessels were of gold... none were of silver; silver was not considered as anything in the days of Solomon (v. 21). The fleet of ships of Tarshish comes every three years with gold, silver, ivory, apes and peacocks (v. 22). Thus King Solomon excelled all the kings of the earth in riches and in wisdom (v. 23), and the whole earth seeks his presence to hear his wisdom, which God had put into his mind (v. 24), bringing tribute year by year (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: Everything here is stated as glory and the writer stages it beautifully — and the law about Israel's kings had said nor shall he acquire for himself excessive silver and gold (Deut. 17:17). This is the third of the three prohibitions, and it is being described in a tone of wonder.
verseByVerse.examples: The figure in verse 14 is six hundred and sixty-six talents in a single year. Readers connect it with the number in Revelation 13:18, and honesty requires saying that the writer of Kings makes nothing whatever of it and that Revelation does not cite this verse. The number is here; what a reader does with it is not something this text authorises.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the weight of gold that came to Solomon in one year was 666 talents of gold, besides that which came from the explorers and from the business of the merchants, and from all the kings of the west and from the governors of the land. King Solomon made 200 large shields of beaten gold; 600 shekels of gold went into each shield. And he made 300 shields of beaten gold; three minas of gold went into each shield. And the king put them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon. The king also made a great ivory throne and overlaid it with the finest gold. The throne had six steps, and the throne had a round top, and on each side of the seat were armrests and two lions standing beside the armrests, while twelve lions stood there, one on each end of a step on the six steps. The like of it was never made in any kingdom. All King Solomon's drinking vessels were of gold, and all the vessels of the House of the Forest of Lebanon were of pure gold. None were of silver; silver was not considered as anything in the days of Solomon. For the king had a fleet of ships of Tarshish at sea with the fleet of Hiram. Once every three years the fleet of ships of Tarshish used to come bringing gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks. Thus King Solomon excelled all the kings of the earth in riches and in wisdom. And the whole earth sought the presence of Solomon to hear his wisdom, which God had put into his mind. Every one of them brought his present, articles of silver and gold, garments, myrrh, spices, horses, and mules, so much year by year.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now the weight of gold that came to Solomon in one year was 666 talents of gold,'

Something in the order of twenty-five tons, in twelve months.

A note on the figure, because a reader will stop at it.

The number six hundred and sixty-six occurs once more in Scripture, at the end of the Bible: this calls for wisdom: let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and his number is 666 (Rev. 13:18).

Some readers connect the two, and there is a certain grim aptness to it, since this chapter is the inventory of a man's accumulation.

What honesty requires is this. The writer of Kings makes nothing of the number; he records it as an annual revenue figure and moves straight on to shields. And Revelation does not cite this verse or allude to Solomon anywhere in the passage. Whatever John meant by the number, he does not tell us he got it from here.

The figure is in the text and a reader may notice it. It should not be built on.

'besides that which came from the explorers and from the business of the merchants, and from all the kings of the west and from the governors of the land.'

That is only the top line. The tribute, the trade, the tolls and the provincial revenue are all on top of it.

'King Solomon made 200 large shields of beaten gold; 600 shekels of gold went into each shield.'

'And he made 300 shields of beaten gold; three minas of gold went into each shield. And the king put them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon.'

Five hundred shields of beaten gold, hung in the great pillared hall.

Gold is a soft metal. These are not fighting equipment; they are ceremonial, carried in procession and displayed on the walls of a room built to be walked through.

Keep them, because the writer comes back for them. Five years after Solomon dies, Shishak king of Egypt comes up against Jerusalem and takes away the treasures of the house of the LORD and of the king's house — he took away everything. He also took away all the shields of gold that Solomon had made (14:26).

Rehoboam replaces them with bronze ones, and gives them to the guard, who carry them in front of him when he goes into the house of the LORD, and take them back to the guardroom afterwards (14:27-28).

The same ceremony, with cheaper metal, and everybody pretending not to notice.

'The king also made a great ivory throne and overlaid it with the finest gold.'

'The throne had six steps, and the throne had a round top, and on each side of the seat were armrests and two lions standing beside the armrests,'

'while twelve lions stood there, one on each end of a step on the six steps. The like of it was never made in any kingdom.'

Six steps, twelve lions, a rounded back, ivory and gold.

The lion is the emblem of Judah — Judah is a lion's cub... he stooped down; he crouched as a lion and as a lioness; who dares rouse him? (Gen. 49:9). Twelve of them, for the tribes, on the way up to the seat.

It is a magnificent object and it is also, precisely, a chair for judging in. This is the seat in the Hall of Judgment, and the man on it asked for a hearing heart.

'All King Solomon's drinking vessels were of gold, and all the vessels of the House of the Forest of Lebanon were of pure gold. None were of silver; silver was not considered as anything in the days of Solomon.'

Silver was not considered as anything.

That sentence is doing more than describing an exchange rate. It is a statement about what happens to a scale of value when enough comes in: the second-best metal in the world stopped registering.

Consider what silver is elsewhere in this book. It is what a threshing floor cost David — fifty shekels of it, and he insisted on paying rather than take the ground free, because I will not offer burnt offerings to the LORD my God that cost me nothing (2 Sam. 24:24).

Fifty shekels of silver was a real price to a real man once. Now the metal is not counted.

'For the king had a fleet of ships of Tarshish at sea with the fleet of Hiram. Once every three years the fleet of ships of Tarshish used to come bringing gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks.'

The last two items are the tell.

Gold, silver and ivory are wealth. Apes and peacocks are not wealth; they are curiosities. Somebody is sending ships on three-year voyages to bring back exotic animals because they are interesting to have.

'Thus King Solomon excelled all the kings of the earth in riches and in wisdom.'

The writer puts the two words in that order.

At Gibeon it was the other way round. Solomon asked for wisdom and did not ask for riches, and God said I give you also what you have not asked (3:13). Riches came second, as an addition.

Here the summary sentence reads in riches and in wisdom.

It may be nothing. It is the sort of small thing this writer does.

'And the whole earth sought the presence of Solomon to hear his wisdom, which God had put into his mind.'

The credit is given correctly: which God had put into his mind.

The historian will not let the wisdom become the man's own property, and he says so at the height of the description of his wealth.

'Every one of them brought his present, articles of silver and gold, garments, myrrh, spices, horses, and mules, so much year by year.'

Note the second-to-last word in the list of gifts.

Horses.

They are arriving as tribute now, year by year, from everyone, and the next verse says where the rest of them came from.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–29 — And Horses Were Imported from Egypt
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: And Solomon gathered together chariots and horsemen. He had 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horsemen, whom he stationed in the chariot cities and with the king in Jerusalem (v. 26). And the king made silver as common in Jerusalem as stone, and he made cedar as plentiful as the sycamore of the Shephelah (v. 27). And Solomon's import of horses was from Egypt and Kue (v. 28); a chariot could be imported from Egypt for six hundred shekels of silver and a horse for a hundred and fifty, and they were exported on to the kings of the Hittites and Syria (v. 29).
verseByVerse.theology: Four verses, and they complete the breach. The law said Israel's king must not acquire many horses for himself or cause the people to return to Egypt in order to acquire many horses, and nor shall he acquire for himself excessive silver and gold (Deut. 17:16-17). Horses, Egypt, and silver like stones, in the space of one paragraph.
verseByVerse.examples: Only one prohibition is left, and it is the one with the reason attached: he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away. The very next verse in the book is now King Solomon loved many foreign women.

verseByVerse.quote: And Solomon gathered together chariots and horsemen. He had 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horsemen, whom he stationed in the chariot cities and with the king in Jerusalem. And the king made silver as common in Jerusalem as stone, and he made cedar as plentiful as the sycamore of the Shephelah. And Solomon's import of horses was from Egypt and Kue, and the king's traders received them from Kue at a price. A chariot could be imported from Egypt for 600 shekels of silver and a horse for 150, and so through the king's traders they were exported to all the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Syria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Solomon gathered together chariots and horsemen. He had 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horsemen, whom he stationed in the chariot cities and with the king in Jerusalem.'

Now the last four verses of the chapter, and they are the indictment.

Fourteen hundred chariots. Twelve thousand horsemen. Cities built to house them, which chapter 9 listed.

The law about Israel's kings is a short paragraph with three prohibitions in it, and this is the first: only he must not acquire many horses for himself or cause the people to return to Egypt in order to acquire many horses, since the LORD has said to you, "You shall never return that way again." (Deut. 17:16).

'And the king made silver as common in Jerusalem as stone, and he made cedar as plentiful as the sycamore of the Shephelah.'

This is the third prohibition, in the same law, two clauses later: nor shall he acquire for himself excessive silver and gold (Deut. 17:17).

Silver as common in Jerusalem as stone.

The image is that you could not walk down a street in that city without stepping over it.

'And Solomon's import of horses was from Egypt and Kue, and the king's traders received them from Kue at a price.'

There it is, in as many words.

Solomon's import of horses was from Egypt.

The law did not merely say a king should not have many horses. It said he should not cause the people to return to Egypt in order to get them, and it gave the reason as a quotation from God himself: you shall never return that way again.

Israel came out of Egypt. That was the founding act, the thing the whole calendar is dated from, the thing Solomon's own prayer went back to six times in one afternoon. And the law's concern was that a king with a taste for cavalry would open a road back to the country God had brought them out of, and that trade would run the wrong way down it.

Which is exactly what has happened. There is now a standing commercial relationship with Egypt for military horseflesh, run by the king's own traders.

'A chariot could be imported from Egypt for 600 shekels of silver and a horse for 150, and so through the king's traders they were exported to all the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Syria.'

The last verse turns him into the middleman.

Israel is now the broker in the arms trade of the region, buying Egyptian chariots and horses and selling them on to the Hittites and the Syrians at a margin.

Two hundred years later the Syrians will besiege Samaria and a king of Israel will watch his people eat their own children. The Hittite and Aramean kings are being supplied with cavalry by the king of Israel, out of Egypt, for cash.

Now stand back and see what the chapter has done, because the writer has done it without a single word of criticism.

Every item in these twenty-nine verses is glorious. The queen is genuinely awestruck and her praise is genuinely good theology. The wisdom is real and God gave it. The throne is magnificent. The trade is skilful. The reputation reaches the ends of the earth and it reaches them, as verse 1 says, concerning the name of the LORD.

The law about Israel's kings had three prohibitions, and this chapter contains all three of them described as achievements.

Horses, in verse 26. Egypt, in verse 28. Silver and gold beyond counting, in verses 14 to 27.

There is one left. It is the third clause of the same law and it is the only one with a reason attached: and he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away (Deut. 17:17).

The next verse in the book is: now King Solomon loved many foreign women, along with the daughter of Pharaoh (11:1).

The writer has spent a chapter describing the summit of Israel's history in tones of wonder, and every rung he described was one the law told a king not to climb. And he does not say so. He puts chapter 10 next to chapter 11 and lets the reader do it.

10.theology:
What crossed the desert (v. 1). Not the wealth and not even the wisdom on its own — the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD. What reached the ends of the earth was something about God, which is exactly the outcome Solomon prayed for over the foreigner at the dedication.

All that was in her heart (v. 2). She arrived with riddles and ended up telling him everything she was carrying. That is what happens when somebody turns out to be worth talking to. And she envies the servants rather than the king — the men who stand in the room every day and listen — having had a few weeks of it and worked out what a lifetime would be worth.

The order of what she saw (vv. 4-5). Wisdom, house, table, officials, servants, clothing, cupbearers, and last of all the burnt offerings at the house of the LORD. The worship is the climax of the list, and it is what took her breath.

Three things a foreigner got right (v. 9). First, she credits God rather than congratulating Solomon, and uses a warm word: delighted in you. Second, because the LORD loved Israel forever, he has made you king — the king is a gift to the nation and not the reverse, which is what David knew at his best (2 Sam. 5:12). Third, and hardest: that you may execute justice and righteousness. She names the purpose of the throne — not glory, not building, not wealth or empire, but that right should be done for people — and she is the first to say it since 2 Samuel 8:15. The visitor from fifteen hundred miles away looked at all of it and identified the point of the thing better than the people living in it. Hold verse 9 for two chapters: the north comes to Rehoboam asking for relief and gets scorpions.

The number in verse 14, handled honestly. Six hundred and sixty-six talents in one year, and readers connect it with the number of the beast... his number is 666 (Rev. 13:18). What honesty requires: the writer of Kings makes nothing whatever of it — he records an annual revenue figure and moves on to shields — and Revelation does not cite this verse or mention Solomon in that passage. The figure is in the text and a reader may notice it. It should not be built on.

The golden shields, and what happened to them (vv. 16-17). Gold is soft; these are ceremonial, carried in procession and hung in a hall built to be walked through. Five years after Solomon dies, Shishak of Egypt takes the treasures of both houses — he took away everything. He also took away all the shields of gold that Solomon had made (14:26) — and Rehoboam replaces them with bronze, and the guard still carries them in front of him into the house of the LORD and puts them back in the guardroom afterwards (14:27-28). The same ceremony, cheaper metal, everybody pretending not to notice.

A magnificent chair for judging in (vv. 18-20). Six steps, twelve lions for the tribes, ivory and gold. The lion is Judah's emblem — Judah is a lion's cub... who dares rouse him? (Gen. 49:9). And this is the seat in the Hall of Judgment, and the man on it asked for a hearing heart.

Silver was not considered as anything (v. 21). More than an exchange rate: a statement about what happens to a scale of value when enough comes in. The second-best metal in the world stopped registering. And consider what silver was earlier in this history — fifty shekels of it bought a threshing floor, and David insisted on paying rather than take the ground free, because I will not offer burnt offerings to the LORD my God that cost me nothing (2 Sam. 24:24). It was a real price to a real man once. Now the metal is not counted.

Apes and peacocks (v. 22). Gold, silver and ivory are wealth; the last two items are not. Somebody is sending ships on three-year voyages to fetch exotic animals because they are interesting to have.

Riches and wisdom, in that order (v. 23). At Gibeon it was the other way round: he asked for wisdom, did not ask for riches, and God said I give you also what you have not asked (3:13). Riches came second, as an addition. The summary sentence here reads in riches and in wisdom. It may be nothing. It is the sort of small thing this writer does. And he immediately refuses to let the wisdom become the man's own property: which God had put into his mind.

The three prohibitions, all three (vv. 26-29). Horses: he must not acquire many horses for himself. Egypt: or cause the people to return to Egypt in order to acquire many horses, since the LORD has said to you, "You shall never return that way again" (Deut. 17:16). Silver and gold: nor shall he acquire for himself excessive silver and gold (Deut. 17:17). All three, in twelve verses, described as achievements.

Why Egypt mattered (v. 28). The law's concern was not economic. Israel came out of Egypt — the founding act, the thing the calendar is dated from, the thing Solomon's own prayer returned to six times in one afternoon — and the danger was that a king with a taste for cavalry would open a road back to the country God brought them out of, and that trade would run the wrong way down it. There is now a standing commercial relationship with Egypt for military horseflesh, run by the king's own traders. And the last verse makes him the middleman: Israel brokers the arms trade of the region, buying Egyptian chariots and selling them on to the Hittites and the Syrians at a margin — the same Syrians who will one day besiege Samaria until its people eat their own children.

What the chapter does without a word of criticism. Every item is genuinely glorious. The queen is genuinely awestruck and her theology is genuinely good. The wisdom is real and God gave it. The reputation reaches the ends of the earth concerning the name of the LORD. And every rung described is one the law told a king not to climb. One prohibition is left, and it is the only one with a reason attached: he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away. The next verse in the book is now King Solomon loved many foreign women. The writer does not say so. He puts chapter 10 next to chapter 11 and lets the reader do it.

She will rise up at the judgment (v. 13). She goes home, and there is no record that Sheba turned to the LORD. And a thousand years later, asked for a sign, the Lord Jesus said: the queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here (Matt. 12:42). She had no Scriptures, no covenant, no prophets and no invitation — only a rumour about the name of a God she did not worship, and she crossed a desert on it because she wanted to know whether it was true. The men he was speaking to were standing in front of the wisdom of God in a body, asking him to do a trick first.
10.examples:
Then: A queen crossed fifteen hundred miles of desert by camel, twice, on the strength of a rumour about the name of a God who was not hers — because she did not believe the reports and wanted to find out. What took her breath in the end was not the gold or the throne but watching the king offer burnt offerings at the house of the LORD.

Now: Three things. Verse 9 is the one to sit with, and it stings: the outsider who had been in the country a few weeks named the purpose of the whole institution more accurately than anybody inside it had for two generations. People at a distance often see what a thing is actually for more clearly than the people running it. Second, silver was not considered as anything is a warning about what abundance does to a scale of value — David paid fifty shekels of it for a threshing floor rather than accept the ground free, and by his son's reign the metal did not register. And third, the shape of the chapter. Nothing in it is condemned and everything in it is against the law, and the writer never once says so. Remember that about seasons when everything is going extremely well: the account is not always presented at the time.

And Genubath was in Pharaoh's house among the sons of Pharaoh.<sup>21</sup>But when Hadad heard in Egypt that David slept with his fathers and that Joab the commander of the army was dead, Hadad said to Pharaoh, "Let me depart, that I may go to my own country."<sup>22</sup>But Pharaoh said to him, "What have you lacked with me that you are now seeking to go to your own country?" Now Ahijah had dressed himself in a new garment, and the two of them were alone in the open country.<sup>30</sup>Then Ahijah laid hold of the new garment that was on him, and tore it into twelve pieces.<sup>31</sup>And he said to Jeroboam, "Take for yourself ten pieces, for thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'Behold, I am about to tear the kingdom from the hand of Solomon and will give you ten tribes<sup>32</sup>(but he shall have one tribe, for the sake of my servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, the city that I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel),<sup>33</sup>because they have forsaken me and worshiped Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, Chemosh the god of Moab, and Milcom the god of the Ammonites, and they have not walked in my ways, doing what is right in my sight and keeping my statutes and my rules, as David his father did.<sup>34</sup>Nevertheless, I will not take the whole kingdom out of his hand, but I will make him ruler all the days of his life, for the sake of David my servant whom I chose, who kept my commandments and my statutes.<sup>35</sup>But I will take the kingdom out of his son's hand and will give it to you, ten tribes.<sup>36</sup>Yet to his son I will give one tribe, that David my servant may always have a lamp before me in Jerusalem, the city where I have chosen to put my name.<sup>37</sup>And I will take you, and you shall reign over all that your soul desires, and you shall be king over Israel.<sup>38</sup>And if you will listen to all that I command you, and will walk in my ways, and do what is right in my eyes by keeping my statutes and my commandments, as David my servant did, I will be with you and will build you a sure house, as I built for David, and I will give Israel to you.<sup>39</sup>And I will afflict the offspring of David because of this, but not forever.'"<sup>40</sup>Solomon sought therefore to kill Jeroboam.
