11.overview:
The previous chapter ended with silver as common as stone and horses arriving from Egypt. This one opens with the last of the three prohibitions in the law about Israel's kings — and it is the only one for which a reason was given: he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away (Deut. 17:17). The writer quotes the warning in verse 2 and reports its exact fulfilment in verse 3: and his wives turned away his heart.

The daughter of Pharaoh is named first, which is the writer collecting a debt. She has been in the account since 3:1 — before Gibeon, before the temple — given a house in chapter 7 and moved out of the city of David in chapter 9 for reasons of holiness, in four flat mentions with no comment attached. Here is the comment.

And three things in verse 4 need taking slowly. When Solomon was old: not in the reckless years but after Gibeon, after the temple, after two appearances of God, after forty years. Not wholly true is shalem — the root of his own name, and the exact word of his own benediction at 8:61, which the writer waits three chapters and then takes off him. And as was the heart of David his father, which is not a whitewash of David: the measure in this book is single, whether a king served the LORD alone, and on that measure David never once in seventy years worshipped another god.

Then the mechanism, and it is not what most people imagine. There is no scene in which Solomon renounces the LORD. He builds his wives their shrines — one reasonable concession at a time, each defensible on its own, because a princess who arrives as a treaty needs somewhere to worship and refusing would insult her father. Verse 8 says he did it for all of them. That is how a heart stops being whole: not by a decision, but by a series of arrangements nobody would have called a decision.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Now King Solomon Loved Many Foreign Women
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now King Solomon loved many foreign women, along with the daughter of Pharaoh: Moabite, Ammonite, Edomite, Sidonian, and Hittite women, from the nations concerning which the LORD had said to the people of Israel, "You shall not enter into marriage with them, neither shall they with you, for surely they will turn away your heart after their gods." Solomon clung to these in love (vv. 1-2). He had 700 wives, who were princesses, and 300 concubines. And his wives turned away his heart (v. 3). For when Solomon was old his wives turned away his heart after other gods, and his heart was not wholly true to the LORD his God, as was the heart of David his father (v. 4). He goes after Ashtoreth and Milcom (v. 5). So Solomon did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and did not wholly follow the LORD, as David his father had done (v. 6). He builds high places for Chemosh and Molech on the mountain east of Jerusalem, and for all his foreign wives (vv. 7-8).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the third of the three prohibitions in the law about Israel's kings, and it is the only one for which a reason was given: lest his heart turn away (Deut. 17:17). Chapter 10 broke the other two. The writer quotes the law's warning in verse 2 and reports its exact fulfilment in verse 3.
verseByVerse.examples: And his heart was not wholly true is shalem — whole, undivided — the word of his own benediction: let your heart therefore be wholly true to the LORD our God (8:61). It is the root of his own name, and it is the word the writer takes away from him.

verseByVerse.quote: Now King Solomon loved many foreign women, along with the daughter of Pharaoh: Moabite, Ammonite, Edomite, Sidonian, and Hittite women, from the nations concerning which the LORD had said to the people of Israel, "You shall not enter into marriage with them, neither shall they with you, for surely they will turn away your heart after their gods." Solomon clung to these in love. He had 700 wives, who were princesses, and 300 concubines. And his wives turned away his heart. For when Solomon was old his wives turned away his heart after other gods, and his heart was not wholly true to the LORD his God, as was the heart of David his father. For Solomon went after Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, and after Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites. So Solomon did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and did not wholly follow the LORD, as David his father had done. Then Solomon built a high place for Chemosh the abomination of Moab, and for Molech the abomination of the Ammonites, on the mountain east of Jerusalem. And so he did for all his foreign wives, who made offerings and sacrificed to their gods.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now King Solomon loved many foreign women, along with the daughter of Pharaoh: Moabite, Ammonite, Edomite, Sidonian, and Hittite women,'

The previous chapter ended with silver as common as stone and horses arriving from Egypt. This one opens with the last of the three prohibitions.

The daughter of Pharaoh is named first, which is the writer collecting a debt. She has been in this account since 3:1, in the first sentence of the reign after the executions, before Gibeon and before the temple. She was given a house of her own in chapter 7 and moved out of the city of David in chapter 9 for reasons of holiness. Four flat mentions with no comment attached to any of them.

Here is the comment.

'from the nations concerning which the LORD had said to the people of Israel, "You shall not enter into marriage with them, neither shall they with you, for surely they will turn away your heart after their gods." Solomon clung to these in love.'

The writer quotes the law, including its reason.

The command is from Deuteronomy 7, and what should be noticed is that the reason given is never about blood or nationality. They will turn away your heart after their gods. It is a warning about worship, and the mechanism is the household.

Scripture is entirely clear about this elsewhere, and it should be said plainly, because this passage has been misused. Rahab of Jericho married into Israel and is in the genealogy of Christ. Ruth was a Moabitess — from one of the nations named in verse 1 — and she is David's great-grandmother, and she is in that genealogy too. Uriah was a Hittite and one of the mighty men. What made the difference in every case was not ancestry but which God they had come to.

Then the verb: Solomon clung to these in love.

It is the word from Genesis 2 — a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife — and it is also the word Deuteronomy uses over and over for what Israel was to do toward God: you shall fear the LORD your God. You shall serve him and hold fast to him (Deut. 10:20).

He clung to them. The verb that belongs to God is used of seven hundred women.

'He had 700 wives, who were princesses, and 300 concubines. And his wives turned away his heart.'

A thousand women, and the writer reports the outcome in the law's own words.

Deuteronomy said lest his heart turn away. This verse says his wives turned away his heart. The law named the mechanism and the history records it working.

It should also be said what seven hundred princesses actually are. These are not romances. Each one is a treaty — a marriage alliance sealing a political relationship with a neighbouring house, which is exactly what the daughter of Pharaoh was. The harem is a foreign policy.

Which makes it worse rather than better, and for a reason the chapter is about to state. A man who marries a princess to secure an alliance has to let her worship her own gods, or the alliance is insulted. Every one of those marriages carried an obligation, and verse 8 is Solomon meeting them.

'For when Solomon was old his wives turned away his heart after other gods, and his heart was not wholly true to the LORD his God, as was the heart of David his father.'

Now this verse should be taken slowly, because there are three things in it and each one matters.

The first is when Solomon was old.

Not in the reckless years. Not as a young king dazzled by his own success. This happened at the end — after Gibeon, after seven years of building, after the dedication and the longest prayer in the Old Testament, after God appeared to him a second time, after forty years on the throne.

He had every advantage a man could have and he had them for four decades, and he went wrong at the end.

That is not the usual shape of a warning and it ought to be felt. There is no age at which a person is past this. A man can pray the finest prayer in the Old Testament and drift in his seventies, and the drift can begin in the part of life that looks safest.

The second is the phrase: his heart was not wholly true.

The word is shalem. It means whole, complete, undivided, at peace — and it is the root of the man's own name.

He used it himself, in front of the whole nation, on the greatest day of his life. Standing in front of the finished temple with the glory of God inside it, his last word to Israel was: let your heart therefore be wholly true to the LORD our God, walking in his statutes and keeping his commandments (8:61).

The writer waits three chapters and then takes the word off him.

Not false. Not apostate. Not he abandoned the LORD. Solomon kept the feasts three times a year and the temple stood and the sacrifices went up. What he lost was the undividedness. His heart had more than one thing in it, and he had told the nation that would not do.

The third is the comparison: as was the heart of David his father.

A reader who has just finished 2 Samuel may find that hard, and it should not be smoothed over. David committed adultery and arranged a murder to cover it, failed to act when his daughter was raped, and handed his son a list of men to kill from his deathbed, one of them under an oath he had sworn himself.

So what is being compared?

Not sinlessness. The measure in this book is single: whether a king served the LORD alone or went after other gods. And on that measure the difference between the two men is total. David never once, in seventy years, worshipped another god or built a shrine to one. Everything he did wrong he did as a man belonging to the LORD, and when he was confronted he broke and said I have sinned against the LORD, and wrote Psalm 51.

Solomon built high places for Chemosh and Molech on the hill facing the temple.

That is the comparison, and it is not a whitewash of David. It is the distinction the whole book of Kings runs on, and it is the reason the verdict on every king who follows is measured against a man who was an adulterer and a murderer — because whatever else he was, he had one God.

'For Solomon went after Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, and after Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites.'

Ashtoreth is the Canaanite fertility goddess, and Milcom is Molech, whose worship involved child sacrifice. The law is explicit about him: any one of the people of Israel who gives any of his children to Molech shall surely be put to death (Lev. 20:2).

The writer calls him the abomination of the Ammonites and does not soften it.

'So Solomon did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and did not wholly follow the LORD, as David his father had done.'

There is the formula, and this is the first time it appears.

Solomon did what was evil in the sight of the LORD.

From here to the end of 2 Kings that sentence will be stamped on king after king, twenty and thirty at a time, until it becomes the drumbeat of the whole history. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD.

And the first man it is used of is the wisest king who ever lived, who built the temple.

'Then Solomon built a high place for Chemosh the abomination of Moab, on the mountain east of Jerusalem, and for Molech the abomination of the Ammonites.'

Read the location.

On the mountain east of Jerusalem. That is the Mount of Olives, directly across the Kidron valley from the temple mount. A person standing in the courtyard of the house of the LORD could look up and see them.

They were still there three hundred years later. When Josiah tore through Judah destroying every shrine he could find, the record says: and the king defiled the high places that were east of Jerusalem, to the south of the mount of corruption, which Solomon the king of Israel had built for Ashtoreth the abomination of the Sidonians, and for Chemosh the abomination of Moab, and for Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites (2 Kings 23:13).

Three centuries, and they were still standing, and they were still called Solomon's.

'And so he did for all his foreign wives, who made offerings and sacrificed to their gods.'

This is how it actually happened, and the mechanism deserves precision, because it is not what most people imagine.

There is no scene in which Solomon renounces the LORD. He does not stop building the temple or abolish the priesthood or declare for Ashtoreth. He builds his wives their shrines.

Each one is a courtesy. A princess arrives from Moab as part of a treaty and she needs somewhere to worship; refusing would insult her father and break the alliance. So a high place goes up. Then another, for the Ammonite. Then another. Verse 8 says he did it for all his foreign wives — and there were seven hundred of them.

It is accommodation, one reasonable concession at a time, each of them defensible on its own, and at the end of it the hill facing the house of God is covered in altars and the king is going up to them.

That is how a heart stops being shalem. Not by a decision. By a series of arrangements nobody would have called a decision.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–25 — Because He Had Appeared to Him Twice
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: And the LORD was angry with Solomon, because his heart had turned away from the LORD, the God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice and had commanded him concerning this thing, that he should not go after other gods. But he did not keep what the LORD commanded (vv. 9-10). So: since this has been your practice and you have not kept my covenant and my statutes that I have commanded you, I will surely tear the kingdom from you and will give it to your servant (v. 11). Yet for the sake of David your father I will not do it in your days, but I will tear it out of the hand of your son. However, I will not tear away all the kingdom, but I will give one tribe to your son, for the sake of David my servant and for the sake of Jerusalem that I have chosen (vv. 12-13). Then the adversaries: Hadad the Edomite, who had fled to Egypt as a boy when Joab killed every male in Edom (vv. 14-22), and Rezon, who gathered men and reigned in Damascus (vv. 23-25).
verseByVerse.theology: Who had appeared to him twice. That is why chapter 9 said a second time: the writer was laying the aggravation in advance. God did not send a prophet or a dream; he came in person, twice, and told him the exact thing to avoid.
verseByVerse.examples: And the mercy is inside the judgment, three times over: not in your days, and not all of it, and one tribe kept — and every clause of the restraint is for the sake of David my servant and of the city God chose. Solomon is spared on somebody else's account.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD was angry with Solomon, because his heart had turned away from the LORD, the God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice and had commanded him concerning this thing, that he should not go after other gods. But he did not keep what the LORD commanded. Therefore the LORD said to Solomon, "Since this has been your practice and you have not kept my covenant and my statutes that I have commanded you, I will surely tear the kingdom from you and will give it to your servant. Yet for the sake of David your father I will not do it in your days, but I will tear it out of the hand of your son. However, I will not tear away all the kingdom, but I will give one tribe to your son, for the sake of David my servant and for the sake of Jerusalem that I have chosen." And the LORD raised up an adversary against Solomon, Hadad the Edomite. He was of the royal house in Edom. For when David was in Edom, and Joab the commander of the army went up to bury the slain, he struck down every male in Edom (for Joab and all Israel remained there six months, until he had cut off every male in Edom). But Hadad fled to Egypt, together with certain Edomites of his father's servants, Hadad still being a little child. They set out from Midian and came to Paran and took men with them from Paran and came to Egypt, to Pharaoh king of Egypt, who gave him a house and assigned him an allowance of food and gave him land. And Hadad found great favor in the sight of Pharaoh, so that he gave him in marriage the sister of his own wife, the sister of Tahpenes the queen. And the sister of Tahpenes bore him Genubath his son, whom Tahpenes weaned in Pharaoh's house. And Genubath was in Pharaoh's house among the sons of Pharaoh. But when Hadad heard in Egypt that David slept with his fathers and that Joab the commander of the army was dead, Hadad said to Pharaoh, "Let me depart, that I may go to my own country." But Pharaoh said to him, "What have you lacked with me that you are now seeking to go to your own country?" And he said to him, "Only let me depart." God also raised up as an adversary to him, Rezon the son of Eliada, who had fled from his master Hadadezer king of Zobah. And he gathered men about him and became leader of a marauding band, after the killing by David. And they went to Damascus and lived there and made him king in Damascus. He was an adversary of Israel all the days of Solomon, doing harm as Hadad did. And he loathed Israel and reigned over Syria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the LORD was angry with Solomon, because his heart had turned away from the LORD, the God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice'

Now the reason chapter 9 bothered to say a second time.

Who had appeared to him twice.

The writer laid that fact down two chapters ago so that it would be available here, and here it is doing its work. This is the aggravation of the charge.

God did not leave this man to work it out. He did not send a prophet with a message, or a dream to be interpreted, or a providence to be discerned. He came himself, twice — once at Gibeon to a young king who asked for a hearing heart, and once in the year the temple was finished — and both times he said the same thing.

'and had commanded him concerning this thing, that he should not go after other gods. But he did not keep what the LORD commanded.'

Concerning this thing. The exact thing. Not a general exhortation to godliness — God had named the specific sin in advance, in person, and Solomon committed that one.

Go back and read it: but if you turn aside from following me, you or your children... and go and serve other gods and worship them, then I will cut off Israel from the land (9:6-7).

He was told. He was told twice, by God, face to face, in the precise terms.

'Therefore the LORD said to Solomon, "Since this has been your practice and you have not kept my covenant and my statutes that I have commanded you, I will surely tear the kingdom from you and will give it to your servant."'

Since this has been your practice.

Not since you did this once. The Hebrew is closer to because this has been with you — a settled state of affairs rather than an incident. The high places had been there for years.

The sentence is the reversal of everything: I will surely tear the kingdom from you and will give it to your servant.

To a servant. Not to a rival dynasty, not to a foreign power — to one of his own officials. The man is named in verse 26 and he is the superintendent of Solomon's forced labour.

'"Yet for the sake of David your father I will not do it in your days, but I will tear it out of the hand of your son."'

Now the mercy, and it is inside the judgment rather than instead of it.

For the sake of David your father.

Solomon is spared the sight of it, and the reason has nothing to do with Solomon. It is on account of a man who has been dead for forty years.

That is the first of three restraints in this chapter and all three have the same ground. Not in your days, for David's sake. Not all the kingdom, for David's sake. One tribe kept, for the sake of David my servant and Jerusalem which I have chosen.

God is honouring a promise made in a night vision to a man in a cedar house who wanted to build him a temple and was told no.

'"However, I will not tear away all the kingdom, but I will give one tribe to your son, for the sake of David my servant and for the sake of Jerusalem that I have chosen."'

One tribe out of twelve, and even that is a kindness rather than a right.

Note also that God says he chose the city. The whole promise now hangs on a man and a place, and both of them are God's own selections.

'And the LORD raised up an adversary against Solomon, Hadad the Edomite. He was of the royal house in Edom.'

The LORD raised up an adversary. The word is satan in the ordinary Hebrew sense of an opponent or accuser, and the writer uses it three times in this section.

What follows is a piece of history with a long fuse in it.

'For when David was in Edom, and Joab the commander of the army went up to bury the slain, he struck down every male in Edom'

'(for Joab and all Israel remained there six months, until he had cut off every male in Edom).'

This is not recorded anywhere in 2 Samuel, and the reader is meeting it for the first time.

Joab spent six months in Edom systematically killing every male he could find. The campaign is mentioned in 2 Samuel 8 in a single verse about eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt; here is what the occupation was like.

'But Hadad fled to Egypt, together with certain Edomites of his father's servants, Hadad being still a little child.'

A small boy is carried out of a massacre by his father's servants.

'They set out from Midian and came to Paran and took men with them from Paran and came to Egypt, to Pharaoh king of Egypt, who gave him a house and assigned him an allowance of food and gave him land.'

'And Hadad found great favor in the sight of Pharaoh, so that he gave him in marriage the sister of his own wife, the sister of Tahpenes the queen.'

He grows up in the Egyptian court and marries the queen's sister.

'And the sister of Tahpenes bore him Genubath his son, whom Tahpenes weaned in Pharaoh's house. And Genubath was in Pharaoh's house among the sons of Pharaoh.'

'But when Hadad heard in Egypt that David slept with his fathers and that Joab the commander of the army was dead, Hadad said to Pharaoh, "Let me depart, that I may go to my own country."'

He waits until both of them are dead, and then goes home.

'But Pharaoh said to him, "What have you lacked with me that you are now seeking to go to your own country?" And he said to him, "Only let me go."'

Only let me go.

He has a house, an allowance, land, a royal marriage, and a son being raised among the sons of Pharaoh. And he wants to go back to the country where his family was slaughtered.

The writer gives him no speech about vengeance and no plan. Three words.

'God also raised up as an adversary to him, Rezon the son of Eliada, who had fled from his master Hadadezer king of Zobah.'

'And he gathered men about him and became leader of a marauding band, after the killing by David. And they went to Damascus and lived there and made him king in Damascus.'

The second adversary, and he comes out of David's Syrian campaign the way Hadad came out of the Edomite one.

Rezon was one of Hadadezer's men, and he ran when David destroyed that army, and gathered a band and took Damascus.

Damascus is going to be the great northern enemy for the next three centuries. Ben-hadad besieges Samaria in chapter 20. Naaman is the commander of the army of the king of Syria. The Syrian wars run through the whole of 2 Kings.

It starts here, with a man who escaped from David's victory.

'He was an adversary of Israel all the days of Solomon, doing harm as Hadad did. And he loathed Israel and reigned over Syria.'

Now stand back and see what the writer has done with these two men.

Both of them are consequences of David's wars. Hadad survived a six-month massacre in Edom; Rezon escaped the destruction of a Syrian army. They were boys and fugitives while Solomon was building his temple, and they have been waiting all his life.

The writer says twice that God raised them up.

The judgment does not arrive out of nowhere. It arrives on legs, from a long way back, using things that were already in the world — a boy carried into Egypt, a soldier who ran. God did not manufacture Solomon's adversaries. He raised up the ones that were already there.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeroboam the son of Nebat, an Ephraimite servant of Solomon, a mighty man of valor set over the forced labour of the house of Joseph, lifts up his hand against the king (vv. 26-28). Ahijah the Shilonite meets him on the road, wearing a new garment, and the two of them were alone in the open country; he tears it into twelve pieces and says take for yourself ten pieces, for thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, "Behold, I am about to tear the kingdom from the hand of Solomon and will give you ten tribes" (vv. 29-31). One tribe is kept for the sake of my servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, the city that I have chosen (v. 32). And then Jeroboam is offered terms: if you will listen to all that I command you, and will walk in my ways, and do what is right in my eyes by keeping my statutes and my commandments, as David my servant did, I will be with you and will build you a sure house, as I built for David, and I will give Israel to you (v. 38). Solomon sought therefore to kill Jeroboam, who flees to Egypt (v. 40).
verseByVerse.theology: A prophet tears a new cloak into twelve pieces on an empty road. The last time a garment was torn in this history, Saul caught the hem of Samuel's robe and Samuel said the LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you this day (1 Sam. 15:27-28).
verseByVerse.examples: And Jeroboam is offered David's own covenant terms, word for word: I will build you a sure house, as I built for David. The offer is genuine and it is conditional, and chapter 12 records what he did with it.

verseByVerse.quote: Jeroboam the son of Nebat, an Ephraimite of Zeredah, a servant of Solomon, whose mother's name was Zeruah, a widow, also lifted up his hand against the king. And this was the reason why he lifted up his hand against the king. Solomon built the Millo, and closed up the breach of the city of David his father. The man Jeroboam was very able, and when Solomon saw that the young man was industrious he gave him charge over all the forced labor of the house of Joseph. And at that time, when Jeroboam went out of Jerusalem, the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite found him on the road. Now Ahijah had dressed himself in a new garment, and the two of them were alone in the open country. Then Ahijah laid hold of the new garment that was on him, and tore it into twelve pieces. And he said to Jeroboam, "Take for yourself ten pieces, for thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'Behold, I am about to tear the kingdom from the hand of Solomon and will give you ten tribes (but he shall have one tribe, for the sake of my servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, the city that I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel), because they have forsaken me and worshiped Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, Chemosh the god of Moab, and Milcom the god of the Ammonites, and they have not walked in my ways, doing what is right in my sight and keeping my statutes and my rules, as David his father did. Nevertheless, I will not take the whole kingdom out of his hand, but I will make him ruler all the days of his life, for the sake of David my servant whom I chose, who kept my commandments and my statutes. But I will take the kingdom out of his son's hand and will give it to you, ten tribes. Yet to his son I will give one tribe, that David my servant may always have a lamp before me in Jerusalem, the city where I have chosen to put my name. And I will take you, and you shall reign over all that your soul desires, and you shall be king over Israel. And if you will listen to all that I command you, and will walk in my ways, and do what is right in my eyes by keeping my statutes and my commandments, as David my servant did, I will be with you and will build you a sure house, as I built for David, and I will give Israel to you. And I will afflict the offspring of David because of this, but not forever.'" Solomon sought therefore to kill Jeroboam. But Jeroboam arose and fled into Egypt, to Shishak king of Egypt, and was in Egypt until the death of Solomon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Jeroboam the son of Nebat, an Ephraimite of Zeredah, a servant of Solomon, whose mother's name was Zeruah, a widow, also lifted up his hand against the king.'

The third adversary, and this one is an Israelite and a servant of the household.

Note the details the writer includes. He is an Ephraimite — from the leading tribe of the north, the tribe of Joshua, the tribe that had never been comfortable under a Judahite king. And his mother's name was Zeruah, a widow.

A widow's son from the north. The writer said the same thing about Hiram the craftsman.

'And this was the reason why he lifted his hand against the king. Solomon built the Millo, and closed up the breach of the city of David his father.'

'The man Jeroboam was very able, and when Solomon saw that the young man was industrious he gave him charge over all the forced labor of the house of Joseph.'

Here is where he came from, and the appointment is almost unbelievable in hindsight.

Solomon noticed a capable young man and promoted him — and the department he put him in charge of was the forced labour of the house of Joseph, which is to say the conscripted work gangs of the northern tribes.

So the man who will take ten tribes away from Solomon's son spent his formative years administering the exact grievance that the ten tribes will secede over.

He knows every man in those gangs. He knows the shift rotas, the quotas, what the levy costs a farming family, and what is said about the king in the north when nobody from Jerusalem is listening.

Solomon gave him that education himself, because he was good at his job.

'And at that time, when Jeroboam went out of Jerusalem, the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite found him on the road. Now Ahijah had dressed himself in a new garment, and the two of them were alone in the open country.'

The scene is set with unusual care, and every detail is doing something.

Ahijah the Shilonite. He is from Shiloh — where the tabernacle stood for centuries, where Hannah prayed and Samuel was called in the night, and which God destroyed and made a byword (Jer. 7:12). A prophet from the ruined sanctuary of the north.

A new garment. He has put on a new cloak specifically for this, because he is about to destroy it.

The two of them were alone in the open country. No witnesses. This is the most seditious conversation in the kingdom and it happens on an empty road.

'Then Ahijah laid hold of the new garment that was on him, and tore it into twelve pieces.'

He rips his own new coat into twelve.

Prophets in Israel did this — acted the message out rather than only saying it — and this particular sign has a history in these books.

When Samuel turned to leave Saul after the Amalekite affair, Saul caught at the hem of his robe and it tore, and Samuel said: the LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you this day and has given it to a neighbour of yours, who is better than you (1 Sam. 15:27-28).

That tear was an accident and this one is deliberate, and the sentence that follows is nearly the same sentence.

'And he said to Jeroboam, "Take for yourself ten pieces, for thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'Behold, I am about to tear the kingdom from the hand of Solomon and will give you ten tribes'"'

Ten pieces handed to a man standing in a field.

'"(but he shall have one tribe, for the sake of my servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, the city that I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel),"'

The one tribe again, and the same reason again. Three times now: David, and the city God chose.

'"because they have forsaken me and worshiped Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, Chemosh the god of Moab, and Milcom the god of the Ammonites, and they have not walked in my ways, doing what is right in my sight and keeping my statutes and my rules, as David his father did."'

Note the pronoun. They have forsaken me.

It is not only Solomon. The high places on the mountain east of Jerusalem were public and they had been there for years, and the nation had grown used to them.

'"Nevertheless, I will not take the whole kingdom out of his hand, but I will make him ruler all the days of his life, for the sake of David my servant whom I chose, who kept my commandments and my statutes."'

'"But I will take the kingdom out of his son's hand and give it to you, ten tribes."'

'"Yet to his son I will give one tribe, that David my servant may always have a lamp before me in Jerusalem, the city where I have chosen to put my name."'

There is the word, and it goes back a long way.

A lamp before me in Jerusalem.

David's own men used it about him on a battlefield when he grew weary and a giant nearly killed him: you shall no longer go out with us to battle, lest you quench the lamp of Israel (2 Sam. 21:17).

Here God takes the word up as his own. And he uses it again when Abijam reigns badly — nevertheless, for David's sake the LORD his God gave him a lamp in Jerusalem (15:4) — and again when Judah deserves destruction: the LORD was not willing to destroy Judah, for the sake of David his servant, since he promised to give a lamp to him and to his sons forever (2 Kings 8:19).

A lamp is a small thing and it is not extinguished. That is the whole promise: not a blaze, not a guarantee of prosperity, just a light God undertakes not to let go out.

It does not go out. It burns down to almost nothing — a king in a Babylonian prison at the end of 2 Kings — and then to a carpenter's family in a village.

'"And I will take you, and you shall reign over all that your soul desires, and you shall be king over Israel."'

'"And if you will listen to all that I command you, and will walk in my ways, and do what is right in my eyes by keeping my statutes and my commandments, as David my servant did, I will be with you and will build you a sure house, as I built for David, and I will give Israel to you."'

Now read what is being offered, because it is astonishing and it is easy to miss.

I will build you a sure house, as I built for David.

That is the language of 2 Samuel 7. God is offering Jeroboam the covenant — the same terms, in the same words, an enduring dynasty in the north on the same footing David got.

The condition is stated and it is not obscure: listen, walk in my ways, do what is right, keep my statutes, as David my servant did.

So the man about to receive ten tribes is not being handed a consolation prize or a temporary arrangement. He is being offered everything, on the one condition that governs everything in this book.

Hold it for one chapter. Jeroboam gets his kingdom, and the first substantial thing he does with it is make two golden calves.

'"And I will afflict the offspring of David because of this, but not forever."'

But not forever. Even the sentence on David's line has a limit written into it.

'Solomon sought therefore to kill Jeroboam. But Jeroboam arose and fled into Egypt, to Shishak king of Egypt, and was in Egypt until the death of Solomon.'

This is the last recorded act of the wisest man who ever lived.

He tries to have him murdered.

Consider what that means. God has told him, in person, that the kingdom will be torn from his son because of what he has done. Solomon's response is not repentance, not the removal of the high places, not a word to God. It is an assassination order.

He is doing what Saul did. Told by a prophet that the kingdom was going to a neighbour, Saul spent the rest of his life trying to kill the neighbour, and threw four spears, and destroyed a town of priests, and hunted a man through the wilderness with three thousand chosen men.

You cannot kill your way out of a word from God. Solomon of all people knew it, and he sent the soldiers anyway.

Note where Jeroboam goes. To Egypt, to Shishak — which is where Hadad went as a boy, and where the daughter of Pharaoh came from. Egypt has now sheltered two of Solomon's three adversaries, and five years after his death Shishak comes up and takes everything in Jerusalem that is not nailed down.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–43 — So Solomon Slept with His Fathers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now the rest of the acts of Solomon, and all that he did, and his wisdom, are they not written in the Book of the Acts of Solomon? (v. 41). And the time that Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel was forty years. And Solomon slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David his father. And Rehoboam his son reigned in his place (vv. 42-43).
verseByVerse.theology: The formula arrives, and from here to the end of both books it will be repeated over king after king: the rest of his acts, the source, the years, the burial, the successor. Solomon is the first to receive it in full.
verseByVerse.examples: Forty years, like his father and like Saul. And the writer, who has told us about the wisdom and the temple and the gold and the seven hundred wives, closes the account by pointing at a book we do not have and telling us there was more.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the rest of the acts of Solomon, and all that he did, and his wisdom, are they not written in the Book of the Acts of Solomon? And the time that Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel was forty years. And Solomon slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David his father. And Rehoboam his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now the rest of the acts of Solomon, and all that he did, and his wisdom, are they not written in the Book of the Acts of Solomon?'

Here the formula appears for the first time, and it will now run through both books to the end.

The pattern is fixed: the rest of his acts, the source where you can read them, the length of the reign, the burial, the successor. It will be applied to something like forty kings, most of them in a few lines, and it is one of the things that gives Kings its relentless quality — a man's whole life summarised, filed, and closed, and then the next one.

Note also that the writer is citing a source. The Book of the Acts of Solomon is a document we do not have, and Kings refers to it and to the chronicles of the kings of Israel and of Judah dozens of times. The historian is telling his readers where to look for more, which means he knows he is not writing an exhaustive account. He is writing a theological one, and he selects.

Which is why we have four chapters on the temple and one on the wives and none at all on the administration of a forty-year empire.

'And the time that Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel was forty years.'

Forty years, like David, and like Saul.

Three kings, forty years each, and then the kingdom breaks.

'And Solomon slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David his father. And Rehoboam his son reigned in his place.'

Now stand back from the whole account, because this is the end of it and the shape of it matters.

He began by asking God for a hearing heart, and God was pleased with the request and gave him more than he asked. He judged two prostitutes rightly when nobody could have. He built the house of God to a pattern given to his father, and stood in front of it and said the truest thing anybody has ever said about a religious building. He prayed for the foreigner and for the exile and for the man who knows the affliction of his own heart. A queen crossed a desert on a rumour about the name of his God.

He also acquired horses, and traded with Egypt, and made silver as common as stone, and married seven hundred princesses, and built shrines for every one of them on the hill facing the temple, and tried to murder the man God had chosen to succeed him.

All of it is the same man, and the writer records all of it, and does not resolve it.

What he does instead is put one word in Solomon's mouth in chapter 8 and take it away in chapter 11. Shalem. Whole, undivided, at peace.

It was his name. He told the nation their hearts must be that toward God. And at the end, when he was old, with every advantage a man has ever had, his was not.

11.theology:
The law's reason, quoted (v. 2). Deuteronomy 7's command is never about blood or nationality: they will turn away your heart after their gods. It is a warning about worship, and the mechanism is the household. Scripture is clear elsewhere and this passage has been misused — Rahab of Jericho married into Israel and is in the genealogy of Christ; Ruth was a Moabitess, from one of the nations named in verse 1, and is David's great-grandmother; Uriah was a Hittite and one of the mighty men. What made the difference was never ancestry but which God they had come to. And the verb in verse 2 is Genesis 2's hold fast, which Deuteronomy uses over and over of what Israel owes God: you shall serve him and hold fast to him (Deut. 10:20). He clung to them. The verb that belongs to God is used of seven hundred women.

Seven hundred princesses are a foreign policy (v. 3). These are not romances; each is a treaty sealing a relationship with a neighbouring house, exactly as the daughter of Pharaoh was. Which makes it worse rather than better: a man who marries a princess to secure an alliance must let her worship her own gods or the alliance is insulted. Every marriage carried an obligation, and verse 8 is him meeting them.

When Solomon was old (v. 4). Not as a young king dazzled by success — at the end, after Gibeon, after seven years of building, after the longest prayer in the Old Testament, after God appeared to him a second time, after forty years on the throne. That is not the usual shape of a warning and it ought to be felt: there is no age at which a person is past this, and the drift can begin in the part of life that looks safest.

The word taken off him (v. 4). Shalem — whole, complete, undivided, at peace, and the root of his own name. He used it himself in front of the whole nation on the greatest day of his life: let your heart therefore be wholly true to the LORD our God (8:61). Note what the writer does not say: not false, not apostate, not that he abandoned the LORD. Solomon kept the feasts, the temple stood, the sacrifices went up. What he lost was the undividedness — his heart had more than one thing in it, and he had told the nation that would not do.

What the comparison with David is and is not (v. 4). Not sinlessness. David committed adultery, arranged a murder, failed his daughter, and left a deathbed list. The measure in this book is single: whether a king served the LORD alone or went after other gods — and on that measure the difference is total. David never once in seventy years worshipped another god or built a shrine to one; everything he did wrong he did as a man belonging to the LORD, and when confronted he broke and wrote Psalm 51. Solomon built high places for Chemosh and Molech facing the temple. That is why the verdict on every king who follows is measured against an adulterer and a murderer: whatever else he was, he had one God.

The formula, used first of Solomon (v. 6). Solomon did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. From here to the end of 2 Kings that sentence is stamped on king after king until it becomes the drumbeat of the whole history — and the first man it is used of is the wisest king who ever lived, who built the temple.

The location, and how long they stood (v. 7). On the mountain east of Jerusalem is the Mount of Olives, across the Kidron from the temple mount: a man standing in the courtyard of the house of the LORD could look up and see them. Three hundred years later Josiah is still tearing them down, and the record still calls them Solomon's (2 Kings 23:13).

Who had appeared to him twice (v. 9). This is why chapter 9 said a second time — the writer laid the fact down so it would be available here. God did not leave him to work it out: no prophet, no dream, no providence to be discerned. He came himself, twice, and said the same thing both times. And concerning this thing means the exact sin was named in advance, in person (9:6-7).

Since this has been your practice (v. 11). Not an incident — the Hebrew is nearer because this has been with you, a settled state of affairs. The high places had stood for years. And the kingdom goes to your servant: not a rival dynasty or a foreign power, but one of his own officials — the superintendent of his forced labour.

Three restraints, all on somebody else's account (vv. 12-13, 32, 34-36). Not in your days; not all the kingdom; one tribe kept — and every clause is for the sake of David my servant and of the city God chose. Solomon is spared the sight of it for the sake of a man dead forty years. The mercy is inside the judgment rather than instead of it.

The judgment arrives on legs (vv. 14, 23). Both adversaries are consequences of David's wars: Hadad a small boy carried out of a six-month massacre in Edom that 2 Samuel never records, and Rezon a soldier who ran when David destroyed Hadadezer's army and took Damascus — which becomes the great northern enemy for three centuries, through Ben-hadad and Naaman and the whole of 2 Kings. God did not manufacture Solomon's adversaries; he raised up the ones already there, who had been waiting all his life. And keep Hadad's three words: he has a house, an allowance, land, a royal marriage and a son raised among the sons of Pharaoh, and what he says is only let me go.

Solomon's own appointment (v. 28). He noticed a capable young man and promoted him — over the forced labour of the house of Joseph, the conscripted gangs of the northern tribes. So the man who takes ten tribes from Solomon's son spent his formative years administering the exact grievance the ten tribes secede over. He knows every man in those gangs, the quotas, what the levy costs a farming family, and what is said about the king in the north when nobody from Jerusalem is listening. Solomon gave him that education himself, because he was good at his job.

Every detail of the scene (v. 29). Ahijah is from Shiloh — where the tabernacle stood for centuries, where Hannah prayed and Samuel was called, and which God destroyed and made a byword (Jer. 7:12). He has put on a new garment specifically in order to destroy it. And they are alone in open country: the most seditious conversation in the kingdom, with no witnesses. The tearing has a history — Saul caught the hem of Samuel's robe and it tore, and Samuel said the LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you this day (1 Sam. 15:27-28). That tear was an accident; this one is deliberate.

The lamp (v. 36). David's own men used the word about him on a battlefield when he grew weary — lest you quench the lamp of Israel (2 Sam. 21:17) — and here God takes it up as his own, and uses it again for Abijam (15:4) and again when Judah deserves destruction (2 Kings 8:19). A lamp is a small thing and it is not extinguished: not a blaze, not a guarantee of prosperity, just a light God undertakes not to let go out. It burns down to almost nothing — a king in a Babylonian prison at the end of 2 Kings — and then to a carpenter's family in a village.

Jeroboam is offered the covenant (v. 38). I will build you a sure house, as I built for David is the language of 2 Samuel 7 — the same terms, in the same words, an enduring dynasty in the north on David's own footing. The condition is not obscure: listen, walk in my ways, keep my statutes, as David my servant did. This is not a consolation prize or a temporary arrangement; it is everything, on the one condition that governs everything in this book. Hold it for one chapter: the first substantial thing he does with his kingdom is make two golden calves. And even the sentence on David's line has a limit written into it — but not forever.

The last recorded act of the wisest man who ever lived (v. 40). He tries to have him murdered. God has told him, in person, that the kingdom will be torn from his son because of what he has done, and the response is not repentance, not the removal of the high places, not a word to God — it is an assassination order. He is doing what Saul did: told that the kingdom was going to a neighbour, Saul spent the rest of his life trying to kill the neighbour. You cannot kill your way out of a word from God, and Solomon of all people knew it. And Jeroboam flees to Egypt, to Shishak — where Hadad went as a boy and where the daughter of Pharaoh came from. Egypt has now sheltered two of his three adversaries, and five years after his death Shishak takes everything in Jerusalem that is not nailed down.

The account, closed (vv. 41-43). The formula appears for the first time and will run to the end of both books over some forty kings, most in a few lines — a man's whole life summarised, filed and closed, and then the next one. And the writer cites a source we do not have, which means he knows he is not writing an exhaustive account. He is writing a theological one, and he selects: four chapters on the temple, one on the wives, and nothing at all on the administration of a forty-year empire. Forty years, like David and like Saul — three kings, forty years each, and then the kingdom breaks.
11.examples:
Then: A king who had asked God for a hearing heart, built him a temple, prayed the longest prayer in the Old Testament and been visited by God twice in person, spent his old age putting up shrines to other gods on the hill facing that temple — one at a time, for one wife at a time — and when a prophet told him the kingdom would be torn away, he sent men to kill the prophet's candidate.

Now: Three things, and they are all uncomfortable. First, the timing: when Solomon was old. Not the reckless years. The end, after every spiritual advantage a human being has ever had. There is no stage of life at which a person becomes safe, and the danger is greatest in the part that looks safest. Second, the mechanism. There was never a moment when he decided to abandon God. There were seven hundred reasonable accommodations, each one defensible on its own, each one owed to somebody, and at the end of them the hill facing the house of God was covered in altars. That is how a heart stops being whole — not by a decision, but by a series of arrangements nobody would call a decision. And third, shalem. He preached it to a nation and lost it, and the writer never says a word about the irony; he simply puts the word in his mouth in chapter 8 and takes it off him in chapter 11. The question the chapter leaves is not whether your religion is functioning. It is whether there is anything else in the room.

And he said to the people, "You have gone up to Jerusalem long enough. Behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt."<sup>29</sup>And he set one in Bethel, and the other he put in Dan.<sup>30</sup>Then this thing became a sin, for the people went as far as Dan to be before one.<sup>31</sup>He also made temples on high places and appointed priests from among all the people, who were not of the Levites.<sup>32</sup>And Jeroboam appointed a feast on the fifteenth day of the eighth month like the feast that was in Judah, and he offered sacrifices on the altar. And he placed in Bethel the priests of the high places that he had made.<sup>33</sup>He went up to the altar that he had made in Bethel on the fifteenth day in the eighth month, in the month that he had devised from his own heart. 12.overview:
The coronation is at Shechem, not Jerusalem — a long way north, on the northern tribes' ground, where Abraham built an altar and Joshua said choose this day whom you will serve. That alone tells you the state of the union before a word is spoken.

And the demand is not religious, not tribal, and not about the succession. Nobody mentions the shrines Solomon built on the hill facing the temple; nobody quotes Ahijah. They have come to make him king, and we will serve you is the last clause of their sentence. It is about the levy — thirty thousand conscripted in monthly shifts, seventy thousand burden-bearers, eighty thousand quarrymen, twenty years of building, and twelve districts drawn across the tribal inheritances. The writer has been laying that down since chapter 4 without a word of comment. Here is the comment, and it comes from the people who carried it, and their word for it is yoke.

The old men give the finest piece of political advice in the Old Testament, and it is not a moral appeal: if you will be a servant to this people today... then they will be your servants forever. One day against a lifetime. They are telling him the arithmetic. And he asks the other set too — which makes it worse, not better: he did not fail to seek advice, he sought two opinions and picked the one he wanted, from men who had grown up in the palace during the richest reign in the nation's history and never carried a stone.

Then the sentence that breaks the kingdom, and it is eighty years old. A worthless man called Sheba blew a trumpet at a river crossing and said those exact words, and his revolt was over inside a chapter. His slogan outlived him and is now the constitutional act of ten tribes. And the writer lifts the curtain twice — a turn of affairs brought about by the LORD, and this thing is from me — over a catastrophe in which not one person is coerced and every one behaves exactly as you would expect.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — My Little Finger Is Thicker
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Rehoboam goes to Shechem, for all Israel had come to Shechem to make him king (v. 1). Jeroboam is sent for out of Egypt (vv. 2-3), and the assembly states its one demand: your father made our yoke heavy. Now therefore lighten the hard service of your father and his heavy yoke on us, and we will serve you (v. 4). He asks three days (v. 5). The old men who had stood before Solomon advise: if you will be a servant to this people today and serve them, and speak good words to them when you answer them, then they will be your servants forever (v. 7). But he abandoned the counsel that the old men gave him and took counsel with the young men who had grown up with him and stood before him (v. 8), who tell him to say my little finger is thicker than my father's thighs... my father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with scorpions (vv. 10-11). He does, harshly (vv. 12-14). So the king did not listen to the people, for it was a turn of affairs brought about by the LORD (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: The demand is not religious, not tribal and not about the succession. It is about the levy. The one thing ten tribes ask of a new king is relief from the conscripted labour that built the temple and the palace and the chariot cities.
verseByVerse.examples: And the old men's sentence is the whole doctrine of leadership: be a servant to this people today, and they will be your servants forever. One day of serving buys a lifetime of loyalty. It is not softness — it is the only arrangement that ever works.

verseByVerse.quote: Rehoboam went to Shechem, for all Israel had come to Shechem to make him king. And as soon as Jeroboam the son of Nebat heard of it (for he was still in Egypt, where he had fled from King Solomon), then Jeroboam returned from Egypt. And they sent and called him, and Jeroboam and all the assembly of Israel came and said to Rehoboam, "Your father made our yoke heavy. Now therefore lighten the hard service of your father and his heavy yoke on us, and we will serve you." He said to them, "Go away for three days, then come again to me." So the people went away. Then King Rehoboam took counsel with the old men, who had stood before Solomon his father while he was yet alive, saying, "How do you advise me to answer this people?" And they said to him, "If you will be a servant to this people today and serve them, and speak good words to them when you answer them, then they will be your servants forever." But he abandoned the counsel that the old men gave him and took counsel with the young men who had grown up with him and stood before him. And he said to them, "What do you advise that we answer this people who have said to me, 'Lighten the yoke that your father put on us'?" And the young men who had grown up with him said to him, "Thus shall you speak to this people who said to you, 'Your father made our yoke heavy, but you lighten it for us,' thus shall you say to them, 'My little finger is thicker than my father's thighs. And now, whereas my father laid on you a heavy yoke, I will add to your yoke. My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with scorpions.'" So Jeroboam and all the people came to Rehoboam the third day, as the king said, "Come to me again the third day." And the king answered the people harshly, and forsaking the counsel that the old men had given him, he spoke to them according to the counsel of the young men, saying, "My father made your yoke heavy, but I will add to your yoke. My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with scorpions." So the king did not listen to the people, for it was a turn of affairs brought about by the LORD that he might fulfill his word, which the LORD spoke by Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam the son of Nebat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Rehoboam went to Shechem, for all Israel had come to Shechem to make him king.'

Note where the coronation is held, because it is not Jerusalem.

Shechem is in the north, in the hill country of Ephraim, and it is one of the oldest covenant sites in the country. Abraham built an altar there when he first entered the land. Joshua gathered all Israel there at the end of his life and said choose this day whom you will serve, and set up a stone under an oak as a witness (Josh. 24). Joseph's bones are buried there.

The new king of Israel is required to travel a long way north and be made king on the northern tribes' ground. That in itself tells you the state of the union before a word is spoken.

'And when Jeroboam the son of Nebat heard of it (for he was still in Egypt, where he had fled from King Solomon), then Jeroboam returned from Egypt.'

'And they sent and called him, and Jeroboam and all the assembly of Israel came and said to Rehoboam,'

'"Your father made our yoke heavy. Now therefore lighten the hard service of your father and his heavy yoke on us, and we will serve you."'

Here is the demand, and what it is and is not deserves precision.

It is not about religion. Nobody mentions the high places on the mountain east of Jerusalem, or Ashtoreth, or Molech, or the fact that the previous king spent his old age building shrines to foreign gods. The word from Ahijah is not quoted at anybody.

It is not about the succession. They have come to Shechem to make him king; the assembly is a coronation, and they are prepared to go through with it.

It is not tribal separatism. We will serve you is the last clause of the sentence, and it is an offer.

It is about the levy.

Thirty thousand men conscripted in monthly shifts to Lebanon. Seventy thousand burden-bearers. Eighty thousand quarrymen. Three thousand three hundred foremen, and a minister of forced labour with a department. Twenty years of building the temple and the palace and the Millo and the wall and Hazor and Megiddo and Gezer and the store cities and the chariot cities. And the twelve districts, drawn across the tribal inheritances, each feeding the court for a month.

The writer has been laying that down since chapter 4 and never once commenting on it. Here is the comment, and it comes from the people who carried it.

Their word for it is yoke — what you put on an animal to make it pull.

'He said to them, "Go away for three days, then come again to me." So the people went away.'

Three days, and he uses them properly. He asks two sets of advisers.

'Then King Rehoboam took counsel with the old men, who had stood before Solomon his father while he was yet alive, saying, "How do you advise me to answer this people?"'

These are the men who ran Solomon's government. They know exactly what the levy was, because they administered it, and they know what the country thinks of it.

'And they said to him, "If you will be a servant to this people today and serve them, and speak good words to them when you answer them, then they will be your servants forever."'

Here is the finest piece of political advice in the Old Testament. Take it apart, because it is not what people assume when they hear that a king was told to be nice.

Read the shape of it: if you will be a servant to this people today... then they will be your servants forever.

One day against a lifetime. The old men are not making a moral appeal and they are not asking him to be soft. They are telling him the arithmetic. Serve them once, at the moment when they have asked for something and it costs you, and you will have them for the rest of your life.

Note the two verbs. Be a servant... and serve them. The word is ebed, the ordinary word for a slave or a bondman — the same word the assembly used of themselves in verse 4, and we will serve you.

They are proposing an exchange of that word. You take the servant's place today; they take it permanently.

And speak good words to them is not a suggestion about tone. In the language of treaties, good words are favourable terms. He is being advised to grant the request and to say so kindly.

Now, a thousand years later, twelve men were arguing about which of them was greatest, and the Son of David said this to them:

You know that those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant, and whoever would be first among you must be slave of all. For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:42-45).

The correspondence should be stated carefully, because they are not the same thing.

The old men are giving prudential advice to a king: serve them and you will keep the kingdom. It works, and it is true, and it is about outcomes.

Jesus is not offering a technique for retaining power. He is describing what greatness actually is in his kingdom, and he grounds it in what he came to do, and the cost is not a day of concessions but his life.

So the verse is not the gospel. It is the shadow the gospel casts backwards over every position of authority anybody has ever held — and what makes it striking is that even at the level of pure statecraft, in a courtroom at Shechem in the tenth century before Christ, the old men had noticed that serving is the only thing that works.

Rehoboam had it in writing from the men who had run the country for forty years, and he had three days.

'But he abandoned the counsel that the old men gave him and took counsel with the young men who had grown up with him and stood before him.'

Who had grown up with him.

That is the whole explanation and the writer gives it in five words. These are his friends. They grew up in the palace during the richest reign in Israel's history, in the generation that saw the gold shields and the ivory throne and the ships bringing apes and peacocks, and never once carried a stone.

Rehoboam is about forty-one years old (14:21), so these are not boys. They are men of his own age who have never done anything except be near power.

He asked both, which is the thing that makes this worse rather than better. He did not fail to seek advice. He sought two opinions and picked the one he wanted.

'And he said to them, "What do you advise that we answer this people who have said to me, 'Lighten the yoke that your father put on us'?"'

Note how he frames the question to the second group.

To the old men he asked: how do you advise me to answer this people? Open.

To his friends he asks: what shall we answer this people who have said to me — and he quotes their demand back in a way that makes it a complaint about his father.

He has already decided how he feels about it. He is looking for support.

'And the young men who had grown up with him said to him, "Thus shall you speak to this people who said to you, 'Your father made our yoke heavy, but you lighten it for us,' thus shall you say to them, 'My little finger is thicker than my father's thighs.'"'

The line is crude and it is meant to be.

It is a boast about virility and force, and it says: whatever you thought my father was, I am more of it.

'"And now, whereas my father laid on you a heavy yoke, I will add to your yoke. My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with scorpions."'

There it is.

A scorpion in this context is generally taken to be a whip with barbs or metal pieces worked into the lashes — a thing designed to tear rather than to sting.

The men asked for the yoke to be lightened. He promises to add to it, and to change the instrument.

Read what he is actually claiming. He is not denying that his father used whips. He accepts the charge in full and offers to escalate it. Solomon's own record is being cited by his son as the baseline he intends to exceed.

Notice what the advice reveals about the men who gave it. They are not stupid about tactics; they are simply certain that the north will do what it is told, because in their experience it always has. They grew up watching the gangs go north to Lebanon ten thousand a month and come back, year after year, and they concluded that this is how the world works.

People who have only ever seen power obeyed cannot imagine it refused.

'So Jeroboam and all the people came to Rehoboam the third day, as the king said, "Come to me again the third day."'

'And the king answered the people harshly, and forsaking the counsel that the old men had given him,'

'he spoke to them according to the counsel of the young men, saying, "My father made your yoke heavy, but I will add to your yoke. My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with scorpions."'

He says it out loud, to their faces, in the assembly.

'So the king did not listen to the people, for it was a turn of affairs brought about by the LORD that he might fulfill his word, which the LORD spoke by Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam the son of Nebat.'

Here the writer lifts the curtain for one sentence, exactly as he did at 2 Samuel 17:14.

It was a turn of affairs brought about by the LORD.

Hold both halves of that, because the verse insists on both and does not explain how they fit.

On the human side, everything in this chapter is fully accounted for. A frightened, vain man of forty-one asked two sets of advisers and chose the flatterers. He was proud, and badly brought up, and afraid of looking weak in his first week. The young men were arrogant because they had never carried anything. The northern tribes had a real grievance, thirty years old, that nobody in Jerusalem had ever taken seriously. Not one person in the chapter is coerced, and every one of them does what you would expect.

The writer says God did it.

This is the structure the books of Samuel and Kings keep using at the great hinges. Ahithophel gave sound advice and Absalom preferred a better speech, for the LORD had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel (2 Sam. 17:14). Joseph's brothers meant evil and God meant good, of the same act (Gen. 50:20). And the cross: delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God and crucified by the hands of lawless men in the same sentence (Acts 2:23).

Scripture never resolves the mechanism and never drops either half. God is not a spectator to whom history happens, and no man in this chapter has an excuse.

Note the purpose clause: that he might fulfill his word, which the LORD spoke by Ahijah. The tearing of the cloak was three chapters ago, on an empty road, with two men present.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–24 — To Your Tents, O Israel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: And when all Israel saw that the king did not listen to them, the people answered the king, "What portion do we have in David? We have no inheritance in the son of Jesse. To your tents, O Israel! Look now to your own house, David." So Israel went to their tents (v. 16). Rehoboam reigns over those in the cities of Judah (v. 17). Then King Rehoboam sent Adoram, who was taskmaster over the forced labor, and all Israel stoned him to death with stones. And King Rehoboam hurried to mount his chariot to flee to Jerusalem (v. 18). So Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David to this day (v. 19). Jeroboam is made king over all Israel; only Judah follows David (vv. 20-21). Rehoboam musters a hundred and eighty thousand to fight, and Shemaiah brings the word of God: you shall not go up or fight against your relatives the people of Israel. Every man return to his home, for this thing is from me (vv. 22-24). And they obey.
verseByVerse.theology: Those words are not new. A worthless man called Sheba blew a trumpet at a river crossing in David's day and said we have no portion in David, and we have no inheritance in the son of Jesse; every man to his tents, O Israel (2 Sam. 20:1). His revolt collapsed in a chapter. His sentence outlived him by eighty years and is now the constitutional act of ten tribes.
verseByVerse.examples: And the man they stone is the minister of forced labour, who has held that office since David's last cabinet list (2 Sam. 20:24) and appears in Solomon's at 4:6 and 5:14. Rehoboam sent the one man in the kingdom who could not be sent, and then ran for his chariot.

verseByVerse.quote: And when all Israel saw that the king did not listen to them, the people answered the king, "What portion do we have in David? We have no inheritance in the son of Jesse. To your tents, O Israel! Look now to your own house, David." So Israel went to their tents. But Rehoboam reigned over the people of Israel who lived in the cities of Judah. Then King Rehoboam sent Adoram, who was taskmaster over the forced labor, and all Israel stoned him to death with stones. And King Rehoboam hurried to mount his chariot to flee to Jerusalem. So Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David to this day. And when all Israel heard that Jeroboam had returned, they sent and called him to the assembly and made him king over all Israel. There was none that followed the house of David but the tribe of Judah only. When Rehoboam came to Jerusalem, he assembled all the house of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin, 180,000 chosen warriors, to fight against the house of Israel, to restore the kingdom to Rehoboam the son of Solomon. But the word of God came to Shemaiah the man of God: "Say to Rehoboam the son of Solomon, king of Judah, and to all the house of Judah and Benjamin, and to the rest of the people, 'Thus says the LORD, You shall not go up or fight against your relatives the people of Israel. Every man return to his home, for this thing is from me.'" So they listened to the word of the LORD and went home again, according to the word of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And when all Israel saw that the king did not listen to them, the people answered the king, "What portion do we have in David? We have no inheritance in the son of Jesse. To your tents, O Israel! Look now to your own house, David." So Israel went to their tents.'

Now go back eighty years and read this.

Now there happened to be there a worthless man, whose name was Sheba, the son of Bichri, a Benjaminite. And he blew the trumpet and said, "We have no portion in David, and we have no inheritance in the son of Jesse; every man to his tents, O Israel!" (2 Sam. 20:1).

It is the same sentence.

Not similar — the same words, in the same order. A man the writer of Samuel called worthless, with no army and no case, blew a trumpet at a river crossing and said twelve words, and his rebellion was over inside a chapter with his head thrown over a wall.

And his sentence survived him by eighty years, and here it is, spoken not by one agitator but by the assembly of ten tribes, as a constitutional act.

Go back further and find where the crack opened. It is the last verse of 2 Samuel 19. David is coming home after Absalom's rebellion, and Israel and Judah are arguing about who had the right to escort him across the Jordan — a quarrel about precedence, about who was asked first, about whose relative he was. And the writer ends the chapter by recording only this: the words of the men of Judah were fiercer than the words of the men of Israel (2 Sam. 19:43).

The very next verse is Sheba's trumpet.

So the line runs: a squabble at a river crossing about who got to walk beside the king; a slogan handed to men who were already humiliated; a revolt that failed; eighty years of the levy; and a young king who would rather sound strong than be obeyed.

Look now to your own house, David is the coldest clause in the verse. It is a dismissal — go and manage your own family — addressed to a dynasty God had promised would last forever.

'But Rehoboam reigned over the people of Israel who lived in the cities of Judah.'

'Then King Rehoboam sent Adoram, who was taskmaster over the forced labor, and all Israel stoned him to death with stones. And King Rehoboam hurried to mount his chariot to flee to Jerusalem.'

This is the single stupidest decision in the book.

Ten tribes have just walked out over the forced labour. The one department they named, the one grievance they stated, the only thing they asked for.

And Rehoboam sends them the minister of forced labour.

Whether he sent him to negotiate or to start collecting, the text does not say, and it barely matters. Adoram is the human face of the thing they have just seceded over.

Keep his name, because he has been in this history a long time. He appears in David's last cabinet list as Adoram... in charge of the forced labor (2 Sam. 20:24), and in Solomon's as Adoniram the son of Abda (4:6), and again running the levy to Lebanon (5:14). The writer has named him four times across three reigns and never once commented.

Here is the comment. They stone him to death.

The king who sent him runs. King Rehoboam hurried to mount his chariot to flee to Jerusalem. The man who three days ago compared his little finger to his father's thighs is now getting into a chariot as fast as he can.

'So Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David to this day.'

To this day. The writer is looking back from a long way off, and the division never healed. The northern kingdom lasted two centuries and was destroyed by Assyria; the southern lasted another century and a half and went to Babylon. They were never one nation again.

'And when all Israel heard that Jeroboam had returned, they sent and called him to the assembly and made him king over all Israel. There was none that followed the house of David but the tribe of Judah only.'

'When Rehoboam came to Jerusalem, he assembled all the house of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin, 180,000 chosen warriors, to fight against the house of Israel, to restore the kingdom to Rehoboam the son of Solomon.'

A hundred and eighty thousand men, mustered to take the north back by force.

'But the word of God came to Shemaiah the man of God:'

'"Say to Rehoboam the son of Solomon, king of Judah, and to all the house of Judah and Benjamin, and to the rest of the people,"'

'"'Thus says the LORD, You shall not go up or fight against your relatives the people of Israel. Every man return to his home, for this thing is from me.'" So they listened to the word of the LORD and went home again, according to the word of the LORD.'

Here is the second half of the theological spine, and it is stronger than the first.

For this thing is from me.

Verse 15 said the refusal was a turn of affairs brought about by the LORD. This says the whole thing — the secession, the loss of ten tribes, the breaking of the kingdom David spent his life uniting — is God's own doing.

Not permitted. Not foreseen. From me.

Note what the prophet calls the northerners: your relatives. Literally your brothers.

That is the same argument Abner shouted across a valley at Joab a hundred years earlier — shall the sword devour forever? Do you not know that it will be bitter in the end? How long will you refrain from telling your people to turn from the pursuit of their brothers? (2 Sam. 2:26). It is what David refused to allow when he walked out of Jerusalem rather than have the city fought over.

'So they listened to the word of the LORD and went home again.'

They obey, which is the one thing anybody in this chapter does right.

A hundred and eighty thousand armed men, already mustered, with a king who wants his kingdom back and a grievance that is entirely legitimate on its own terms — and a prophet says one sentence and they all go home.

That is remarkable and it should be said so. Rehoboam would not listen to the old men who had run the government, or to ten tribes standing in front of him. He listens to Shemaiah.

It is the only good decision he makes in the chapter, and it is also the shape of what is wrong with him: he can obey God when a prophet tells him plainly, and he cannot govern people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–33 — Behold Your Gods, O Israel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeroboam builds Shechem and Penuel (v. 25), and reasons: now the kingdom will turn back to the house of David. If this people go up to offer sacrifices in the temple of the LORD at Jerusalem, then the heart of this people will turn again to their lord, to Rehoboam king of Judah, and they will kill me (vv. 26-27). So the king took counsel and made two calves of gold. And he said to the people, "You have gone up to Jerusalem long enough. Behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt" (v. 28). One is set in Bethel and the other in Dan, and this thing became a sin (vv. 29-30). He makes temples on high places and appoints priests who were not of the Levites (v. 31), and a feast in the eighth month like the feast that was in Judah (v. 32), going up to the altar he had made in Bethel in the month that he had devised from his own heart (v. 33).
verseByVerse.theology: He had been offered David's own covenant on condition of obedience — I will build you a sure house, as I built for David (11:38) — and his first act as king is the thing that forfeits it. And his stated reasoning is entirely about security: they will kill me. He does it because he is afraid.
verseByVerse.examples: Behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt is Aaron's sentence at the foot of Sinai, almost word for word (Ex. 32:4, 8). And the chapter ends on the writer's verdict on all invented worship: a festival in the month that he had devised from his own heart.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jeroboam built Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim and lived there. And he went out from there and built Penuel. And Jeroboam said in his heart, "Now the kingdom will turn back to the house of David. If this people go up to offer sacrifices in the temple of the LORD at Jerusalem, then the heart of this people will turn again to their lord, to Rehoboam king of Judah, and they will kill me and return to Rehoboam king of Judah."
