So the king took counsel and made two calves of gold. And he said to the people, "You have gone up to Jerusalem long enough. Behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt." And he set one in Bethel, and the other he put in Dan. Then this thing became a sin, for the people went as far as Dan to be before one. He also made temples on high places and appointed priests from among all the people, who were not of the Levites. And Jeroboam appointed a feast on the fifteenth day of the eighth month like the feast that was in Judah, and he offered sacrifices on the altar. So he did in Bethel, sacrificing to the calves that he made. And he placed in Bethel the priests of the high places that he had made. He went up to the altar that he had made in Bethel on the fifteenth day in the eighth month, in the month that he had devised from his own heart. And he instituted a feast for the people of Israel and went up to the altar to make offerings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Jeroboam built Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim and lived there. And he went out from there and built Penuel.'

He fortifies a capital and a crossing point east of the Jordan.

Penuel is where Jacob wrestled all night and was named Israel.

'And Jeroboam said in his heart, "Now the kingdom will turn back to the house of David."'

Said in his heart.

The reader has met that phrase before, at a bad moment. Then David said in his heart, "Now I shall perish one day by the hand of Saul. There is nothing better for me than that I should escape to the land of the Philistines" (1 Sam. 27:1). No priest, no ephod, no prophet — a man doing his own thinking in a crisis, and it cost him sixteen months in enemy country.

Jeroboam is doing the same thing, and he has more reason not to than David had. He has a word from a prophet, delivered in person on an empty road, with an offer attached.

'"If this people go up to offer sacrifices in the temple of the LORD at Jerusalem, then the heart of this people will turn again to their lord, to Rehoboam king of Judah, and they will kill me, and they will return to Rehoboam king of Judah."'

Here is the reasoning, and every step of it is politically sound.

Three times a year every male in Israel was required to go up to Jerusalem for the feasts. That means his entire adult population walking south into his rival's capital, three times a year, to worship at a temple built by the dynasty he has just replaced, in a city God had chosen.

No new state could survive that. Any competent adviser would have said so.

Note where the reasoning ends: they will kill me.

That is the actual engine. Not theology, not a vision for the north, not even ambition. Fear.

Now set that against what he had been given. Ahijah tore a new cloak into twelve pieces on an empty road and said: if you will listen to all that I command you, and will walk in my ways, and do what is right in my eyes by keeping my statutes and my commandments, as David my servant did, I will be with you and will build you a sure house, as I built for David, and I will give Israel to you (11:38).

He has been offered David's own covenant, in David's own words, on one condition.

The security he is frightened about has already been guaranteed by God, in person, through a prophet, before he was king. And within a few verses of getting the kingdom he sets about protecting it by means that forfeit the promise.

That is the tragedy of the man, and it is a very ordinary one. He believed the prophecy enough to take the throne and not enough to trust the God who gave it.

'So the king took counsel and made two calves of gold. And he said to the people, "You have gone up to Jerusalem long enough. Behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt."'

Now read the last sentence and then read Exodus 32.

Aaron, at the foot of Sinai, with Moses on the mountain and the people restless, took their gold and made a calf, and they said, "These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!" (Ex. 32:4). God repeats it back to Moses in verse 8 in the same words.

Jeroboam says it almost exactly, and makes two.

This is not an accidental echo. Everybody in Israel knew that story; it was the worst day in the nation's history, three thousand men died for it, and Moses ground the calf to powder and made them drink it. Jeroboam is repeating it deliberately and at national scale.

Be precise about what he is doing, because it is subtler than simple idolatry and that is what makes it work.

He is not introducing a foreign god. He does not name Baal or Ashtoreth or Chemosh. The sentence he uses is about the God who brought Israel out of Egypt — the right God, correctly identified by the right act.

In the surrounding cultures a bull was not usually the god itself but the pedestal the god was imagined to stand on, and it is likely enough that Jeroboam presented these as thrones for the invisible LORD rather than as rivals to him. That is precisely what Aaron did: he made the calf and then proclaimed a feast to the LORD (Ex. 32:5), using the covenant name.

So this is a worship of the true God by means he has forbidden, and it breaks the second commandment rather than the first.

Which is exactly why it is so dangerous. Nobody in the north had to decide to abandon the LORD. They had to accept a more convenient way of approaching him, sanctioned by the state, closer to home, and requiring no journey.

'And he set one in Bethel, and the other he put in Dan.'

The placement is expert.

Dan is at the far northern end of the kingdom and Bethel is at the southern border, a few miles from Jerusalem. Between them they cover the whole country, and nobody has to travel far.

Both sites already had religious history, which is the shrewdest part. Bethel is where Jacob slept with a stone for a pillow and saw the ladder and said surely the LORD is in this place, and I did not know it... this is none other than the house of God (Gen. 28:16-17). The name means house of God. Dan had housed an illegitimate shrine since the days of the judges, with a stolen idol and a hired Levite (Judg. 18).

He is not inventing anything. He is using ground people already felt religious about.

'Then this thing became a sin, for the people went as far as Dan to be before one.'

This thing became a sin. The writer says it flatly, and the phrase becomes his shorthand for the whole northern kingdom. From here to the fall of Samaria, king after king is condemned in the same formula: he did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin.

Nineteen kings, two centuries, and every one of them is measured against this afternoon.

'He also made temples on high places and appointed priests from among all the people, who were not of the Levites.'

Now the second thing, and it is as serious as the calves.

The priesthood in Israel was not an office anybody could hold. It belonged to Aaron's line within the tribe of Levi, and the whole tribe had no territorial inheritance precisely so that they would be distributed through the country and dependent on the tithe. Uzziah, a king of Judah, was struck with leprosy for going into the temple to burn incense (2 Chron. 26:16-21).

Jeroboam appoints priests from among all the people.

Chronicles records what happened next: the Levites in the north left their pasturelands and their property and came south to Judah, for Jeroboam and his sons cast them out from serving as priests of the LORD (2 Chron. 11:14).

He emptied the northern kingdom of the men whose job was to teach the law.

'And Jeroboam appointed a feast on the fifteenth day of the eighth month like the feast that was in Judah, and he offered sacrifices on the altar. So he did in Bethel, sacrificing to the calves that he made. And he placed in Bethel the priests of the high places that he had made.'

A festival one month later than the real one.

The Feast of Booths was the fifteenth day of the seventh month — the feast Solomon chose for the dedication of the temple. Jeroboam moves it to the fifteenth day of the eighth.

Everything is almost right. Almost the same festival, almost the same date, almost the same God, at sites with genuine history, with priests and altars and sacrifices, and it is all one month and one tribe and one commandment out.

'He went up to the altar that he had made in Bethel on the fifteenth day in the eighth month, in the month that he had devised from his own heart. And he instituted a feast for the people of Israel and went up to the altar to make offerings.'

There is the last phrase of the chapter, and it is the writer's verdict on the whole enterprise.

In the month that he had devised from his own heart.

Not the month God appointed. The month he thought of.

That is the charge, and it is not primarily that he was irreligious. He was extremely religious. He built the sanctuaries, appointed the clergy, instituted the festival, and went up to the altar himself to make the offerings. The north had a full and functioning national worship from this day onward.

Every element of it came out of a man's own head, for reasons he had stated: they will kill me.

Set the phrase beside the one from the beginning of the chapter. The old men told Rehoboam what would keep his kingdom and he preferred what his friends said. Ahijah told Jeroboam what would build him a sure house and he preferred what he had worked out himself.

Both men had the answer in their hands. Both looked at it, and did the thing they had devised from their own heart, and between them they broke the kingdom of God's people in half.

12.theology:
Where the coronation is held (v. 1). Shechem is in the hill country of Ephraim — Abraham's first altar in the land, the place Joshua gathered all Israel and set a stone under an oak as a witness (Josh. 24), where Joseph's bones are buried. The new king of Judah's house has to travel north and be made king on the other tribes' ground.

What the demand is not (v. 4). Not religion — nobody mentions the high places, or Ashtoreth, or Molech, and Ahijah's word is not quoted at anybody. Not the succession — they came to make him king and are prepared to go through with it. Not separatism — we will serve you is an offer. It is the levy, and the writer has been documenting it since chapter 4 in silence.

The arithmetic in the old men's advice (v. 7). A servant today against servants forever: they are not asking him to be soft, they are telling him what works. And the word in both halves is ebed, the ordinary word for a bondman — the same word the assembly used of themselves. They are proposing an exchange of that word: take the servant's place today and they take it permanently. Speak good words is not about tone either; in treaty language good words are favourable terms.

Mark 10:42-45, stated carefully. The old men are giving prudential advice to a king — serve them and you keep the kingdom — and it is true and it is about outcomes. Jesus is not offering a technique for retaining power; he is describing what greatness is in his kingdom, grounds it in what he came to do, and the cost is not a day of concessions but his life. The verse is not the gospel. It is the shadow the gospel casts backwards over every position of authority — and what is striking is that even at the level of pure statecraft, in a courtroom at Shechem, the old men had noticed that serving is the only thing that works.

Who had grown up with him (v. 8). Five words and the whole explanation. Rehoboam is about forty-one (14:21), so these are not boys but men of his own age who grew up in the palace during the gold shields and the ivory throne and the ships bringing apes and peacocks, and never carried a stone. And note how he frames the question differently to each group: to the old men, how do you advise me to answer this people?, open; to his friends, what shall we answer this people who have said to me, with the demand quoted back as a complaint about his father. He had already decided how he felt and was looking for support.

He accepts the charge and escalates it (v. 11). A scorpion is generally taken to be a whip with barbs or metal worked into the lashes — designed to tear. And he does not deny that his father used whips; he takes Solomon's record as the baseline he intends to exceed. What the advice reveals about the young men is not stupidity about tactics but certainty: they grew up watching gangs go north to Lebanon ten thousand a month and come back, year after year, and concluded that this is how the world works. People who have only ever seen power obeyed cannot imagine it refused.

Both halves, and no mechanism (v. 15). On the human side everything is fully accounted for: a frightened, vain man of forty-one asked two sets of advisers and chose the flatterers; the young men were arrogant because they had never carried anything; the north had a thirty-year grievance nobody in Jerusalem had taken seriously. Not one person is coerced. And the writer says God did it. This is the structure Samuel and Kings use at every great hinge — Ahithophel's good counsel defeated because the LORD had ordained it (2 Sam. 17:14); Joseph's brothers meaning evil and God meaning good of the same act (Gen. 50:20); and the cross, according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God and by the hands of lawless men in one sentence (Acts 2:23). Scripture never resolves it and never drops either half.

Sheba's sentence, eighty years later (v. 16). The same words in the same order, from a man the writer of Samuel called worthless, who had no army and no case and whose head went over a wall inside a chapter (2 Sam. 20:1). And the crack opened one verse earlier than that, in a quarrel about precedence at a river crossing — who had the right to escort the king home — which the writer ended by recording only that the words of the men of Judah were fiercer than the words of the men of Israel (2 Sam. 19:43). And look now to your own house, David is the coldest clause: a dismissal addressed to a dynasty God had promised would last forever.

The stupidest decision in the book (v. 18). Ten tribes have walked out over the forced labour, and he sends them the minister of forced labour. Whether to negotiate or to start collecting the text does not say and it hardly matters: Adoram is the human face of the thing they seceded over. He has been in this history across three reigns — David's last cabinet list (2 Sam. 20:24), Solomon's (4:6), and running the levy to Lebanon (5:14) — named four times without comment. Here is the comment. And the king who three days earlier compared his little finger to his father's thighs gets into a chariot as fast as he can.

This thing is from me (v. 24). Stronger than verse 15. Not permitted, not foreseen — the secession, the loss of ten tribes, the breaking of the kingdom David spent his life uniting, is God's own doing. And the prophet calls the northerners your relatives, literally your brothers, which is Abner's argument shouted across a valley a century earlier (2 Sam. 2:26) and the reason David walked out of Jerusalem rather than have the city fought over. They obey, which is the one thing anybody in this chapter does right: a hundred and eighty thousand armed men with a legitimate grievance go home on one sentence from a prophet. Rehoboam would not listen to the men who ran the government or to ten tribes in front of him, and he listens to Shemaiah — which is his one good decision and also the shape of what is wrong with him. He can obey God when told plainly, and he cannot govern people.

Said in his heart (v. 26). The reader has met the phrase at a bad moment: then David said in his heart, "Now I shall perish one day by the hand of Saul" (1 Sam. 27:1) — a man doing his own thinking in a crisis with a priest and an ephod and a prophet in his camp. Jeroboam has less excuse: he has a word from a prophet delivered in person with an offer attached.

The reasoning is sound, and the engine is fear (v. 27). Three times a year every male in Israel was required at Jerusalem; that is his whole adult population walking into his rival's capital to worship at a temple built by the dynasty he replaced. No new state could survive it, and any competent adviser would have said so. And the reasoning ends they will kill me. Set that against 11:38, where he was offered David's own covenant in David's own words on one condition. The security he is frightened about had already been guaranteed by God through a prophet before he was king — and he sets about protecting it by means that forfeit the promise. He believed the prophecy enough to take the throne and not enough to trust the God who gave it.

Aaron's sentence, deliberately (v. 28). These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt (Ex. 32:4, 8). Everybody in Israel knew that story: the worst day in the nation's history, three thousand dead, the calf ground to powder and drunk. Jeroboam repeats it at national scale, and makes two. And it is subtler than simple idolatry, which is what makes it work: he names no foreign god, and the sentence is about the God who brought Israel out of Egypt — the right God, correctly identified by the right act. In the surrounding cultures a bull was usually the pedestal a god stood on rather than the god, and he very likely presented these as thrones for the invisible LORD, which is exactly what Aaron did before proclaiming a feast to the LORD (Ex. 32:5). It breaks the second commandment rather than the first — and that is why it is dangerous. Nobody in the north had to decide to abandon the LORD. They had to accept a more convenient way of approaching him, sanctioned by the state, closer to home, requiring no journey.

Expert placement (v. 29). Dan at the far north and Bethel at the southern border cover the whole country; nobody travels far. And both sites already had religious history, which is the shrewdest part: Bethel is where Jacob slept on a stone and said surely the LORD is in this place... this is none other than the house of God (Gen. 28:16-17), and the name means house of God; Dan had housed an illegitimate shrine with a stolen idol and a hired Levite since the days of the judges (Judg. 18). He invents nothing. He uses ground people already felt religious about.

The formula for two centuries (v. 30). This thing became a sin, and from here to the fall of Samaria king after king is condemned in the same words: he did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin. Nineteen kings, and every one measured against this afternoon.

He emptied the north of its teachers (v. 31). The priesthood belonged to Aaron's line within Levi, and the whole tribe held no territory precisely so that they would be distributed through the country and dependent on the tithe; a king of Judah was struck with leprosy for burning incense in the temple (2 Chron. 26:16-21). Jeroboam appoints priests from among all the people — and Chronicles records the result: the Levites left their pasturelands and property and came south, for Jeroboam and his sons cast them out from serving as priests of the LORD (2 Chron. 11:14).

Everything almost right (vv. 32-33). The Feast of Booths was the fifteenth of the seventh month — the feast Solomon chose for the dedication. He moves it to the fifteenth of the eighth. Almost the same festival, almost the same date, almost the same God, at sites with genuine history, with priests and altars and sacrifices — one month and one tribe and one commandment out. And the last phrase is the verdict on the whole enterprise: in the month that he had devised from his own heart. The charge is not that he was irreligious; he was extremely religious, and the north had a full and functioning national worship from that day. Every element of it came out of a man's own head, for a reason he had stated: they will kill me. The old men told Rehoboam what would keep his kingdom and he preferred what his friends said; Ahijah told Jeroboam what would build him a sure house and he preferred what he had worked out himself. Both had the answer in their hands, and between them they broke the kingdom of God's people in half.
12.examples:
Then: Ten tribes asked a new king for one thing — that the conscripted labour be lightened — and offered to serve him if it was. The men who had run the government for forty years told him that one day of serving them would buy him their loyalty for life. He asked his friends instead, promised to beat them with something worse than his father had used, and then sent them the minister of forced labour, who was stoned to death in the road.

Now: Three things. The old men's sentence is the one to keep, and its force is that it is not sentiment but arithmetic: a day of genuine service, at the moment when somebody has asked for something and it costs you, buys what no amount of authority can command. Anyone who has charge of anybody is standing in Rehoboam's three days. Second, he did not fail to seek counsel — he sought two opinions and chose the one he already wanted, and framed the question differently to each set of advisers. That is the ordinary way people get bad advice, and it is not a failure of information. And third, Jeroboam, whose golden calves were not apostasy but convenience: the right God, correctly named, approached by a method he had devised himself, closer to home, requiring no journey. Worship that has been quietly redesigned to cost less is the danger this chapter is actually about, and two centuries of a nation's history are measured against the afternoon he set it up.

13.text: <sup>1</sup>And behold, a man of God came out of Judah by the word of the LORD to Bethel. Jeroboam was standing by the altar to make offerings.<sup>2</sup>And the man cried against the altar by the word of the LORD and said, "O altar, altar, thus says the LORD: 'Behold, a son shall be born to the house of David, Josiah by name, and he shall sacrifice on you the priests of the high places who make offerings on you, and human bones shall be burned on you.'"<sup>3</sup>And he gave a sign the same day, saying, "This is the sign that the LORD has spoken: 'Behold, the altar shall be torn down, and the ashes that are on it shall be poured out.'"<sup>4</sup>And when the king heard the saying of the man of God, which he cried against the altar at Bethel, Jeroboam stretched out his hand from the altar, saying, "Seize him." And his hand, which he stretched out against him, dried up, so that he could not draw it back to himself.<sup>5</sup>The altar also was torn down, and the ashes poured out from the altar, according to the sign that the man of God had given by the word of the LORD.<sup>6</sup>And the king said to the man of God, "Entreat now the favor of the LORD your God, and pray for me, that my hand may be restored to me." And the man of God entreated the LORD, and the king's hand was restored to him and became as it was before.<sup>7</sup>And the king said to the man of God, "Come home with me, and refresh yourself, and I will give you a reward."<sup>8</sup>And the man of God said to the king, "If you give me half your house, I will not go in with you. And I will not eat bread or drink water in this place,<sup>9</sup>for so was it commanded me by the word of the LORD, saying, 'You shall neither eat bread nor drink water nor return by the way that you came.'"<sup>10</sup>So he went another way and did not return by the way that he came to Bethel.<sup>11</sup>Now an old prophet lived in Bethel. And his sons came and told him all that the man of God had done that day in Bethel. They also told to their father the words that he had spoken to the king.<sup>12</sup>And their father said to them, "Which way did he go?" And his sons showed him the way that the man of God who came from Judah had gone.<sup>13</sup>And he said to his sons, "Saddle the donkey for me." So they saddled the donkey for him and he mounted it.<sup>14</sup>And he went after the man of God and found him sitting under an oak. And he said to him, "Are you the man of God who came from Judah?" And he said, "I am."<sup>15</sup>Then he said to him, "Come home with me and eat bread."<sup>16</sup>And he said, "I may not return with you, or go in with you, neither will I eat bread nor drink water with you in this place,<sup>17</sup>for it was said to me by the word of the LORD, 'You shall neither eat bread nor drink water there, nor return by the way that you came.'"<sup>18</sup>And he said to him, "I also am a prophet as you are, and an angel spoke to me by the word of the LORD, saying, 'Bring him back with you into your house that he may eat bread and drink water.'" But he lied to him.<sup>19</sup>So he went back with him and ate bread in his house and drank water.<sup>20</sup>And as they sat at the table, the word of the LORD came to the prophet who had brought him back.<sup>21</sup>And he cried to the man of God who came from Judah, "Thus says the LORD, 'Because you have disobeyed the word of the LORD and have not kept the command that the LORD your God commanded you,<sup>22</sup>but have come back and have eaten bread and drunk water in the place of which he said to you, "Eat no bread and drink no water," your body shall not come to the tomb of your fathers.'"<sup>23</sup>And after he had eaten bread and drunk, he saddled the donkey for the prophet whom he had brought back.<sup>24</sup>And as he went away a lion met him on the road and killed him. And his body was thrown in the road, and the donkey stood beside it; the lion also stood beside the body.<sup>25</sup>And behold, men passed by and saw the body thrown in the road and the lion standing by the body. And they came and told it in the city where the old prophet lived.<sup>26</sup>And when the prophet who had brought him back from the way heard of it, he said, "It is the man of God who disobeyed the word of the LORD; therefore the LORD has given him to the lion, which has torn him and killed him, according to the word that the LORD spoke to him."<sup>27</sup>And he said to his sons, "Saddle the donkey for me." And they saddled it.<sup>28</sup>And he went and found his body thrown in the road, and the donkey and the lion standing beside the body. The lion had not eaten the body or torn the donkey.<sup>29</sup>And the prophet took up the body of the man of God and laid it on the donkey and brought it back to the city to mourn and to bury him.<sup>30</sup>And he laid the body in his own grave. And they mourned over him, saying, "Alas, my brother!"<sup>31</sup>And after he had buried him, he said to his sons, "When I die, bury me in the grave in which the man of God is buried; lay my bones beside his bones.<sup>32</sup>For the saying that he called out by the word of the LORD against the altar in Bethel and against all the houses of the high places that are in the cities of Samaria shall surely come to pass."<sup>33</sup>After this thing Jeroboam did not turn from his evil way, but made priests for the high places again from among all the people. Any who would, he ordained to be priests of the high places.<sup>34</sup>And this thing became sin to the house of Jeroboam, so as to cut it off and to destroy it from the face of the earth.
13.overview:
He is never named. The writer calls him the man of God twelve times in thirty-two verses, and the timing of his arrival is exact: Jeroboam is standing at the altar he devised, at the festival he moved to the eighth month, in the middle of the ceremony. And he addresses the altar rather than the king, which is its own comment — then names a man three hundred years before he is born. There is nothing else quite like it in the Old Testament; prophecies of a coming ruler are common, a personal name given three centuries in advance is not. And it happened, and the historian stops the narrative at 2 Kings 23:16 to point back at this verse.

Everything about him so far is admirable. He interrupts a state ceremony in a foreign kingdom, faces down an arrest, prays immediately for the king who ordered it, and refuses half a kingdom — because his instructions were no bread, no water, and do not go home the way you came. The third part is stranger than the others and never explained, and it is the one that kills him. A command you can see the sense of is not much of a test.

Then an old prophet finds him sitting under an oak — not walking; stopped, tired, and under command to eat and drink nothing all day — and says the sentence that kills him. Peer credentials, a higher authority, and the exact formula the man of God has just used twice: I also am a prophet as you are, and an angel spoke to me by the word of the LORD. It does not contradict the mission or ask him to bless anything; it revises one small logistical detail, and it flatters. And the writer ends the verse with four words that leave no room to wonder: but he lied to him.

He had the word himself. He had already refused a king with it and quoted it twice, accurately — and then weighed the messenger instead of the message. Paul states the principle at its strongest and includes himself in it: even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed (Gal. 1:8).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A man of God comes out of Judah to Bethel while Jeroboam is standing by the altar, and cries against it: O altar, altar, thus says the LORD: "Behold, a son shall be born to the house of David, Josiah by name, and he shall sacrifice on you the priests of the high places who make offerings on you, and human bones shall be burned on you" (vv. 1-2). He gives a sign: the altar will be torn down and its ashes poured out (v. 3). Jeroboam stretches out his hand and says seize him, and his hand, which he stretched out against him, dried up, so that he could not draw it back to himself (v. 4), and the altar splits (v. 5). The king asks him to entreat the LORD, and his hand is restored (v. 6). Offered hospitality and a reward, he refuses: if you give me half your house, I will not go in with you... for so was it commanded me by the word of the LORD, saying, "You shall neither eat bread nor drink water nor return by the way that you came" (vv. 7-9). So he goes another way (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: He names a king three hundred years before the man is born, and it happens. Josiah tore down this altar, burned human bones on it, and the historian stops the narrative to say according to the word of the LORD that the man of God proclaimed (2 Kings 23:15-16).
verseByVerse.examples: And the instruction he has been given is threefold and strange: no bread, no water, and do not go home the way you came. It is not explained to him and he does not ask. He is to have no fellowship in that place at all.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, a man of God came out of Judah by the word of the LORD to Bethel. Jeroboam was standing by the altar to make offerings. And the man cried against the altar by the word of the LORD and said, "O altar, altar, thus says the LORD: 'Behold, a son shall be born to the house of David, Josiah by name, and he shall sacrifice on you the priests of the high places who make offerings on you, and human bones shall be burned on you.'" And he gave a sign the same day, saying, "This is the sign that the LORD has spoken: 'Behold, the altar shall be torn down, and the ashes that are on it shall be poured out.'" And when the king heard the saying of the man of God, which he cried against the altar at Bethel, Jeroboam stretched out his hand from the altar, saying, "Seize him." And his hand, which he stretched out against him, dried up, so that he could not draw it back to himself. The altar also was torn down, and the ashes poured out from the altar, according to the sign that the man of God had given by the word of the LORD. And the king said to the man of God, "Entreat now the favor of the LORD your God, and pray for me, that my hand may be restored to me." And the man of God entreated the LORD, and the king's hand was restored to him and became as it was before. And the king said to the man of God, "Come home with me, and refresh yourself, and I will give you a reward." And the man of God said to the king, "If you give me half your house, I will not go in with you. And I will not eat bread or drink water in this place, for so was it commanded me by the word of the LORD, saying, 'You shall neither eat bread nor drink water nor return by the way that you came.'" So he went another way and did not return by the way that he came to Bethel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And behold, a man of God came out of Judah by the word of the LORD to Bethel. Jeroboam was standing by the altar to make offerings.'

He is not named, in this chapter or anywhere else, and the writer calls him only the man of God — twelve times in thirty-two verses.

And the timing is exact. Jeroboam is standing at the altar he devised, on the festival he moved to the eighth month, in the sanctuary he built at Bethel, in the middle of the ceremony.

'And the man cried against the altar by the word of the LORD and said, "O altar, altar, thus says the LORD: 'Behold, a son shall be born to the house of David, Josiah by name, and he shall sacrifice on you the priests of the high places who make offerings on you, and human bones shall be burned on you.'"'

He addresses the altar rather than the king, which is its own comment, and then names a man three hundred years before he is born.

Josiah by name.

There is nothing else quite like this in the Old Testament. Prophecies of a coming ruler are common; a personal name, given three centuries in advance, is not.

It happened. When Josiah came to the throne of Judah and tore through the country destroying every shrine he could find, the historian records what he did at this altar and then stops the narrative to point at this verse:

Moreover, the altar at Bethel, the high place erected by Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin, that altar with the high place he pulled down and burned... And as Josiah turned, he saw the tombs there on the mount. And he sent and took the bones out of the tombs and burned them on the altar and defiled it, according to the word of the LORD that the man of God proclaimed, who had predicted these things (2 Kings 23:15-16).

Human bones burned on that altar, exactly as this man said, by a king with exactly this name.

'And he gave a sign the same day, saying, "This is the sign that the LORD has spoken: 'Behold, the altar shall be torn down, and the ashes that are on it shall be poured out.'"'

The long prophecy needs three hundred years to be verified, so he gives a short one for today.

'And when the king heard the saying of the man of God, which he cried against the altar at Bethel, Jeroboam stretched out his hand from the altar, saying, "Seize him." And his hand, which he stretched out against him, dried up, so that he could not draw it back to himself.'

The hand he stretches out to have the prophet arrested seizes up where it is.

Not struck off, not paralysed at his side — frozen in the gesture, pointing at the man, where everybody at the festival can see it. He cannot even pull it back.

'The altar also was torn down, and the ashes poured out from the altar, according to the sign that the man of God had given by the word of the LORD.'

The sign happens in front of the whole assembly.

'And the king said to the man of God, "Entreat now the favor of the LORD your God, and pray for me, that my hand may be restored to me." And the man of God entreated the LORD, and the king's hand was restored to him and became as it was before.'

Now notice two things about this exchange.

The first is what the king asks for. Not forgiveness, not an explanation, not what must I do. He wants his hand back.

And note how he refers to God: the LORD your God. Standing at an altar he built for the God who brought Israel out of Egypt, he calls him the prophet's God.

The second is that the man of God prays for him, immediately, without conditions. The prophet who has just announced the destruction of this altar and this priesthood intercedes for the king who tried to arrest him, and the hand is restored on the spot.

That is mercy, and it is more than Jeroboam asked for and much more than he deserved.

'And the king said to the man of God, "Come home with me, and refresh yourself, and I will give you a reward."'

Now the second attack, and it is more dangerous than the first.

The soldiers failed. The hospitality is the real threat.

A prophet who denounces an altar in the morning and dines at the king's table in the evening has unsaid everything he said. Jeroboam would not need to answer the prophecy; he would only need to be photographed with the prophet.

'And the man of God said to the king, "If you give me half your house, I will not go in with you. And I will not eat bread or drink water in this place,"'

'"for so was it commanded me by the word of the LORD, saying, 'You shall neither eat bread nor drink water nor return by the way that you came.'"'

He quotes the command, and it has three parts and none of them is explained to him.

No bread. No water. And do not go home by the road you came on.

Eating and drinking with somebody in that world was not a meal; it was fellowship, and a measure of peace between the parties. To take bread at Bethel would be to say that there was something here a man of God could sit down with.

The third part is stranger, and it is the one that kills him. Why should the route matter? He is not told. It looks like an arbitrary instruction attached to a reasonable one — and the arbitrariness is the point, because a command you can see the sense of is not much of a test.

'So he went another way and did not return by the way that he came to Bethel.'

He obeys all three, at the moment when obeying costs most.

Hold that, because everything about this man so far is admirable. He walked into a foreign kingdom, interrupted a state ceremony, denounced the altar to its face, faced down an arrest, prayed for the man who ordered it, and refused half a kingdom.

He is one chapter away from being one of the great figures of the Old Testament, and he has about an hour left.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–19 — But He Lied to Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: An old prophet lives in Bethel; his sons tell him what happened (vv. 11-12). He saddles a donkey, rides after the man of God, finds him sitting under an oak, and invites him home to eat (vv. 13-15). The man refuses and repeats the command word for word (vv. 16-17). And he said to him, "I also am a prophet as you are, and an angel spoke to me by the word of the LORD, saying, 'Bring him back with you into your house that he may eat bread and drink water.'" But he lied to him (v. 18). So he went back with him and ate bread in his house and drank water (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: Look at the credentials offered: a fellow prophet, an angel, and the phrase by the word of the LORD. Every one is exactly what would be needed to make it convincing, and the writer ends the verse with four words that leave no room to wonder: but he lied to him.
verseByVerse.examples: And the man of God had the word himself. He had it directly, he had already refused a king with it, and he quoted it accurately twice within two verses — and then a stranger with better standing gave him a newer one, and he sat down and ate.

verseByVerse.quote: Now an old prophet lived in Bethel. And his sons came and told him all that the man of God had done that day in Bethel. They also told to their father the words that he had spoken to the king. And their father said to them, "Which way did he go?" And his sons showed him the way that the man of God who came from Judah had gone. And he said to his sons, "Saddle the donkey for me." So they saddled the donkey for him and he mounted it. And he went after the man of God and found him sitting under an oak. And he said to him, "Are you the man of God who came from Judah?" And he said, "I am." Then he said to him, "Come home with me and eat bread." And he said, "I may not return with you, or go in with you, neither will I eat bread nor drink water with you in this place, for it was said to me by the word of the LORD, 'You shall neither eat bread nor drink water there, nor return by the way that you came.'" And he said to him, "I also am a prophet as you are, and an angel spoke to me by the word of the LORD, saying, 'Bring him back with you into your house that he may eat bread and drink water.'" But he lied to him. So he went back with him and ate bread in his house and drank water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now an old prophet lived in Bethel. And his sons came and told him all that the man of God had done that day in Bethel. They also told to their father the words that he had spoken to the king.'

There is a prophet living in Bethel.

Stop on that, because it raises a question the text never answers. He is a prophet of the LORD — he receives a genuine word in verse 20 — and he has been living in the capital of Jeroboam's counterfeit religion, apparently without saying anything.

His sons went to the festival at the calf-altar. They came home and told him what a visitor from Judah had done.

Whatever he is, he is not a man who has been crying out against that altar himself.

'And their father said to them, "Which way did he go?" And his sons showed him the way that the man of God who came from Judah had gone.'

'And he said to his sons, "Saddle the donkey for me." So they saddled the donkey for him, and he mounted it.'

An old man gets on a donkey and goes after him.

Why he does it is not stated, and the temptation to fill it in should be resisted. It may be admiration. It may be loneliness — here at last is a real prophet, doing what he has not been doing. It may be something worse.

The text tells us what he did, not why.

'And he went after the man of God and found him sitting under an oak. And he said to him, "Are you the man of God who came from Judah?" And he said, "I am."'

Sitting under an oak.

That small detail is doing something. He is not walking; he has stopped. He has been on his feet since morning, has had nothing to eat or drink all day by command, and has sat down under a tree in the heat.

Attacks come when a man is tired and has stopped moving.

'Then he said to him, "Come home with me and eat bread."'

'And he said, "I may not return with you, or go in with you, neither will I eat bread nor drink water with you in this place,"'

'"for it was said to me by the word of the LORD, 'You shall neither eat bread nor drink water there, nor return by the way that you came.'"'

He refuses a second time, and he quotes the command a second time, accurately.

Note how well he is doing. He has now stated the word of God twice in one day, to two different men, under two different pressures. He knows exactly what he was told.

'And he said to him, "I also am a prophet as you are, and an angel spoke to me by the word of the LORD, saying, 'Bring him back with you into your house that he may eat bread and drink water.'"'

Here is the sentence that kills him, and every element of it is chosen.

I also am a prophet as you are. Peer credentials. Not a king, not a courtier — somebody in the same office, who would know.

And an angel spoke to me. Higher authority than a mere prophetic impression. An angel is a step up.

By the word of the LORD. The exact formula the man of God has just used twice. He is being answered in his own vocabulary.

And the content is designed to be plausible. It does not contradict the mission or ask him to praise the altar or bless Jeroboam. It only revises one small logistical detail, and it comes with a reason that flatters: an angel was sent about you specifically.

It is a better word from a better source, delivered to a tired man under a tree.

'But he lied to him.'

Four words, and the writer refuses to leave any ambiguity.

Not he was mistaken. Not he had a false impression. He lied, deliberately, in the name of God, about an angel.

Why he did it is never told us, in this verse or any other. The writer gives us the lie and withholds the motive, and a reader who wants one has to supply it, which is a discipline worth noticing in itself.

'So he went back with him and ate bread in his house and drank water.'

He goes.

Now here is the thing this chapter exists to say, and it should be stated plainly before anything else is said about fairness.

He had the word himself.

God spoke it to him directly. He had already refused a king with it and quoted it twice, word for word. And then a man with better credentials brought a newer word that contradicted it, and he did not test it against the one he already had. He weighed the messengers instead of the messages.

The New Testament states the principle in the strongest terms available, and it is aimed at exactly this situation: but even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed (Gal. 1:8).

Paul includes himself and he includes angels. It does not matter who is bringing it. A new revelation that contradicts a clear one is to be refused no matter what it arrives in.

And notice what the old prophet did not have to do. He did not have to argue that God had not said it. He only had to say that God had said something else, more recently, to someone qualified.

That is how it is nearly always done.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: And as they sat at the table, the word of the LORD came to the prophet who had brought him back (v. 20), and he cries out against his guest: because you disobeyed and came back and ate and drank in the place God forbade, your body shall not come to the tomb of your fathers (vv. 21-22). He saddles the donkey and the man rides away (v. 23). And as he went, a lion met him on the road and killed him. And his body was thrown in the road, and the donkey stood beside it; the lion also stood beside the body (v. 24) — and men passing by see it and report it (v. 25). The old prophet knows at once: it is the man of God who disobeyed the word of the LORD (v. 26). He goes and takes up the body, mourning alas, my brother!, and buries him in his own grave (vv. 27-30). Then to his sons: when I die, bury me in the grave in which the man of God is buried; lay my bones beside his bones. For the saying that he called out by the word of the LORD... shall surely come to pass (vv. 31-32).
verseByVerse.theology: The word comes to the liar, at his own table, while his deceived guest is eating the meal he lied to obtain. God speaks a true word through a man who has just told a deliberate untruth, and the writer does not pause over it.
verseByVerse.examples: And the lion neither eats the body nor the donkey nor runs away, and the writer says so twice so that nobody can read it as an accident on a dangerous road. Then the old prophet weeps over him, calls him my brother, gives him his own grave, and arranges to be buried beside him — and three centuries later Josiah spares that tomb for exactly that reason (2 Kings 23:17-18).

verseByVerse.quote: And as they sat at the table, the word of the LORD came to the prophet who had brought him back. And he cried to the man of God who came from Judah, "Thus says the LORD, 'Because you have disobeyed the word of the LORD and have not kept the command that the LORD your God commanded you, but have come back and have eaten bread and drunk water in the place of which he said to you, "Eat no bread and drink no water," your body shall not come to the tomb of your fathers.'" And after he had eaten bread and drunk, he saddled the donkey for the prophet whom he had brought back. And as he went away a lion met him on the road and killed him. And his body was thrown in the road, and the donkey stood beside it; the lion also stood beside the body. And behold, men passed by and saw the body thrown in the road and the lion standing by the body. And they came and told it in the city where the old prophet lived. And when the prophet who had brought him back from the way heard of it, he said, "It is the man of God who disobeyed the word of the LORD; therefore the LORD has given him to the lion, which has torn him and killed him, according to the word that the LORD spoke to him." And he said to his sons, "Saddle the donkey for me." And they saddled it. And he went and found his body thrown in the road, and the donkey and the lion standing beside the body. The lion had not eaten the body or torn the donkey. And the prophet took up the body of the man of God and laid it on the donkey and brought it back to the city to mourn and to bury him. And he laid the body in his own grave. And they mourned over him, saying, "Alas, my brother!" And after he had buried him, he said to his sons, "When I die, bury me in the grave in which the man of God is buried; lay my bones beside his bones. For the saying that he called out by the word of the LORD against the altar in Bethel and against all the houses of the high places that are in the cities of Samaria shall surely come to pass."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And as they sat at the table, the word of the LORD came to the prophet who had brought him back.'

Now the strangest verse in the chapter.

The word of the LORD comes to the liar.

He is sitting at his own table, eating a meal he obtained by inventing an angel, opposite a man he has just deceived into disobedience — and God speaks through him. A genuine word, which is fulfilled within the hour.

The writer does not pause over this and does not explain it, and it should not be smoothed away. It tells us something about how God works that is uncomfortable and true: the truth of a message is not guaranteed by the character of the man carrying it, and a man's usefulness is not evidence of his integrity. Balaam prophesied truly. Caiaphas prophesied truly and did not know he was doing it (John 11:51).

'And he cried to the man of God who came from Judah, "Thus says the LORD, 'Because you have disobeyed the word of the LORD and have not kept the command that the LORD your God commanded you,'"'

'"'but have come back and have eaten bread and drunk water in the place of which he said to you, "Eat no bread and drink no water," your body shall not come to the tomb of your fathers.'"'

Imagine the table.

The old man opposite him, mid-meal, suddenly delivering the judgment — and every word of it is true, and he is the reason for it.

The charge is stated with care: you have disobeyed the word of the LORD and have not kept the command that the LORD your God commanded you. Not you were deceived. The offence is located in the man who had the command, and the deception is not mentioned.

That is severe, and the severity should be faced rather than argued down.

He was lied to. He was tired, hungry, thirsty, and a long way from home, and a fellow prophet invoked an angel. Most people would have gone.

And he was responsible, because the word had been given to him, and he was the one who knew what it said, and he had already proved he could refuse a king with it. Being deceived is a reason and it is not a defence, and Scripture is consistent about this from Eden onward — the woman said the serpent deceived me, and I ate, which was entirely true and changed nothing.

'And after he had eaten bread and drunk water, he saddled the donkey for the prophet whom he had brought back.'

The old man saddles the donkey for him, after telling him he is going to die.

'And as he went, a lion met him on the road and killed him. And his body was thrown in the road, and the donkey stood beside it; the lion also stood beside the body.'

Now read the details, because the writer is being very deliberate.

A lion kills him. And then nothing else happens.

The donkey does not bolt, which is the one thing a donkey certainly does when a lion is nearby. The lion does not eat the body. It does not take the donkey either. And it does not leave.

Three animals in a road, one of them dead, and the other two standing.

'And behold, men passed by and saw the body thrown in the road and the lion standing by the body. And they came and told it in the city where the old prophet lived.'

People walk past a lion.

The writer wants it established beyond doubt that this was not a hungry animal on a dangerous road. It is a judgment carried out under orders, and it stops the instant it is done.

'And when the prophet who had brought him back from the way heard of it, he said, "It is the man of God who disobeyed the word of the LORD; therefore the LORD has given him to the lion, which has torn him and killed him, according to the word that the LORD spoke to him."'

He knows immediately, and he says the theology correctly, and he is the reason for all of it.

'And he said to his sons, "Saddle the donkey for me." And they saddled it.'

'And he went and found his body thrown in the road, and the donkey and the lion standing beside the body. The lion had not eaten the body or torn the donkey.'

The writer says it again, in case anyone missed it. The lion had not eaten the body or torn the donkey.

The lion is still there when the old man arrives, and lets him take the body.

'And the prophet took up the body of the man of God and laid it on the donkey and brought it back to the city to mourn and to bury him.'

'And he laid the body in his own grave. And they mourned over him, saying, "Alas, my brother!"'

Here is where this man becomes genuinely difficult to read.

He puts the body in his own grave — the plot he had prepared for himself — and mourns over it, and the words are alas, my brother.

The grief appears to be real. Nothing in the text suggests otherwise.

So we have, in one person: a prophet living quietly in the capital of a false religion; a man who invented an angel to get a stranger to his table; a man through whom God then spoke a true word; a man who wept over the consequence of his own lie and called the dead man his brother; and a man who gave away his own grave.

The writer records all of it and reconciles none of it. He does not tell us whether the old prophet repented, or what he thought he was doing, or what became of him.

People are like this, and Scripture declines to tidy them up.

'And after he had buried him, he said to his sons, "When I die, bury me in the grave in which the man of God is buried; lay my bones beside his bones."'

This is a strange and rather moving request, and it is not sentimental.

'"For the saying that he called out by the word of the LORD against the altar in Bethel and against all the houses of the high places that are in the cities of Samaria shall surely come to pass."'

There is the reason.

He believes the prophecy. He has heard a man name a king three centuries early and announce that human bones will be burned on that altar, and he has watched the same man die within the day for disobedience — which has convinced him that every word of it was from God.

So he makes a practical arrangement about his own bones. If Josiah is coming, and bones are going to be dug up and burned on that altar, then the safest place in the country to be buried is beside the man who said so.

It worked.

Three hundred years later Josiah is at Bethel, burning bones taken from the tombs on the mount, and the account continues:

Then he said, "What is that monument that I see?" And the men of the city told him, "It is the tomb of the man of God who came from Judah and predicted these things that you have done against the altar at Bethel." And he said, "Let him be; let no man move his bones." So they let his bones alone, with the bones of the prophet who came out of Samaria (2 Kings 23:17-18).

The old prophet's bones were left alone because they were lying next to the right man's.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After this thing Jeroboam did not turn from his evil way, but made priests for the high places again from among all the people. Any who would, he ordained to be priests of the high places (v. 33). And this thing became sin to the house of Jeroboam, so as to cut it off and to destroy it from the face of the earth (v. 34).
verseByVerse.theology: After this thing. After an altar split in front of him, after his own hand withered and was healed by the prayer of the man he had tried to arrest, after a prophet from Judah named his kingdom's end and died on the road for eating a meal.
verseByVerse.examples: And nothing changed. He went back to ordaining anybody who wanted the job. That is the chapter's last word on signs: they can split an altar and heal a hand and leave a man exactly where he was.

verseByVerse.quote: After this thing Jeroboam did not turn from his evil way, but made priests for the high places again from among all the people. Any who would, he ordained to be priests of the high places. And this thing became sin to the house of Jeroboam, so as to cut it off and to destroy it from the face of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'After this thing Jeroboam did not turn from his evil way, but made priests for the high places again from among all the people. Any who would, he ordained to be priests of the high places.'

After this thing.

Stop and count what this thing includes.

A stranger walked out of Judah into his festival and denounced the altar to its face. He named a king three hundred years in advance who would burn human bones on it. He gave a sign, and the altar split in front of the whole assembly and the ashes poured out on the ground.

Jeroboam pointed at him and his own hand seized up in the air where everybody could see it, and he could not pull it back. He had to ask the man he was arresting to pray for him, and the man did, at once, and the hand was healed.

And then, within the day, that same prophet was killed by a lion on the road for eating a meal he had been told not to eat — which proved to everybody who heard about it that his words were God's.

All of it, in one day, in front of the king.

Jeroboam did not turn from his evil way.

He went back to ordaining priests. And the phrase the writer uses is contemptuous: any who would, he ordained. Anybody who wanted the job could have it.

Now here is the lesson of the chapter's last two verses, and it runs against most people's instincts about what would change a person.

Signs do not produce repentance.

He saw an altar destroyed by a word and a hand restored by a prayer, and he was not moved an inch. The evidence was overwhelming and the evidence was not the problem.

The Lord Jesus said this in a story about a rich man who wanted somebody sent back from the dead to warn his brothers: if they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead (Luke 16:31).

And he said it about his own generation, who had watched him heal and feed and raise the dead, and who asked him for a sign.

What Jeroboam lacked was never information.

'And this thing became sin to the house of Jeroboam, so as to cut it off and to destroy it from the face of the earth.'

The chapter ends on the sentence that will be the epitaph of the whole northern kingdom.

This thing became sin to the house of Jeroboam.

His dynasty lasts one more generation. His son Nadab reigns two years and is murdered, and Baasha kills every member of the house of Jeroboam, according to the word of the LORD that he spoke by his servant Ahijah the Shilonite (15:29).

The formula outlives the family. Nineteen kings of Israel over two centuries, and the verdict on almost every one of them is the same: he walked in all the way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, and in his sin which he made Israel to sin.

The man who was offered David's own covenant — I will build you a sure house, as I built for David — becomes the standing measure of what went wrong with a nation.

13.theology:
Josiah by name (v. 2). Three hundred years before the man is born, and the fulfilment is recorded with the writer pointing back: Josiah pulled down that altar, took bones out of the tombs and burned them on it, according to the word of the LORD that the man of God proclaimed (2 Kings 23:15-16). And he cries against the altar rather than the king, which is where the offence actually is.

The hand frozen in the gesture (v. 4). Not struck off and not paralysed at his side — seized up pointing at the prophet, where every worshipper at the festival can see it, and he cannot pull it back. And note what he asks for: not forgiveness, not what must I do, but his hand. And note what he calls God: the LORD your God, standing at an altar he built for the God who brought Israel out of Egypt.

The prophet prays for him at once (v. 6). Without conditions, having just announced the destruction of that altar and that priesthood, for the king who ordered his arrest — and the hand is restored on the spot. More than Jeroboam asked for and much more than he deserved.

The hospitality is the real attack (v. 7). The soldiers failed; this is more dangerous. A prophet who denounces an altar in the morning and dines at the king's table in the evening has unsaid everything he said. Jeroboam would not need to answer the prophecy, only to be seen with the prophet.

Three commands, one of them arbitrary (v. 9). Eating with somebody in that world was fellowship and a measure of peace between the parties; to take bread at Bethel would say there was something there a man of God could sit down with. The third part — do not go home the way you came — is never explained, and the arbitrariness is the point, because a command whose sense you can see is not much of a test.

A prophet living in Bethel (v. 11). The text never answers the question it raises. He is a genuine prophet — he receives a true word in verse 20 — and he has been living in the capital of Jeroboam's counterfeit religion, apparently saying nothing; his sons attended the calf-festival. Whatever he is, he is not a man who has been crying out against that altar himself. Why he saddles a donkey and rides after the visitor is also not stated, and filling it in should be resisted: admiration, loneliness, something worse. The text gives the act, not the motive.

Sitting under an oak (v. 14). He is not walking. He has stopped, on his feet since morning, with nothing to eat or drink all day by command, in the heat. Attacks come when a man is tired and has stopped moving.

Every element of the lie is chosen (v. 18). I also am a prophet as you are — peer credentials, somebody in the same office who would know. An angel spoke to me — a step up in authority. By the word of the LORD — the exact formula the man of God has used twice, so he is answered in his own vocabulary. And the content is plausible: it does not contradict the mission or ask him to bless Jeroboam, it revises one logistical detail, and it flatters him with the news that an angel was sent about him specifically. A better word from a better source, delivered to a tired man under a tree.

But he lied to him (v. 18). Not mistaken, not confused about an impression — a deliberate untruth in the name of God about an angel. And the writer gives the lie and withholds the motive, which is a discipline worth noticing.

What the chapter exists to say (v. 19). He had the word himself, directly, and had already refused a king with it, and quoted it twice word for word. Then a man with better credentials brought a newer word that contradicted it, and he did not test the message against the one he already had. He weighed the messengers instead. Paul states the principle at its strongest and includes himself and angels in it (Gal. 1:8) — a new revelation contradicting a clear one is refused regardless of what it arrives in. And notice what the old prophet never had to do: he did not have to argue that God had not said it. He only had to say God had said something else, more recently, to someone qualified. That is how it is nearly always done.

The word comes to the liar (v. 20). At his own table, mid-meal, opposite the man he has just deceived, God speaks a true word through him — and the writer does not pause over it. It says something uncomfortable and true: the truth of a message is not guaranteed by the character of the man carrying it, and usefulness is not evidence of integrity. Balaam prophesied truly; so did Caiaphas, without knowing he was doing it (John 11:51).

Deceived, and responsible (vv. 21-22). The charge is stated with care — you have disobeyed the word of the LORD and have not kept the command — and the deception is not mentioned. That is severe, and the severity should be faced rather than argued down. He was lied to, tired, hungry, thirsty and far from home, and a fellow prophet invoked an angel; most people would have gone. And he was responsible, because the word had been given to him. Scripture is consistent about this from Eden: the serpent deceived me, and I ate was entirely true and changed nothing.

The lion is under orders (vv. 24-28). The donkey does not bolt, which is the one thing a donkey certainly does near a lion. The lion does not eat the body, does not take the donkey, and does not leave — and men walk past it. The writer says it twice so that nobody can read it as a hungry animal on a dangerous road. It is a judgment carried out under orders, and it stops the instant it is done.

All of it is the same man (vv. 30-31). A prophet living quietly in the capital of a false religion; a man who invented an angel to get a stranger to his table; a man through whom God then spoke truly; a man who wept over the consequence of his own lie and called the dead man my brother; and a man who gave away his own grave. The writer records all of it and reconciles none of it, and never tells us whether he repented or what became of him. People are like this, and Scripture declines to tidy them up.

A practical arrangement about bones (v. 32). Not sentiment — he believes the prophecy. He has heard a man name a king three centuries early and announce that bones will be burned on that altar, and watched him die within the day for disobedience, which convinced him every word was from God. So if bones are going to be dug up, the safest place in the country to be buried is beside the man who said so. And it worked: let him be; let no man move his bones. So they let his bones alone, with the bones of the prophet who came out of Samaria (2 Kings 23:17-18).

Signs do not produce repentance (v. 33). Count what after this thing includes: an altar split by a word in front of the assembly, his own hand seized in the air and healed by the prayer of the man he was arresting, and that prophet dead on the road within the day for eating a meal — which proved to everyone that his words were God's. All of it in one day, in front of the king. And he went back to ordaining priests, and the phrase is contemptuous: any who would, he ordained. The evidence was overwhelming and the evidence was not the problem. If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead (Luke 16:31).

The epitaph of a kingdom (v. 34). His dynasty lasts one more generation: Nadab reigns two years and is murdered, and Baasha kills every member of the house according to the word of the LORD that he spoke by his servant Ahijah the Shilonite (15:29). And the formula outlives the family — nineteen kings over two centuries, and the verdict on almost every one is he walked in all the way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, and in his sin which he made Israel to sin. The man who was offered David's own covenant becomes the standing measure of what went wrong with a nation.
13.examples:
Then: A prophet who had faced down a king, watched an altar split at his word, and refused half a kingdom because God had told him not to eat or drink in that place, sat down under a tree at the end of a long day — and an older prophet told him an angel had said it was all right now, and he went back and ate, and was dead before evening.

Now: Three things. The first is the whole chapter: a newer word from a better-credentialled person does not overrule a clear word you already have. Notice the shape of the lie, because it is always this shape — nobody says God did not say it; they say God has said something else, more recently, to someone qualified. And the test is never who is speaking. Second, the severity, which should not be argued down. He was genuinely deceived and he was genuinely responsible, because the word had been given to him and he was the one who knew what it said. Being lied to is a reason and it is not a defence. And third, verse 33. Jeroboam saw an altar destroyed by a word and his own hand healed by a prayer, in one afternoon, and changed nothing. If you are waiting for evidence dramatic enough to shift somebody, this chapter says the evidence was never what was missing.
