14.overview:
His son is dying, and he sends to a prophet of the LORD. Jeroboam has two golden calves, sanctuaries at Bethel and Dan, a priesthood he appointed himself and a festival he devised — and he consults none of it. He knows perfectly well that the calves cannot help him, and the writer never says a word about it.

And the disguise is useless, because Ahijah is blind. She walks twenty miles in clothes good enough to fool everybody on the road, to consult a man who does not get his information by looking — and God tells him her footsteps are at the door before she reaches it. Why do you pretend to be another? is a real question, and it hangs over the chapter: a great deal of religion is exactly this shape, approaching God in a costume, keeping the arrangement anonymous, bringing the right sort of gift, when the whole point of him is that he already knows who is at the door.

Then verse 13, which is one of the most tender verses in Kings and is easy to read past in the middle of a judgment oracle. In that house — the family of the man who made the calves and cast God behind his back — God looked, and in one child found something pleasing to him. We are told nothing else about the boy. He is the only one of that family who will get a grave, and all Israel will mourn him. And he dies first, which is the mercy: the righteous man is taken away from calamity; he enters into peace (Isa. 57:1-2).

And then Judah, five years after Solomon: an Egyptian army at the gates, he took away everything, including the gold shields. Rehoboam makes bronze replacements, and the guard still carries them in procession and still puts them back in the guardroom afterwards. The same ceremony, the same order, a cheaper metal, and nobody says anything.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — Why Do You Pretend to Be Another?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Abijah the son of Jeroboam falls sick, and Jeroboam sends his wife in disguise to Ahijah at Shiloh, who said of me that I should be king over this people, with a present of loaves and cakes and honey (vv. 1-3). Now Ahijah could not see, for his eyes were dim because of his age (v. 4) — but the LORD has told him she is coming (v. 5). He hears her feet at the door: come in, wife of Jeroboam. Why do you pretend to be another? For I am charged with unbearable news for you (v. 6). The message: I exalted you from among the people and tore the kingdom from David and gave it to you, and yet you have not been like my servant David, who kept my commandments and followed me with all his heart, but have made other gods and metal images and have cast me behind your back (vv. 7-9). The house of Jeroboam will be cut off and burned like dung (vv. 10-11). Arise therefore, go to your house. When your feet enter the city, the child shall die. And all Israel shall mourn for him and bury him, for he only of Jeroboam's house shall come to the grave, because in him there is found something pleasing to the LORD (vv. 12-13). And Israel will be uprooted and scattered beyond the Euphrates (vv. 14-16). She goes home, and the child dies as she crosses the threshold (vv. 17-18).
verseByVerse.theology: The disguise fails because the prophet is blind. She fooled everybody in Israel except the one man in it who could not see her — and God told him her footsteps were at the door before she reached it.
verseByVerse.examples: And verse 13 is a mercy inside a judgment, and it should be read slowly. The one member of that household with something pleasing to the LORD found in him is the one who dies first — and he is the only one who gets a grave and a nation's mourning. He is taken before the rest of it comes.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Abijah the son of Jeroboam fell sick. And Jeroboam said to his wife, "Arise, and disguise yourself, that it not be known that you are the wife of Jeroboam, and go to Shiloh. Behold, Ahijah the prophet is there, who said of me that I should be king over this people. Take with you ten loaves, some cakes, and a jar of honey, and go to him. He will tell you what shall happen to the child." Jeroboam's wife did so. She arose and went to Shiloh and came to the house of Ahijah. Now Ahijah could not see, for his eyes were dim because of his age. And the LORD said to Ahijah, "Behold, the wife of Jeroboam is coming to inquire of you concerning her son, for he is sick. Thus and thus shall you say to her." When she came, she pretended to be another woman. But when Ahijah heard the sound of her feet, as she came in at the door, he said, "Come in, wife of Jeroboam. Why do you pretend to be another? For I am charged with unbearable news for you. Go, tell Jeroboam, 'Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: "Because I exalted you from among the people and made you leader over my people Israel and tore the kingdom away from the house of David and gave it to you, and yet you have not been like my servant David, who kept my commandments and followed me with all his heart, doing only that which was right in my eyes, but you have done evil above all who were before you and have gone and made for yourself other gods and metal images, provoking me to anger, and have cast me behind your back, therefore behold, I will bring harm upon the house of Jeroboam and will cut off from Jeroboam every male, both bond and free in Israel, and will burn up the house of Jeroboam, as a man burns up dung until it is all gone. Anyone belonging to Jeroboam who dies in the city the dogs shall eat, and anyone who dies in the open country the birds of the heavens shall eat, for the LORD has spoken it."' Arise therefore, go to your house. When your feet enter the city, the child shall die. And all Israel shall mourn for him and bury him, for he only of Jeroboam shall come to the grave, because in him there is found something pleasing to the LORD, the God of Israel, in the house of Jeroboam. Moreover, the LORD will raise up for himself a king over Israel who shall cut off the house of Jeroboam today. And henceforth, the LORD will strike Israel as a reed is shaken in the water, and root up Israel out of this good land that he gave to their fathers and scatter them beyond the Euphrates, because they have made their Asherim, provoking the LORD to anger. And he will give Israel up because of the sins of Jeroboam, which he sinned and made Israel to sin." Then Jeroboam's wife arose and departed and came to Tirzah. And as she came to the threshold of the house, the child died. And all Israel buried him and mourned for him, according to the word of the LORD, which he spoke by his servant Ahijah the prophet. Now the rest of the acts of Jeroboam, how he warred and how he reigned, behold, they are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel. And the time that Jeroboam reigned was twenty-two years. And he slept with his fathers, and Nadab his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'At that time Abijah the son of Jeroboam fell sick.'

At that time — that is, after the altar split and the hand withered and the man of God died on the road, and after Jeroboam went back to ordaining anybody who wanted to be a priest.

'And Jeroboam said to his wife, "Arise, and disguise yourself, that it not be known that you are the wife of Jeroboam, and go to Shiloh. Behold, Ahijah the prophet is there, who said of me that I should be king over this people."'

Now read what he is doing, because every part of it is revealing.

His son is dying, and he sends to a prophet of the LORD.

He has two golden calves, sanctuaries at Bethel and Dan, a priesthood he appointed himself, a national festival he devised, and altars on every high place in his kingdom. And when his child is sick he does not consult any of it. He sends to Shiloh.

He knows perfectly well that the calves cannot help him. That is the most damning thing in the chapter and the writer never says a word about it.

And note who he sends to: Ahijah the prophet... who said of me that I should be king over this people. He remembers the man who gave him ten pieces of a torn cloak on an empty road, along with the offer of David's own covenant on condition of obedience.

So he sends his wife in disguise to the one man in Israel who knows exactly what he was promised and exactly what he did with it.

'"Take with you ten loaves, some cakes, and a jar of honey, and go to him. He will tell you what shall happen to the child."'

The gift is a peasant's gift, chosen to match the costume.

Bread, some cakes, and a jar of honey is what a village woman would bring a holy man. It is exactly what a queen would not bring.

'Jeroboam's wife did so. She arose and went to Shiloh and came to the house of Ahijah. Now Ahijah could not see, for his eyes were dim because of his age.'

And here is the detail that makes the whole scene, and the writer places it precisely.

Ahijah could not see.

She has walked twenty miles in a disguise good enough that nobody on the road knew her, to consult a man who is blind.

There is something almost comic about it, and it is the sort of comedy Scripture does when it wants to expose a way of thinking. Jeroboam has calculated the deception carefully — the clothes, the gift, the anonymity — and he has forgotten that the man he is deceiving does not get his information by looking.

'And the LORD said to Ahijah, "Behold, the wife of Jeroboam is coming to inquire of you concerning her son, for he is sick. Thus and thus shall you say to her."'

God tells him before she arrives.

'"When she comes, she will pretend to be another woman."'

Even the pretence is announced in advance.

'But when Ahijah heard the sound of her feet, as she came in at the door, he said, "Come in, wife of Jeroboam. Why do you pretend to be another? For I am charged with unbearable news for you."'

He hears her feet and says her name.

She has not spoken. She is standing in the doorway of a blind man's house in borrowed clothes, and before she can say anything at all he greets her by the identity she has spent a day concealing.

Why do you pretend to be another?

It is a real question and it hangs over the chapter. What did they think they were doing? The disguise could only ever have fooled a man; it was never going to touch the thing they actually wanted, which was a word from God.

And a great deal of religion is exactly this shape. People approach God in a costume — presenting a version of themselves, keeping the arrangement anonymous, offering the right sort of gift — when the whole point of him is that he already knows who is at the door.

I am charged with unbearable news for you. Literally, I am sent to you with hard things. He tells her before he begins that this will not be what she came for.

'"Go, tell Jeroboam, 'Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: "Because I exalted you from among the people and made you leader over my people Israel"'"'

The indictment starts where every indictment in Scripture starts: with what God did first.

I exalted you from among the people. He was a labour foreman. Solomon noticed him and promoted him, and God gave him a kingdom.

'"'"and tore the kingdom away from the house of David and gave it to you, and yet you have not been like my servant David, who kept my commandments and followed me with all his heart, doing only that which was right in my eyes,"'"'

And there is the standard, and it is the same one Solomon was measured by.

My servant David, who kept my commandments and followed me with all his heart.

The comparison is not about sinlessness — this book knows what David did — and it is about one thing only: he never went after another god. That is the measure in Kings, and it does not change from the first page to the last.

'"'"but you have done evil above all who were before you and have gone and made for yourself other gods and metal images, provoking me to anger, and have cast me behind your back,"'"'

You have cast me behind your back.

The picture is of throwing something over your shoulder — discarded, out of sight, not worth turning round for.

And you have done evil above all who were before you is the phrase the writer will now use of king after king in the north, each one worse than the last. Jeroboam is the first.

'"'"therefore behold, I will bring harm upon the house of Jeroboam and will cut off from Jeroboam every male, both bond and free in Israel, and will burn up the house of Jeroboam, as a man burns up dung until it is all gone."'"'

The judgment is total and the image is contemptuous.

'"'"Anyone belonging to Jeroboam who dies in the city the dogs shall eat, and anyone who dies in the open country the birds of the heavens shall eat, for the LORD has spoken it."'"'

No burial. In that world it was the final indignity, and Ahijah says it about an entire dynasty.

Hold it for one verse, because of what comes next.

'"Arise therefore, go to your house. When your feet enter the city, the child shall die."'

She came to ask whether her son would live.

The answer is that he will die the moment she gets home — and that her walking through the gate is the thing that will do it. She has to carry that for twenty miles.

'"And all Israel shall mourn for him and bury him, for he only of Jeroboam's house shall come to the grave, because in him there is found something pleasing to the LORD, the God of Israel, in the house of Jeroboam."'

And now stop, because this is one of the most tender verses in the books of Kings and it is easy to read past in the middle of a judgment oracle.

Take the three things in it.

First: in him there is found something pleasing to the LORD.

In that house. In the family of the man who made the calves, appointed anybody who wanted to be a priest, moved the festival, and cast God behind his back — God looked, and in one child he found something he was pleased with.

The Hebrew is literally a good thing toward the LORD was found in him. We are told nothing else about the boy. Not his age, not what he did, not what he said. Something in him pleased God, and God noticed it, and it is recorded in Scripture three thousand years later.

Second: he is the only one who gets a grave. He only of Jeroboam's house shall come to the grave. Every other member of that family will be eaten by dogs or by birds. This child will be buried properly, and all Israel will mourn him.

Third, and this is the part that changes how the verse reads: he dies first.

The child in that house with something of God in him is the one taken early — and the writer puts his death immediately after the sentence about dogs and birds, so that the reader cannot miss what he is being spared.

Isaiah says the same thing in a sentence that people find difficult until they have needed it: the righteous man perishes, and no one lays it to heart; devout men are taken away, while no one understands. For the righteous man is taken away from calamity; he enters into peace (Isa. 57:1-2).

That is what is happening here. It looks like the worst thing in the chapter and it is the one mercy in it.

This should be said carefully, because it is not a general explanation of why children die, and it must not be turned into one. Scripture does not offer that, and anybody who has buried a child has been offered enough tidy explanations already.

What this verse does say is smaller and steadier: that God saw something good in a boy nobody else in that house had any use for, that he said so, and that taking him early was kindness rather than carelessness.

'"Moreover, the LORD will raise up for himself a king over Israel who shall cut off the house of Jeroboam today. And henceforth,"'

'"the LORD will strike Israel as a reed is shaken in the water, and root up Israel out of this good land that he gave to their fathers and scatter them beyond the Euphrates, because they have made their Asherim, provoking the LORD to anger."'

And here, in the first generation of the northern kingdom, is its ending.

Scatter them beyond the Euphrates.

That is Assyria, and it is two hundred years away. The northern tribes were deported in 722 BC and never came back; 2 Kings 17 records it and gives the same reasons Ahijah gives here.

The image is exact: as a reed is shaken in the water. A reed has no root worth the name. Nothing holds it.

'"And he will give Israel up because of the sins of Jeroboam, which he sinned and made Israel to sin."'

There is the formula again, and it will be repeated over nineteen kings.

'Then Jeroboam's wife arose and departed and came to Tirzah. And as she came to the threshold of the house, the child died.'

She walks twenty miles knowing what will happen when she arrives, and it happens as she crosses the threshold.

The writer gives her no words. She came, she was told, she went home, and her son died at the door. Not one line of what she said or thought is recorded, here or anywhere.

'And all Israel buried him and mourned for him, according to the word of the LORD, which he spoke by his servant Ahijah the prophet.'

'Now the rest of the acts of Jeroboam, how he warred and how he reigned, behold, they are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.'

'And the time that Jeroboam reigned was twenty-two years. And he slept with his fathers, and Nadab his son reigned in his place.'

Twenty-two years, and the formula, and the son who will be murdered within two.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–28 — He Made Bronze Shields Instead
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Rehoboam reigns seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city that the LORD had chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, and his mother's name was Naamah the Ammonite (v. 21). And Judah did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and they provoked him to jealousy with their sins that they committed, more than all that their fathers had done (v. 22): high places, pillars and Asherim on every high hill and under every green tree (v. 23), and male cult prostitutes in the land, and they did according to all the abominations of the nations that the LORD drove out before the people of Israel (v. 24). In the fifth year Shishak king of Egypt comes up against Jerusalem and took away the treasures of the house of the LORD and the treasures of the king's house. He took away everything. He also took away all the shields of gold that Solomon had made (vv. 25-26). And King Rehoboam made in their place shields of bronze, and committed them to the hands of the officers of the guard, who kept the door of the king's house. And as often as the king went into the house of the LORD, the guard carried them and brought them back to the guardroom (vv. 27-28).
verseByVerse.theology: Five years. Solomon's gold shields hung in the House of the Forest of Lebanon and Sheba's queen had no breath left in her, and five years after his death an Egyptian army carries the lot away and the writer says he took away everything.
verseByVerse.examples: And then the bronze. The same procession, the same guard, the same route into the house of the LORD, the same shields put back in the same room afterwards — in a cheaper metal, with everybody carrying on as though nothing had changed. It is the most exact picture of religious decline in the Old Testament.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Rehoboam the son of Solomon reigned in Judah. Rehoboam was forty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city that the LORD had chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, to put his name there. His mother's name was Naamah the Ammonite. And Judah did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and they provoked him to jealousy with their sins that they committed, more than all that their fathers had done. For they also built for themselves high places and pillars and Asherim on every high hill and under every green tree, and there were also male cult prostitutes in the land. They did according to all the abominations of the nations that the LORD drove out before the people of Israel. In the fifth year of King Rehoboam, Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem. He took away the treasures of the house of the LORD and the treasures of the king's house. He took away everything. He also took away all the shields of gold that Solomon had made, and King Rehoboam made in their place shields of bronze, and committed them to the hands of the officers of the guard, who kept the door of the king's house. And as often as the king went into the house of the LORD, the guard carried them and brought them back to the guardroom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now Rehoboam the son of Solomon reigned in Judah. Rehoboam was forty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city that the LORD had chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, to put his name there. His mother's name was Naamah the Ammonite.'

Two things in that verse, set side by side without comment.

Jerusalem, the city that the LORD had chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, to put his name there. The writer takes a whole clause to say it, which he did not need to do.

And: his mother's name was Naamah the Ammonite.

The king ruling in the city God chose is the son of an Ammonite woman — one of the seven hundred, from one of the nations named in the warning at 11:1. Ammon is Milcom's country, the god Solomon built a high place for on the hill facing the temple.

The writer repeats her name in the last verse of the chapter, which means he wants it noticed.

'And Judah did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and they provoked him to jealousy with their sins that they committed, more than all that their fathers had done.'

And now the south, and the verdict is as bad as anything said about the north.

This matters, because a reader coming out of chapter 12 might have formed the impression that the calves were the problem and Judah was the faithful remnant. The writer will not allow it. Judah did evil, and more than all that their fathers had done.

Note also the word: they provoked him to jealousy. It is the language of a marriage, and it is the word God uses of himself in the second commandment — the one about images. God is not indifferent about this the way a landlord is indifferent about a tenant. It is the offence of a husband.

'For they also built for themselves high places and pillars and Asherim on every high hill and under every green tree,'

The full apparatus of Canaanite religion, and the phrase on every high hill and under every green tree becomes the standard description of it through the prophets.

'and there were also male cult prostitutes in the land. They did according to all the abominations of the nations that the LORD drove out before the people of Israel.'

And here is the sentence that ought to stop a reader.

They did according to all the abominations of the nations that the LORD drove out before the people of Israel.

The reason God gave for dispossessing the Canaanites was that the land had become intolerable — the land vomited out its inhabitants (Lev. 18:25), and the practices listed there include exactly this. Israel was warned in the same passage that the land would do the same to them.

Judah is now doing the things the previous occupants were expelled for, on the same ground, five years after the temple was dedicated.

'In the fifth year of King Rehoboam, Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem.'

Five years.

Solomon has been dead five years. The temple has stood for about thirty. And an Egyptian army is at the gates of Jerusalem.

Shishak is one of the few figures in this history who is independently documented: he is Sheshonq I, and he left a record of this campaign carved on a wall at Karnak, listing the towns he took.

Note also who he is. He is the man who sheltered Jeroboam when Solomon tried to kill him (11:40).

'He took away the treasures of the house of the LORD and the treasures of the king's house. He took away everything. He also took away all the shields of gold that Solomon had made.'

He took away everything.

Three chapters ago the reader was standing in a room where silver was not considered as anything, where a fleet came every three years with gold and ivory and apes and peacocks, and where a foreign queen ran out of breath.

It lasted five years past its owner.

And the writer specifies the shields, because they are what he wants us watching: all the shields of gold that Solomon had made. Two hundred large and three hundred small, hanging in the House of the Forest of Lebanon.

'And King Rehoboam made in their place shields of bronze, and committed them to the hands of the officers of the guard, who kept the door of the king's house.'

He makes replacements.

'And as often as the king went into the house of the LORD, the guard carried them and brought them back to the guardroom.'

And here is the most exact picture of religious decline anywhere in the Old Testament, and the writer draws it in one sentence about a routine.

Everything continues.

The king still goes up to the house of the LORD. The guard still turns out. The shields are still carried in front of him in procession, and afterwards they are still taken back and put away in the guardroom, and presumably somebody still polishes them.

The form is intact down to the last detail. The metal is not.

Nobody stopped the ceremony. Nobody stood up and said that gold shields carried before the king had meant something and bronze ones do not. They made the replacements the same size and carried on exactly as before, and within a generation nobody in that guardroom would have remembered that they were ever gold.

That is how it goes. Not a repudiation and not a scandal — a substitution, quietly made, with the liturgy unaltered.

And the detail that finishes it is brought them back to the guardroom. They are not even displayed. Solomon's shields hung in a hall built to be walked through; these are locked away between uses, because they are for the procession and nothing else.

A reader ought to feel the question the verse asks without asking it. What in your own practice is bronze now, carried with the same ceremony, in the same order, by people who have never seen the gold?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–31 — And There Was War Continually
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now the rest of the acts of Rehoboam and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? (v. 29). And there was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam continually (v. 30). And Rehoboam slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David. His mother's name was Naamah the Ammonite. And Abijam his son reigned in his place (v. 31).
verseByVerse.theology: Shemaiah stopped the war in chapter 12 with one sentence and a hundred and eighty thousand men went home. It did not stay stopped. War between Rehoboam and Jeroboam continually — two Israelite kings, brothers by the prophet's own word, fighting for the rest of their lives.
verseByVerse.examples: And the writer names his mother a second time in the last verse of the chapter. Naamah the Ammonite. He said it in verse 21 and he says it again here, and he does not explain why.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the rest of the acts of Rehoboam and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? And there was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam continually. And Rehoboam slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David. His mother's name was Naamah the Ammonite. And Abijam his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now the rest of the acts of Rehoboam and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?'

The formula, and from here it will alternate: the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah, the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel, back and forth, for the rest of both books.

Chronicles fills in a good deal that Kings leaves out about Rehoboam, including a moment this account does not mention: when Shishak came up, Shemaiah told the king and the princes you abandoned me, so I have abandoned you to the hand of Shishak, and they humbled themselves and said the LORD is righteous, and God said they have humbled themselves. I will not destroy them (2 Chron. 12:5-7).

So Jerusalem was stripped rather than sacked, and the reason was a moment of repentance the writer of Kings does not record.

He is writing a theological account and he selects. What he wants us to see here is the bronze.

'And there was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam continually.'

Continually.

Go back two chapters. A hundred and eighty thousand men were mustered to take the north back by force, and a prophet said one sentence — you shall not go up or fight against your relatives the people of Israel... for this thing is from me — and every one of them went home (12:24).

They obeyed. And then they spent the rest of their lives at war anyway.

Not the invasion they were forbidden; something slower. Border raids, skirmishes, garrison towns, two Israelite kings fighting over a frontier that ran through the middle of Benjamin, for seventeen years.

A man can obey the letter of a prohibition and give his whole life to the thing it was meant to prevent.

'And Rehoboam slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David. His mother's name was Naamah the Ammonite. And Abijam his son reigned in his place.'

And there she is again, in the last verse of the chapter.

Naamah the Ammonite.

The writer said it in verse 21 and there was no need to say it twice. He repeats it in the sentence about the man's burial, and he offers no comment either time.

What he is doing, quietly, is closing an account that was opened in 3:1 and left running for eight chapters.

Solomon married foreign women. His wives turned away his heart. He built high places for all of them on the mountain east of Jerusalem. God tore the kingdom in two.

And the king left sitting in the city God chose, ruling one tribe, doing more evil than his fathers, with male cult prostitutes in the land and an Egyptian army walking off with the gold — is the son of one of those women.

The writer does not draw the line. He writes her name at the top of the reign and at the bottom of it, and leaves it there.

14.theology:
He sends to Shiloh (v. 2). With calves at Bethel and Dan, a priesthood of his own appointing and altars on every high place, his sick child sends him to a prophet of the LORD — and specifically to the man who gave him ten pieces of a torn cloak and the offer of David's own covenant. He knows what the calves are worth. That is the most damning thing in the chapter and the writer never remarks on it. Note too that the gift is chosen to match the costume: bread, cakes and honey are what a village woman brings a holy man, and exactly what a queen would not.

The blind prophet (vv. 4-6). There is something almost comic in it, and it is the comedy Scripture uses to expose a way of thinking: Jeroboam calculated the clothes, the gift and the anonymity, and forgot that the man he was deceiving does not see. God announces her arrival and even her pretence in advance, and Ahijah names her by the sound of her feet before she has spoken. I am charged with unbearable news — literally I am sent to you with hard things — tells her before he begins that this will not be what she came for.

The indictment starts with what God did (v. 7). I exalted you from among the people. He was a labour foreman; Solomon promoted him and God gave him a kingdom. And the standard is the one Solomon was measured by: my servant David, who kept my commandments and followed me with all his heart. Not sinlessness — this book knows what David did — but that he never went after another god. That measure does not change from the first page of Kings to the last. You have cast me behind your back is the picture of throwing something over your shoulder: discarded, out of sight, not worth turning round for.

Verse 13, taken slowly. Three things. In him there is found something pleasing to the LORD — literally a good thing toward the LORD was found in him, in that household, and we are told nothing else about the boy: not his age, not what he did or said. Something in him pleased God, God noticed, and it is recorded in Scripture three thousand years later. Second, he alone of that house comes to a grave, while the rest are given to dogs and birds. And third, he dies first — and the writer places his death immediately after the sentence about dogs and birds so that the reader cannot miss what he is spared. Isaiah says it plainly: the righteous man is taken away from calamity; he enters into peace (Isa. 57:1-2).

And what it does not say. This is not a general explanation of why children die and must not be turned into one; Scripture does not offer that, and anyone who has buried a child has been offered enough tidy explanations already. What the verse says is smaller and steadier: God saw something good in a boy nobody else in that house had any use for, said so, and took him early as kindness rather than carelessness.

The end of the north, in its first generation (v. 15). Scatter them beyond the Euphrates is Assyria, two centuries away; the northern tribes were deported in 722 and never returned, and 2 Kings 17 gives the same reasons Ahijah gives here. And the image is exact — as a reed is shaken in the water: a reed has no root worth the name, and nothing holds it.

She is given no words (v. 17). She walks twenty miles knowing what will happen when she arrives, and it happens as she crosses the threshold. Not one line of what she said or thought is recorded, here or anywhere.

Naamah the Ammonite, twice (vv. 21, 31). The king ruling in the city that the LORD had chosen is the son of an Ammonite woman — one of the seven hundred, from one of the nations named in the warning at 11:1, and Ammon is Milcom's country, for whom Solomon built a high place on the hill facing the temple. The writer names her at the top of the reign and again at the burial, and comments neither time. He is closing an account opened at 3:1 and left running for eight chapters.

Judah is not the faithful remnant (v. 22). A reader coming out of chapter 12 might think the calves were the problem and the south was sound. The verdict here is as bad as anything said of the north: more than all that their fathers had done. And the word is jealousy — the language of a marriage, and the word God uses of himself in the commandment about images. This is not a landlord's indifference; it is a husband's offence.

Doing what the Canaanites were expelled for (v. 24). The reason God gave for dispossessing them was that the land had become intolerable — the land vomited out its inhabitants (Lev. 18:25) — and the practices listed there include exactly this. Israel was warned in the same passage that the land would do the same to them. Judah is now doing it on the same ground, five years after the temple was dedicated.

He took away everything (v. 26). Three chapters ago silver was not considered as anything and a foreign queen had no breath left in her. It lasted five years past its owner. Shishak is Sheshonq I, one of the few figures here independently documented — he carved a record of this campaign on a wall at Karnak — and he is the man who sheltered Jeroboam when Solomon tried to kill him (11:40).

The bronze shields (vv. 27-28). The most exact picture of religious decline in the Old Testament, drawn in one sentence about a routine. Everything continues: the king still goes up to the house of the LORD, the guard still turns out, the shields are still carried before him and still taken back and put away afterwards. The form is intact to the last detail; the metal is not. Nobody stopped the ceremony and nobody said that gold shields had meant something and bronze ones do not — they made replacements the same size and carried on, and within a generation nobody in that guardroom would remember they were ever gold. Not a repudiation and not a scandal: a substitution, quietly made, with the liturgy unaltered. And they are not even displayed — Solomon's hung in a hall built to be walked through; these are locked away between uses, because they are for the procession and nothing else.

What Kings leaves out (v. 29). Chronicles records that when Shishak came, Shemaiah said you abandoned me, so I have abandoned you to the hand of Shishak, and the king and princes humbled themselves and said the LORD is righteous, and God said they have humbled themselves. I will not destroy them (2 Chron. 12:5-7). So Jerusalem was stripped rather than sacked, for a reason this writer does not mention. He is writing a theological account and he selects, and what he wants us watching is the bronze.

Continually (v. 30). Two chapters ago a hundred and eighty thousand men were mustered to take the north by force, and one sentence from a prophet sent every one of them home (12:24). They obeyed — and then spent the rest of their lives at war anyway. Not the invasion they were forbidden; something slower, over a frontier running through the middle of Benjamin, for seventeen years. A man can obey the letter of a prohibition and give his whole life to the thing it was meant to prevent.
14.examples:
Then: A king sent his wife twenty miles in disguise, dressed as a villager and carrying a villager's gift, to get a word from God about their dying son — and the prophet she was deceiving was blind, and greeted her by name from the sound of her feet in the doorway before she had said anything at all.

Now: Three things. Why do you pretend to be another? is the question the chapter leaves standing: the costume could only ever have fooled a man, and it was never going to touch the thing they actually wanted. A great deal of religious practice is that shape — a version of yourself presented, the right sort of offering, the arrangement kept anonymous — and the whole point of God is that he knows who is at the door. Second, verse 13, which is for anybody who has stood at a small grave: it does not explain why children die and it is not offered as one, and what it does say is that God found something good in a boy his own family had no use for, said so, and took him early to spare him. And third, the bronze shields. The procession went on, the guard turned out, the shields came back to the guardroom — and within a generation nobody remembered they had ever been gold. The question the verse asks without asking it is which parts of your own practice are bronze now, carried in the same order, by people who never saw the gold.
