He left to the house of Jeroboam not one that breathed, until he had destroyed it, according to the word of the LORD that he spoke by his servant Ahijah the Shilonite.<sup>30</sup>It was for the sins of Jeroboam that he sinned and that he made Israel to sin, and because of the anger to which he provoked the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>31</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Nadab and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?<sup>32</sup>And there was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel all their days.<sup>33</sup>In the third year of Asa king of Judah, Baasha the son of Ahijah began to reign over all Israel at Tirzah, and he reigned twenty-four years.<sup>34</sup>He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and walked in the way of Jeroboam and in his sin which he made Israel to sin.
15.overview:
Here the book changes shape. From this chapter to the end of 2 Kings the narrative runs on a fixed pattern, alternating between the kingdoms and dating each reign by the other. It can feel like a filing system, and it is doing something: by dating Judah's kings from Israel's and Israel's from Judah's, the writer refuses to let either half be read alone. They are one people who have broken in two, and he keeps making the reader look across the border.

And he has found his yardstick. His heart was not wholly true — shalem, the word Solomon preached at the dedication and lost in his old age — is applied to Abijam in exactly the terms it was taken off his grandfather. It will be the measure for four hundred years.

Verse 5 is one of the most carefully weighed sentences in the Old Testament. David did not turn aside from anything that he commanded him all the days of his life — an enormous claim, which a reader of 2 Samuel may want to object to — and then in five words the writer objects for him: except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite. He names the worst thing David did, by the man's name, in a verse about why God kept the promise. It is not a whitewash, and the exception is narrow, and both facts are deliberate.

Then Asa, who removes his own grandmother from the office of queen mother and burns her Asherah image at the Kidron in public — and leaves the high places standing. The writer puts the failure and the verdict in one verse, in that order: but the high places were not taken away. Nevertheless, the heart of Asa was wholly true to the LORD all his days. That is shalem, given to somebody at last — to a man who is nowhere near as gifted as Solomon, who strips the temple to hire a Syrian, and who in his old age sought physicians and not the LORD.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Abijam reigns three years in Jerusalem; his mother is Maacah the daughter of Abishalom (vv. 1-2). And he walked in all the sins that his father did before him, and his heart was not wholly true to the LORD his God, as the heart of David his father (v. 3). Nevertheless, for David's sake the LORD his God gave him a lamp in Jerusalem, setting up his son after him, and establishing Jerusalem, because David did what was right in the eyes of the LORD and did not turn aside from anything that he commanded him all the days of his life, except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite (vv. 4-5). War with Jeroboam continues all his days (vv. 6-8).
verseByVerse.theology: His heart was not wholly true — shalem again, the word Solomon lost. It is becoming the writer's yardstick, and it is applied to grandfather and grandson in the same terms.
verseByVerse.examples: And the exception in verse 5 is astonishing for its precision. David did not turn aside from anything that he commanded him all the days of his life — and then, in five words, except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite. The writer will not pretend it did not happen and he will not let it define the man.

verseByVerse.quote: Now in the eighteenth year of King Jeroboam the son of Nebat, Abijam began to reign over Judah. He reigned for three years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Maacah the daughter of Abishalom. And he walked in all the sins that his father did before him, and his heart was not wholly true to the LORD his God, as the heart of David his father. Nevertheless, for David's sake the LORD his God gave him a lamp in Jerusalem, setting up his son after him, and establishing Jerusalem, because David did what was right in the eyes of the LORD and did not turn aside from anything that he commanded him all the days of his life, except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite. Now there was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam all the days of his life. The rest of the acts of Abijam and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? And there was war between Abijam and Jeroboam. And Abijam slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city of David. And Asa his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now in the eighteenth year of King Jeroboam the son of Nebat, Abijam began to reign over Judah.'

Here the book changes shape.

From this chapter to the end of 2 Kings the narrative runs on a fixed pattern, alternating between the two kingdoms and dating each reign by the other. It is a filing system, and it can feel like one — but it is doing something.

By dating Judah's kings from Israel's and Israel's from Judah's, the writer refuses to let either half be read alone. They are one people who have broken in two, and he keeps making the reader look across the border.

'He reigned for three years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Maacah the daughter of Abishalom.'

'And he walked in all the sins that his father did before him, and his heart was not wholly true to the LORD his God, as the heart of David his father.'

There is the word again.

His heart was not wholly true — shalem, whole and undivided.

Solomon used it in his benediction at the dedication and the writer took it off him at 11:4. Here it is applied to his grandson in exactly the same form, and the standard is exactly the same man: as the heart of David his father.

The writer has found his yardstick and he is going to use it for four hundred years.

'Nevertheless, for David's sake the LORD his God gave him a lamp in Jerusalem, setting up his son after him, and establishing Jerusalem,'

Nevertheless.

A bad king, whose heart was divided, who walked in his father's sins — and the dynasty survives him. Not because of anything in him.

For David's sake.

The word is the one from Ahijah's oracle: a lamp in Jerusalem. David's own soldiers used it about him when he grew weary on a battlefield — lest you quench the lamp of Israel (2 Sam. 21:17) — and God took it up as his own at 11:36, and uses it again here, and again when Judah deserves destruction: he was not willing to destroy Judah, for the sake of David his servant, since he promised to give a lamp to him and to his sons forever (2 Kings 8:19).

A lamp is a small light and the promise is that it will not go out. Not that it will blaze, and not that the men holding it will be worth much. It burns through Abijam, and Ahaz, and Manasseh, down to almost nothing, and it does not go out.

'because David did what was right in the eyes of the LORD and did not turn aside from anything that he commanded him all the days of his life, except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite.'

Here is one of the most carefully weighed sentences in the Old Testament.

Read the whole of it. David did what was right in the eyes of the LORD and did not turn aside from anything that he commanded him all the days of his life.

That is an enormous claim, and a reader who has just finished 2 Samuel may want to object.

Then, in five words, the writer objects for him: except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite.

Two things about that exception, and both matter.

The first is that he makes it. He does not let the summary stand unqualified. The worst thing David ever did is named, by the man's name, in a verse about why God kept the promise — and the man named is not Bathsheba but Uriah, which is exactly how 2 Samuel ended, with his name last on the roll of the mighty men.

The second is how narrow the exception is. One matter, named once. Everything else in a seventy-year life is on the other side of it.

That is not a whitewash and it is not indulgence. It is the same judgment Kings makes everywhere: the question is whether a man belonged to the LORD alone, and David did, and what he did to Uriah was the great exception in a life that otherwise went one way.

The fact that it is named at all is the point. God kept the promise for David's sake, and the writer will not let anybody think that means David was better than he was.

'Now there was war between Abijam and Jeroboam all the days of his life.'

'The rest of the acts of Abijam and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? And there was war between Abijam and Jeroboam.'

Said twice in three verses. The war that began when a hundred and eighty thousand men went home is still running in the second generation.

'And Abijam slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city of David. And Asa his son reigned in his place.'

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–24 — The Heart of Asa Was Wholly True
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Asa reigns forty-one years (vv. 9-10). And Asa did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, as David his father had done (v. 11). He puts away the male cult prostitutes and removes the idols his fathers had made (v. 12). He also removed Maacah his mother from being queen mother because she had made an abominable image for Asherah. And Asa cut down her image and burned it at the brook Kidron (v. 13). But the high places were not taken away. Nevertheless, the heart of Asa was wholly true to the LORD all his days (v. 14). Baasha of Israel fortifies Ramah against him (v. 17), so Asa takes all the silver and gold left in the house of the LORD and the king's house and sends it to Ben-hadad of Syria to break his treaty with Baasha (vv. 18-19); Ben-hadad does, and Asa carries away the stones of Ramah (vv. 20-22). But in his old age he was diseased in his feet (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: The heart of Asa was wholly true to the LORD all his days. That is shalem — whole, undivided — the word Solomon preached at the dedication and lost in his old age. Here it is, given to somebody.
verseByVerse.examples: And it sits immediately after but the high places were not taken away. The writer puts the failure and the verdict in the same verse, in that order, and lets both stand. A man can be wholly true to God and still leave something standing that should have come down.

verseByVerse.quote: In the twentieth year of Jeroboam king of Israel, Asa began to reign over Judah, and he reigned forty-one years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Maacah the daughter of Abishalom. And Asa did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, as David his father had done. He put away the male cult prostitutes out of the land and removed all the idols that his fathers had made. He also removed Maacah his mother from being queen mother because she had made an abominable image for Asherah. And Asa cut down her image and burned it at the brook Kidron. But the high places were not taken away. Nevertheless, the heart of Asa was wholly true to the LORD all his days. And he brought into the house of the LORD the sacred gifts of his father and his own sacred gifts, silver, and gold, and vessels. And there was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel all their days. Baasha king of Israel went up against Judah and built Ramah, that he might permit no one to go out or come in to Asa king of Judah. Then Asa took all the silver and the gold that were left in the treasures of the house of the LORD and the treasures of the king's house and gave them into the hands of his servants. And King Asa sent them to Ben-hadad the son of Tabrimmon, the son of Hezion, king of Syria, who lived in Damascus, saying, "Let there be a covenant between me and you, as there was between my father and your father. Behold, I am sending to you a present of silver and gold. Go, break your covenant with Baasha king of Israel, that he may withdraw from me." And Ben-hadad listened to King Asa and sent the commanders of his armies against the cities of Israel and conquered Ijon, Dan, Abel-beth-maacah, and all Chinneroth, with all the land of Naphtali. And when Baasha heard of it, he stopped building Ramah, and he lived in Tirzah. Then King Asa made a proclamation to all Judah, none was exempt, and they carried away the stones of Ramah and its timber, with which Baasha had been building, and with them King Asa built Geba of Benjamin and Mizpah. Now the rest of all the acts of Asa, all his might, and all that he did, and the cities that he built, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? But in his old age he was diseased in his feet. And Asa slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David his father, and Jehoshaphat his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And in the twentieth year of Jeroboam king of Israel, Asa began to reign over Judah,'

'and he reigned forty-one years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Maacah the daughter of Abishalom.'

Forty-one years, which is the longest reign in Judah so far, and one of the longest in the book.

A note on his mother, since verse 2 said the same woman was Abijam's mother. The likeliest explanation is that Maacah is Asa's grandmother, and that the Hebrew word is being used in its wider sense of a female ancestor — which also explains why she is still holding the office of queen mother into a new reign, and why removing her from it is a formal act rather than a family quarrel.

'And Asa did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, as David his father had done.'

The first good verdict in the book since Solomon's early years, and it is unqualified.

'He put away the male cult prostitutes out of the land and removed all the idols that his fathers had made.'

All the idols that his fathers had made.

His father Abijam made them, and his great-grandfather Solomon built the high places on the mountain east of Jerusalem, and Asa takes them out.

That is not a small thing to do. Every one of those installations had a constituency, and some of them had been standing for two generations and had acquired the respectability that anything acquires if it stands long enough. Removing them means telling people that what their fathers did was wrong.

'He also removed Maacah his mother from being queen mother because she had made an abominable image for Asherah. And Asa cut down her image and burned it at the brook Kidron.'

Here is the costliest thing he does.

The queen mother in Judah held a real office, not merely a title. She sat at the king's right hand, had standing in the court, and in a country where the king had many wives she was frequently the most powerful woman in the kingdom.

Asa removes her.

The grounds are stated: she had made an abominable image for Asherah, the Canaanite goddess. The word for the image is unusual and carries a suggestion of something obscene.

He does not simply confiscate it. He cuts it down and burns it at the Kidron — the brook below the city, in public, where everybody could see the smoke.

Now consider what that took. This is his grandmother, in her old age, in an office she has held through two reigns. He is not removing a stranger's shrine; he is stripping his own family's matriarch of her position and destroying her religious property in front of the capital.

There is a hard principle underneath it, and Scripture does not soften it anywhere. The Lord Jesus said whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me (Matt. 10:37), and the same passage warns that a man's enemies will be those of his own household.

Most obedience is not costly because a stranger opposes it. It is costly because somebody at the table does.

'But the high places were not taken away.'

There is the qualification, and this writer will attach it to almost every good king from here to the end.

Hezekiah is the one who finally does it, and Josiah, and nobody else.

What the high places were should be stated, because it is not simple idolatry. Many of them were places where the LORD himself was worshipped — local hilltop sanctuaries, convenient, ancient, often with genuine history attached, exactly like Bethel. The trouble was that they were not the place God had chosen, and they were the mechanism by which Canaanite practice kept seeping in.

So the failure is not that Asa served other gods. It is that he tidied the country and left the alternative structures standing, because they were popular and long-established and taking them down would have cost more than removing his grandmother's idol.

'Nevertheless, the heart of Asa was wholly true to the LORD all his days.'

Now the verse the chapter exists for.

The heart of Asa was wholly true to the LORD all his days.

The word is shalem.

It is the word Solomon used standing in front of the finished temple with the glory of God inside it, telling the whole nation: let your heart therefore be wholly true to the LORD our God (8:61). It is the root of Solomon's own name. And it is the word the writer took off him three chapters later, when he was old and his wives had turned his heart: his heart was not wholly true to the LORD his God (11:4).

It was taken off Abijam eleven verses ago.

Here it is given to somebody.

Asa is not a better man than Solomon. He is nowhere near as gifted, he leaves the high places standing, he strips the temple to buy a foreign alliance, and Chronicles records that he ended badly. And the writer says his heart was whole toward God all his days.

That is the distinction this book keeps making and it should be had exactly. Shalem is not a measure of achievement or even of consistency. It is a question about whether there is anything else in the room. Solomon had seven hundred marriages and a hill full of altars; Asa had one God and a job half done.

The two clauses are in the same verse, in that order: but the high places were not taken away. Nevertheless, the heart of Asa was wholly true.

The writer records the failure and refuses to let it cancel the verdict. Both are true at once, and a reader who can only hold one of them will misread every king in this book.

'And he brought into the house of the LORD the sacred gifts of his father and his own sacred gifts, silver, and gold, and vessels.'

He puts treasure back into the temple — which had been stripped by Shishak in his grandfather's fifth year.

Hold that for four verses.

'And there was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel all their days.'

'Baasha king of Israel went up against Judah and built Ramah, that he might permit no one to go out or come in to Asa king of Judah.'

Ramah is about five miles north of Jerusalem, on the main road. Fortifying it is a blockade.

'Then Asa took all the silver and the gold that were left in the treasures of the house of the LORD and the treasures of the king's house and gave them into the hands of his servants. And King Asa sent them to Ben-hadad the son of Tabrimmon, the son of Hezion, king of Syria, who lived in Damascus, saying,'

Here is the other side of the man, and it should be stated as plainly as the verdict was.

He takes the silver and gold out of the house of the LORD — including, presumably, what he had just put in — and sends it to a foreign king to buy a military favour.

Damascus, incidentally, is the kingdom founded by Rezon, the man who escaped David's Syrian campaign and became one of the adversaries God raised up against Solomon (11:23-25).

'"Let there be a covenant between me and you, as there was between my father and your father. Behold, I am sending to you a present of silver and gold. Go, break your covenant with Baasha king of Israel, that he may withdraw from me."'

Go, break your covenant.

He is paying a pagan king to be treacherous, and he says so in the letter.

'And Ben-hadad listened to King Asa and sent the commanders of his armies against the cities of Israel and conquered Ijon, Dan, Abel-beth-maacah, and all Chinneroth, with all the land of Naphtali.'

'And when Baasha heard of it, he stopped building Ramah, and he lived in Tirzah.'

It works. Baasha has to pull north to defend his own border and the blockade lifts.

'Then King Asa made a proclamation to all Judah, none was exempt, and they carried away the stones of Ramah and its timber, with which Baasha had been building, and with them King Asa built Geba of Benjamin and Mizpah.'

He dismantles the enemy fortress and rebuilds his own frontier with the materials.

Now, the strategy was a complete success and Chronicles records what God thought of it.

Hanani the seer came to Asa and said: because you relied on the king of Syria, and did not rely on the LORD your God, the army of the king of Syria has escaped you. Were not the Ethiopians and the Libyans a huge army with very many chariots and horsemen? Yet because you relied on the LORD, he gave them into your hand. For the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to give strong support to those whose heart is blameless toward him (2 Chron. 16:7-9).

Asa put the seer in the stocks.

Note the last clause of the rebuke: those whose heart is blameless toward him. That is shalem — the same word Kings uses of Asa's heart, quoted back at him as the thing he had just stopped acting on.

So the record on this man is genuinely mixed and the two books make no attempt to harmonise it. Kings says his heart was whole toward God all his days, and it says he stripped the temple to hire a Syrian. Both.

'Now the rest of all the acts of Asa, all his might, and all that he did, and the cities that he built, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? But in his old age he was diseased in his feet.'

The last clause is put in almost as an afterthought and Chronicles supplies what is behind it.

In the thirty-ninth year of his reign Asa was diseased in his feet, and his disease became severe. Yet even in his disease he did not seek the LORD, but sought help from physicians (2 Chron. 16:12).

Be careful with that verse, because it has been badly used.

It is not a rule against doctors. Scripture nowhere condemns medicine; Isaiah prescribed a poultice of figs for Hezekiah's boil, Paul told Timothy to take a little wine for his stomach, and Luke is called the beloved physician.

The charge is in the first half of the sentence: he did not seek the LORD. A man whose heart had been whole toward God for forty years, at the end, in pain, went everywhere except to him.

It is the same pattern as the Syrian alliance. Not apostasy — competence. He handled the problem himself, effectively, and did not ask.

'And Asa slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David his father, and Jehoshaphat his son reigned in his place.'

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–34 — According to the Word of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nadab the son of Jeroboam reigns two years and walked in the way of his father (vv. 25-26). Baasha conspires against him at Gibbethon and kills him (v. 27), and as soon as he was king, he killed all the house of Jeroboam. He left to the house of Jeroboam not one that breathed, until he had destroyed it, according to the word of the LORD that he spoke by his servant Ahijah the Shilonite (v. 29) — because of the sins of Jeroboam that he sinned and that he made Israel to sin (v. 30). And Baasha reigns twenty-four years in Tirzah (vv. 32-33), and he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and walked in the way of Jeroboam and in his sin which he made Israel to sin (v. 34).
verseByVerse.theology: The word Ahijah gave to a woman in a disguise is carried out to the letter: not one that breathed. God said the house of Jeroboam would be burned up like dung until it was all gone, and a conspirator with a knife at Gibbethon completed it.
verseByVerse.examples: And then the last verse. The man God used to execute judgment on Jeroboam's calves walked in the way of Jeroboam. Being the instrument of a judgment teaches a man nothing at all.

verseByVerse.quote: Nadab the son of Jeroboam began to reign over Israel in the second year of Asa king of Judah, and he reigned over Israel two years. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and walked in the way of his father, and in his sin which he made Israel to sin. Baasha the son of Ahijah, of the house of Issachar, conspired against him. And Baasha struck him down at Gibbethon, which belonged to the Philistines, for Nadab and all Israel were laying siege to Gibbethon. So Baasha killed him in the third year of Asa king of Judah and reigned in his place. And as soon as he was king, he killed all the house of Jeroboam. He left to the house of Jeroboam not one that breathed, until he had destroyed it, according to the word of the LORD that he spoke by his servant Ahijah the Shilonite. It was for the sins of Jeroboam that he sinned and that he made Israel to sin, and because of the anger to which he provoked the LORD, the God of Israel. Now the rest of the acts of Nadab and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? And there was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel all their days. In the third year of Asa king of Judah, Baasha the son of Ahijah began to reign over all Israel at Tirzah, and he reigned twenty-four years. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and walked in the way of Jeroboam and in his sin which he made Israel to sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Nadab the son of Jeroboam began to reign over Israel in the second year of Asa king of Judah, and he reigned over Israel two years.'

Two years, and then the house of Jeroboam is finished.

'He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and walked in the way of his father, and in his sin which he made Israel to sin.'

There is the formula, arriving for the first of many times.

He walked in the way of his father, and in his sin which he made Israel to sin.

From here to the fall of Samaria this sentence, or something almost identical, is stamped on nineteen kings across two centuries. Jeroboam is dead, and every one of them is measured against an afternoon at Bethel when he set up a calf because he was afraid.

The phrase which he made Israel to sin is the part that will not go away. He did not merely sin; he built it into the machinery of a nation, with sanctuaries and clergy and a festival, so that ordinary people went on doing it without ever choosing it.

'Baasha the son of Ahijah, of the house of Issachar, conspired against him. And Baasha struck him down at Gibbethon, which belonged to the Philistines, for Nadab and all Israel were laying siege to Gibbethon.'

He is murdered by one of his own officers in the middle of a siege.

'So Baasha killed him in the third year of Asa king of Judah and reigned in his place.'

'And as soon as he was king, he killed all the house of Jeroboam. He left to the house of Jeroboam not one that breathed, until he had destroyed it, according to the word of the LORD that he spoke by his servant Ahijah the Shilonite,'

Now the writer stops and tells us what has happened.

According to the word of the LORD that he spoke by his servant Ahijah the Shilonite.

Go back one chapter. A blind man in Shiloh said to a woman in a disguise: I will cut off from Jeroboam every male, both bond and free in Israel, and will burn up the house of Jeroboam, as a man burns up dung until it is all gone (14:10).

Not one that breathed.

The word was given in a private house to a woman who told nobody, and it is executed by a soldier from the tribe of Issachar who had never heard it, for reasons entirely his own.

Baasha is not obeying anything. He is a conspirator eliminating a rival dynasty, which is standard practice; he would have done exactly this if Ahijah had never spoken. And the writer says the word of the LORD was fulfilled.

It is the same structure as 12:15 and 2 Samuel 17:14: a man acting freely, from his own motives, completing something God said.

'it was because of the sins of Jeroboam that he sinned and that he made Israel to sin, and because of the anger to which he provoked the LORD, the God of Israel.'

The reason is given plainly, and the family is not being punished for Baasha's ambition. They are being cut off for what their father built.

'Now the rest of the acts of Nadab, and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?'

'And there was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel all their days.'

'In the third year of Asa king of Judah, Baasha the son of Ahijah began to reign over all Israel at Tirzah, and he reigned twenty-four years.'

'He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and walked in the way of Jeroboam and in his sin which he made Israel to sin.'

There is the last verse of the chapter, and it is the one to take away.

Baasha has just destroyed the house of Jeroboam. He killed every male in it. He was the instrument by which God's word against the calves and the priesthood and the invented festival was carried out.

The first thing recorded about his own reign is that he walked in the way of Jeroboam and in his sin which he made Israel to sin.

He wiped out a family for a sin and then committed it.

The calves at Bethel and Dan are still standing. He does not remove them. The priesthood Jeroboam appointed from among all the people is still functioning; he does not touch it. The festival in the eighth month goes on. Baasha changes the dynasty and leaves the religion exactly as he found it, because the religion was the thing that made the northern kingdom possible and he needs it as much as Jeroboam did.

That is why the judgment does not fix anything. Chapter 16 opens with a prophet coming to Baasha with almost word for word the same oracle Ahijah gave Jeroboam, and Baasha's house is destroyed the same way.

Being the instrument of a judgment teaches a man nothing. He can carry out God's sentence on somebody else's sin in the morning and take it up himself in the afternoon, and it will not occur to him that there is any connection.

15.theology:
Why the dates cross the border (v. 1). Each reign is fixed by the other kingdom's calendar, which is a way of insisting that these are one people in two halves. The writer will not let the reader settle into either.

The yardstick (v. 3). Shalem — whole, undivided. Solomon used it in his benediction (8:61), the writer took it off him at 11:4, and here it is denied to his grandson in the same words, against the same standard: as the heart of David his father.

Nevertheless, for David's sake (v. 4). A bad king with a divided heart, and the dynasty survives him for nothing in himself. The word is Ahijah's from 11:36, and David's own soldiers used it of him when he grew weary on a battlefield (2 Sam. 21:17); God uses it again when Judah deserves destruction (2 Kings 8:19). A lamp is a small light, and the promise is only that it will not go out — not that it will blaze, and not that the men holding it will be worth much. It burns through Abijam and Ahaz and Manasseh, down to almost nothing.

Except in the matter of Uriah (v. 5). The writer will not let the summary stand unqualified, and the man he names is not Bathsheba but Uriah — which is exactly how 2 Samuel ended, with that name last on the roll of the mighty men. And notice how narrow the exception is: one matter, named once, with everything else in a seventy-year life on the other side of it. That is the judgment Kings makes everywhere — whether a man belonged to the LORD alone — and naming the exception at all is the point: God kept the promise for David's sake, and nobody is to think that means David was better than he was.

All the idols that his fathers had made (v. 12). His father made them and his great-grandfather built the high places on the mountain east of Jerusalem. Every one had a constituency, and some had stood for two generations and acquired the respectability anything acquires if it stands long enough. Removing them means telling people that what their fathers did was wrong.

He removed his own grandmother (v. 13). Queen mother in Judah was a real office, not a courtesy: she sat at the king's right hand and was frequently the most powerful woman in the kingdom. (Verse 2 makes Maacah Abijam's mother, so she is almost certainly Asa's grandmother, the Hebrew being used of a female ancestor — which also explains why she still held the office into a new reign.) He does not simply confiscate the image; he cuts it down and burns it at the Kidron where the city could see the smoke. And the principle underneath is one Scripture never softens: whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me (Matt. 10:37). Most obedience is not costly because a stranger opposes it, but because somebody at the table does.

What the high places were (v. 14). Not simple idolatry — many were places where the LORD himself was worshipped: local hilltop sanctuaries, convenient, ancient, often with real history attached, exactly like Bethel. The trouble was that they were not the place God had chosen, and they were the channel by which Canaanite practice kept seeping in. Asa's failure is not that he served other gods; it is that he tidied the country and left the alternative structures standing, because they were popular and long-established and taking them down would have cost more than removing his grandmother's idol. Only Hezekiah and Josiah ever finish the job.

The word restored (v. 14). The heart of Asa was wholly true to the LORD all his days — shalem, the word Solomon preached to a nation and lost. And Asa is not a better man than Solomon: he is nowhere near as gifted, he leaves the high places, he strips the temple to buy an alliance, and Chronicles records that he ended badly. That is the distinction this book keeps making. Shalem is not a measure of achievement or even of consistency; it is a question about whether there is anything else in the room. Solomon had seven hundred marriages and a hill full of altars; Asa had one God and a job half done. And the two clauses sit in one verse in that order — the failure recorded, and refused permission to cancel the verdict. A reader who can only hold one of them will misread every king in this book.

The other side of the man (vv. 18-19). He takes the silver and gold out of the house of the LORD — including, presumably, what he had just put back in at verse 15 — and sends it to Damascus to buy a military favour, writing go, break your covenant. He is paying a pagan king to be treacherous and says so in the letter. (Damascus is the kingdom founded by Rezon, one of the adversaries God raised up against Solomon, 11:23-25.) It works perfectly, and Chronicles records what God thought of it: because you relied on the king of Syria, and did not rely on the LORD your God, the army of the king of Syria has escaped you... the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to give strong support to those whose heart is blameless toward him (2 Chron. 16:7-9). The last phrase is shalem, quoted back at him as the thing he had stopped acting on — and Asa put the seer in the stocks. The two books make no attempt to harmonise the record. Kings says his heart was whole all his days, and says he stripped the temple to hire a Syrian. Both.

Diseased in his feet (v. 23). Chronicles supplies what is behind the afterthought: yet even in his disease he did not seek the LORD, but sought help from physicians (2 Chron. 16:12). Be careful with that verse, because it has been badly used: it is not a rule against doctors. Scripture nowhere condemns medicine — Isaiah prescribed figs for Hezekiah's boil, Paul told Timothy to take a little wine, and Luke is the beloved physician. The charge is in the first half: he did not seek the LORD. A man whose heart had been whole toward God for forty years went everywhere except to him — which is the same pattern as the Syrian alliance. Not apostasy: competence. He handled it himself, effectively, and did not ask.

Which he made Israel to sin (v. 26). The formula arrives, and it or something almost identical is stamped on nineteen kings across two centuries. Jeroboam is dead, and every one of them is measured against an afternoon at Bethel when he set up a calf because he was afraid. And the phrase that will not go away is which he made Israel to sin: he did not merely sin, he built it into the machinery of a nation — sanctuaries, clergy, a festival — so that ordinary people went on doing it without ever choosing it.

A free man completing a word he never heard (v. 29). Ahijah spoke it in a private house to a woman in a disguise who told nobody, and it is executed by a soldier of Issachar for reasons entirely his own. Baasha is not obeying anything; he is a conspirator eliminating a rival dynasty, which was standard practice, and he would have done it if Ahijah had never spoken. And the writer says the word of the LORD was fulfilled — the same structure as 12:15 and 2 Samuel 17:14.

Being the instrument teaches nothing (v. 34). Baasha destroyed the house of Jeroboam, every male in it, as the instrument of God's word against the calves — and the first thing recorded of his own reign is that he walked in the way of Jeroboam and in his sin which he made Israel to sin. He wiped out a family for a sin and then committed it. The calves are still standing; he does not remove them. The priesthood still functions; he does not touch it. The festival goes on. He changes the dynasty and leaves the religion exactly as he found it, because the religion is what made the northern kingdom possible and he needs it as much as Jeroboam did. That is why the judgment fixes nothing, and why chapter 16 opens with a prophet bringing Baasha almost word for word the oracle Ahijah brought Jeroboam. A man can carry out God's sentence on somebody else's sin in the morning and take it up himself in the afternoon, and never see a connection.
15.examples:
Then: A young king stripped his own grandmother of the highest office a woman could hold in Judah, cut down the idol she had made, and burned it in the valley below the city where everybody could watch the smoke — and left the hilltop shrines standing all over the country, because they were popular and old and everybody used them.

Now: Three things. Verse 14 is the one to keep, and it is the most encouraging sentence in the chapter: shalem is not a score for achievement or even consistency — it asks whether there is anything else in the room. Asa left a job half done, hired a pagan army with temple silver, and put a prophet in the stocks, and God's verdict on his heart stands in the same verse as the failure. Second, Maacah. Obedience is rarely expensive because strangers object; it is expensive because somebody at your own table does, and the higher their standing the more it costs. And third, Baasha, who is the warning nobody expects: he executed God's judgment on another man's sin and then walked straight into it, and it never occurred to him that the two things were related. Being right about somebody else's failure is not the same as being free of it.

16.text: <sup>1</sup>And the word of the LORD came to Jehu the son of Hanani against Baasha, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Since I exalted you out of the dust and made you leader over my people Israel, and you have walked in the way of Jeroboam and have made my people Israel to sin, provoking me to anger with their sins,<sup>3</sup>behold, I will utterly sweep away Baasha and his house, and I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam the son of Nebat.<sup>4</sup>Anyone belonging to Baasha who dies in the city the dogs shall eat, and anyone of his who dies in the field the birds of the heavens shall eat."<sup>5</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Baasha and what he did, and his might, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?<sup>6</sup>And Baasha slept with his fathers and was buried at Tirzah, and Elah his son reigned in his place.<sup>7</sup>Moreover, the word of the LORD came by the prophet Jehu the son of Hanani against Baasha and his house, both because of all the evil that he did in the sight of the LORD, provoking him to anger with the work of his hands, in being like the house of Jeroboam, and also because he destroyed it.<sup>8</sup>In the twenty-sixth year of Asa king of Judah, Elah the son of Baasha began to reign over Israel in Tirzah, and he reigned two years.<sup>9</sup>But his servant Zimri, commander of half his chariots, conspired against him. When he was at Tirzah, drinking himself drunk in the house of Arza, who was over the household in Tirzah,<sup>10</sup>Zimri came in and struck him down and killed him, in the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, and reigned in his place.<sup>11</sup>When he began to reign, as soon as he had seated himself on his throne, he struck down all the house of Baasha. He did not leave him a single male of his relatives or his friends.<sup>12</sup>Thus Zimri destroyed all the house of Baasha, according to the word of the LORD, which he spoke against Baasha by Jehu the prophet,<sup>13</sup>for all the sins of Baasha and the sins of Elah his son, which they sinned and which they made Israel to sin, provoking the LORD God of Israel to anger with their idols.<sup>14</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Elah and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?<sup>15</sup>In the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, Zimri reigned seven days in Tirzah. Now the troops were encamped against Gibbethon, which belonged to the Philistines,<sup>16</sup>and the troops who were encamped heard it said, "Zimri has conspired, and he has killed the king." Therefore all Israel made Omri, the commander of the army, king over Israel that day in the camp.<sup>17</sup>So Omri went up from Gibbethon, and all Israel with him, and they besieged Tirzah.<sup>18</sup>And when Zimri saw that the city was taken, he went into the citadel of the king's house and burned the king's house over him with fire and died,<sup>19</sup>because of his sins that he committed, doing evil in the sight of the LORD, walking in the way of Jeroboam, and for his sin which he committed, making Israel to sin.<sup>20</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Zimri, and the conspiracy that he made, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?<sup>21</sup>Then the people of Israel were divided into two parts. Half of the people followed Tibni the son of Ginath, to make him king, and half followed Omri.<sup>22</sup>But the people who followed Omri overcame the people who followed Tibni the son of Ginath. So Tibni died, and Omri became king.<sup>23</sup>In the thirty-first year of Asa king of Judah, Omri began to reign over Israel, and he reigned for twelve years; six years he reigned in Tirzah.<sup>24</sup>He bought the hill of Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver, and he fortified the hill and called the name of the city that he built Samaria, after the name of Shemer, the owner of the hill.<sup>25</sup>Omri did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and did more evil than all who were before him.<sup>26</sup>For he walked in all the way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, and in the sins that he made Israel to sin, provoking the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger by their idols.<sup>27</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Omri that he did, and the might that he showed, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?<sup>28</sup>And Omri slept with his fathers and was buried in Samaria, and Ahab his son reigned in his place.<sup>29</sup>In the thirty-eighth year of Asa king of Judah, Ahab the son of Omri began to reign over Israel, and Ahab the son of Omri reigned over Israel in Samaria twenty-two years.<sup>30</sup>And Ahab the son of Omri did evil in the sight of the LORD, more than all who were before him.<sup>31</sup>And as if it had been a light thing for him to walk in the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, he took for his wife Jezebel the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians, and went and served Baal and worshiped him.<sup>32</sup>He erected an altar for Baal in the house of Baal, which he built in Samaria.<sup>33</sup>And Ahab made an Asherah.
