He laid its foundation at the cost of Abiram his firstborn, and set up its gates at the cost of his youngest son Segub, according to the word of the LORD, which he spoke by Joshua the son of Nun.
16.overview:
The chapter is built as an accelerating collapse. Baasha gets Ahijah's oracle with the name changed — I exalted you out of the dust, the same charge, the same dogs and birds — and he had stood over the corpses of Jeroboam's family, so he will have recognised it. Elah is stabbed while drinking himself drunk in his palace manager's house, with his whole army in the field. Zimri holds the throne for seven days, sees the city taken, and burns the palace down on top of himself. Then four years of civil war, and a fourth dynasty. Fifty years earlier there was one kingdom and a house on the temple mount that a foreign queen had run out of breath looking at.

Verse 7 carries a clause worth stopping on. Baasha is condemned for being like the house of Jeroboam and also because he destroyed it — and chapter 15 said that destruction was according to the word of the LORD. The same act is the fulfilment of God's word and a crime the man answers for. Assyria is the rod of God's anger and is punished for the arrogance with which it swung (Isa. 10:5-12); men did what God's plan had predestined at the cross and were lawless men (Acts 2:23). Being used by God is not the same as being commissioned by him.

And Omri is the point of the middle of the chapter, though not in the way a historian of the ancient world would tell it. He founded Samaria, which held out against Assyria for three years and stood as the northern capital until 722; his dynasty lasted four generations where the previous three managed fifty years between them; Assyrian records call Israel the house of Omri for a century after his family was wiped out, and the Moabite Stone names him. He gets six verses, four of them about how he took the throne, and the international reputation is not mentioned. That is not ignorance. It is a scale of measurement, and this writer's is not the world's.

Then Ahab, and something genuinely new: not the wrong worship of the right God, but another god installed in the capital, with a temple and an altar — and a wife whose father's name means with Baal. And the chapter's last verse is a five-hundred-year-old curse collected in full, placed immediately before Elijah walks in.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The word of the LORD comes to Jehu the son of Hanani against Baasha: since I exalted you out of the dust and made you leader over my people Israel, and you have walked in the way of Jeroboam and have made my people Israel to sin, provoking me to anger with their sins, behold, I will utterly sweep away Baasha and his house (vv. 1-3) — word for word the oracle Ahijah brought Jeroboam, down to the dogs and the birds (v. 4). Baasha reigns twenty-four years and dies (vv. 5-6). The writer repeats the reason: he did evil in provoking him to anger with the work of his hands, in being like the house of Jeroboam, and also because he destroyed it (v. 7). Elah his son reigns two years, and Zimri, commander of half his chariots, strikes him down as he was in Tirzah, drinking himself drunk in the house of Arza, who was over the household (vv. 8-10), and kills every male of Baasha's house (vv. 11-14).
verseByVerse.theology: The oracle against Baasha is Ahijah's oracle against Jeroboam with the name changed, including I exalted you out of the dust — the same opening, the same charge, the same sentence. He wiped out one house for a sin and is destroyed for it himself.
verseByVerse.examples: And verse 7 adds a clause that repays attention: he is condemned for being like the house of Jeroboam and also because he destroyed it. He was the instrument of a judgment, and he is answerable for how he carried it out. Being used by God is not the same as being commissioned.

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of the LORD came to Jehu the son of Hanani against Baasha, saying, "Since I exalted you out of the dust and made you leader over my people Israel, and you have walked in the way of Jeroboam and have made my people Israel to sin, provoking me to anger with their sins, behold, I will utterly sweep away Baasha and his house, and I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam the son of Nebat. Anyone belonging to Baasha who dies in the city the dogs shall eat, and anyone of his who dies in the field the birds of the heavens shall eat." Now the rest of the acts of Baasha and what he did, and his might, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? And Baasha slept with his fathers and was buried at Tirzah, and Elah his son reigned in his place. Moreover, the word of the LORD came by the prophet Jehu the son of Hanani against Baasha and his house, both because of all the evil that he did in the sight of the LORD, provoking him to anger with the work of his hands, in being like the house of Jeroboam, and also because he destroyed it. In the twenty-sixth year of Asa king of Judah, Elah the son of Baasha began to reign over Israel in Tirzah, and he reigned two years. But his servant Zimri, commander of half his chariots, conspired against him. When he was at Tirzah, drinking himself drunk in the house of Arza, who was over the household in Tirzah, Zimri came in and struck him down and killed him, in the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, and reigned in his place. When he began to reign, as soon as he had seated himself on his throne, he struck down all the house of Baasha. He did not leave him a single male of his relatives or his friends. Thus Zimri destroyed all the house of Baasha, according to the word of the LORD, which he spoke against Baasha by Jehu the prophet, for all the sins of Baasha and the sins of Elah his son, which they sinned and which they made Israel to sin, provoking the LORD God of Israel to anger with their idols. Now the rest of the acts of Elah and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the word of the LORD came to Jehu the son of Hanani against Baasha, saying,'

A prophet named Jehu, not to be confused with the king of the same name later on. His father Hanani is the seer who rebuked Asa about the Syrian alliance and was put in the stocks for it (2 Chron. 16:7-10).

Two generations of one family telling kings on both sides of the border what they did not want to hear.

'"Since I exalted you out of the dust and made you leader over my people Israel, and you have walked in the way of Jeroboam and have made my people Israel to sin, provoking me to anger with their sins,"'

Now read that against 14:7, and read it slowly, because the writer is repeating himself on purpose.

To Jeroboam, through Ahijah: because I exalted you from among the people and made you leader over my people Israel... but you have done evil above all who were before you.

To Baasha, through Jehu: since I exalted you out of the dust and made you leader over my people Israel, and you have walked in the way of Jeroboam.

The same opening, the same charge, and the same sentence is coming.

Out of the dust is if anything more pointed. Jeroboam was a labour foreman; Baasha was an officer of Issachar with a knife and an opportunity. God took him off the ground.

'"behold, I will utterly sweep away Baasha and his house, and I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam the son of Nebat."'

'"Anyone belonging to Baasha who dies in the city the dogs shall eat, and anyone of his who dies in the field the birds of the heavens shall eat."'

Word for word what Ahijah said about Jeroboam's house, down to the dogs and the birds (14:11).

Baasha stood over the corpses of Jeroboam's family. He heard how they died and why. And the oracle that comes to him is the same oracle, in the same words, and he will have recognised it.

'Now the rest of the acts of Baasha and what he did, and his might, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?'

'And Baasha slept with his fathers and was buried at Tirzah, and Elah his son reigned in his place.'

'Moreover, the word of the LORD came by the prophet Jehu the son of Hanani against Baasha and his house, both because of all the evil that he did in the sight of the LORD, provoking him to anger with the work of his hands, in being like the house of Jeroboam, and also because he destroyed it.'

And here is a clause that repays close attention: and also because he destroyed it.

Baasha is condemned on two counts. The first is that he was like the house of Jeroboam. The second is that he destroyed it.

And chapter 15 said that destruction happened according to the word of the LORD that he spoke by his servant Ahijah the Shilonite (15:29).

So the same act is both the fulfilment of God's word and a crime the man is answerable for.

That is not a contradiction and the Bible states it in several places. Assyria is the rod of God's anger against Israel, and God then punishes Assyria for the arrogance with which it swung (Isa. 10:5-12). Men did what God's hand and plan had predestined at the cross, and they were lawless men (Acts 2:23).

Being used by God is not the same as being commissioned by him. Baasha was not obeying an order; he was a conspirator murdering a rival dynasty for his own advancement, and God's word was fulfilled through what he freely chose to do for his own reasons. The purpose was God's. The motive was his, and he answers for it.

Anybody inclined to think that a good outcome vindicates how they got there is looking at the verse that says otherwise.

'In the twenty-sixth year of Asa king of Judah, Elah the son of Baasha began to reign over Israel in Tirzah, and he reigned two years.'

'But his servant Zimri, commander of half his chariots, conspired against him when he was at Tirzah, drinking himself drunk in the house of Arza, who was over the household in Tirzah.'

And the detail is contemptuous, and it is meant to be.

The king of Israel is killed while drinking himself drunk in the house of his palace manager.

Note where he is not. His army is in the field — the next verse says the whole force is besieging Gibbethon. His father was murdered at that same siege line by an officer. Elah is at home, in a subordinate's house, incapable.

The Hebrew makes the point sharply by what it puts next to it: the men are at Gibbethon, and the king is drunk in Tirzah.

'And Zimri came in and struck him down and killed him, in the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, and reigned in his place.'

'When he began to reign, as soon as he had seated himself on his throne, he struck down all the house of Baasha. He did not leave him a single male of his relatives or his friends.'

The same thing again, one generation later. Baasha did it to Jeroboam's house; Zimri does it to Baasha's.

And or his friends is new. Zimri goes wider than the family.

'Thus Zimri destroyed all the house of Baasha, according to the word of the LORD, which he spoke against Baasha by Jehu the prophet,'

'for all the sins of Baasha and the sins of Elah his son, which they sinned and which they made Israel to sin, provoking the LORD God of Israel to anger with their idols.'

The word is fulfilled exactly, by a man who is about to last a week.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zimri reigned seven days in Tirzah (v. 15). When the army besieging Gibbethon hears he has killed the king, they make Omri their commander king on the spot and go up and besiege Tirzah (vv. 16-17). And when Zimri saw that the city was taken, he went into the citadel of the king's house and burned the king's house over him with fire and died (v. 18), because of his sins that he committed, doing evil in the sight of the LORD, walking in the way of Jeroboam (v. 19). Half the people follow Tibni and half Omri; Omri prevails and Tibni dies (vv. 21-22). Omri reigns twelve years, buys the hill of Samaria for two talents of silver and builds a city on it (vv. 23-24). Omri did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and did more evil than all who were before him (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: Seven days, and a verdict. Zimri held the throne for a week and the writer still applies the full formula to him — he walked in the way of Jeroboam — because a week was long enough to show what he would have done with it.
verseByVerse.examples: And Omri is the most historically important king the north ever had. He founded Samaria, which was its capital until Assyria destroyed it; Assyrian records call Israel the house of Omri for a century after his dynasty ended; the Moabite Stone names him. He gets six verses. The historian's measure is not the world's.

verseByVerse.quote: In the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, Zimri reigned seven days in Tirzah. Now the troops were encamped against Gibbethon, which belonged to the Philistines, and the troops who were encamped heard it said, "Zimri has conspired, and he has killed the king." Therefore all Israel made Omri, the commander of the army, king over Israel that day in the camp. So Omri went up from Gibbethon, and all Israel with him, and they besieged Tirzah. And when Zimri saw that the city was taken, he went into the citadel of the king's house and burned the king's house over him with fire and died, because of his sins that he committed, doing evil in the sight of the LORD, walking in the way of Jeroboam, and for his sin which he committed, making Israel to sin. Now the rest of the acts of Zimri, and the conspiracy that he made, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? Then the people of Israel were divided into two parts. Half of the people followed Tibni the son of Ginath, to make him king, and half followed Omri. But the people who followed Omri overcame the people who followed Tibni the son of Ginath. So Tibni died, and Omri became king. In the thirty-first year of Asa king of Judah, Omri began to reign over Israel, and he reigned for twelve years; six years he reigned in Tirzah. He bought the hill of Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver, and he fortified the hill and called the name of the city that he built Samaria, after the name of Shemer, the owner of the hill. Omri did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and did more evil than all who were before him. For he walked in all the way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, and in the sins that he made Israel to sin, provoking the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger by their idols. Now the rest of the acts of Omri that he did, and the might that he showed, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? And Omri slept with his fathers and was buried in Samaria, and Ahab his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'In the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, Zimri reigned seven days in Tirzah.'

Seven days.

He is the shortest reign in either book and the writer still gives him the full treatment: an accession formula, a verdict, a cause of death, and a summary. Seven days was long enough to be judged.

'Now the troops were encamped against Gibbethon, which belonged to the Philistines, and the troops who were encamped heard it said, "Zimri has conspired, and he has killed the king." Therefore all Israel made Omri, the commander of the army, king over Israel that day in the camp.'

Gibbethon again. The same Philistine town the army was besieging when Baasha murdered Nadab twenty-seven years earlier, and they are still besieging it.

Two kings have been assassinated on the strength of that one siege line, and the town is still not taken.

And the army makes its own commander king that day in the camp. No prophet, no anointing, no elders, no assembly. The soldiers vote and the general is king.

'So Omri went up from Gibbethon, and all Israel with him, and they besieged Tirzah.'

'And when Zimri saw that the city was taken, he went into the citadel of the king's house and burned the king's house over him with fire and died,'

He sets fire to the palace with himself inside it.

It is a strange and grim end and the writer gives it four words of explanation in the next verse. Whatever drove him — despair, defiance, refusal to be taken alive — is not recorded. He had the throne for a week and burned it down on top of himself.

'because of his sins that he committed, doing evil in the sight of the LORD, walking in the way of Jeroboam, and for his sin which he committed, making Israel to sin.'

And the formula, applied to a man who reigned seven days.

Walking in the way of Jeroboam... making Israel to sin.

A week. He cannot have instituted anything or changed any policy. What the verdict means is that in seven days he did nothing about the calves either, and that he was going to be exactly what all of them were.

'Now the rest of the acts of Zimri, and the conspiracy that he made, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?'

'Then the people of Israel were divided into two parts. Half of the people followed Tibni the son of Ginath, to make him king, and half followed Omri.'

'But the people who followed Omri overcame the people who followed Tibni the son of Ginath. So Tibni died, and Omri became king.'

A civil war inside the northern kingdom, and the writer disposes of it in two verses.

So Tibni died. He does not say how, and the placement leaves little doubt.

Now count what this chapter has done so far. Baasha's house destroyed. Elah drunk and stabbed. Zimri for seven days, burning the palace down on himself. Then four years of civil war between two factions. And a fourth dynasty.

Fifty years earlier there was one kingdom, one throne in Jerusalem, and a house on the temple mount that a foreign queen had run out of breath looking at.

'In the thirty-first year of Asa king of Judah, Omri began to reign over Israel, and he reigned for twelve years; six years he reigned in Tirzah.'

'He bought the hill of Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver, and he fortified the hill and called the name of the city that he built Samaria, after the name of Shemer, the owner of the hill.'

And here is the one solid achievement, and it is real.

He buys a hill and builds a capital on it, and Samaria is a superb site — isolated, defensible, commanding the trade roads. It became and remained the capital of the northern kingdom until the Assyrians took it after a three-year siege in 722, which is a considerable testimony to the man's judgment.

And note that he bought it, and the writer records the price and the seller's name. That is a proper transaction, not a seizure.

Now here is the thing about Omri, and it is the point of these six verses.

He is by any external measure the most significant king the northern kingdom ever had.

He founded a dynasty that lasted four generations, where the previous three lasted a combined fifty-odd years. He established a capital that outlived his line by a century and a half. He was strong enough that Assyrian royal inscriptions refer to Israel as the house of Omri for over a hundred years after his family was wiped out — long after his descendants were dead, foreign chancelleries were still calling the country by his name. The Moabite Stone, set up by King Mesha, names him and describes his conquest of Moab.

He is one of the few figures in this book who left a mark on the wider records of the ancient world.

The writer of Kings gives him six verses, four of which are about how he got the throne, and never mentions the international reputation at all.

That is not ignorance. It is a scale of measurement.

This historian is not writing about power, and he is not impressed by it. He gives four chapters to a building and one line to an empire's foreign policy; he spends thirty-four verses on a man of God who ate a meal he should not have eaten, and six on the king whose name a superpower used for Israel for a century.

What he wants to know about a man is one thing, and he asks it in the next verse.

'Omri did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and did more evil than all who were before him.'

That is the entry in the ledger.

More evil than all who were before him. The formula is escalating, and it will escalate again in three verses.

'For he walked in all the way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, and in the sins that he made Israel to sin, provoking the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger by their idols.'

'Now the rest of the acts of Omri that he did, and the might that he showed, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?'

The might that he showed. The writer knows about it. He simply files it elsewhere and refers the interested reader to another book.

'And Omri slept with his fathers and was buried in Samaria, and Ahab his son reigned in his place.'

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ahab the son of Omri reigned over Israel in Samaria twenty-two years. And Ahab the son of Omri did evil in the sight of the LORD, more than all who were before him (vv. 29-30). And as if it had been a light thing for him to walk in the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, he took for his wife Jezebel the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians, and went and served Baal and worshiped him (v. 31). He erected an altar for Baal in the house of Baal, which he built in Samaria. And Ahab made an Asherah (vv. 32-33). In his days Hiel of Bethel built Jericho. He laid its foundation at the cost of Abiram his firstborn, and set up its gates at the cost of his youngest son Segub, according to the word of the LORD, which he spoke by Joshua the son of Nun (v. 34).
verseByVerse.theology: Something new has happened, and the writer marks it. Jeroboam's calves were the wrong worship of the right God — a breach of the second commandment. Ahab builds a temple to a different god in the capital. And Jezebel's father is Ethbaal, whose name means with Baal: the Tyrian alliance Solomon began comes home two centuries later as a marriage.
verseByVerse.examples: And the last verse is a five-hundred-year-old curse being collected. Joshua said of Jericho cursed before the LORD be the man who rises up and rebuilds this city. At the cost of his firstborn shall he lay its foundation, and at the cost of his youngest son shall he set up its gates (Josh. 6:26). A man does it anyway, and buries two sons, and the writer puts it in the last verse before Elijah walks in.

verseByVerse.quote: In the thirty-eighth year of Asa king of Judah, Ahab the son of Omri began to reign over Israel, and Ahab the son of Omri reigned over Israel in Samaria twenty-two years. And Ahab the son of Omri did evil in the sight of the LORD, more than all who were before him. And as if it had been a light thing for him to walk in the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, he took for his wife Jezebel the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians, and went and served Baal and worshiped him. He erected an altar for Baal in the house of Baal, which he built in Samaria. And Ahab made an Asherah. Ahab did more to provoke the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger than all the kings of Israel who were before him. In his days Hiel of Bethel built Jericho. He laid its foundation at the cost of Abiram his firstborn, and set up its gates at the cost of his youngest son Segub, according to the word of the LORD, which he spoke by Joshua the son of Nun.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'In the thirty-eighth year of Asa king of Judah, Ahab the son of Omri began to reign over Israel, and Ahab the son of Omri reigned over Israel in Samaria twenty-two years.'

Twenty-two years, and the next six chapters belong to his reign.

The writer has been moving fast — five kings in twenty-eight verses — and he is about to slow down almost completely. From here to chapter 22 the pace changes entirely, because Elijah is about to arrive.

'And Ahab the son of Omri did evil in the sight of the LORD, more than all who were before him.'

His father was more evil than all who were before him four verses ago. Now the same sentence is used of the son.

The formula has been climbing all through the book. Jeroboam did evil above all who were before him; Omri did more than all before him; Ahab does more than all of them.

'And as if it had been a light thing for him to walk in the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, he took for his wife Jezebel the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians, and went and served Baal and worshiped him.'

And here the whole northern story changes, and the writer marks it with a phrase.

As if it had been a light thing. The calves were not enough for him. A hundred years of Jeroboam's religion was, in Ahab's estimation, a small matter.

Now be precise about what is new, because the distinction is the point of the verse.

Jeroboam's calves were an offence against the second commandment. He never named another god; he used the covenant name, quoted the exodus, and called his images thrones for the God who brought Israel out of Egypt. It was the wrong worship of the right God.

Ahab went and served Baal and worshiped him.

That is a different commandment and a different sin. It is not a corrupted approach to the LORD; it is another god, brought in and installed.

And note where she comes from. Jezebel the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians.

Sidon is Phoenicia. Tyre and Sidon are the same coast, the same people, the same gods — and the reader has been there before. Hiram of Tyre loved David, sent him cedar unasked, blessed the LORD by name and credited him with Solomon's wisdom, and supplied every beam in the temple.

Two centuries later the alliance comes home as a marriage.

And her father's name is a sentence in itself. Ethbaal means with Baal, or Baal is with him. Josephus records that he was a priest of Astarte before he took the throne.

She is not a princess who happens to have brought her own religion. She is the daughter of a priest of a fertility cult, married to the king of Israel, and chapter 18 will say she keeps four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and four hundred of Asherah at her own table, and has been killing the prophets of the LORD.

'He erected an altar for Baal in the house of Baal, which he built in Samaria.'

A temple to Baal in the capital.

Jeroboam put calves at Bethel and Dan and called it the worship of the LORD. Ahab builds a house for a Canaanite storm god in the city his father founded, and puts an altar in it.

'And Ahab made an Asherah. Ahab did more to provoke the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger than all the kings of Israel who were before him.'

The third time in six verses the writer says he exceeded everybody.

'In his days Hiel of Bethel built Jericho. He laid its foundation at the cost of Abiram his firstborn, and set up its gates at the cost of his youngest son Segub, according to the word of the LORD, which he spoke by Joshua the son of Nun.'

And here is the last verse of the chapter, and its placement is entirely deliberate.

Go back five hundred years. Jericho has fallen; the walls came down; and Joshua puts the city under a curse:

Cursed before the LORD be the man who rises up and rebuilds this city, Jericho. At the cost of his firstborn shall he lay its foundation, and at the cost of his youngest son shall he set up its gates (Josh. 6:26).

Jericho was the firstfruits of the land — the first city taken, devoted entirely to God, with everything in it destroyed. It was to be left as it lay.

Now a man from Bethel rebuilds it.

And the writer records the price with terrible precision: at the cost of Abiram his firstborn — when the foundation went in — and at the cost of his youngest son Segub — when the gates went up.

Which means it took years, and he buried his eldest son at the beginning and his youngest at the end, and he kept building.

That is the detail that makes the verse unbearable. It was not a single catastrophe he could not have foreseen. The first son died at the foundation, and there was the curse, five centuries old and public, and he went on and finished the gates.

Two things follow.

The first is the writer's own comment, which is the only interpretation offered: according to the word of the LORD, which he spoke by Joshua the son of Nun. Five hundred years, and it was still live.

The second is why this verse is here, in this chapter, in this position.

It has nothing to do with Ahab. Hiel is a private citizen from Bethel and the king is not mentioned in the verse except as a date: in his days.

And the writer puts it last, immediately before chapter 17 begins, and chapter 17 begins with a man walking in from nowhere and saying as the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand, there shall be neither dew nor rain these years, except by my word.

The last thing we are told before Elijah arrives is that a word God spoke five centuries ago just came true, exactly, and cost a man his two sons.

The country is worshipping Baal, who is the god of storm and rain and fertility. His temple is in the capital and his prophets eat at the queen's table. And into that, on the far side of a verse about a curse that took five hundred years and did not fail, walks a man who says it will not rain again until he says so.

16.theology:
Two generations of one family (v. 1). Jehu the son of Hanani brings this word; his father is the seer who rebuked Asa over the Syrian alliance and was put in the stocks for it (2 Chron. 16:7-10). Father and son, telling kings on both sides of the border what they did not want to hear.

The same oracle with the name changed (vv. 2-4). To Jeroboam: because I exalted you from among the people and made you leader over my people Israel... but you have done evil (14:7). To Baasha: since I exalted you out of the dust and made you leader over my people Israel, and you have walked in the way of Jeroboam. Same opening, same charge, same dogs and birds. Out of the dust is if anything more pointed — an officer of Issachar with a knife and an opportunity.

Used, and answerable (v. 7). Two counts: being like the house of Jeroboam, and destroying it — and 15:29 called that destruction the fulfilment of God's word through Ahijah. Not a contradiction: Baasha was not obeying an order but murdering a rival dynasty for his own advancement, and God's word was fulfilled through what he freely chose for his own reasons. The purpose was God's; the motive was his. Anyone inclined to think a good outcome vindicates how they reached it is looking at the verse that says otherwise.

The contempt in the detail (v. 9). The king is killed drinking himself drunk in a subordinate's house — and the very next verse says the whole army is in the field besieging Gibbethon, which is where his own father murdered the previous king. The Hebrew makes the point by juxtaposition: the men at Gibbethon, the king drunk in Tirzah.

Seven days, and a full verdict (vv. 15, 19). The shortest reign in either book still gets an accession formula, a verdict, a death and a summary. He cannot have instituted anything in a week — what the verdict means is that in seven days he did nothing about the calves either, and that he was going to be exactly what all of them were. And Gibbethon is still not taken: two kings assassinated on the strength of one siege line, twenty-seven years apart, and the town holds.

The army makes its own king (v. 16). That day in the camp — no prophet, no anointing, no elders, no assembly. The soldiers vote and the general is king.

The one solid achievement, and it is real (v. 24). Samaria is a superb site — isolated, defensible, commanding the roads — and it remained the northern capital until Assyria took it after a three-year siege. Note that he bought it, and the writer records the price and the seller's name: a proper transaction, not a seizure.

The historian's measure is not the world's (vv. 23-28). By any external standard Omri is the most significant king the north ever had: a dynasty of four generations where the previous three managed fifty years between them, a capital that outlived his line by a century and a half, and enough weight that Assyrian royal inscriptions called Israel the house of Omri for over a hundred years after his family was destroyed — foreign chancelleries still using his name for the country long after his descendants were dead. The Moabite Stone names him. He is one of the few figures here who marked the wider records of the ancient world. And he gets six verses, four about how he took the throne, with the international reputation never mentioned — though the writer knows about it, since he files the might that he showed in another book and refers the interested reader to it. He gives four chapters to a building and one line to an empire's foreign policy; thirty-four verses to a man of God who ate a meal he should not have eaten, and six to this.

The formula escalating (vv. 25, 30, 33). Jeroboam did evil above all before him; Omri did more than all before him; Ahab does more than all of them, and the writer says it three times in six verses.

As if it had been a light thing (v. 31). A hundred years of Jeroboam's religion was, in Ahab's estimation, a small matter. And be precise about what is new: Jeroboam never named another god — he used the covenant name, quoted the exodus, and called his images thrones for the God who brought Israel out of Egypt. That was the wrong worship of the right God, a breach of the second commandment. Ahab went and served Baal and worshiped him, and built him a house in the capital. Different commandment, different sin: not a corrupted approach to the LORD but another god installed.

The Tyrian alliance comes home (v. 31). Sidon is Phoenicia — the same coast, the same people, the same gods as Tyre, and the reader has been there. Hiram loved David, sent cedar unasked, blessed the LORD by name and supplied every beam in the temple. Two centuries later it returns as a marriage. And Ethbaal means with Baal; Josephus records that he was a priest of Astarte before he took the throne. She is not a princess who happens to have brought her own religion — she is a priest's daughter, and chapter 18 says she keeps four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and four hundred of Asherah at her own table, and has been killing the prophets of the LORD.

Five hundred years, and still live (v. 34). Joshua cursed the man who would rebuild Jericho — at the cost of his firstborn shall he lay its foundation, and at the cost of his youngest son shall he set up its gates (Josh. 6:26). It was the firstfruits of the land, devoted entirely to God, to be left as it lay. And the writer records the price with terrible precision, which means the work took years: the eldest son died when the foundation went in, and the youngest when the gates went up, and Hiel kept building in between. That is what makes the verse unbearable. It was not one catastrophe he could not have foreseen; the first son died at the foundation, with a five-hundred-year-old public curse on record, and he finished the gates.

Why the verse is placed here. It has nothing to do with Ahab — Hiel is a private citizen and the king appears only as a date, in his days. And the writer puts it last, immediately before a man walks in from nowhere and says there shall be neither dew nor rain these years, except by my word. The country is worshipping Baal, who is the god of storm and rain and fertility, with his temple in the capital and his prophets at the queen's table — and the last thing we are told before Elijah arrives is that a word God spoke five centuries ago just came true, exactly, and cost a man two sons.
16.examples:
Then: A man from Bethel rebuilt Jericho against a curse five hundred years old, buried his eldest son when the foundations went in, and went on building for years until the gates were finished — and buried his youngest son the week they were hung.

Now: Three things. Verse 7 is the one that will not let anybody off: Baasha carried out God's own judgment and is condemned for how he did it. A right outcome does not sanctify the motive that produced it, and being useful to God's purposes is not the same as being sent. Second, Omri, who is the quiet rebuke to every way of keeping score. He was the most consequential man in that kingdom's history by every measure the world uses, and this historian — who knows all about it and files it elsewhere — gives him six verses and one sentence of verdict. And third, Hiel. The first death was the warning, and he had a public five-hundred-year-old curse in front of him, and he finished the gates anyway. Most people who go on with something ruinous are not ignorant of the cost. They have already paid an instalment of it.
